Senator Murray also met with farmworkers, advocates, and community members in Burlington last year to listen to their concerns amid a recent spike in ICE activity—including large-scale raids and the detention of local activists and leaders—in Northwest Washington, particularly in Whatcom and Skagit counties.

Murray has been outspoken against the Trump administration’s inhumane immigration agenda from the start, strongly opposing passage of the Laken Riley Act. Murray was one of the few Senate Democrats to take to the floor to speak out forcefully against its passage.

(GEO), a private prison operator with a record of mistreatment and abuse of people detained in its custody. In short, taxpayers are sending nearly $2 billion to GEO Group to execute President Trump’s cruel immigration agenda.

ICE’s use of taxpayer dollars follows a trend of gross mismanagement of appropriated funds that Republicans approved for ICE without any meaningful guardrails. Even so, and in the midst of a follow-on GAO engagement that would result in its November 19, 2026, report’s findings that “ICE has neither determined the scope and costs to purchase more facilities nor updated its spending plan to reflect its current efforts” and “hasn’t assessed the cost effectiveness of these investments,” ICE is reportedly still moving ahead with this $453 million purchase of a detention facility with seemingly no financial benefit or control.

text:
Dive Brief:

A coalition of local governments and public housing authorities filed a lawsuit Monday to halt a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule that would block households with mixed immigration statuses from receiving federal housing assistance.

The rule, scheduled to go into effect Dec. 14, is “callous, ill-conceived, and illegal,” and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act, the lawsuit states.

HUD’s rule change could displace at least 15,500 mixed-status families, according to the suit, placing additional burden on localities’ already-strained homeless shelter and support systems.

Dive Insight:

Households with mixed immigration statuses have for decades been able to receive federal housing assistance, prorated based on the number of household members who verify they are U.S. citizens or have eligible immigration status, according to plaintiffs.

On Nov. 10, HUD announced all recipients of federal housing aid would be required to provide proof of eligibility for all household members. “The final rule includes any tenants currently living in ‘mixed status’ households that have exploited regulatory loopholes by enabling illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens to latch on to those with eligible status,” the agency stated.

The coalition filed their lawsuit Monday in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts. Other lawsuits challenging the rule have also been filed by states and Los Angeles-area tenant organizations and housing advocacy groups.

“HUD’s Final Rule is a radical departure from the law and decades of past practice and regulations,” San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu, representing the city in the Nov. 23 lawsuit, said in a news release. “Cities across the country are coming together to fight this callous and illegal change that is designed to push immigrant families into homelessness.”

Along with San Francisco, plaintiffs include Boston; Chicago; the City and County of Los Angeles; King County, Washington; New York City; Providence, Rhode Island; San Diego; Santa Clara County, California; Seattle, and eight public housing authorities.

text:
A former private prison in western Minnesota that just reopened as a detention facility for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is sparking pushback.

The detention facility in Appleton, three hours west of Minneapolis, opened Nov. 9 after the Department of Homeland Security purchased it for nearly $500 million from CoreCivic, which still manages the site. It was formerly Prairie Correctional Facility, which closed in 2010.

Immigrant rights advocates say 70 people are currently in custody at the site, which can hold up to 1,600 detainees. In response to an inquiry from WCCO News, ICE said the number of detainees is "subject to change" and not publicly released.

The agency in a statement on Nov. 12 said the facility "gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction."

Dozens of people gathered at the Minnesota State Capitol in St. Paul on Monday, calling for oversight and its closure. In 2023, the Minnesota Legislature passed a law banning the use of private prisons for people incarcerated in the state system.

"Whether it's civil or criminal, the Constitution protects everyone. Due process matters. Access to the court matters. Human dignity matters, and that's why we're here today," said Julio Zelaya, director of advocacy for the ACLU of Minnesota.

Protestors held signs with messages like "abolish ICE now," "close the camps" and "due process, not profits."

In a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, DFL U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum questioned why the federal government paid what it did for the facility when the state was offered the site for a fraction of the price just a year earlier.

"The facility opened during the deadliest period for people in ICE custody in more than two decades. It is also the product of a costly and hasty detention expansion that jeopardizes local property tax dollars and that Congress's own watchdog has found is wasting taxpayer money," McCollum and others wrote.

In a statement, a spokesperson for CoreCivic said that the federal government determined the sale price "following its assessment process."

The ICE detention center's opening comes 10 months after the thousands of federal immigration agents descended on Minnesota in Operation Metro Surge, an unprecedented operation during which two American citizens were shot and killed.

Democrats are set to take back total control of the State Capitol — the House, Senate and governor's office — after November's election, and they promise future action on ICE accountability measures that passed the Minnesota Senate earlier this year but didn't clear the tied House.

Those measures include banning face masks for federal agents and prohibiting them from making arrests at schools, hospitals and courthouses. Republicans have questioned if the Legislature has the authority to implement those rules since ICE is a federal agency. State lawmakers have little power to restrict the facility's operation, as protestors demand.

"I want to say it is our priority to make sure that what happened in Minnesota last winter never happens again," said Rep. Samantha Sencer-Mura, the newly elected majority whip for the DFL-led House, at the Monday rally.

But not everyone is opposed to the Appleton detention site. Sen. Torrey Westrom, a Republican from Alexandria, Minnesota, who represents the town, praised the federal purchase of it. In a statement, he said it creates 450 new jobs and provides an economic boost to the region.

"Although this is a lost opportunity for the state of Minnesota, this is a practical solution that puts an existing facility back to use, brings back good jobs for rural Minnesota, and represents a wise use of taxpayer resources," Westrom said in August at the time of the announcement of the sale.

title: ICE's own investigations expose deadly medical neglect in US immigrant detention centers
description:
Internal investigators for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement found that 23 of the 29 immigrants whose deaths they reviewed had received deficient medical care.
The findings directly contradict the Trump administration’s repeated claims that detainees receive comprehensive medical care.
A June investigation by the Associated Press and KFF Health News documented widespread allegations of medical neglect in ICE detention facilities across at least 33 states.
The detention center has offloaded responsibility for emergency medical care to local services that lack the resources to meet its demands.
Despite a bullet lodged near his spine, Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital after about four hours and then transported 135 miles to an ICE detention center in Pearsall.
text:
Internal investigators for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement found that 23 of the 29 immigrants whose deaths they reviewed had received deficient medical care. The immigrants died in ICE custody from January 2025 through January 2026. The San Francisco Chronicle, which obtained the reviews under the Freedom of Information Act, reported the findings on November 6. The findings directly contradict the Trump administration’s repeated claims that detainees receive comprehensive medical care.

Among the victims was 39-year-old Ismael Ayala-Uribe, who died of septic shock in September 2025 after being detained at the Adelanto Processing Center in California. ICE investigators found that the facility’s medical department, which they determined was understaffed, failed to examine an abscess that became a fatal infection, to respond promptly to his complaints or to properly administer prescribed medications.

In another case, Huabing Xie complained of chest pain at a California detention facility, but neither of the supervising medical providers evaluated him or provided treatment. He died of a heart attack less than two hours later.

As the WSWS reported in September, immigrants in ICE detention across the country were denied access to medical care as the agency went more than 11 months without paying claims from outside providers. Hospitals and ambulance services were owed millions of dollars. For detainees who depended on outside specialists, the consequences included canceled appointments and months-long delays in obtaining cancer care.

The latest mortality reports were not voluntarily released. ICE briefly posted some of them online in September, then removed them. The Chronicle obtained the reviews through a Freedom of Information Act request after months of delay.

Despite the damning revelations, the agency has announced no disciplinary action against the personnel or private contractors responsible. ICE also declined to answer the Chronicle’s questions about whether anyone had been held accountable.

The revelations come as the Trump administration pours billions of dollars into expanding the immigration detention apparatus, imprisoning tens of thousands more immigrants while failing to provide adequate medical care. Across the country, detainees face denial of essential medications, inadequate treatment for serious illnesses, insufficient mental health care and dangerous delays in emergency treatment.

By November 6, the Chronicle had documented at least 62 deaths in ICE custody since Trump returned to office. A Reuters analysis published in June found that the death rate in ICE detention had more than doubled under his administration, from one death annually per 3,848 detainees from 2009 through 2024, compared with one per 1,630 under Trump.

A June investigation by the Associated Press and KFF Health News documented widespread allegations of medical neglect in ICE detention facilities across at least 33 states. Reporters reviewed thousands of federal court filings and interviewed more than 50 detainees, relatives and attorneys, uncovering more than 300 cases alleging delayed, denied or inadequate medical treatment.

Among the detainees was a 52-year-old Romanian immigrant recovering from multiple heart surgeries, including a triple bypass, who required 16 medications daily. He was hospitalized three times for chest pain. After the second hospitalization, he received only eight of his 16 prescribed medications, according to discharge papers cited by his lawyer. His court filing says he suffered a stroke during a video call with his daughter in August 2025. A federal judge ordered his release that November.

The neglect reaches even the basic conditions necessary to sustain life. At the GEO Group-operated Folkston Processing Center in Georgia, detainees described a diet consisting almost entirely of canned or frozen food, sometimes spoiled, with hot drinks and raw vegetables unavailable. At North Lake in Michigan, where hundreds of detainees staged a hunger strike in April, strikers reported receiving protein only once a week while food was thrown away. “The food here is absolute garbage,” one North Lake detainee said. At Delaney Hall in Newark, New Jersey, where 300 detainees struck in May, detainees reported finding live worms in their food.

The failures are not confined to the facilities themselves. A Scripps News investigation found that the CoreCivic-operated Stewart Detention Center in rural Lumpkin, Georgia, which holds approximately 2,000 immigrants, has repeatedly overwhelmed local ambulance services. Emergency dispatch records documented 206 calls for medical assistance, and ambulances were summoned from neighboring counties on at least 14 occasions because none were available locally.

In one incident, three detainees required emergency transport simultaneously—one with an elevated heart rate, another vomiting blood and a third with an abnormal electrocardiogram. Only one ambulance was immediately available in the county. Even after emergency responders reached the facility, patients still faced a 35-mile trip to the nearest hospital. The detention center has offloaded responsibility for emergency medical care to local services that lack the resources to meet its demands.

ICE’s internal mortality reviews document the fatal outcomes of these conditions. In at least eight cases, on-site medical personnel failed to administer cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) properly or not at all.

The disregard for immigrant workers’ health and lives does not end at the detention centers. On September 20, an ICE agent shot 28-year-old Venezuelan delivery driver Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez during a traffic stop in Austin, Texas. Despite a bullet lodged near his spine, Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital after about four hours and then transported 135 miles to an ICE detention center in Pearsall.

Garcés Pérez later reported that he had received no medication and was experiencing loss of sensation and movement on the left side of his body. He was taken back to a hospital for further treatment before being transferred back into ICE custody. Austin police confirmed that ICE agents had not provided medical assistance before local officers arrived at the scene of the shooting.

While the federal government allows the healthcare of those it imprisons to collapse, it pours unprecedented resources into expanding the detention apparatus. Under Trump’s 2025 spending legislation, Congress allocated $45 billion for detention capacity through 2029. Between January 2025 and July 2026, the number of detention facilities more than doubled, from 134 to 272, and the average daily detainee population rose from about 39,000 to 66,000.

The federal government finances, directs and oversees this apparatus, which has grown under successive Democratic and Republican administrations. Under Barack Obama, millions of immigrants were deported, and his administration expanded family detention and maintained contracts with private prison corporations. The Biden administration continued operating the detention system despite extensive documentation of medical neglect, deaths in custody and abuses at facilities under federal supervision.

The aftermath of the November 3 midterm elections has made the detention system’s bipartisan nature unmistakable. The elections inflicted a sweeping defeat on Trump and the Republicans, reflecting, in part, widespread popular opposition to the administration’s attacks on immigrants. Yet the electoral repudiation has not halted collaboration. Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller, the principal architect of his anti-immigrant policies, as White House chief of staff after the Republican defeat signals an escalation rather than a retreat.

The Democrats, meanwhile, only posture as opponents of Miller while openly seeking bipartisanship with Trump. On November 8, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries denounced Miller as “the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine.” Yet Jeffries has declined to call for abolishing ICE. Two days after the election, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee summed up their program for the agency, declaring it was “time for ICE to take the masks off, turn the body cameras on, and start answering to the American people.”

Since the election, the immigration Gestapo has continued to seize immigrants and assault citizens who document its raids. On November 15 in Modesto, California, ICE agents pepper-sprayed 23-year-old Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, a US citizen who was 12 weeks pregnant, according to her attorney. Video shows agents forcing her to the ground and handcuffing her on her stomach as her husband shouted that she was pregnant.

The healthcare crisis in the detention camps is not a separate phenomenon but a concentrated expression of the capitalist healthcare system, in which tens of millions of workers face substandard treatment, crushing medical debt and the denial of essential care, all for the enrichment of insurance and hospital corporations.

The same government that denies medical care to workers in its custody has turned the threat of imprisonment and deportation against opponents of the US-backed genocide in Gaza. ICE detained Mahmoud Khalil, a lawful permanent resident who represented the Columbia student protesters in negotiations with the university. It jailed Ya’akub Ira Vijandre, a photojournalist protected under DACA, because he refused to become an FBI informant. Cornell doctoral student Momodou Taal left the country under threat of deportation after the administration revoked his student visa over his participation in campus protests.

Immigrant workers are an integral part of the working class, not a separate population whose rights can be attacked without consequences for all workers. The persecution of immigrants is intended to intimidate and divide the working class while strengthening the state’s repressive power. The attack on immigrants is an attack on all workers—as the January murders and cover-up of two US citizens, Renée Good and Alex Pretti, by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis made brutally clear.

Defending immigrant workers’ right to healthcare, freedom and democratic rights requires the political unity of immigrant and native-born workers. Such unity cannot be achieved through the AFL-CIO and the trade union bureaucracy, which have promoted nationalist divisions on which the anti-immigrant crackdown depends and have subordinated workers to the Democratic Party and the defense of American capitalism.

Workers must draw lessons from the bipartisan assault on immigrants and build an independent socialist movement against both capitalist parties and the profit system they defend. Its demands must include abolishing ICE and the entire detention apparatus, ending deportations, releasing all detainees and securing full and equal rights for all immigrant workers.

The incident sparked a tense clash between protesters and agents outside of Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center Monday night.

Burbank police responded to the scene shortly after. Activists then accused officers of escorting that elderly detainee out of the hospital and into ICE custody.

"We can't handle this happening, not only in our state and our cities, but in this country," said Toby, a community activist. "It's gotten to the point where this is pure facism. This is way overboard."

What happened in Burbank is eerily similar to another incident earlier this month at a hospital in Boyle Heights, where the LAPD was called during a confrontation between federal agents and protesters with yet another injured detainee.

In that instance, the LAPD denied helping ICE, saying their role was simply limited to responding to reports of disturbance, maintaining public safety and keeping the peace.

As for Monday's incident in Burbank, Eyewitness News has reached out to the Burbank Police Department, the Department of Homeland Security and ICE for more information.

Foronda Farro, who specializes in human rights, migration and environmental law, said one of the tribunal’s goals is to be able to denounce the human rights violations it has documented before international organizations, including the United Nations and international courts that hear human rights cases.
The report calls for protection of migrants’ rights to mobility and for the U.S. to stop considering migration a crime.

In a call with Witness at the Border members earlier last week, Pérez-Bustillo pointed out that Dec. 10 is Human Rights Day.
text:
Human rights monitors from across the Americas met twice in Mexico earlier this year to hold a people’s tribunal over aggressive actions committed by the United States under the Trump administration.

On Thursday, the jury from that tribunal announced its preliminary findings during a press conference in Mexico City, with some participants joining virtually from as far away as Brazil. Based on testimony and evidence from more than 50 cases heard over four days, ranging from military attacks on fishing boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean to deportations of immigrants to countries where they do not have ties, the group roundly condemned the United States’ human rights violations and called on international organizations — including the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights — to launch investigations.

“There’s an overwhelming number of cases and issues that are presented there, but from the most local to the more global geopolitical issues that are at stake, we see this common thread of breaking with the rule of law in an advanced stage of capitalism that requires, for its own survival, intensification of looting and land grabs and violation of rights and extermination and even ecocide and genocide of certain populations,” said Laura Carlsen, director of MIRA: Feminisms and Democracies, in a call with Capital & Main.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment from Capital & Main.

“All illegal aliens receive full due process and have their claims heard,” said Lauren Bis, a spokesperson for the White House. “No lawbreakers in the history of human civilization have been treated better than illegal aliens.”

The tribunal, co-founded about 16 years ago by roughly a half-dozen people from several countries and known as Tribunal Internacional de Conciencia de los Pueblos en Movimiento, or International Tribunal of Conscience of Peoples in Movement, met in Ciudad Juarez, Mexico, in September and in Mexico City in October after a series of pre-hearings in several countries including Colombia and the U.S.

Camilo Pérez-Bustillo, co-founder of Witness at the Border and of the tribunal, explained that the people’s tribunal traces back to a tribunal organized in 1967 by acclaimed philosophers and writers Bertrand Russell and Jean-Paul Sartre to examine war crimes committed during the Vietnam War. That tribunal took its inspiration from the Nuremberg Trials that prosecuted Nazi officials after World War II, Pérez-Bustillo said.

A similar, international tribunal has operated in Italy since the late 1970s.

“The first commitment of the tribunal is to center the victim in the process,” José Antonio Foronda Farro, an attorney who is leading the jury’s legal review process and co-founded the tribunal, said in Spanish during Thursday’s press conference.

Foronda Farro, who specializes in human rights, migration and environmental law, said one of the tribunal’s goals is to be able to denounce the human rights violations it has documented before international organizations, including the United Nations and international courts that hear human rights cases. He said the people’s tribunal itself doesn’t have any sentencing power over the government officials that it is judging, but he still sees the practice as worthwhile.

“It’s good to make it visible,” Foronda Farro said in an interview with Capital & Main. “It’s good to spread it.”

He said he sees the people’s tribunal as a process rather than an event and emphasized that even the conclusions that the group will share in December won’t be truly final because of the ongoing witnessing, documenting and listening the group will be doing.

Carlsen, who participated on the jury, said beyond examining rights violations and broken laws, the tribunal is also looking at what it sees as the impunity that the U.S. government and its officials operate with.

“We have seen this leading to a level of dispossession, disappearance, discrimination and displacement, among many other crimes — many against humanity — and that we have not seen in other moments in history,” Carlsen said in Spanish during the press conference.

Julio Moreira, professor of sociology and law at Universidade Federal da Integração Latino-Americana in Foz do Iguaçu, Brazil, said he was particularly concerned about the U.S. government’s attempts to meddle in other countries’ elections, including in Brazil and Honduras.

“We are connected to political issues in a way that isn’t tied to any specific partisan politics,” Moreira said in Spanish. “Rather, it is a politics of humanity.”

The jury will release a final report in December that will include a specific review of individual international laws and conventions it said was broken by the U.S. government. In the meantime, the preliminary findings provide a resounding indictment of the Trump administration’s policies and practices.

The jury organized its findings around four themes — genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity; neofascism and U.S. intervention; migrant genocide and carceral imperialism; and environmental justice and ecocide.

“In the United States, migrant people are assassinated and persecuted, creating a regime of terror that reaches even U.S. citizens who dare to intervene in the arbitrary detention of migrants,” the report says.

In addition, the jury writes in the report that the U.S. also promotes similar policies in other countries, such as Mexico’s use of its National Guard to block migrants heading north. It says that throughout the hemisphere, migrants are treated as criminals, and their rights are taken away — even their right to life.

According to the report, the testimony and evidence that the jury received regarding migration practices included information about unaccompanied migrant children, Indigenous migrants, forced displacement, mass deportation, Haitians stuck at the border in Tijuana, migrants living in a camp in Mexico City and deportation flights to Brazil. The final report will include more specific details from the cases, Carlsen said.

The report says that migrants experience different types of economic exploitation on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border, noting that many immigration detention facilities are run by private companies. As of January 2025, nearly 90% of people in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody were in facilities run by private prisons, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, which gathers and analyzes government data.

The U.S. government often transfers people in immigration custody to detention centers far away from their families, friends and lawyers, making it more difficult for them to fight their cases, according to the report.

“The United States expands the carceral system as a form of torture to dehumanize migrants,” the report says.

It says that deportations occur without following a legal process and that the U.S. government doesn’t necessarily deport people to their countries of origin, but rather to other places.

It calls out what it says is the racism, xenophobia and discrimination involved in these policies as detrimental to the mental and physical well-being of migrants by exposing them to violence, isolating them and breaking up family and other social ties.

The report notes that many groups, including U.S. citizens creating networks to protect Latino migrants, cross-border legal defense networks, shelters and sanctuary cities, are resisting the Trump administration’s policies and trying to support migrants both in the U.S. and abroad.

The report calls for protection of migrants’ rights to mobility and for the U.S. to stop considering migration a crime. It urges the U.S. to implement a right to refuge and asylum and guarantee migrants’ rights to health, food, education and work.

It calls for an end to attacks, persecution and torture of migrants and human rights defenders as well as to arbitrary detentions and deportations. It says the U.S. should end third country agreements and close detention centers.

The report calls on the U.S. to guarantee the return of essential documents to migrants, which, the jury learned during testimony, often does not happen.

And, the report says the U.S. should guarantee the right to truth, justice and reparations for the victims of the country’s harmful policies.

Elena Gutiérrez, from Movimiento de los Pueblos por la Paz con Justicia, or Movement of the Peoples for Peace and Justice, and Global Exchange called on people in the U.S., Mexico, Canada and the whole of Latin America to organize across borders to defend human rights.

The group will present its final report in different locations throughout December, beginning in Mexico City on Dec. 9, the anniversary of the U.N. adopting the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, and ending in New York in front of the United Nations on Dec. 18, International Migrants Day.

In a call with Witness at the Border members earlier last week, Pérez-Bustillo pointed out that Dec. 10 is Human Rights Day.

“It was the same body of human beings who were thinking about the same issues, who had sort of the same questions in mind that adopted the Genocide Convention one day, and the next day adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, so we want to think about those two instruments and what they represent and sort of the thinking that went into them in a convergent way,” Pérez-Bustillo said.

“And that’s the grounding from which the tribunal emerges.”

text:
A Centreville-based nonprofit is suing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in a class-action federal lawsuit alleging that agents have been making warrantless immigration arrests without probable cause throughout Virginia.

The 84-page complaint, filed earlier this month on behalf of the Centreville Immigration Forum and six Virginia residents, argues that federal immigration agents have taken an “arrest-first, investigate-later approach,” sometimes involving allegedly unprovoked physical force, under the current Trump administration.

ICE’s Washington Field Office in Chantilly appears to have operated as a junction point in many of the detainments cited in the suit.

The lawsuit seeks a judicial order requiring ICE and DHS “to comply with the limits Congress imposed on warrantless civil immigration arrests,” prohibit “arrests that lack the individualized probable-cause determinations required by law,” and set aside “the unlawful agency policy and practice” described in the complaint.

DHS and ICE did not respond to a list of questions FFXnow sent about the incidents in question.

ICE activities undermining mission, nonprofit says

The Centreville Immigration Forum, founded in 2007 to help day laborers who often gathered outside the Centreville Regional Library looking for work, says in the complaint that the surge in ICE detentions has “directly impaired” its “ability to carry out its mission and core activities.”

The nonprofit, which has just five full-time paid staff, is now diverting resources to emergency response efforts and legal referrals that would otherwise support established programs like its Centreville Labor Resource Center, which matches workers with potential employers.

According to the complaint:

“Defendants’ practices have led to a significant decrease in member participation in CIF’s employment, educational, wage-theft, and leadership programs; caused CIF staff to divert substantial time from those programs to address urgent arrest- and detention-related requests; and caused CIF to incur additional expenses including maintaining a separate incident database and security protocols.”

Since February 2025, CIF has documented about 61 arrests involving its members, or their family and friends, the complaint says. Longtime and founding members are among those affected. In comparison, only two members were arrested between 2022 and 2024.

Many of those arrests have been conducted “without any warrant, and without any individualized determinations regarding immigration status or likelihood of escape,” according to the nonprofit.

Some plaintiffs held at Chantilly field office

ICE’s Chantilly field office, the site of regular protests by activists, typically serves as an administrative site, but immigration rights advocates alleged that it had been turned into a makeshift detention facility holding as many as 100 people at a time in August 2025, when federal agents and National Guard troops began occupying D.C.

The office at 14797 Murdock Street is mentioned in several of the plaintiffs’ accounts, even though they may not have been picked up in Fairfax County.

For instance, Edgar Chavez Calix had been working and living in the U.S. on humanitarian parole since October 2024 when officers wearing ICE vests surrounded the vehicle he was traveling in with his father and brother near Woodbridge on Feb. 27.

“Although the officers indicated that they were looking for Mr. Chavez Calix’s brother, they handcuffed Mr. Chavez Calix before asking his name and then searched him and took his Honduran identification from his wallet,” the complaint says. “Before handcuffing him or placing him in their vehicle, officers did not ask about his immigration status, present a warrant, or otherwise inquire whether he was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”

Chavez Calix was taken to a school and fire station before being transported to the Chantilly office. He was later taken to the Riverside jail and then to the Farmville Detention Center, ultimately being detained for 200 days.

Another plaintiff, 24-year-old Jose Rosito Roca Estrada, also a Woodbridge resident, was arrested on June 27 by apparent immigration officers who allegedly crashed into his work van, smashed the windows, pepper-sprayed the occupants and forcibly removed him. Like in Chavez Calix’s case, the officers didn’t ask Roca Estrada about his immigration history or current circumstances during his arrest, the complaint says.

Even though Roca Estrada sustained serious injuries from his arrest, including a broken clavicle and injured lung, he wasn’t given immediate medical treatment and was instead funneled through West Virginia, Chantilly, Caroline County and Farmville before being taken to a hospital nearly two days later, according to the complaint.

Pepper spray during early-morning stop in Centreville

Another plaintiff, 24-year-old Catarina Rebeca Us Lopez, was riding through Centreville with her partner and 3-year-old child when the car was surrounded by officers in unmarked vehicles and blocked at a traffic light at around 6 a.m. on April 22.

Multiple agents, some of whom were masked, surrounded the car, knocked on windows, and forced the door open. One said her partner was subject to a deportation order, which was incorrect, according to the lawsuit.

“When Ms. Us Lopez’s partner tried to explain as much, an agent pepper sprayed him and threatened to draw a weapon,” the complaint says. “Agents forced both Ms. Us Lopez and her partner into one of the unmarked vehicles and only then asked them their names for the first time.”

While Us Lopez is a native of Guatemala, she has lived in the U.S. since 2019 with work authorization, which her partner also has. The child is a U.S. citizen. Even after she explained that, agents continued to search the car, tossed her partner’s driver’s license and other paperwork into the street, taunted the couple, and threatened to pick up their child too, the suit alleges.

Before being taken to a detention facility, both were taken to “a remote location,” where the partner was given “a small cup of water to wash the pepper spray from his face,” but officers “laughed at him when he requested more.”

Us Lopez was released, but has been wearing an ankle monitor since the April incident.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs said the arrests documented in the complaint demonstrate a pattern of ICE targeting everyday people going about their lives, and justifying their detentions after the fact.

“ICE agents are arresting people first and assuming they’ll figure out a reason to justify it later, flagrantly ignoring federal law that’s been in place for decades,” ACLU of Virginia Senior Supervising Attorney Sophia Gregg said in a press release. “The law is clear: ICE must have a warrant or probable cause before it can arrest someone.”

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court of the Eastern District of Virginia in Alexandria on Nov. 16.

In addition to the ACLU of Virginia, the plaintiffs are represented by attorneys from Bailey & Glasser LLP, Covington & Burling LLP, Legal Aid Justice Center, and the Washington Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs.

title: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism - SCOTUSblog
description:
American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself.
And then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law.
It also mandated expedited removal to asylum seekers who had crossed the border seeking to apply for asylum and provided for expedited removal of such persons.
Surprising as it may seem, the United States is not exceptional in having to grapple with immigration, refugees, and asylum.
Section 1158’s grant of authority to the executive to grant asylum applications can be construed at least in two ways.
text:
American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself. The founders of New England, in words echoed by President Ronald Reagan, famously declared that it was to be “as a citty upon a Hill. The eies of all people are upon us.”

At best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result. In time the New England states would become leaders in the abolition of slavery. Closer to our time, the United States would translate its victory in the Second Word War into the Marshall Plan, the World Bank, and the currently embattled international legal order under the aegis of the United Nations. The 18th Amendment, the juvenile death penalty (until 2005), and the failure to guarantee a right to healthcare furnish examples of exceptionalism gone wrong.

And then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law. At the Founding and for decades thereafter, the court tended to embrace “the law of nations,” either as a guide to interpreting relevant statutes or even as furnishing a rule of decision in appropriate circumstances. In more recent times, however, majorities have balked at viewing treaties as self-executing, taking guidance from the International Court of Justice, or applying statutes that expressly incorporate “the law of nations” into domestic law.

A grant of certiorari just this month will likely confirm the trend. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, in which the justices will review one of the Trump administration’s earliest attempts to restrict immigration. On the administration’s first day, a presidential proclamation declared that “an invasion is ongoing on the southern border.” The proclamation, among other things, sought to suspend entry to the United States for non-citizens “engaged in the invasion,” even for refugees fleeing persecution and seeking to apply for asylum. But the edict went one step further. It also mandated expedited removal to asylum seekers who had crossed the border seeking to apply for asylum and provided for expedited removal of such persons.

The proclamation was issued notwithstanding a congressional framework that seeks to facilitate asylum – indefinite lawful residence – to those escaping persecution in their home country, set forth primarily in the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act as amended by the 1980 Refugee Act and later amendments (codified under Title 8 of the U.S. Code). This framework: a) ensures a right to apply for asylum, b) links eligibility for asylum to refugee status, and c) provides protections against the government removing persons who would be likely to face persecution or torture.

Section 1158 establishes the right to seek asylum. It provides that “Any alien who is physically present in the United States … irrespective of such alien’s status, may apply for asylum.” The same section makes eligibility for asylum conditional, among other things, on a demonstration of refugee status. For this the statute relies on the definition of refugee in section 1101(a)(42) as a person who is unwilling or unable to return to their home country “because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.”

In turn, safeguards from removal come from two sources. The Immigration statute itself states that noncitizens cannot be removed to a country where the attorney general determines that the “alien’s life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien’s race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” In addition, the Foreign Affairs Reform & Restructuring Act of 1998 restricts removal to a country when “there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.”

The Trump administration initially justified the denial of asylum and removal projections to those within the United States by invoking the president’s authority to suspend entry “of any aliens or of any class of aliens into the United States [that] would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The logic is that no one who violated the suspension by entering should be entitled to asylum and removal protections. To this defense the administration has added the formal role of the attorney general and director of Homeland Security. The INA grants each official the authority to grant asylum to eligible applicants as well as withhold removal for those who qualify. At the same time, the statute makes clear that these decisions are subject to individualized judicial review under an “abuse of discretion” standard. (At least until the second Trump administration, decisions not to grant relief to those who had demonstrated that they had qualified for asylum were the “exceedingly rare“ exception.)

The lower courts rejected both justifications. Judge Randolph Moss of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia dismissed the administration’s claim that the president’s suspension of entry to those “engaged in [the] invasion” invalidated asylum and removal protections that expressly applied to persons physically in the country. The D.C. Circuit agreed with a slightly different emphasis. Writing for the majority, Judge Michelle Childs also rejected the idea that a suspension of entry justified eliminating asylum and removal safeguards for those present in the United States. To this point she added that, as a grant of asylum is discretionary, the express right to apply it entails individualized consideration rather than blanket elimination. (Judge Justin Walker issued a partial dissenting argument that the grant of discretionary authority permits a blanket denial of asylum claims.)

The D.C. courts’ holdings are not wrong so far as they go. Suspending entry would appear to be a different power from removing someone after they had entered. The provisions for asylum strongly imply individualized consideration and even suggest a presumption of granting asylum to those who meet the detailed eligibility requirements. The relevant provisions plainly bar removal of those who qualify for that protection. But whether this reasoning will be sufficient at the Supreme Court is another matter. This is so not least given the justices’ recent penchant for giving the executive wide latitude on immigration.

But the justices should take into account some additional perspective.

One relevant perspective comes from international law. Surprising as it may seem, the United States is not exceptional in having to grapple with immigration, refugees, and asylum. More surprising still, these common global challenges has yielded what should be familiar, common legal standards that apply, and to a great extent which owe their development to, the United States. Perhaps most surprising of all, standard domestic doctrines invite reference to this body of law when interpreting applicable federal statutes.

Consider first asylum. As an initial matter, the domestic asylum framework incorporates international standards as a function of congressional intent. As the court itself recognized in 1987’s INS v. Cardozo-Fonseca, Congress enacted the Refugee Act of 1980 to bring U.S. law in conformity with the nation’s obligations as a state party to the 1967 Protocol to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Crucially, in determining those obligations, the court sensibly drew upon the views of the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees.

What do those obligations contemplate? The Refugee Conventions do not expressly provide for a right to apply for long-term asylum, as opposed to specifying rights for refugees fleeing persecution. But the UNCHR has maintained that international law presupposes individualized consideration of refugee status, especially before that status is denied. Given that Congress made the requirements for refugee status the basis for being eligible for asylum, it would be odd to conclude that the U.S. would remain in conformity with the convention as interpreted by the UN’s most authoritative body should the executive reject the right to seek asylum by means of a categorial denial of all asylum claims.

Not surprisingly, categorical rejection of asylum claims would also be at variance with widespread international practice, especially as mandated in Europe. And neither last nor least, the administration’s position would also be inconsistent with the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights’ express guarantee of a right to asylum. Though not binding, the UDHR was adopted without dissent by the UN General Assembly, reflects the dominant position of the Member States, and informs their practice.

The Charming Betsy canon leads to the same conclusion. In the 1804 case Murray v. the Schooner Charming Betsy, Chief Justice John Marshall famously stated that “an act of Congress ought never to be construed to violate the law of nations if any other possible construction remains.” Marshall’s reference to the “law of nations” is generally understood to apply to modern customary international law. International custom arises given a near consensus of state practice perused out of a sense of legal obligation.

Section 1158’s grant of authority to the executive to grant asylum applications can be construed at least in two ways. It might mean a complete categorical discretion to deny. Or it might be better understood to assume individualized consideration. The latter clearly better comports with international practice. Yet there is even a stronger consideration. Customary, and for that matter treaty law, clearly prohibits removal to countries where a refugee has a well-founded fear of facing persecution or torture. When the result is expedited removal, the categorical denial of asylum status to persons claiming to escape from persecution and torture places the U.S. in obvious jeopardy of violating exactly this well-established international prohibition.

Which brings up the matter of removal itself. Here the upshot of Congress’ intent is more direct. Article 33.1 of the 1951 Refugee Convention provides: “No Contracting State shall expel or return (“refouler”) a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.” Likewise, Article 3.1 of the Convention Against Torture mandates that “No State Party shall expel, return ("refouler") or extradite a person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” As noted, the Refugee Act in the first instance sought to place the U.S. in conformity with the Refugee Convention. FARRA sought to do the same with CAT. Categorically removing persons in the U.S. seeking asylum all but guarantees violations of the treaties that Congress sought to uphold.

So strong is the congressional intent argument that the Charming Betsy need not set sail. Yet even if the relevant statutory provisions were somehow ambiguous, the Charming Betsy canon would compel rejection of the administration’s position. Assume that section 1182(f), which grants the executive discretion to deny asylum claims, authorizes a categorial denial of applications across the board. Assume further that this section, along with section 1185(a)(1), can be read to permit removal of persons within the United States denied the opportunity to apply for asylum on the basis of persecution or torture. Even without the conventions, international practice has separately established “non-refoulement” – the prohibition of returning, or “refouling,” a person to return to a territory where he may be exposed to persecution as a matter of binding customary international law. Reading the relevant statutes to permit removal would then constitute a clear violation of non-refoulement. That reading would therefore also run counter to the Charming Betsy canon.

It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation.

A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border.

text:
Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled.

However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders.

That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation.

In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

The deliberately caused crisis was part of various “hybrid actions” undertaken by Belarus and its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile.

In response, those EU states took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus.

On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus.

The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”.

This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”.

The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention.

However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”.

That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus.

In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants.

For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis.

The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure for the Afghan national, ordering that he not be returned to Belarus.

However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR.

It also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation.

In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”.

At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk.

However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention.

It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures.

In response to today’s ruling on Poland, deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Kaciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”.

He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies.

The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration

“In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC.

A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards.

In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border.

Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted.

The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution.

Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration.

This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross.

text:
Port of Seattle commissioners unanimously criticized ICE agents Monday and called for a review of badging and security procedures, while simultaneously acknowledging the jurisdictional restraints after masked federal agents detained two travelers on an Alaska Airlines jet bridge Saturday as passengers were boarding a flight to Los Angeles.

“ICE is a rogue agency,” Port of Seattle Commissioner Toshiko Hasegawa said bluntly during a sparsely attended special meeting.

“It is a fundamental question of public safety and airport security. The traveling public and our airport employees should not be left wondering whether they are witnessing a lawful arrest or an abduction. Period,” Port of Seattle Commissioner Sam Cho added. “I could wear a mask, go into the airport, and claim to be ICE. No one in this room will tell me that's appropriate or OK.”

RELATED | ICE airport arrests: Attorney says detainees have pending asylum, no criminal record

“Immigration is a civil matter; it is not a criminal matter,” Port of Seattle Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed said in an interview. She is pushing the Port to review the badging mechanisms internally while also acknowledging the agents might have entered the area using another tactic.

“We'll have to go through legal review to ensure that if we can deactivate any badges under our control, then we should deactivate any badges that's under our control that they may have,” she said. “They do have federal credentials and federal badges that they can use in different parts of the airport, but I think it's still important that we send a clear message that we're not complicit in this, and we do not support what it is that they're doing.”

Furthermore, the two passengers, Ricardo Larrando Mendoza and Sofia Hernandez-Mejia, had already been passed through by TSA agents at the airport.

“These individuals were already cleared,” Mohamed said in an interview. “There was no logic that supports what those officers did.”

A passenger who witnessed the arrest told KOMO News the arresting agents had “no sign of law enforcement whatsoever” and looked like passengers wearing masks. The family’s attorney said the agents did not identify themselves before the arrest. The attorney described the family as distraught and said the father and daughter had pending immigration applications and valid work permits. The two are being held in an immigration detention center in Tacoma.

PREVIOUS COVERAGE | ICE arrests 2 on Sea-Tac Airport jetway, disrupting flight boarding and sparking outrage

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said the agents were enforcing the law and making sure people “in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport. The fact of the matter is those who are in this country illegally have a choice. They can use the CBP Home app and receive a free flight and a $3,000 check, or they can be arrested, detained, and deported.”

The Port’s public guidance says federal agents have broad access to airport property, including areas before and after security, and that the Port cannot interfere with federal law enforcement operations or legally restrict access to the airport. The Port says it has no jurisdiction over ICE operations, which occur without its participation or knowledge.

The agents’ face coverings also raise questions under Washington’s SB 5855, which took effect in March. The law includes federal employees and agents who have authority to carry firearms and make warrantless arrests while enforcing federal criminal, customs or immigration laws.

It generally bars law enforcement officers from wearing an opaque face covering while interacting with the public in the course of their duties.

However, the law provides an exception for an officer working as an undercover operative during an active undercover operation. Whether that exception applies to Saturday’s arrest has not been determined.

text:
Parents and children detained at the family immigration detention center in Dilley, Texas, have been pressured to leave the country, held longer than allowed under court rules, and not informed of their legal rights, according to declarations filed in federal court.

Legal advocacy organizations alleged in the filing over weekend that federal immigration authorities have repeatedly violated the Flores Settlement Agreement, a 1997 court settlement that sets standards for the treatment and release of detained migrant children, including the limitation that they cannot be held for more than 20 days.

The declarations were filed with a motion asking a federal judge to require the enforcement of the settlement.

In the declarations, parents and children said they were not told about their Flores rights or their rights regarding conditions and release. Several also described enduring prolonged detention and delayed or inadequate medical care, as well as pressure to sign deportation documents.

"My daughter and I have been detained at Dilley for 15 days," Genesis Zerpa Rodriguez, a 30-year-old mother from Venezuela, said in her declaration. "We were picked up by ICE officers a couple of weeks ago after I had dropped off my baby at day care. We had just gotten some empanadas for breakfast and were about to go back-to-school shopping to get some new shoes for my seven-year-old when ICE agents suddenly swerved and surrounded our car in the front and the back."

Zerpa Rodriguez said she was detained at Dilley with her 7-year-old daughter, who suffers from asthma and had allergic reactions and rashes at the facility. While she said her daughter received an inhaler after repeated requests, she said it is not enough, and that her daughter needs more serious treatment for her condition.

Zerpa Rodriguez also said she has a hernia near her uterus for which she had a surgical procedure scheduled in Chicago, and that medical staff have offered only Tylenol.

"If I could, I would change everything about this place," she said. "I wish there could be more empathy from everyone, and I especially wish there were better care for children."

The Dilley facility, which is the only family detention center in the country, was closed during the Biden administration but was reopened last year as part of the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees the nation's immigration detention centers, did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

Karen Ortiz Castellanos, a 25-year-old mother from Venezuela who is detained with her 7-year-old daughter, said in her declaration that she was working as a delivery driver when three large black cars surrounded her vehicle.

"They forced open the door and pulled on my arm very painfully," Ortiz Castellanos said. "I was trembling, and I began to scream. It was one of the worst things that has happened to me. They handcuffed my hands and my ankles. I fainted twice and vomited."

Ortiz Castellanos said she signed a paper upon arrival without knowing what it said in English. She also said members of the staff threw away corn flakes she had brought to her room from the cafeteria for her daughter, who barely eats at the facility.

"I pleaded with them, telling them it's the only thing she'll eat, but they did not care," Ortiz Castellanos said.

Pablo Guerrero-Pimentel, a 49-year-old man from Venezuela, said in his declaration that he has been detained at Dilley for 13 days with his partner and their 17- and 11-year-old daughters. He said he had lived in El Paso for about four years and worked as a local mechanic before ICE agents surrounded his car while he was driving his daughters to school.

"They handcuffed me in front of my daughters and took us to the ICE office in El Paso," he said. "It was horrible for my daughters to see their dad handcuffed."

Guerrero-Pimentel said officers at Dilley tried to get his family to sign a paper to self-deport, telling them they would each receive $3,000.

"They told us that if we signed, we'd each get $3,000," he said. "Being here has affected my health so much."

text:
By Ryan Schwach

New York City joined Attorney General Letitia James in a lawsuit over a new federal rule that could cost thousands of immigrant New Yorkers their homes.

James, the city and a coalition of several other state attorneys general and municipalities argued that the Trump administration violated federal law when the Department of Housing and Urban Development created a new rule that would require every member of a household receiving federal subsidies – including under Section 8 – to be a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant, effectively stripping benefits from mixed-status families.

It could put 78,000 Americans at risk of losing their homes, according to James. In New York City, an estimated 2,540 mixed-status families would be displaced under the new rule.

“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. Denying a child that security because of who they live with is cruel and indefensible,” James said in a statement. “With our country already in the throes of a housing crisis, it is outrageous that the federal government would push even more families out of their homes. This rule runs counter to our nation’s values and the very purpose of these housing programs.”

The coalition challenged the rule, which would require all U.S. citizens in federal housing programs to prove their citizenship, arguing it violates federal law and 30 years of precedent.

On Monday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the city would also be joining James in the lawsuit.

“The federal government’s new mixed-status rule threatens to rip that security away from tens of thousands of people,” Mamdani said. “We will not stand by while families are put at risk.”

New York City Corporation Counsel Steven Banks said that the new HUD rule “defies the longstanding intent of Congress to protect mixed-status households.”

“No parent should ever have to face the heartbreaking choice of separating from their family in order to prevent their children from losing their housing assistance,” he said. “Yet that is the choice this new HUD rule would force families to make – children will be at risk of losing their homes simply because of their parents’ immigration status.”

The 56-page lawsuit was filed on Monday in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts.

“No family should have to choose between keeping a roof over their heads and keeping their family together,” said Lucy Newman, a supervising attorney in the Public Housing Unit at The Legal Aid Society. “HUD’s rule threatens to upend that protection and put families’ homes and stability at risk. We will keep fighting this unlawful policy in court and alongside the families whose lives it would disrupt. We thank Mayor Mamdani and the elected officials joining our fight to protect families and keep them housed.”
