title: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?
description:
So what can we say about the different justices’ support for the Trump administration on the emergency docket?
Thomas supported the executive in 83% of eligible Trump I decisions, 39% under Biden, and 92% under Trump II.
Kagan supported executive positions in 43% of eligible Trump I decisions, 94% under Biden, and 24% under Trump II.
Roberts supported the executive in 10 of 11 immigration decisions under Trump I, three of six under Biden, and 11 of 13 under Trump II.
Thomas supported the government in 10 of 10 eligible Trump I immigration decisions, two of six under Biden, and 12 of 13 under Trump II.
text:
When the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson to leave Cook in office while the case proceeded. Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett dissented. The administration lost, but the court’s disagreement did not reflect the familiar ideological split.

Four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners. In Trump v. Kingdom, Thomas and Alito indicated that they would have granted the requested stay, but no other justice publicly held that position. Unlike Trump v. Cook, which produced a signed opinion after oral argument, the Kingdom order disclosed nothing about the reasoning or votes behind the court’s denial.

The contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief. And whereas some justices have supported federal executive positions at broadly similar rates across presidencies, others appear far more likely to do so depending on whether the president is a Republican or Democrat.

The prior article in this series examined how frequently the Trump and Biden administrations prevailed. In turning to the individual justices, I reviewed federal executive-action decisions from 2017 through November 12, 2026, consolidated into 106 distinct substantive decisions. The three administrations account for 32, 36, and 38 decisions, respectively.

There is a very important qualification throughout: the court often publishes emergency orders without identifying each justice’s vote. The analysis thus assigned a justice to the court’s majority ruling when they were silent, absent an express position or other evidence indicating otherwise.

So what can we say about the different justices’ support for the Trump administration on the emergency docket?

Different presidents, different justices

The most consistent record belongs to Roberts. He aligned with federal executive positions in 23 of 31 eligible decisions during Trump’s first administration, 26 of 36 under Biden, and 28 of 38 during Trump’s second administration. Those figures amount to 74%, 72%, and 74%. The disputes changed markedly, but Roberts’ aggregate willingness to leave the federal government’s position intact – or grant it relief – barely moved. In other words, Roberts has typically supported executive power on the emergency docket regardless of who is president.

The next most consistent justice, Barrett (though with a much lower sample size), aligned with Biden in 69% of her eligible decisions and Trump II in 78%. Third was Kavanaugh, with rates of 78%, 67%, and 79%. Then came Gorsuch, with rates of 83%, 54%, and 84%.

Thomas and Alito present a very different picture. Thomas supported the executive in 83% of eligible Trump I decisions, 39% under Biden, and 92% under Trump II. Alito’s corresponding figures were 83%, 47%, and 92%.

The liberal justices show the opposite movement, although their individual records differ. Kagan supported executive positions in 43% of eligible Trump I decisions, 94% under Biden, and 24% under Trump II. Sotomayor’s rates were 27%, 94%, and 16%. Jackson, who joined the court during Biden’s presidency, supported its executive position in 21 of 24 eligible decisions (88%), compared with three of 38 (8%) under Trump II.

The figure above makes these distinctions particularly clear. Roberts remains between 72% and 74% across the three periods, while Thomas’ support moves from 83% under Trump I to 39% under Biden and 92% under Trump II. The middle group of Barrett, Kavanaugh, and Gorsuch is more varied, but each supported Biden’s executive position more frequently than a simple Republican-versus-Democratic framing might suggest.

These numbers are telling, but they do not establish the reasons for why the justices decided as they did. For example, a president defending an environmental rule presents a very different legal issue from one seeking permission to remove an independent agency official. To determine how much of the observed variation is associated with presidential identity, the next step is to examine the kinds of cases that produced it.

The issues that unite and divide the justices

Immigration provides a useful point of comparison because it generated substantial emergency litigation under all three administrations. Roberts supported the executive in 10 of 11 immigration decisions under Trump I, three of six under Biden, and 11 of 13 under Trump II. Thomas supported the government in 10 of 10 eligible Trump I immigration decisions, two of six under Biden, and 12 of 13 under Trump II. Kagan’s comparable figures were six of eleven, six of six, and five of 13.

This is revealing. Roberts and Thomas both supported Trump’s immigration positions at high rates but not as much when Biden defended his administration’s policies. Kagan and Sotomayor supported Biden in all six coded immigration decisions, then opposed most of Trump II positions. But there is, of course, a key caveat: This category covers different immigration rules, as opposed to simple support for one president over another.

Public-health and related health litigation under Biden revealed a sharper division within the conservative majority. In 10 eligible health-coded decisions, Roberts and Kavanaugh each supported the federal executive in seven, compared with one each for Thomas and Alito. Barrett supported it in five; Gorsuch in two. Kagan and Sotomayor each supported the government in nine such cases. (Jackson’s two favorable positions came from only three eligible decisions in this category, making her figure much less informative.)

The court’s January 2022 vaccination decisions supply a concrete example. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in allowing the administration to enforce a vaccination requirement for workers at healthcare facilities receiving Medicare or Medicaid funding, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. On the same day, Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the conservatives in blocking OSHA’s broader vaccination-or-testing standard. To Roberts and Kavanaugh, health litigation was clearly treated issue-by-issue.

Let’s move on to personnel decisions, or the president’s control over the executive branch. In the nine Trump II personnel and removal decisions, Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett supported the executive in eight, while Roberts and Kavanaugh did so in seven. In four foreign-affairs and national-security decisions, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch aligned with the government in all of these, compared with two for Roberts and Barrett.

Subject matter therefore helps explain how things break down. The same conservative justice may support emergency intervention in a dispute over immigration enforcement while resisting it in a case involving agency regulation. The legal authority being asserted, the posture of the case, and the requested remedy all shape the decision.

The coalitions inside the conservative majority

So which justices most frequently aligned? At the front of the pack are Thomas and Alito, who agreed in all 38 coded Trump II decisions. Their alignment is particularly visible when the administration lost. In seven events, both of their positions favored more relief for the administration than the majority granted or would otherwise provide.

Other pairings are almost as cohesive. Roberts and Barrett agreed in 35 of 36 Trump II decisions (97%). Roberts and Kavanaugh agreed in 36 of 38 of these (95%), as did Gorsuch and Kavanaugh. The next figure displays those pairings alongside the liberal and cross-ideological relationships. The high agreement rates show how often the conservatives arrive at the same apparent disposition, but the exceptions reveal competing views about the scope of emergency judicial intervention.

The foreign-assistance dispute in Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, for instance, separated Roberts and Barrett from Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh. The four dissenters would have granted the administration relief from an order requiring payment for foreign-aid work already completed. Roberts and Barrett did not join that position. Their disagreement concerned what a district court could require of the government while the underlying funding litigation continued.

A different alignment emerged in NIH v. American Public Health Association. There, the court granted partial relief in litigation over terminated research grants. Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh would have granted the administration’s request in full, while Roberts joined Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson in seeking to deny it altogether. Barrett supported an intermediate outcome.

In Cook, the division shifted again. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in rejecting the administration’s attempt to immediately remove a Federal Reserve governor, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. In Trump v. Illinois, concerning the Trump administration’s deployment of National Guard forces, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch disagreed with the court’s denial of relief to Trump, while Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment on narrower grounds.

The evidence points toward distinctive approaches to removal authority, spending, the judicial supervision of agencies, and emergency remedies. Justices who agree in one field can diverge in another, and partial orders sometimes put a justice between two groups seeking opposing forms of relief.

The liberal justices and the unusual alliances across ideological lines

The three liberal justices also exhibited some meaningful disagreements. Under Trump II, Jackson aligned with the executive in only three of 38 emergency decisions (8%), compared with six for Sotomayor (16%) and nine for Kagan (24%). Kagan and Sotomayor agreed in 35 of 38 such decisions; Kagan and Jackson in 32. The differences are not as dramatic as those dividing the conservatives, but they complicate the assumption that the liberal trio behaves as a single bloc in every emergency dispute.

Their publicly registered dissents differ as well. Jackson expressly opposed a Trump II executive position in 26 decisions, Sotomayor in 23, and Kagan in 20. In FCC v. Brown, for example, Sotomayor and Jackson publicly indicated that they would deny the agency’s stay application, while Kagan registered no public disagreement.

Trump’s second term has produced more than one identifiable cross-ideological alignment. The five-justice majority in Cook included Roberts, Kavanaugh, and the three liberals, while the NIH grants dispute placed Roberts and the liberals together against complete relief. Barrett also joined certain portions of Sotomayor’s dissent in Trump v. J.G.G., a dispute involving the Alien Enemies Act, although her partial join should not necessarily be counted as agreement with the liberals on the case.

These examples again highlight why the distinction between shared results and shared legal reasoning is important. A justice can favor the same outcome as an ideological opponent while arriving there for entirely different reasons (we see this with concurrences in merits cases all the time). Separate opinions can also reveal agreement on a particular procedural or statutory question even when the justices disagree on the ultimate relief. At the same time, the emergency docket makes these relationships especially difficult to measure comprehensively because many orders contain no individual vote information at all.

Where this leaves us

My analysis of the emergency docket shows a chief most reluctant to favor one administration over another, with Barrett and Kavanaugh following closely behind; Gorsuch acting more favorably towards the Trump administration, although not overwhelmingly so; Thomas and Alito disproportionately favoring Trump over Biden; and the three liberal justices acting as a near mirror image of Thomas and Alito – although to varied degrees.

We thus see a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.

text:
Two human rights groups and others convinced a federal court to permanently halt enforcement of part of President Donald Trump’s executive order authorizing sanctions against those that help the International Criminal Court.

The executive order seeks to regulate speech-based services in violation of the First Amendment, Judge Jesse M. Furman of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York said in Monday order. Trump is excluded from the injunction, Furman also said.

Democracy for the Arab World Now and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide sued in July over Executive Order 14203, which declared a national emergency based on the ICC’s purportedly improper actions targeting America and Israel. They said the executive order violates the First Amendment to the extent it prohibits the provision or receipt of services by, to, or for the benefit of any person designated for sanctions connected with the ICC’s work.

Furman granted a preliminary injunction Oct. 13. He said in that order that this case paralleled Rona v. Trump, where another Southern District of New York judge enjoined application of the executive order against two law professors.

The plaintiffs are entitled to permanent relief “substantially for the reasons” in the October order and Rona, Furman said.

“Every application of the Services Prohibition to a speech-based service turns on the function or purpose of the speech and, thus, triggers strict scrutiny. And every such application suffers from the same lack of narrow tailoring, the judge said.

Joseph Pace of New York City represents the plaintiffs.

text:
A magistrate judge who authorized a recent search of Ilhan Omar’s home by federal agents ruled that the Minnesota Democratic congresswoman was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search, according to court documents unsealed on Monday.

The unsealed filings reveal how federal justice department attorneys and US magistrate judge Matthew Sharbaugh resolved their initial disagreement over the thorny constitutional implications of searching a member of Congress’s private residence for a criminal investigation.

The heavily redacted documents – released in response to a lawsuit filed by media organizations – do not appear to shed new light on the reason or outcome of the search itself. They also do not disclose new details of an immigration-fraud investigation launched by the Trump administration – that Omar claims is politically motivated.

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, the Associated Press reported in October, citing a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an active investigation.

The unsealed filings show that Sharbaugh – before authorizing the search of Omar’s home – raised concerns about the “speech or debate clause” implications of searching a private residence belonging to a member of Congress. The clause, which is designed to protect legislators from executive branch interference or intimidation, includes a privilege against compelled disclosures.

Sharbaugh said he disagreed with the government’s argument that the privilege is limited only to official congressional offices and certain electronic devices.

“That logic does not hold,” the magistrate wrote.

Sharbaugh concluded that the government’s law-enforcement interests needed to be balanced against Omar’s constitutional rights as a member of Congress. He said the government ultimately agreed to a search protocol allowing Omar to invoke a privilege over any speech or debate clause material before agents carried out the search.

Omar, a naturalized US citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by Donald Trump and many of the president’s Republican allies. She hasn’t been charged with any crimes and has denied any wrongdoing.

Washington DC federal court chief judge James Boasberg ordered the partial unsealing of court filings related to the 12 October search of Omar’s home in the nation’s capital, which was carried out by US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents.

He ruled after more than a dozen news organizations, including the AP, argued that the public has a right to access the records under the US constitution’s first amendment free press rights.

Boasberg agreed with the government that it would be premature to unseal a 67-page search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government’s investigation. In a court filing in October, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made.

An attorney for Omar didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment Monday on the unsealed documents.

Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the 3 November midterm elections, when Omar won her re-election bid and Trump’s Republican party lost control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency.

The US justice department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election.

text:
Some community members are calling for a boycott of a popular coffee shop in West Humboldt Park, and workers have walked off the job over a viral social media post alleging the shop has ties to ICE.

On Monday, the business also was egged.

Jackie Marquez owns Tasa Coffee Roasters, a roastery and coffee shop at 4136 W. North Ave. The shop opened in 2022 and quickly became a neighborhood favorite for its “Latina-owned and woman-forward” approach.

But a post that began circulating on social media Monday morning alleges someone with the same name as a man connected to the coffee shop appears in a database of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees leaked at the end of October.

WBEZ/Sun-Times can confirm the leaked documents list this individual as having been a supervisory detention and deportation officer at the agency. Public records reviewed by WBEZ/Sun-Times state that an individual by this name has been employed by DHS, but the agency did not provide direct confirmation of his status or position with the agency.

WBEZ/Sun-Times has been unable to confirm if the man listed in the leak is in fact the same person identified in the viral post, and as a result, is not naming him.

A search using the Nexis public records database showed an ICE email address and DHS employment location associated with the man’s name. But WBEZ/Sun-Times could not independently confirm the man is, or was ever, employed by ICE.

The shop’s publicly available business license and grants are all solely in Jackie Marquez’s name. Public records link the couple via mortgage and marriage documents.

On Monday afternoon, a few neighbors gathered around the shop to get a look at the signs left by workers that read: “After finding out from Reddit that there are allegations … we the baristas and roasters, have closed for the day. We do not stand beside, condone, support or accept anyone or any org associated with ICE. As the baristas, we are discussing what steps will be necessary for us. We intend to do our best as employees to be as honest and transparent as we can be. Thank you.”

By 4 p.m. Monday, Marquez herself had posted an Instagram story that briefly addressed the situation: “I’m Jackie, the sole owner of Tasa Coffee Roasters. I am a chef. Food and coffee have been my only career. I personally disagree with current immigration policy, and I believe in civil dialogue and mutual respect, even when we disagree. I ask that my employees not be targeted or held responsible for matters outside their control. My commitment remains firmly with my employees, my customers, and my community.”

Neither Marquez nor the man being targeted had responded to a request for comment by early Monday night.

Esme Segura, 28, heard about the Tasa allegations and decided to check things out with a friend.

They arrived with the intention of grabbing some photos and videos of the signs posted by the workers. But once they began recording video of the closed shop, a man inside started tearing down the posters and gestured to a small handgun in his waistband. The video was reviewed by WBEZ/Sun-Times.

“He just started banging on the door and flicking us off and then he also just flashed his gun or he was pointing at it. He raised his shirt and showed that he had it,” Segura said.

Police were called to the scene and the man was temporarily detained. Nobody on scene wanted to file a police report, so police released the man after confirming he is legally allowed to carry a firearm, officers at the scene said. The man’s identity has not been confirmed.

Since Chicago has been an ongoing target of federal immigration enforcement, Segura said it matters to the community if there are ties to the agency carrying out detentions and deportations.

“It is a Latino space, or they claim it to be a Latino space,” she said. “I feel like, you know, the neighborhood should feel safe going in.”

text:
The arrest of an Encinitas mother near an elementary school is galvanizing the community against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activities near schools.

According to ICE, Griselda Velasquez-Carrillo, an immigrant from Guatemala, was detained during a “targeted enforcement” on Nov. 18. The agency said she crossed into the United States illegally in 2016 near the Tecate border and was released into the U.S. with an order to attend court hearings.

“All of her claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and she will receive due process,” a statement from a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson said. “This administration will not ignore the rule of law."

In video footage shared with KPBS News, Velasquez-Carrillo was stopped near St. John the Evangelist Catholic Church, two blocks away from Ocean Knoll Elementary School, where her son attends kindergarten.

“I was very affected by opening a car door and seeing a kid's school photo,” Leigh Ratcliffe said. “But this is one of many, many families that are being destroyed.”

Ratcliffe is part of a rapid response network monitoring ICE activities in North County. Before the arrest, she said another community member saw an ICE agent following Velasquez-Carrillo’s car out of the parking lot where she had just dropped her son off at school.

When she and another community member found Velasquez-Carrillo’s car parked in the back lot of the nearby church, the passenger-side window was smashed, and a bag of groceries sat on the passenger seat.

That was a bag she had picked up from the school’s food drive.

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said ICE does not target schools.

“This is just another false narrative to try and demonize our brave ICE law enforcement who are facing a 1,600% increase in assaults against them and an 8,000% increase in death threats,” the spokesperson said.

Ratcliffe said that was a disingenuous statement. She’s seen ICE agents' vehicles at every elementary school in Encinitas.

“The kids in the school are traumatized. They're hearing about parents who disappear,” she said. “So I don't care if they say they're not here. They're traumatizing kids in this school.”

In a statement, the Encinitas Union School District said it is working with the family to provide all the needed support.

“No family should fear for their safety on their way to and from school,” the statement said.

Ratcliffe said the family was devastated. Several family members were detained in the past year, leaving only one breadwinner, she said. It was especially heartbreaking when Ratcliffe saw a 16-year-old girl come by to pick up the car.

“She was very worried about her mother, who has to go to work every day and is vulnerable. And she has a job now; she said she just got a second job after school.” Ratcliffe said. “She was very worried about the little kids that were left and herself. She said she was born here.”

San Diego Unified School District, the state’s second-largest school district, said ICE’s actions have a real impact on students’ mental health.

In a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin following the detainment of an 8-year-old Haitian boy on Nov. 4, the district said actions such as that “place children at significant risk of academic regression, mental health challenges, and long-term instability.”

Rattcliffe said these are members of the community, not criminals and these arrests must stop.

text:
New York state Attorney General Letitia James joined 21 other attorneys general to announce a lawsuit against the Trump administration as a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule revokes assistance for families of “mixed immigration statuses.”

“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. Denying a child that security because of who they live with is cruel and indefensible. With our country already in the throes of a housing crisis, it is outrageous that the federal government would push even more families out of their homes,” James said during a press conference Monday.

James filed the lawsuit against HUD and Secretary Scott Turner with attorneys general from California, Massachusetts, Arizona, Colorado, Washington, D.C., Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico and Oregon, as well as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.

James said that the rule would force families to choose between keeping their housing and staying together. She said Congress wrote that into law in 1997.

“For nearly 30 years, families with mixed immigration statuses have been able to receive housing assistance for eligible household members and that assistance is already reduced to exclude anyone who is ineligible; Congress expressly protected that arrangement. In fact, when Congress established this prorated housing assistance, it explicitly said mixed-status families could not lose their assistance simply because an ineligible family member lived with them and HUD has no authority to rewrite a law Congress wrote,” James said during the press conference.

The new rules would only allow a family to stay in HUD-assisted housing if every person is a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant. They estimate that 20,000 mixed-status families will lose their housing assistance, which equals about 78,000 individuals.

“There are children who could lose their bedrooms, their schools, and the stability every child needs to thrive, but this rule reaches even further, it would require American citizens receiving federal housing assistance to undergo citizenship checks using a system with a documented record of errors and then produce additional documents if that system fails to recognize them,” James said.

Secretary Scott Turner released a statement Monday:

“HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars," Turner said. "This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

In New York City, James said that approximately 2,540 mixed-status families would be displaced from federally subsidized housing. James and the other attorneys general are asking that the courts strike down the rule, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it.

The rule is set to go into effect on Dec. 14 but was proposed in February.

“I can say that during the period of time where individuals were submitting comments, despite the thousands of comments that were filed with HUD, the rule remains unchanged,” James said. “We are confident again that this rule will be struck down by the courts because HUD does not have the power to erase a protection Congress wrote into federal law.”

Maura Healey and Campbell take action against the ICE arrests.

text:
Above: Attorney General Andrea Campbell addresses reporters during a press conference on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026 at her One Ashburton Place office. Yawu Miller photo

Attorney General Andrea Campbell has filed a lawsuit in federal court against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for making civil immigration arrests in Massachusetts court houses in violation of the PROTECT Act, which bars such arrests in courts, schools and other facilities.

“Under the Tenth Amendment of the US Constitution, Massachusetts retains sovereign authority over its judicial system and its administration of justice and, with the passage of the Protect Act, Massachusetts has established clear restrictions on civil immigration arrest in its courthouses,” Campbell said, speaking to reporters during a press conference on Monday. “By openly violating these restrictions, ICE is unlawfully interfering with the Commonwealth’s sovereign authority, and unlawfully using state, courts, and resources to carry out federal immigration enforcement.”

Campbell said ICE agents have arrested at least 38 individuals in Massachusetts courthouses since the PROTECT Act was enacted in November. The lawsuit seeks an injunction barring ICE agents from making arrests on court property.

While police and court officers in Massachusetts can cooperate with ICE in cases where immigrant defendants have been convicted of crimes and have deportation orders, the PROTECT Act bars them from participating in civil immigration enforcement — cases in which an person’s only infraction is entering the country without documentation or authorization. The law bars ICE agents from making such arrests without a judicial warrant.

Since Trump took office in 2025, his administration has ramped up efforts to detain and deport immigrants. On its website, ICE claims to have arrested 74,082 immigrants since Dec. 31, 2024 through Nov. 23, the vast majority of whom have no criminal record. ICE has also detained immigrants who are here legally, including those here on student visas and immigrants with refugee status.

LUCE member Leela Ramachandran spoke during a Nov. 18 press conference on the steps of the State House in Boston. Yawu Miller photo

Immigration advocates last Wednesday (Nov. 18) gathered in front of the State House to demand Gov. Maura Healey and Campbell take action against the ICE arrests.

“When we have a policing system in which Black and brown folks are disproportionately criminalized, a court system that allows our people to be picked up inside of courts and immigration courts that feel like a joke with severe consequences, we are complicit in the mass deportation project of the Trump administration,” said Leela Ramachandran, a member of the group LUCE.

Ramachandran said she and other LUCE volunteers have witnessed court officials working in collaboration with ICE agents.

“We have seen court officers continuing to trade personal cell phone numbers with ICE agents, showing agents footage from cameras inside the courthouse and being disrespectful with volunteers,” she said.

Ramachandran told reporters that LUCE volunteers have reported all suspected violations to the Attorney General’s Office of Civil Rights.

On Monday, Campbell told reporters her office would follow up with any complaints received of violations of the PROTECT Act.

Campbell’s lawsuit challenges a May 2025 memo ICE issued stating that its officers have the authority to enter courthouses to make civil arrests even when states forbid it. While a federal court in California ruled against the policy in June, ICE has continued to make such arrests.

Campbell told reporters her office has informed ICE of the provisions of the PROTECT Act and how they should comply, but received no response. Asked how her office would respond if ICE ignores a judgment in the Commonwealth’s favor, she said she would bring the agency back into court.

“If we have to go back into court to get a court to enforce a particular order, we will do that,” she said. “There are other tools that the court has in order to hold the federal government accountable and to ensure their compliance with the court order. We will take those additional steps if required here.

“Right now, though, we want the court to move as quickly as possible, and we will, of course, work with the court on this complaint, and strategy going forward in order to stop these arrests from happening.”

text:
Two Columbus law firms representing multiple plaintiffs are preparing to sue the Franklin County Sheriff's Office, alleging the county jails unlawfully hold detainees past their release times so U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents can arrest them.

Attorneys at Marshall, Forman & Schlein sent a letter on Nov. 16 requesting the Sheriff's Office preserve records in anticipation of litigation they intend to file in early 2027. Gittes Law Group will also be part of the lawsuit, said John Marshall, an attorney on the planned suit. The planned legal action will allege that the county jails are violating immigrants' rights under the U.S. Constitution, including Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable seizure.

Franklin County Sheriff Dallas Baldwin's office told The Dispatch that he cannot comment on pending litigation. The Dispatch has reported multiple times in 2026 on how the jails work with ICE. The jail's official policy is to not hold people for ICE unless presented with a criminal warrant signed by a judge. Baldwin has maintained that his deputies follow his written policy "99% of the time." He said his staff cannot stop ICE agents from showing up at the jail.

Attorneys contend what is on paper differs from what is done in practice.

"The sheriff is keeping people in violation of their constitutional rights in order to hand them off to ICE for political reasons," Marshall told The Dispatch. "If he says he's not doing it, that's not true."

ICE arrested at least 161 people at the Franklin County jails in 2026 through early August, according to available ICE data published by the Deportation Data Project. That's nearly double the 88 arrested there in all of 2025.

Marshall said he does not know if the jails violated policy or detainees' rights in each of those cases, but he said the jail has done so for multiple individuals who plan to join the pending lawsuit.

The Dispatch reported on the case of one young mother, an asylum-seeker from Venezuela, who was still nursing her baby when they were separated by ICE agents picking her up at the jail. Baldwin maintains his deputies followed his policy in that case. Attorneys and records say the jail released her to ICE.

"It's sad to see the dehumanization of immigrants, which has been going on now for years in this country," Marshall said. "It causes people to think that somehow it's okay to treat them this way."

Marshall said his legal team is building on an opinion issued in a case they brought earlier in 2026 against the Department of Homeland Security and ICE. In that case, U.S. District Court Judge Sarah Morrison granted the government's request to dismiss the case because plaintiffs lacked standing to sue over what ICE might do to them in the future.

Morrison went further though, Marshall said. She issued an opinion over 70 pages long in which she laid out the evidence that ICE is acting illegally in Ohio.

"It is clear that Defendants have, in some instances, unlawfully arrested and detained non-citizens in Ohio without a warrant and without a probable cause determination of their likelihood of escape," Morrison wrote. "Some of the accounts offered by Plaintiffs and those they wish to represent about how individual agents effectuated arrests deeply trouble the Court."

Lawyers have filed requests with the Sheriff's Office for records from a period of weeks in October and November. They are seeking copies of ICE detainers received by the jail, jail management notes for each detainee released from the jail and telephone logs and audio recordings from calls between jail staff and ICE.

title: This Moderate Democrat Thinks Trump Could Help Rein In ICE - TIME
description:
While many of his colleagues want to battle the Trump Administration to rein in ICE, Cuellar sees things differently.
Trump has never been given an opportunity to sign or veto an immigration bill at the White House.
Instead of passing a standalone bill, Democrats may find it easier to reshape the immigration system through the budget process.
Cuellar’s congressional district in South Texas is home to three ICE detention centers.
In January, he was one of just seven House Democrats to join Republicans in voting for an ICE funding bill.
text:
Representative Henry Cuellar has been in Congress for more than 20 years, representing a South Texas district that includes a big chunk of Texas' border with Mexico. Over the years, he has fended off pressures from both parties: Democrats have tried and failed to replace him with someone more liberal; Republicans have tried and failed to convince him to join the GOP.

Now he's about to start a new term as part of the largest Democratic majority this century. While many of his colleagues want to battle the Trump Administration to rein in ICE, Cuellar sees things differently. He thinks Washington may be on the verge of the perfect conditions to finally fix the country's immigration system for good.

“I told my Republican friends, the last time we had real immigration reform was [when] President Reagan was a Republican, and the House was controlled by Democrats," Cuellar tells TIME. "That's how you get the work done. It's got to be bipartisan.”

Cuellar says discussions are already underway behind the scenes on how to work with the White House to actually pass immigration reform, something Congress has repeatedly tried and failed to accomplish for decades. He points to Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, and Reps. Sylvia Garcia and Rep. Veronica Escobar, both from Texas, as other Democrats who are helping craft language for the measures. “A good number” of congressional Republicans willing to talk seriously about immigration reform are also involved in the discussions, he says.

Cuellar is set to chair the House subcommittee that oversees funding for the Department of Homeland Security. At the top of Cuellar’s wish list: put new guardrails on Immigration and Customs Enforcement, redirect billions of unspent funding allocated to immigration enforcement in the One Big Beautiful Bill, and streamline the visa process for millions of immigrant guest-workers.

Cuellar’s optimism on immigration reform stems in part from how Trump softened his tone on immigration right after the election. During a “60 Minutes” interview, Trump acknowledged that some of the immigration policies pushed by hardline Republicans were “too tough” and that he was open to a pathway to permanent residency for undocumented immigrants who have been staying in the U.S. for more than a decade.

But around the same time, Trump also promoted Stephen Miller as the White House Chief of Staff, elevating the architect of the mass deportation agenda to the most powerful unelected position in Washington.

Any potential immigration deal is further complicated by Cuellar and Trump’s unusual history. In 2025, President Trump pardoned Cuellar and his wife after both were indicted for accepting thousands of dollars from the Azerbaijan government and a Mexican commercial bank. Following his pardon, Cuellar continued to run and won his reelection as a Democrat, which enraged Trump who expected Cuellar to switch parties. Last month, Trump slammed Cuellar in a Truth Social post, calling him “disloyal” and “ungrateful.”

While Cuellar saw signs of hope from Trump’s comments on “60 Minutes,” other Democratic lawmakers and some immigration policy experts were far more skeptical. Trump, after all, is behind the federal government’s most aggressive immigration enforcement operation in decades.

Trump’s comments also drew pushback from his closest allies, who interpreted the President’s comments as amnesty. Vice President JD Vance on Thursday criticized the idea of offering a legal pathway to undocumented immigrants, saying that any effort to “give amnesty to people who have broken our laws” is “morally and electorally disastrous.” But none of those comments dented Cuellar’s excitement.

Jorge Loweree, the managing director of programs at the American Immigration Council, says that Trump has long floated the idea of offering undocumented immigrants a legal pathway to stay in the country, but previous efforts among congressional Republicans during Trump’s first term failed due to the GOP’s internal divisions. Trump has never been given an opportunity to sign or veto an immigration bill at the White House.

“If Congress managed to get it [a legalization bill] through both chambers and send it to the President and call his bluff, it's not clear what he would do,” Loweree says.

Instead of passing a standalone bill, Democrats may find it easier to reshape the immigration system through the budget process. Cuellar is set to chair the House subcommittee that oversees funding for the Department of Homeland Security.

An American Immigration Council analysis estimates that ICE had roughly $91 billion remaining from two Republican reconciliation laws as of October, with another $45.6 billion available to Customs and Border Protection—guaranteeing both agencies the ability to carry out mass deportation operations for years without congressional oversight. Last week, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries reiterated his interest in redirecting ICE funding.

“We believe that taxpayer dollars should actually be spent to make life affordable for the American people, not to brutalize or kill American citizens, or law-abiding immigrants,” Jeffries said during a press conference.

Democrats in both chambers have previously introduced bills either redirecting tens of billions of dollars to fund Medicaid or clawing back the funding altogether. Cuellar suggested that legislators are looking into whether that money could be redirected to other agencies inside DHS that have been impacted by the layoffs implemented by DOGE last year.

“Can it be moved from ICE into other items? You've got FEMA. You've got other agencies that certainly could use more assistance. We are looking at all the legalities as to what is possible and what is not,” he explains.

Cuellar’s congressional district in South Texas is home to three ICE detention centers. He has also examined the conditions inside Dilley, the country’s largest family immigration detention facility, which is in Texas but not in his district, and has drawn a string of accusations of medical neglect.

And he’s been watching how ICE has been buying up properties around the country to drastically expand its network of detention facilities. The agency overpaid by at least 50% for nine of the 11 warehouses that it had intended to convert to detention centers, but is now trying to offload, according to a recent report from the Government Accountability Office. The report also estimated that ICE pays more than $13 million a month for detention beds that sit empty.

All of that is shaping his approach to trying to overhaul ICE, as is a ticking clock. There is likely little time to rein in ICE’s spending on detention centers before the agency signs more contracts with private prison companies. The One Big Beautiful Bill signed by Trump in 2025 granted ICE $45 billion for immigration detention centers and made the funds available through the 2029 fiscal year. The GAO report found that ICE’s current plans indicate that the agency expects to obligate the remaining detention funds by the end of the 2027 fiscal year.

Cuellar has a history of being a staunch supporter of border security. In January, he was one of just seven House Democrats to join Republicans in voting for an ICE funding bill. Among the broader party, support for pairing ICE reform with border security has been gaining more traction among Democrats since the end of the Biden administration. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, the state’s first Democratic governor since 1990, said in a Fox News interview on Thursday that she wants to see the federal government shore up funds for border security.

“Texas has spent $20 billion on border security,” she says. “It is the responsibility of the federal government to keep our borders intact and secure, and Texas taxpayers should not be footing that bill to such an extent.”

text:
A federal court on Monday evening released documents regarding last month's raid at the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.

The majority of the 169 pages of court documents are heavily redacted and consist of exchanges between federal prosecutors and a magistrate judge over probable cause, constitutional privilege, warrant execution and public unsealing.

According to one of the documents, federal government officials applied for a search warrant on Oct. 2 to search Omar's home for "[a]ll records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of." The document then contains redacted text before stating, "those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present."

Federal officials provided two ex parte briefs in support of the warrant to the court before the judge signed it on Oct. 9. According to Cornell Law School, ex parte refers to "communication with a judge or opposing party without the presence or knowledge of the other party's attorney."

Homeland Security Investigations agents executed the warrant on Oct. 12. HSI has jurisdiction over federal offenses including immigration document fraud, identity fraud and immigration benefit fraud.

The court documents, released by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, said federal investigators were authorized to seize documents, records, photos, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers and cellphones "registered or used by" Omar.

Three days before the raid, a judge granted a request to have the warrant sealed, stating that "because of such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation," according to the court documents.

A document filed by the federal government on Oct. 16 said, "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades—beginning long before she was ever in Congress," though the filing did not identify the alleged crimes.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro asked that a judge on Monday not release any of the files because they may be needed in a future trial. WCCO sources have said there are several immigration issues that authorities are investigating.

Criminal defense attorney Joe Tamburino says this case is highly unusual.

"First of all it's unusual because you have a sitting member of Congress, I don't know when that has ever happened, if ever," Tamburino said. "Second, you have a situation where somebody could be in jeopardy of losing their citizenship, and I have never seen that."

WCCO reached out to Omar's office on Monday and has not yet heard back. Her office said in a statement on Oct. 12 that Omar had "done nothing wrong" and called the raid an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

text:
Attorney General Jennifer Davenport today joined 21 other attorneys general and the governor of Pennsylvania in challenging a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule that would strip federal housing assistance from families with mixed immigration status. Under the new rule, any eligible person, including a U.S. citizen, who shares a household with a non-U.S. citizen or ineligible immigrant would be cut off from HUD assistance entirely. The rule would also require all U.S. citizens in federal housing programs to prove their citizenship or risk eviction.

View Complaint

In a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Attorney General Davenport and the coalition argue that the rule illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal law and policy allowing mixed-status families to stay together. They also argue it violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) by exceeding HUD’s authority to enact this arbitrary new restriction.

“This unnecessary and heartless rule will put children on the street,” said Attorney General Davenport. "Families should not have to choose between staying together or keeping a roof over their heads—and Congress did not impose that choice on families. HUD is straying beyond its authority to implement housing programs in the way Congress has directed.”

For nearly 30 years, federal housing programs have provided housing assistance to low-income families even if not every household member is eligible for assistance. If every household member is not eligible for assistance, HUD reduces the family’s subsidy so it covers only the eligible household members. Congress codified this protection in 1997, explicitly stating that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them.

The new HUD rule effectively eliminates this protection. Under the rule, a family can stay in HUD-assisted housing only if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant. As a result, U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants who live with an ineligible relative will be forced to choose between maintaining their housing and keeping their family together.

HUD estimates that around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, will lose their housing assistance. This includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. The agency also acknowledges that the rule will lead to evictions and displacement, and that many of these families could become homeless.

The rule would also make it harder for millions of U.S. citizens to keep the housing they already qualify for. Under the new rule, every U.S. citizen would also need to provide their Social Security number and consent to have their citizenship status checked through the federal SAVE database. If SAVE cannot automatically confirm their citizenship, U.S. citizens would have to produce official documents to prove their status, such as an original or certified birth certificate, naturalization certificate, or passport. Nationwide, an estimated 3.8 million adult U.S. citizens lack a document proving their citizenship, and another 17.5 million face barriers to getting one.

The coalition asserts that the rule will increase homelessness and shift major costs onto state and local governments. By HUD’s own estimates, sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per affected person each year. The rule would also shrink the supply of affordable housing more broadly. HUD acknowledges that losing rental assistance could leave many subsidized units vacant, reduce rental income for housing providers, and drive private landlords out of the Section 8 voucher program, making it even harder for eligible families to find a home.

Attorney General Davenport and the coalition argue that HUD’s new rule exceeds the agency’s authority and violates federal law, which expressly allows prorated assistance for mixed-status families and establishes different documentation requirements for U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants aged 62 and older. They argue that HUD also violated the APA by issuing an arbitrary and capricious rule. The coalition is asking the court to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities.

Joining Attorney General Davenport in filing this lawsuit, which is led by the attorneys general of New York, California, and Massachusetts, are the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania.

text:
Federal immigration law says that a person who has been "granted asylum" and meets certain other criteria, including being "physically present in the United States for at least one year after being granted asylum," may apply to have their status adjusted to that of "an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence." In other words, they may seek to obtain a green card.

But what about those whose asylum status was later terminated? Are they now categorically barred from trying to obtain a green card, even though they were technically "granted asylum" at one point, which is what the law seemingly requires? Should the fact that the law is unclear about whether the termination of asylum also effectively erases the prior granting of asylum now cut in favor of the person or of the executive branch that wants to categorically prohibit all such people from getting green cards?

The Supreme Court will tackle these weighty matters of statutory interpretation later this month when it hears oral arguments in the case of Wassily v. Blanche. In other words, fresh off of their Thanksgiving break, the justices will weigh an immigration-related dispute that could impact the lives of many people now peacefully living in the U.S. who lost their asylum status through no fault of their own.

This case well illustrates how seemingly dry and technical debates over statutory interpretation can have profound real-world consequences. As the National Immigrant Justice Center points out in the amicus brief it filed in the case, when an immigrant receives asylum in the U.S., his or her spouse and/or minor children may also receive what's called "derivative" asylum. But "when a principal's asylum is terminated," the brief points out, "a federal regulation automatically terminates the status of any spouse or child who holds asylum status derivatively."

The principal may have lost asylum status for valid reasons while the spouse or children may not have done anything wrong and would still have an otherwise valid case to make when seeking a green card. Yet as the National Immigrant Justice Center explains, those family members will now face the same categorical ban on seeking a green card if the government wins:

Under the government's reading [of federal immigration law], these family members are barred from even applying for adjustment to [lawful permanent resident] status, no matter the merits of their individual cases. Indeed, under the government's theory, an asylee spouse or child who becomes the victim of domestic violence or abuse risks the automatic loss of her status and mandatory removal proceedings if she reaches out to the police for protection.

A divided three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit sided with the Trump administration when it decided this case last year, holding that "the plain text of 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) allows only noncitizens with current asylum status to adjust to lawful permanent resident status."

Writing in dissent, 2nd Circuit Judge Beth Robinson rejected the majority's confident claim, countering that "the best understanding" of the statute at issue "is that it encompasses 'any' noncitizen 'granted asylum,' regardless of whether the asylum was subsequently terminated."

The 2nd Circuit's ruling is now up for review by the Supreme Court. We'll get our first indications of what the justices are thinking when they hear oral arguments on November 30.

text:
A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

“They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people,” Catala said of the father and daughter. “She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it’s just heartbreaking.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa “in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia’s husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

“When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee,” Catala said.

“It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are,” Catala said. ”There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on.”

“They just lunged forward. They didn’t identify themselves and then sort of hit this family from behind,” John Gaedeke, who was in line waiting to board the flight and filmed part of the confrontation on his cellphone, said of the officers.

Gaedeke said passengers on the jet bridge were screaming or crying “because it was just so emotional, and just to see the pain and anguish and then the speed and violence with which it happened.”

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

[An asylum seeker’s traffic stop, a teenage UAF student’s airport detention: Contested ICE tactics come to Anchorage]

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.

text:
Federal immigration agents are using license plate cameras to identify people for deportation, sometimes during random vehicle checks, according to a Nov. 23 investigation by The Atlantic that documented three shootings involving the technology, two of them fatal. The findings raise new concerns in the District, where police operate dozens of license plate readers that can record the movements of residents who are not suspected of crimes.

“We have a lot of concerns about whether or not there’s a constitutional question that needs to be addressed there,” D.C. police union President Gregg Pemberton said in September.

The Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) reported operating 98 fixed license plate readers and 68 mobile readers as of January, including 71 cameras supplied by Flock Safety. The technology photographs passing vehicles, records their locations, and allows investigators to search for particular license plates.

The Atlantic described a Sept. 20 encounter in Austin, Texas, where ICE officers identified a Toyota Corolla registered to Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan man facing deportation. Officers attempted to stop him, and he drove away, striking an officer with his side mirror. During a subsequent confrontation, an officer shot him in the back. Garcés Pérez survived and faces a federal assault charge.

At a court hearing, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) investigator Rick Bazan testified that officers had been “doing random checks on vehicles and at random places.”

The Atlantic also connected license plate reader use to fatal ICE shootings in Houston and Maine in July.

Peter Mina, a former senior DHS civil rights official, warned that the technology “creates the potential for rampant civil-rights and civil-liberties abuses.”

“I can’t imagine that all of a sudden someone in the chain of command is going to start monitoring and disciplining people, or counseling them, because they are indiscriminately using license-plate readers,” Mina told The Atlantic. “Because they’re probably feeling the same pressure to produce.”

A July 22 investigation by The Washington Informer documented the nationwide reach of the cameras through DeFlock Maps, a public project identifying more than 117,000 readers and 6,424 law enforcement agencies participating in information-sharing networks.

Only about 900 agencies maintained public transparency portals, while roughly 530 disclosed their data-sharing partners.

“We’ve already seen how this mass surveillance tool can be weaponized and abused by law enforcement,” ACLU officials said.

MPD defended the cameras as “vital proactive investigative tools” for recovering stolen vehicles and weapons and locating missing or wanted people.

ICE is testing a mobile application connected to ELITE, a Palantir-developed system that combines immigration files, addresses, vehicle registrations, criminal records and biometric information. Officers can photograph a plate and retrieve a person’s case file, and the system also generates neighborhood maps identifying concentrations of potential immigration targets.

Department of Homeland Security privacy rules prohibit random plate searches and stops based solely on database results. The Atlantic reported that ICE is developing additional restrictions, but they have not been finalized.

Flock Safety denies providing its technology directly to DHS, and the company says local police departments control access to their records, although privacy advocates have documented immigration-related searches through participating agencies.

Public acceptance of such surveillance depends heavily on its purpose. A September National Policing Institute survey found that 54.4% opposed local license plate reader programs. While 88.3% accepted their use to locate missing children, only 26.4% approved of their use for immigration enforcement. Nearly 58% said stronger safeguards would increase their support.

“Our survey finds that not everyone rejects the technology outright, though the public is very clear about the limits of its consent,” institute President Jim Burch said.

text:
☀️Sunny and cooler, with highs in the 40s. Start defrosting your turkey if you haven’t already! Sunset is at 4:15 p.m.

Federal immigration agents have arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants since the PROTECT Act, a state law prohibiting them from doing so, went into effect three weeks ago. Now Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell is suing, saying the federal government is violating the state’s sovereignty.

“These unlawful ICE arrests have also created unnecessary fear, making it less likely that defendants, victims and witnesses will appear when summoned for a criminal case, creating serious public safety concerns,” Campbell said.

Campbell also said ICE agents are using state resources like court schedules and security screenings to target immigrants in local courthouses. She pointed to one case in which Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested a man who was about to stand trial in a domestic violence case. Now, without a defendant to prosecute, the case can’t go to trial. GBH’s Sarah Betancourt has more details on this lawsuit here.

Four Things to Know

1. Warren questions NVIDIA CEO’s return: Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts called the chip maker NVIDIA’s decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang “reckless.” Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman accused of being a spy. Both President Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance reportedly had input on Huang’s reinstatement.

“Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Warren said. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”

2. Thankful for the journey: Today and tomorrow will be the busiest days on the road before Thanksgiving, according to AAA. Slightly fewer people will be on the roads compared with last year. Gas prices are at $3.80 a gallon, lower than they’ve been in recent months but higher than the $3.04 they were this time last year.

“That’s about 200,000 fewer travelers, and that’s really a representation of the high fuel prices people have been paying all year,” said Mark Schieldrop, a spokesperson for AAA Northeast. “But it’s important to note that the total decrease is literally 0.1%, so relatively small in terms of steps back.”

3. Gender affirming care back in Springfield: Baystate Health in Springfield will once again provide gender-affirming care to minors starting Dec. 15. The hospital suspended those services in February after federal officials threatened that continuing to provide gender-affirming care to minors could jeopardize its federal funding. The care includes puberty blockers, hormones and talk therapy.

“They were so quick to take it away, just based on a verbal threat,” said a woman whose transgender son was getting treatment at Baystate before February. “I’m glad they’re opening it back up. I hope that more kids can get care, but I also don’t have a lot of faith in them to keep it going.”

4. Bringing the food pantry to you: The Salem Pantry has a truck that brings fresh produce, meat and prepared foods to people who need them around Salem and Lynn. They make stops at senior housing, community centers and outside doctor’s offices. Here’s a video from GBH’s Emma Jacques that takes you inside the Salem Pantry’s warehouse and on the road with its mobile food pantry truck.

“Some people don’t have a means of transportation. Some people are working at specific hours, and when they have time they just need to rest,” said Ranfy Chavez, the mobile pantry manager. “Having the truck come to them makes it much more convenient.” If you’re on the North Shore, you can find a truck stop near you here. They’ll also deliver food right to your home if you qualify.

From the Curiosity Desk: This day in history

By Edgar B. Herwick III, host of GBH’s Curiosity Desk

History is littered with examples of great works of art, literature and science not being appreciated in their time: “The Wizard of Oz” and “It’s a Wonderful Life” both lost money for their film studios on initial release.

“Moby-Dick” received mixed reviews upon publication. One influential British magazine called it “bedlam literature,” and it sold poorly in Herman Melville’s lifetime.

And I don’t have to tell you what happened to Galileo.

This was by no means the case with “On the Origin of Species” by Charles Darwin. Darwin’s magnum opus was first published on this date, Nov. 24, back in 1859. It was an immediate scientific and commercial blockbuster. Its initial run of 1,250 copies was oversubscribed from pre-orders — essentially already sold-out when it hit the shelves.

The book itself was the culmination of years of travel, study and research by a scientist who, by this time, was well-known and well-respected within the scientific community. And while the work did have its detractors, within a dozen or so years Darwin would release five more editions, and the book had been translated into nearly 40 different languages.

As for its influence, it’s obviously hard to overstate. Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection is the foundational framework of modern life sciences. In a 2009 piece for Scientific American, Ernst Mayr put it this way: “Almost every component in modern man’s belief system is somehow affected by Darwinian principles.”

Fun Fact: The phrase “survival of the fittest” did not appear in Darwin’s first edition. It was coined by English polymath Herbert Spencer as a way to succinctly explain Darwin’s mechanism of natural selection. Darwin would eventually incorporate Spencer’s phrase in later editions.

HARTFORD, CT — Connecticut has joined 21 other states in challenging a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule that would strip federal housing assistance from mixed-status families.

Under the new rule, any household with at least one member who is not a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant would be cut off from HUD assistance entirely, even though federal subsidies are already prorated to only include eligible individuals, according to Attorney General William Tong. The rule would also require all U.S. citizens in federal housing programs to prove their citizenship or risk eviction.

In a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Tong and the coalition argue that the rule illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal policy allowing mixed-status families to stay together and violates the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding HUD’s authority to enact this arbitrary new restriction.

“We have a full-blown housing affordability crisis in this country right now. Trump’s response? Let’s throw entire families on the street if a single person doesn’t have their papers in order,” Tong said. “This is a cruel and unlawful attempt to weaponize housing assistance for vulnerable, mixed-status families. We’re suing to protect Connecticut families and to ensure Trump cannot ignore the law in order to advance his extreme immigration agenda.”

For nearly 30 years, federal housing programs have provided housing assistance to low-income families even if not every household member is eligible for assistance, Tong said. Under this system, known as proration, HUD reduces the family’s subsidy so it covers only the eligible household members. Congress codified this protection in 1997, explicitly stating that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them.

The new HUD rule eliminates this protection. Under the rule, a family can stay in HUD-assisted housing only if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant. As a result, U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants who live with an ineligible relative will be forced to choose between maintaining their housing and keeping their family together, Tong said.

HUD estimates that around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, will lose their housing assistance. This includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. The agency also acknowledges that the rule will lead to evictions and displacement, and that many of these families could become homeless.

The rule would also make it harder for millions of U.S. citizens to keep the housing they already qualify for. Under the new rule, every U.S. citizen would also need to provide their Social Security number and consent to have their citizenship status checked through the federal SAVE database. If SAVE cannot automatically confirm their citizenship, U.S. citizens would have to produce official documents to prove their status, such as an original or certified birth certificate, naturalization certificate, or passport.

Nationwide, an estimated 3.8 million adult U.S. citizens lack a document proving their citizenship, and another 17.5 million face barriers to getting one, Tong said.

The coalition asserts that the rule will increase homelessness and shift major costs onto state and local governments. By HUD’s own estimates, sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per person each year. The rule would also shrink the supply of affordable housing more broadly. HUD acknowledges that losing rental assistance could leave many subsidized units vacant, reduce rental income for housing providers, and drive private landlords out of the Section 8 voucher program, making it even harder for eligible families to find a home.

Tong and the coalition argue that HUD’s new rule exceeds the agency’s authority and violates federal law, which expressly allows prorated assistance for mixed-status families and establishes different documentation requirements for U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants aged 62 and older. They argue that HUD also violated the Administrative Procedure Act by issuing an arbitrary and capricious rule. The coalition is asking the court to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities.

The lawsuit is led by the attorneys general of New York, California, and Massachusetts, and in addition to Connecticut, includes the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Delaware, Hawai’i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania.

Following the now-viral video of an ICE arrest of two travelers at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport over the weekend, the Port of Seattle expressed support for a new proposal to limit when and how ICE agents operate in airports.

The Travel Without Fear Act, sponsored by Democratic senators from Nevada, California, and Illinois, would restrict ICE from using TSA and airline data to carry out civil immigration enforcement and require notification to airports before enforcement operations.

"We join local, state, and federal leaders in calling for an end to domestic ICE enforcement activities at SEA Airport," the Port of Seattle said in a statement Monday. “While the Port operates Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, the security of the airport is subject to federal security regulations. These regulations require federal law enforcement access to airports with federal law enforcement credentials. We are heartened and strongly support federal actions on this issue, including the recently-introduced Travel without Fear Act, led by Senator Rosen."

RELATED | Port of Seattle commissioners call ICE agents 'rogue,' demand airport security review

STATEMENT: Federal Immigration Enforcement at SEA Airport

"Federal staff regularly operate at SEA for immigration enforcement of passenger and cargo flights, and only the Department of Homeland Security can confirm cases or incidents," the statement said. "The Port of Seattle is working with our congressional delegation and others in the state of Washington to explore additional actions or steps to improve information-sharing between jurisdictions and safe and secure travel for those who come through our airport."

Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nevada), a co-sponsor of the Travel Without Fear Act, said ICE enforcement in airports brings chaos and fear to travelers.

"It's clear that ICE needs to be reigned in," Rosen said. "Their actions are instilling fear in entire communities ... I believe that stopping these broad ICE enforcement operations in airports is a place to start."
