title: New Jersey joins lawsuit challenging federal housing rule affecting mixed-status immigrant families
description:
Under the new rule, families receiving federal housing assistance would be required to have every household member qualify as a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant.
Otherwise, the entire household could lose its housing assistance, including benefits for U.S. citizens and other eligible residents.
The rule would also require U.S. citizens participating in federal housing programs to verify their citizenship or risk losing their housing.
Of those affected, approximately 55,000 people are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, including children and older adults.
The lawsuit also challenges new citizenship verification requirements that would apply to U.S. citizens receiving federal housing assistance.
text:
TRENTON, N.J. — New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport has joined a coalition of 22 attorneys general and Pennsylvania’s governor in a federal lawsuit challenging a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule that would eliminate housing assistance for families with mixed immigration status.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, argues that the rule unlawfully reverses nearly 30 years of federal policy allowing eligible individuals to receive housing assistance even when they live with family members who are not eligible.

Under the new rule, families receiving federal housing assistance would be required to have every household member qualify as a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant. Otherwise, the entire household could lose its housing assistance, including benefits for U.S. citizens and other eligible residents.

The rule would also require U.S. citizens participating in federal housing programs to verify their citizenship or risk losing their housing.

“This unnecessary and heartless rule will put children on the street,” said Attorney General Davenport. “Families should not have to choose between staying together or keeping a roof over their heads—and Congress did not impose that choice on families. HUD is straying beyond its authority to implement housing programs in the way Congress has directed.”

For nearly three decades, federal housing programs have allowed mixed-status families to receive prorated assistance, meaning subsidies are calculated based only on household members who qualify for federal benefits.

Congress established that protection in federal law in 1997, specifying that families receiving prorated assistance could not lose their benefits solely because an ineligible family member lived in the household.

According to the lawsuit, the new HUD rule would effectively eliminate that protection, forcing eligible residents to choose between maintaining federal housing assistance and continuing to live with relatives who do not qualify.

HUD estimates that approximately 20,000 mixed-status families, representing 78,100 people, would lose housing assistance under the rule.

Of those affected, approximately 55,000 people are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, including children and older adults.

The agency has also acknowledged that the rule could result in evictions, displacement and homelessness among affected families, according to the Attorney General’s Office.

The lawsuit also challenges new citizenship verification requirements that would apply to U.S. citizens receiving federal housing assistance.

Under the rule, citizens would be required to provide their Social Security numbers and consent to citizenship verification through the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, database.

If the database cannot automatically verify their citizenship, individuals would be required to provide official documentation, such as an original or certified birth certificate, naturalization certificate or passport.

According to the Attorney General’s Office, an estimated 3.8 million adult U.S. citizens nationwide lack documentation proving their citizenship, while another 17.5 million face barriers to obtaining such documents.

The coalition argues that the requirements could place additional burdens on eligible residents and increase the risk of housing instability.

State officials also contend that the rule could impose significant financial costs on state and local governments if displaced families require emergency housing assistance.

According to HUD estimates cited in the lawsuit, providing shelter for individuals displaced by the rule could cost governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per person annually.

The coalition further argues that eliminating rental assistance for affected households could leave subsidized housing units vacant, reduce income for housing providers and discourage private landlords from participating in the federal Section 8 housing voucher program.

The attorneys general allege that HUD exceeded its authority under federal law and violated the Administrative Procedure Act by adopting a rule they contend is arbitrary and capricious.

The lawsuit also argues that the rule conflicts with federal provisions allowing prorated housing assistance for mixed-status families and establishing different documentation requirements for certain eligible residents.

The coalition is asking the federal court to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down and prevent HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the participating states, their local governments and public housing authorities.

The lawsuit is led by the attorneys general of New York, California and Massachusetts.

Joining New Jersey are the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, along with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.

The legal challenge remains pending, and the allegations against HUD have not been resolved by the court.

text:
Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration on Monday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses, arguing that such arrests without judicial warrants are illegal under state law.

The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3.

Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion.

"The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement.

DOJ SUES TO STOP OHIO COURT BLOCKING COURTHOUSE ARRESTS

"ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved," she continued.

The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, including more than 600 people in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026.

Campbell said ICE has ignored the new state law and arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants in the two and a half weeks since the courthouse protections went into effect.

"I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime," Campbell said.

FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS

Campbell said that ICE's courthouse arrests have continued in Massachusetts despite a federal ruling handed down in June by U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in California that vacated the Trump administration's courthouse arrest policy ​in a separate class action lawsuit.

In Monday's lawsuit, Campbell argues the ICE policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act since it was adopted without taking into account the impact it would have on states and because the Immigration and Nationality Act does not explicitly authorize courthouse arrests.

The lawsuit also alleges that the ⁠policy violates the U.S. Constitution's Tenth Amendment, which protects states' rights to maintain authority over their own judicial systems.

"The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe," Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. "We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law."

In a statement to Reuters, a DHS spokesperson argued that making immigration arrests at courthouses "conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already ​know where a target will ​be," adding that "the ability of law enforcement ⁠to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense."

A similar lawsuit against ICE arrests at state courthouses was filed in October by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

text:
Transcript

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

Several federal judges in Colorado have expressed anger with the Trump administration, specifically with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, for failing to comply with court orders to release immigrants from detention. Colorado Public Radio's Allison Sherry has found at least 18 recent cases like this in that state and joins us now. Hi there.

ALLISON SHERRY, BYLINE: Hi.

SUMMERS: Allison, catch us up if you can. What are judges saying there in Colorado?

SHERRY: Well, U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney recently issued a blistering 15-page ruling to top officials at the Department of Homeland Security, holding them in civil contempt of court for not following judicial orders in Colorado. You know, basically, this amounts to a stern legal scolding, but Judge Sweeney said in no uncertain terms that they better start heeding orders or it could get worse for them.

SUMMERS: How did we get here? What brought the judge to the point of issuing a legal rebuke like this one?

SHERRY: Yeah. I mean, federal judges around the country are increasingly seeing thousands more requests from immigration attorneys to get their clients out of detention while their immigration cases move forward. And in Colorado, a handful of judges were ordering people out of detention, and then ICE would turn around, literally a few seconds later, and rearrest them and send them back to detention. And I talked to a man who went through this at the end of October. His name is Carlos Garcia. He's a painter and was held in detention. And a judge ordered him released while he fights his immigration case. Garcia said the release and then the rearrest felt intentional.

CARLOS GARCIA: I asked one of the officers under what circumstance? He said, you guys found a loophole to get out legally. With a smirk on his face, he said, so we found a way to rearrest you guys.

SHERRY: Garcia was among four or five people this happened to on the same day in late October.

SUMMERS: Allison, do you know if this is happening in states other than Colorado?

SHERRY: ICE is doing this across the country, including Louisiana, Pennsylvania and Minnesota. And in Pennsylvania, a judge also held top ICE officials in civil contempt for similar violations.

SUMMERS: And what about ICE? What has been the response to all of this?

SHERRY: Well, for this story, ICE referred me to their parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, and they did not respond to my request. But in federal court in Denver, several judges have hauled top ICE officials to the stand in their courtrooms and put them under oath, where these officials have mostly claimed confusion about all this. One assistant field office director said she hadn't read the judicial orders and was following her boss' instructions, but then her boss took the stand, the acting field office director. He said an ICE official in Minnesota told him it was OK to rearrest immigrants after their release. And some advocates, I will say, don't buy that ICE officials are just confused. This is Tim Macdonald at the Colorado American Civil Liberties Union.

TIM MACDONALD: How high up does this go, and does - is it really credible that it was done without direction from the administration in Washington, D.C.?

SUMMERS: Allison, so the judge held these ICE officials in contempt. Practically, though, what does that mean?

SHERRY: It's a really good question. It's civil contempt, so they won't be arrested for this. But Judge Sweeney basically said that she stopped short of issuing stronger sanctions because these ICE leaders swore under oath they'd stop the practice of rearresting people in Colorado. Now, if she or another judge gets wind that they're violating judicial orders, criminal contempt of court is an option, which can lead to jail time.

SUMMERS: Colorado Public Radio's Allison Sherry. Allison, thank you so much.

SHERRY: You're welcome, Juana.

text:
A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

“They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people,” Catala said of the father and daughter. “She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it’s just heartbreaking.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa “in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia’s husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

“When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee,” Catala said.

“It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are,” Catala said. “There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on.”

“They just lunged forward. They didn’t identify themselves and then sort of hit this family from behind,” John Gaedeke, who was in line waiting to board the flight and filmed part of the confrontation on his cellphone, said of the officers.

Gaedeke said passengers on the jet bridge were screaming or crying “because it was just so emotional, and just to see the pain and anguish and then the speed and violence with which it happened.”

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.

BASILE, La – Today, four people filed a federal lawsuit for rape, sexual abuse, harassment, and forced labor while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at a for-profit detention center run by the GEO Group, Inc. in Basile, Louisiana. Defendants include the GEO Group and two former GEO employees at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center (SLIPC): then-assistant warden Emmanuel Reyes and former detention officer David Courvelle.

The plaintiffs, Luis Renteria-Gonzalez, Mario Garcia-Valenzuela, Kenia Campos-Flores, and Jane Doe*, claim the for-profit group and its employees targeted primarily transgender and nonbinary immigrants at SLIPC. Among other abuses, the lawsuit cites instances of rape, groping, voyeurism, physical abuse, denial of medical care, and retaliatory solitary confinement.

The lawsuit states that Renteria-Gonzales, Garcia-Valenzuela, Campos-Flores and Doe were detained at SLIPC between 2023 and 2025 and repeatedly abused by Reyes and other GEO employees. Using his position of authority as assistant warden, Reyes coerced plaintiffs to perform hard physical labor, sex acts, or both, threatening them with death, deportation, further sexual abuse, physical harm, and harm to their families and loved ones. Plaintiffs were also denied basic necessities, life-sustaining medical care, and placed in solitary confinement in retaliation for filing complaints against these abuses.

“The treatment and the conditions that they had us living in, nobody should go through that,” said Renteria-Gonzales. “It’s unbelievable that this happened under the care of the people who are supposed to protect us.”

Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela, who are transgender men, and Campos-Flores, who is nonbinary, were targeted by Reyes for an off-the-books “work program” of predominantly LGBTQ+ individuals. Assigned hard manual labor without proper protective equipment, they were forced to work through the night. At one point, while stripping floors, the harsh chemicals dissolved the fabric on Luis’ shoes and burned his feet. The lawsuit also details sexual harassment and abuse from Reyes and other SLIPC officers.

Doe was detained in November 2023. In the complaint, she stated that after she turned down Reyes’ offer to join his night “cleaning crew,” he began stalking and harassing her with aggressive, inappropriate sexual comments. Within months, he escalated his attacks, cornering Jane and forcibly groping her. From February to May 2024, Reyes regularly forced Jane to perform oral sex on him, threatening her life and her family if she refused.

The abuse didn’t end with Reyes. In 2025, GEO detention officer David Courvelle sexually assaulted Garcia-Valenzuela three times and forced Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela Luis and Mario to stand guard outside a closet while he raped a woman detained at SLIPC. Courvelle later pleaded guilty to sexual abuse of a ward and was sentenced in June to three years in federal prison.

The plaintiffs reported this abuse through Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA) complaints, grievances, the Department of Homeland Security inspector general’s hotline, and interviews with ICE officials and the FBI. Reyes left SLIPC of his own accord in July 2024.

“Enough is enough,” said Garcia-Valenzuela. “This is America. We’re supposed to have a voice, to be able to speak out. I’m sharing my story so that other people can have the courage to speak up about what happens in these detention centers.”

The lawsuit, filed by the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, National Immigration Project, National Immigrant Justice Center, ACLU of Louisiana, and Southern Poverty Law Center under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA) and Louisiana state law in the Western District of Louisiana, follows prior complaints in September 2025.

“Despite these failures long and thoroughly documented by detained people, non-governmental organizations, and ICE itself, GEO has continued to operate SLIPC without taking steps to meaningfully address mistreatment or otherwise improve conditions of detention,” said the representing organizations in a joint statement. . “It was under these conditions of lax oversight that Defendants Reyes and Courvelle were allowed to wage abuse against plaintiffs.”

*Jane Doe is proceeding under a pseudonym.

Trying to protect your wife and they're taking your father-in-law," Castillo told CBS News in an interview Monday.
DHS has said Hernandez Mejia "will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."
Hernandez Mejia and her father remain in ICE custody in Tacoma, Washington, according to their attorney.
Last week, video captured ICE agents pushing a pregnant woman and U.S. citizen to the ground in Modesto, California.
Hernandez Mejia, Catala said, applied for a green card as the spouse of a U.S. citizen.
text:
The husband of a woman whose arrest by immigration agents inside a jetway at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport gained national attention says he felt "useless" when seeing his wife and father-in-law be taken into federal custody, calling the episode "unjust."

Jose Castillo, an American citizen, teared up when recounting the moment on Saturday when masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detained his wife, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, and his father-in-law, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza.

"You black out. You don't even know what's going on. You don't even know what's happening. Everything is moving so fast. Trying to protect your wife and they're taking your father-in-law," Castillo told CBS News in an interview Monday. "As a U.S. citizen, you feel useless."

Castillo said he felt "disgusted."

"How can you sit with yourself and strip somebody away like that in broad daylight, in front of families?" Castillo added.

The arrest was captured on videos that have gone viral. Hernandez Mejia is heard wailing and saying she has a valid work permit, while bystanders demand answers from the federal agents.

Department of Homeland Security officials identified Hernandez Mejia and Larrondo Mendoza as Mexican nationals living in the U.S. illegally after overstaying their visas. The agency said ICE officers were targeting Larrondo Mendoza for arrest when "other passengers began obstructing federal officers."

DHS accused Hernandez Mejia of assaulting agents, alleging she threw hot coffee on them. Castillo pushed back on the allegations.

"There was no assault on her end," Castillo said. "She did nothing. She was being shoved. They came directly at us."

"When you're coming at me and my wife and you're shoving us, obviously coffee's going to be spilled," he added.

DHS has said Hernandez Mejia "will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."

Castillo said he was traveling with his wife and father-in-law to a family event when they were approached by ICE agents in plainclothes on the jetway to an Alaska Airlines flight. The flight was delayed by over two hours, and the flight crew had to be replaced, the airline said.

Officials at Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, said they were not given prior notice of the ICE operation. The Port of Seattle said it was "outraged."

Hernandez Mejia and her father remain in ICE custody in Tacoma, Washington, according to their attorney. Castillo pleaded for their release.

"They don't deserve to be in there," he said. "It was done in such an unjust manner."

The incident is the latest in a string of ICE operations that have gone awry in recent weeks, even after President Trump acknowledged to 60 Minutes that his crackdown on illegal immigration may have been "too tough."

Last week, video captured ICE agents pushing a pregnant woman and U.S. citizen to the ground in Modesto, California. ICE accused her of interfering with the arrest of a man with a criminal record. In Texas, an ICE agent is facing criminal charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly striking a Mexican immigrant with an unmarked SUV. His attorney has called the incident an "accident."

The detention at Sea-Tac airport is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to send ICE officers to major airports across the country to arrest travelers who are in the U.S. illegally or with a tenuous legal status. Those arrested have included travelers with pending legal immigration applications but whose underlying permission to be in the U.S. expired.

Olia Catala, who is representing the father and daughter detained at Sea-Tac, said her clients entered the U.S. as tourists and that both have pending immigration applications. Hernandez Mejia, Catala said, applied for a green card as the spouse of a U.S. citizen.

She said the family was trying to follow the immigration process prior to being arrested.

"Congress created legal pathways and Sofia and her father were using them," Catala said. "We can't tell immigrants to use the legal pathways, to follow the law and then punish them for doing just that."

title: Two U.S. citizens released from ICE detention, Rep. Simon says as she vows to investigate
authors: Chase Hunter, Harry Harris, Sam Mulick
description:
“There is no reason for federal agents to throw community members to the ground, wreak havoc on the streets, and use tear gas unprovoked.
Beginning Sunday morning, federal immigration agents began conducting an operation near 87th Avenue and E Street.
Two other residents were also shoved to the ground by federal immigration agents, she said.
Lee said the East Bay was witnessing a “disturbing and unacceptable” surge in aggressive ICE operation.
“I am heartened that we have helped secure the release of both U.S. citizens, including a minor, who were unjustly detained by ICE,” Simon said.
text:
After federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested two U.S. citizens, including a minor, from East Oakland over the weekend and sent at least two women to the hospital, Oakland Rep. Lateefah Simon’s office said she and other East Bay officials had secured the citizens’ release.

Simon, in a statement, said ICE had unjustly detained the two U.S. citizens and reiterated that federal immigration agents would not be welcomed in the East Bay, adding that she is demanding more accountability from the Trump administration and the Department of Homeland Security regarding enforcement tactics.

“There is no reason for federal agents to throw community members to the ground, wreak havoc on the streets, and use tear gas unprovoked. It’s simply not right, and I will continue working to end this Administration’s terror campaign against immigrant communities,” Simon said in a statement.

Beginning Sunday morning, federal immigration agents began conducting an operation near 87th Avenue and E Street. Agents patrolled the streets, deploying flash-bang grenades and tear gas that spread through the residential neighborhood, according to witnesses and numerous videos posted to social media. One of the videos showed an ICE agent in a gas mask knocking a woman to the ground and another officer picking her up and tossing her aside.

Agents tackled a 17-year-old boy and detained him in one of their vehicles, according to East Oakland resident Celia Davis, 64, who exited her home around 1 p.m. to see the scene. She began recording video with her cell phone when one agent sprayed her with mace multiple times before another violently shoved her to the ground, she said. Two other residents were also shoved to the ground by federal immigration agents, she said.

“I was maced so much that I couldn’t open my eyes, it hurt so badly,” Davis said.

Davis was taken to the hospital in an ambulance where she said she had a CT scan that came back negative, though she continued to have severe eye and skin irritation. She said what happened to her and other observers “was totally uncalled for, they were attacking people who were just observing.”

Davis said what happened to her will not deter her from being involved if she hears of similar ICE activity.

“I am a firm believer in supporting people in my community and my neighbors who are just living their lives,” she said. “I will go right out and observe and record their activities.”

Hospital officials did not immediately return a phone call asking for the condition of the other woman.

The two detainees were taken by federal agents to an ICE detention center in downtown San Francisco before being released later that evening at approximately 8:30 p.m. because they were both citizens. Their names have not been released.

Oakland is a sanctuary city, and its agencies do not assist ICE officials, Mayor Barbara Lee reiterated in a news release Monday.

“ICE is not wanted in Oakland, the Oakland Police Department does not cooperate with ICE, and I am profoundly grateful to our residents for standing together to protect their neighbors,” Lee said. “Instead of respecting their First Amendment rights, federal agents escalated the situation, deploying what witnesses described as smoke bombs and chemical sprays, violently pushing observers to the ground, and arresting two U.S. citizens. Stay vigilant, and report any ICE activity or information to the ACILEP hotline at 510-241-4011.”

The Alameda County Immigration Legal and Education Partnership, a nonprofit partnered with Alameda County, is reviewing footage of the immigration operation in East Oakland and is in contact with families to ensure they are connected with legal support.

Lee said the East Bay was witnessing a “disturbing and unacceptable” surge in aggressive ICE operation. Simon echoed that sentiment saying federal agents had no reason to “wreak havoc” in Oakland by throwing community members to the ground and using tear gas without provocation.

“I am heartened that we have helped secure the release of both U.S. citizens, including a minor, who were unjustly detained by ICE,” Simon said. “My office will continue working around the clock to support the families impacted.”

Bay Area News Group asked ICE and the Department of Homeland Security about their immigration operation in East Oakland and why they did not determine the citizenship stats of two U.S. citizens before they were detained. Neither agency replied as of Monday afternoon.

description:

text:
More than 100 people showed up to a rally Monday in support of a Princeton University doctoral student currently being held in custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Eva Yi Xie is being held at the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia, about 90 miles south of Washington, D.C. She had been waiting for a flight back to New Jersey at Reagan National Airport, after attending a conference, when federal immigration officers took her into custody.

Members of the university’s community, who gathered on campus near the Princeton School of Public and International Affairs, remain shocked and in disbelief that Xie would be arrested in the first place.

“I can still almost cry every time I think about it,” said Carlos Brody, a neuroscience professor at Princeton and one of Xie’s academic advisors. He described her as “the gentlest, kindest, most generous person that you can imagine.”

“[She] is just brilliant and hell bent on contributing her brilliance to our community and our country.”

Others who spoke at the rally shared the same sentiment about Xie, including Adrian Bondy, an associate research scholar, who described her as “a whirlwind in the lab.”

“We always say you can’t keep up with her,” Bondy said. “You give her a task and she does three times as much in half the amount of time you thought.”

The rally was organized by several members of the Princeton Progressive Coalition after they learned of Xie’s detainment through the campus newspaper. In addition to the rally, organizers put together a phone bank to urge supporters to contact their federal representatives on Xie’s behalf.

“We liaised with her colleagues and peers in the Princeton Neuroscience Institute who have been talking with her lawyers,” said Isaac Barsoum, one of the organizers. “We’re hopeful that all of our community organizing, bringing people out, getting them to call their senators and representatives, getting them to call the people who can help get Eva out will eventually make a difference in her case.”

Xie is waiting for a response from the government to the habeus corpus petition filed on her behalf by Kerry Doyle, the lawyer the university arranged to represent Xie. Doyle expects a bond hearing before an immigration judge. Xie was born in China and came to this country on a visa.

“We still filed the habeus petition because we are arguing that her arrest and detention are illegal at its core,” Doyle said.

Senior U.S. District Judge Anthony J. Trenga gave immigration officials until 5 p.m. Wednesday to present “factual and legal issues” in relation to the petition filed by Xie. Trenga also ordered that Xie be kept within the Eastern District of Virginia, the court’s jurisdiction.

Immigration officials and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond to emails from WHYY News seeking comment.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told the Daily Princetonian, the university’s campus newspaper, that Xie was “admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, but chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016.”

Doyle confirmed that Xie came to the country with her family on a temporary visa, but she is learning the details. Xie and her parents have a pending asylum application that is scheduled to be heard in January 2028.

Xie is the first known Princeton student to be detained by ICE. Her detention has added to the concerns of international students at the Ivy League institution who live in fear due to the current immigration crackdown by the Trump administration.

Narges Anzali, another student organizer, read a statement during the rally from a group of international students who wished to remain anonymous. Relaying their concerns, Anzali shared that many of the students are from countries who are on the Trump administration’s banned travel list.

“An international student in our community who could not go home to her own father’s funeral because she cannot be sure of getting a visa for her reentry because she’s from one of the countries that is mentioned in the current travel ban,” Anzali said.

Annabelle Luo, who also assisted in organizing the rally, said many international students expressed their fear to her that if they appear at a rally, like the one calling for the release of Xie, they would be targeted by the administration.

“I have friends where they also are scared about the status of their abilities to continue their education here and see their families and just be able to stay in this country for many different reasons,” Luo said.

Xie’s colleagues at her lab are encouraged by the outpouring of support, including from state Sen. Andrew Zwicker, who also works for the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and spoke at the rally.

“When I sent a student to a conference … I never worried that they wouldn’t come home,” Zwicker said.

Brody said the rally’s turnout is a testament to the fact that Xie “is such a wonderful member of our community.”

“I knew that she was great, but I didn’t know until I met all these people and heard all the stories that they say about her,” he said.

Bondy was equally encouraged by the crowd. He said he has been in contact with colleagues online over the weekend. Many of them saw each other in person Monday. They will have their weekly lab meeting on Tuesday. But, Bondy said, he doesn’t think they’ll be talking about science much at that time.

“I think we’ll just be processing and trying to support each other,” he said.

text:
Standing outside the federal building downtown, some of San Diego’s representatives in the House on Monday outlined their priorities on immigration when Democrats retake control of Congress in January. At the same time inside, an immigration judge ordered two children, ages 9 and 15, deported back to Guatemala.

“On Nov. 3rd, voters sent the president and they sent the nation a message: They reject President Trump and Republicans’ reckless, anti-American agenda,” said Rep. Scott Peters. “It wasn’t just about cost. It’s about the way we’re treating people.”

Top of mind was the Nov. 4 detention of an 8-year-old Haitian boy at an ICE check-in. Video of three agents leading the boy, a third grader at Fay Elementary School in City Heights, into an elevator sparked outrage and protest.

“We don’t want murderers and rapists running around. Absolutely not,” Rep. Juan Vargas said Monday. “We want them, of course, not to be in our society. I completely agree with that. That’s not who he’s going after. He’s going after a little boy, an 8-year-old boy.”

That child, who previously had Temporary Protected Status, was taken to a federal facility in Texas but has since been released to his family.

“He held me tight, so tight I had to tell him to loosen up,” said Guerline Jozef, of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, which advocated for his return. “And he said, ’Thank you, but I’m afraid. I’m afraid of what could happen again. Will they take me again?’”

Peters, Vargas and Rep.-elect Marni von Wilpert said one of their priorities in the new Congress is to pass the American Dream and Promise Act, offering legal pathways to TPS holders and DACA recipients.

They also want to bar immigration arrests within 1,000 feet of so-called sensitive locations like schools, churches and hospitals, except in the case of an emergency.

“As this administration exploits the places we trust the most and turns them into hunting grounds, protecting our schools has to be a priority,” Peters said.

“We demand safe passage for students, families and educators,” said Monique Barrett, president of the San Diego Education Association. “Advance comprehensive immigration reform. Protect due process. Prevent family separation. Use your oversight authority.”

The members of Congress said they also wanted to investigate conditions at detention centers, and institute stricter background checks and vetting for ICE agents, as well as limiting their use of force.

“ICE’s actions in our community are not law enforcement. They are chaos and violence, and they need to stop,” von Wilpert said. “Parents are afraid to take their children to school. Families are afraid to go to the doctor. Children are afraid their parents won’t come home from work. That is not public safety. And our communities deserve better.”

They also floated the possibility of clawing back billions of dollars already allocated to the Department of Homeland Security that haven’t yet been spent.

“Republicans in the Big Beautiful Bill funded ICE and Border Patrol to a level higher than the United States Marines. They got more money than the Israeli military,” Peters said. “Those dollars and those resources were turned back on our own communities. And that’s wrong. We’ve got to put an end to it.”

As they spoke, a father and his two children walked out of the federal building alongside volunteer court observers. They said an immigration judge had just ordered the children, a 9-year-old boy and a 15-year-old girl, deported back to Guatemala.

“They tried to express to the judge the problems that they felt that they had, the fear that they had, but the judge did not feel that was sufficient enough for the asylum request to be approved,” said FAITH volunteer Belinda Mayes.

“Clearly they were, in talking to the children afterwards, extremely disappointed. Very nervous, very anxious,” Mayes continued. “The father, basically at a loss not knowing what to do, because we’re only talking about an order against the children so it’s basically their future and what they’re going to be facing alone.”

Speaking in Spanish, the teenager, a freshman at a San Diego high school, said her family feared threats of violence against them in Guatemala, calling the process inside immigration court “ugly.”

The family said the judge gave them 30 days to appeal the decision, opening the window for their deportation on Dec. 23.

“They want to deport them two days before Christmas, one day before Christmas Eve,” Vargas said after speaking with the family. “Can you imagine that? How ridiculous is that? ’Merry Christmas kids, we’re deporting you.’”

name: Human Rights
title: Guantánamo Bay 2.0? The rise of legal violence inside US detention centers
description:
Detainees’ testimonies of violent punishments by ICE agents are all too reminiscent of the experiences of Guantánamo Bay prisoners.
There has been very little pressure from legislators or the courts to dissuade the government from using legal violence—a direct failure of the very systems that allowed this kind of violence to become legal in the first place.
This violence was carried out in one of the largest detention centers in the country, located at the Fort Bliss military base in Texas.
Ending legal violence Like many who were imprisoned in Guantánamo Bay, most of the migrants in detention today have not been convicted of any crime.
If these steps are not taken, the use of legal violence and the policies of impunity that underpin them will only grow.
text:
The United States government has a long history of dehumanizing foreigners both inside and outside its borders. The treatment of prisoners in Guantánamo Bay and of migrants currently detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) provide just two recent examples of the extensive use of criminalizing language to justify targeting these groups. The George W. Bush administration routinely labeled those incarcerated in Guantánamo Bay as “terrorists” and associated them with the September 11 attacks, often without direct evidence. Today, the Donald J. Trump administration labels migrants as “animals”, “criminals”, and “rapists”. This type of dehumanizing language suggests that detainees do not deserve legal rights, and it leads to the broad erosion of the civil protections that shield people—whether or not they are US citizens—from arrest without charge and trial or harsh and unusual punishment.

The state’s curtailment of due process and other civil rights in these cases has led to a rise in legal violence: harm inflicted by a government body while enforcing state policy. Many held in Guantánamo Bay have claimed that members of the United States military physically and mentally assaulted them during their detention. Similar abuse is still taking place today against migrants in ICE detention centers. Detainees’ testimonies of violent punishments by ICE agents are all too reminiscent of the experiences of Guantánamo Bay prisoners.

The US government and military have not taken the lessons of the War on Terror to heart, and the United States is still using violence against people it detains. There has been very little pressure from legislators or the courts to dissuade the government from using legal violence—a direct failure of the very systems that allowed this kind of violence to become legal in the first place.

Mass incarceration and violence toward migrants

Since Trump took office as president of the United States for the second time, his administration has pushed ICE to detain anyone deemed to be residing in the country illegally. This has led to the mass incarceration of Latinos and other migrants all over the nation. According to The Guardian, a total of 68,400 individuals were held in detention as of December 2025. The majority of detainees have no previous criminal record. A recent Human Rights Watch report documented dozens of executive orders rolling back migrants’ right to due process, guaranteed by the Fifth Amendment, and limiting their ability to seek legal redress while detained.

These new executive orders have systematically allowed the state to punish those detained prior to legal due process or the filing of charges. The result is legal violence inflicted against migrants detained in defiance of their constitutional rights. For example, officers are now legally allowed to interrogate suspected illegal migrants using violence and make arrests without warrants.

The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) has done very little to limit the powers granted to ICE. In fact, some recent SCOTUS rulings have expanded ICE’s powers. In September 2025, SCOTUS eliminated restrictions on ICE’s use of racial profiling when making arrests. In the case of Noem v. Vasquez-Perdomo SCOTUS ruled that ICE could conduct raids in public places opening the door to using race, ethnicity, and language to determine their targets. This is unambiguously racial profiling and encourages violence toward especially Latinos regardless of their immigration status.

Several reports documenting migrant accounts of violence committed by detention officers and ICE have been released since Trump’s executive orders and SCOTUS’s legal decisions on immigration enforcement. One of many migrants who spoke with the ACLU reported that detention officers had beaten him, breaking his tooth and damaging his ear to the point that he began to lose hearing. This violence was carried out in one of the largest detention centers in the country, located at the Fort Bliss military base in Texas.

One man in a Florida detention center, speaking to Human Rights Watch, recalled officers turning up the air conditioning to intentionally freezing levels in the cells. Several people in the same location are also being denied life-saving medications needed to treat chronic illnesses.

Are detention centers the new Guantánamo Bay?

Guantánamo Bay was established in 2002 to detain individuals believed to be linked with the perpetrators of the September 11 attacks. The Center for Constitutional Rights has outlined the violent experiences of prisoners detained at Guantánamo Bay, which included practices like those used today in ICE detention centers.

The Bush administration authorized the use of violent practices in Guantánamo Bay by declaring that those imprisoned there were “unlawful enemy combatants” and thus ineligible for the protections of the Geneva Conventions. By eliminating application of the Geneva Conventions, the Bush administration removed a major barrier imposed by international law to prevent the torture of prisoners. More recently, the Trump administration has similarly rejected the Geneva Conventions by cutting funding for the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and condemning their operations.

The Center for Constitutional Rights has shared the experience of Abu Zubaydah, who was subjected to waterboarding, sleep deprivation, stress positions, and confinement inside a coffin-sized box. Ahmed al-Darbi similarly reported that officers played painfully loud music for several hours and chilled his cell to extremely cold temperatures until he confessed to the crime he was accused of. The government framed these practices as interrogation, but it’s clear that they constitute torture.

Many of the prisoners in Guantánamo Bay were never formally charged with any crime. Instead, they were imprisoned indefinitely and subjected to intense and violent interrogation tactics in hopes of eliciting confessions. These abusive practices were justified by a Military Order that allowed prisoners suspected of terrorism to be held outside US jurisdiction. This was an intentional move to limit the court’s reach and provide for increased use of force against those held in Guantánamo Bay and impunity for the officers who carried it out.

Ending legal violence

Like many who were imprisoned in Guantánamo Bay, most of the migrants in detention today have not been convicted of any crime. Legal violence does not change; only its target does.

To prevent the continuation of legal violence, we must challenge the system. The executive and military orders that allowed violence and mistreatment of prisoners in Guantánamo Bay laid the foundation for the laws currently supporting ICE’s violent and indiscriminate campaign of immigration enforcement. The United States Constitution already prohibits abuse inside penitentiaries and detention centers. Cruel and unusual punishments are strictly prohibited.

The courts must consistently apply the protections provided by the United States Constitution, and they must disempower ICE. This includes protecting due process rights for migrants, firing officers who act with racial bias, eliminating officers’ rights to interrogate detainees using violence, and investigating each facility where abuse has been reported. If these steps are not taken, the use of legal violence and the policies of impunity that underpin them will only grow.

name: Human Rights
title: The Way Forward After Mass Deportation | Connecting California - Zócalo Public Square
description:
To clean up the disaster of mass deportation, the United States will eventually need more than an amnesty.
Many of those removed were legal immigrants who followed the rules and obtained visas or work authorization—and got kicked out anyway.
The 1986 amnesty law championed by President Reagan legalized nearly 3 million people—and, eventually, many of their family members.
Given the U.S. immigration and federal court systems’ complicity in the deportation campaigns, such prosecutions might have to take place overseas.
We cannot move forward while millions of our neighbors have not been compensated for harm from the deportation campaign.
text:
To clean up the disaster of mass deportation, the United States will eventually need more than an amnesty.

It will need two amnesties. One for the millions of victims of the cruel, violent, and flagrantly unlawful deportation campaign tearing through American communities. And another for those who took part in making the deportations happen.

The Trump administration is deporting people without due process, including to faraway continents and unfamiliar countries. Many of those removed were legal immigrants who followed the rules and obtained visas or work authorization—and got kicked out anyway. Families have been shattered, human rights cancelled, local economies damaged, and whole segments of society forced into hiding.

When this nightmare finally ends, California and the United States will face a monumental challenge: How do we reunite families, uncover the full scale of what was done in our name, compensate victims, restore the rule of law, and hold official perpetrators accountable?

The solution is what I am calling the Double Amnesty.

The first amnesty is straightforward: a comprehensive, unencumbered program granting permanent residency, and creating a speedy process for obtaining citizenship for everyone caught in the U.S. regime’s anti-immigrant pogrom.

This first amnesty starts with allowing readmission for deported people, with priority going to immigrants the Trump administration sent to third-party countries. Restitution must apply universally—to undocumented immigrants, long-term legal residents, migrants with temporary status, and U.S. citizens mistaken for migrants. The amnesty must also cover citizens and residents who were punished or injured for defending their neighbors against deportation. They are heroes, not criminals.

This is the only practical way to return millions of human beings to the light, stabilize our economy, and shrink the unauthorized population. The 1986 amnesty law championed by President Reagan legalized nearly 3 million people—and, eventually, many of their family members.

It also reduced unauthorized immigration to the country. Immigration restrictionists claim that relentless enforcement deters unauthorized presence. In reality, the opposite is true. When people are arrested in immigration courts or naturalization appointments, the message is: Stay undocumented, stay in the shadows.

The current administration has manufactured more undocumented immigration, not reduced it. By stripping legal status en masse—revoking Temporary Protected Status (TPS), ending protection for Dreamers, rescinding humanitarian parole, and ripping away valid visas—the government deliberately and illegally created more than 1 million so-called “illegal” immigrants.

Which brings me to the second amnesty of the Double Amnesty—in which the U.S. would offer administrative and legal relief to the government employees, ICE agents, CBP officers, and bureaucrats who participated in executing this campaign. This amnesty may be harder to swallow. Many of us would prefer to prosecute law enforcement officials who broke the law and hurt immigrants, but the scale of the lawless deportation campaign makes mass prosecutions impractical.

But the second amnesty does not offer forgiveness automatically. This amnesty must be strictly contingent on first establishing personal and institutional accountability, and on exposing violations.

The Trump deportation machine operates in the dark, with masked law enforcement personnel, secret deportations to third countries, concealed detainee facilities, and undisclosed transfers of migrants between centers and prisons to keep them from being found by families and lawyers.

As a result, deportations have been executed with staggering incompetence, shielded by bureaucratic deception, and deliberately hidden from federal courts, defense lawyers, and the public. We still do not know the true number of missing children, falsified records, or unconstitutional orders carried out in field offices across the country.

To earn this second amnesty, agents and officials must go through a process of mandatory truth-telling. They must step forward and disclose every secret directive and unwritten quota, every illegal detention and unconstitutional maneuver, and every document or record withheld from courts, defense counsel, and the public.

In addition, the top executives of private companies that knew of the immigration abuses and personally profited must report their activities—and forfeit every dollar they made, for their business and personally—to a restitution fund for the campaign’s victims.

Once perpetrators provide full, verifiable documentation of their actions, they should receive immunity. If they lie, destroy evidence, or refuse to disclose, they must face full criminal prosecution.

There is one non-negotiable exception to the amnesty:

No mercy at the top.

You Might Also Like

Architects of the deportation campaign do not get a deal. No matter how much they disclose, no matter how many documents they hand over, there can be zero amnesty for the president, for Stephen Miller, or for senior political and law enforcement leaders who designed, ordered, and directed this campaign.

Given the U.S. immigration and federal court systems’ complicity in the deportation campaigns, such prosecutions might have to take place overseas. Since the U.S. is likely to block using the International Criminal Court (which the U.S. has sought to dismantle), accountability may require holding trials in foreign courts.

Under the principle of universal jurisdiction, Germany, Spain, France, and Argentina allow their national courts to prosecute non-citizens for grave crimes committed anywhere in the world. An international tribunal might be formed by multiple countries, with Canada as the natural host, because of its strong legal system and proximity to the U.S. This is not a new idea. International tribunals have long been held outside the ICC system, from Nuremberg and the Tokyo trial after World War II to more recent tribunals examining systematic rights violations in Sierra Leone, Rwanda, Cambodia, and the former Yugoslavia.

The Double Amnesty would offer a moral and practical way forward for a broken country. It would repair the lives of millions of victims targeted by state terror, while forcing the American deportation apparatus to document its own abuses in service of accountability.

We cannot move forward while millions of our neighbors have not been compensated for harm from the deportation campaign. And we cannot fix what remains hidden. A Double Amnesty won’t be a surrender or a compromise—it is a realistic blueprint for exposing the truth, restoring the rule of law, and preventing such evils from being repeated.

Joe Mathews writes the Connecting California column for Zócalo Public Square and is founder-columnist of Democracy Local, a planetary publication. He is working on a book, One Law to Save the World, for the University of California Press.

text:
The government has been accused of a "dereliction of its duty to protect citizens" by allowing a planned asylum centre.

The shadow minister for women and equalities, Joy Morrisey, said Labour had ignored warnings raised by residents and police when it granted permission for the redevelopment of part of MoD Bicester in Oxfordshire.

She was speaking at the launch of a think tank report called Mass Immigration is a Women's Issue, attended by women from Piddington, a village near the military site.

The Home Office said other large sites had been operating for a number of years with no rising crime. The Refugee Council said "there is no evidence refugees commit crimes...more than any other groups".

But the report's author, human rights and equality barrister Dr Anna Loutfi, said the government has not disclosed data on how crime rates change when large-scale male encampments are created.

That is backed by a University of Oxford Migration Observatory report from August 2026 that said there is no published data on convicted offenders' immigration status, such as whether they are an asylum seeker, refugee, work migrant or international student.

Some villagers in Piddington - home to 350 people, including 133 women - have said they will be living in fear if 1,256 male asylum seekers are housed nearby.

Planning permission for the MoD Bicester site was approved by the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner earlier this month after the Home Office used a fast-track route for projects deemed to be urgently needed and of national importance.

It said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.

Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site, which has also been legally challenged by campaigners.

A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against and one in support.

Loutfi said the concerns they were raising were common sense: "Even if this was a group of football fans it would be of concern.

"But these men often come from countries where there are culturally incompatible ways of viewing women, they're viewed as available if they are unaccompanied or dressed a certain way or drinking alcohol.

"Most of the men are single, young, excitable with nothing to do all day, it doesn't take a rocket scientist to see putting a large number of them into a population of a lot less women will be trouble."

Essex Police covers the area around MDP Wethersfield which has been used to house 800 single male migrants since 2023.

The Chief Constable of the force said in September that crime linked to the site is "very low" with 15 offences since it opened in which a member of the public was the victim and the suspect was identified as, or alleged to be, a Wethersfield "service user".

Imran Hussain, Director of External Affairs at the Refugee Council, said: "Violence against women and girls is a problem across society that needs to be addressed to ensure that people feel safe in their homes and communities.

"But public debate and narratives must reflect the fact that there is no evidence refugees commit crimes towards women and girls more than any other groups."

The Women's Policy Centre, that commissioned Loufi's report, is an independent think tank. It invited MPs from all political parties to the launch of the report and said the issue of mass immigration and women's safety is a cross party issue.

Sandra Innes, a Piddington resident of 23 years, said she felt the government was being "hugely naive" in stating that the chance of crime was negligible.

She said women in the village were "living on the edge" and said their huge frustration was the lack of communication from ministers.

"Why isn't someone coming to us engaging and talking about how they will safeguard us?" she added.

The Home Office has said it is working closely with local authorities, police, health partners and community representatives to ensure any impact is carefully managed and local concerns are addressed.

In the conditions of planning permission, it said the site would be closely managed through 24-hour staffing, controlled access, CCTV and security patrols which would "reduce" the risk.

In August, the government created a nine-page booklet for asylum seekers explaining rape, sexual harassment and domestic abuse are illegal in the UK and giving guidance on how UK laws and customs may be different from their home countries.

Reform's Fareham and Waterlooville MP Suella Braverman attended the meeting.

She is the party's spokesperson on equalities and said she was concerned to see campaigners in Piddington accused of racism on social media for voicing concerns about the development.

"It is not racist to want to keep women and girls safe. Just recently we have seen an Iranian migrant arrested in Crowborough (another former military site being used to house migrants).

"That is coming to Piddington unless the government changes course and listens to the women," she added.

text:
(CN) — A coalition of states led by California and New York sued the Trump administration Monday to block enforcement of a change in federal housing policy that would leave more than 55,000 U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens without federally subsidized affordable housing.

Joined by 20 other attorneys general, the states say President Donald Trump’s new policy would upend three decades of federal Housing and Urban Development policy by cutting off a family’s entire housing subsidy if even one household member is ineligible, forcing mixed-status families to choose between separating from their loved ones or losing their homes.

“Despite being the federal agency charged with administering programs to provide low-income housing and reduce homelessness, HUD now seeks to implement a policy that will have the opposite effect, causing the mass displacement of U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens from their homes,” the states write in a 56-page civil complaint filed in Massachusetts federal court.

Previously under this system, known as proration, federal housing programs have helped low-income families afford rent even when not every household member is eligible for assistance.

The new HUD rule — unveiled earlier this month and set to take effect Dec. 14 — eliminates this protection by only allowing a family to stay in HUD-assisted housing if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant.

The states brings two counts of violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, accusing the policy change of lacking a rational connection between the facts it found and the decision it made.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said Monday the new rule “runs counter to our nation’s values and the very purpose of these housing programs.”

“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. Denying a child that security because of who they live with is cruel and indefensible,” she wrote in a statement announcing the lawsuit. “With our country already in the throes of a housing crisis, it is outrageous that the federal government would push even more families out of their homes.”

James said the displacement from the new HUD policy could further strain New York City’s shelter system that already has limited capacity to support new families.

The states say Congress drafted this approach into law in 1997 and explicitly stated that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them.

California and New York are joined in the complaint by the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania.

The coalition is asking a federal judge to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down and block HUD from enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments and their public housing authorities.

The states target the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and its secretary, Scott Turner, as co-defendants.

Shortly into his second term in office, Trump appointed Turner, a former NFL player, Texas state representative and White House senior aide, as housing secretary in February 2025.

The changes to HUD policy during Trump’s second term were explicitly laid out in the Heritage Foundation’s so-called Project 2025 policy blueprint, titled “Mandate for Leadership: The Conservative Promise.”

The conservative policy overhaul called for the HUD secretary to strip all mixed-status families of federally assisted housing.

The Project 2025 playbook suggested local welfare organizations “step up to provide welfare for the housing of noncitizens” in the absence of federal housing.

Housing advocates have criticized the changes to HUD’s policies and functions as a shift toward tax credits, mortgage boosts and regulatory cuts for property developers and owners.

The agency defended the policy change as a guarantee that “only American citizens and certain eligible noncitizens” will reside in HUD-funded housing.

“HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars," Turner wrote in a statement Monday afternoon. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”
