title: Legal, LGBTQ+, and Immigration Organizations Urge U.S. Supreme Court to Block Unlawful ...
description:
The coalition includes Immigration Equality, Lambda Legal, Oasis Legal Services, the Council for Global Equality (CGE), Outright International, the Organization for Refuge, Asylum, and Migration (ORAM), and Rainbow Railroad.
Denying them the chance to object violates decades-long immigration policy and due process guarantees.
Some of those countries have sent refugees back to the very places a U.S. judge said they could not be sent.
The Supreme Court paused the district court’s early orders in June 2025, allowing these deportations to continue while the case proceeded.
The organizations supporting the amicus brief are committed to advocating for the rights and safety of LGBTQ+ refugees and will continue to monitor the case closely.
text:
“Outrageous and cruel.” Immigration Equality, Lambda Legal, the Council for Global Equality, Oasis Legal Services, Outright International, the Organization for Refuge, Asylum, and Migration, and Rainbow Railroad file a friend-of-the-court brief highlighting the absurdity and bad faith of the Trump administration’s treatment of LGBTQ+ refugees.

Para leer este artículo en español, haga clic aquí.

A coalition of leading LGBTQ+ immigration and rights advocacy, research, and support organizations filed today a friend-of-the-court brief in the U.S. Supreme Court highlighting the unlawfulness of the Trump administration’s practice of deporting LGBTQ+ refugees to third countries without legally adequate notice and the opportunity to object based on fears of persecution or torture in the country selected by the government.

The coalition includes Immigration Equality, Lambda Legal, Oasis Legal Services, the Council for Global Equality (CGE), Outright International, the Organization for Refuge, Asylum, and Migration (ORAM), and Rainbow Railroad. In its amicus curiae brief in Department of Homeland Security (DHS) v. D.V.D., the coalition shows that the administration is violating the rights of individuals already shielded by U.S. immigration judges from deportation back to their countries of origin due to credible fears of persecution or torture there. The administration is doing so by failing to provide fair notice and a reasonable opportunity to explain why deportation to a third country the government has chosen is too dangerous for them because of who they are.

The brief includes powerful examples of clients represented by these amici, which show vividly the particular vulnerability of LGBTQ+ refugees who, after fleeing severe abuse, have been granted protection by U.S. immigration judges from being returned to their countries of origin, but are being deported instead to other countries where they will face similar risks of violence, persecution, and even torture based on their LGBTQ+ identities. Because same-sex relationships and expressions of an LGBTQ+ identity are criminalized and/or systematically persecuted by governmental and non-governmental actors in many of the countries that the administration has chosen for its aggressive deportation efforts, the legally required opportunity to object to a particular destination country is essential for LGBTQ+ people who are subject to deportation.

Quotes From Friend-of-the-Court Organizations

Lambda Legal

“The Trump administration’s illegal policy of hastily deporting LGBTQ+ refugees to countries the government knows are extremely dangerous for them because of who they are – without giving them the legally required chance to object to that danger – is outrageous and cruel,” said Jenny Pizer, a co-author of the brief and Senior Director of Strategic Initiatives at Lambda Legal. “The administration knows full well that many of these countries criminalize LGBTQ+ people simply for existing, with some even imposing the death penalty, and many more subject them to pervasive societal violence with no access to police protection. Denying them the chance to object violates decades-long immigration policy and due process guarantees. The case examples provided in this brief show starkly that this administration’s unlawful practice creates life-or-death consequences for real people who already have been horribly traumatized.”

“In short, the Trump administration is deporting immigrant people, including LGBTQ+ refugees, who have already been granted protection by the U.S. government due to credible fear of persecution or torture in their home countries, to third countries they don’t know and might never have heard of, where they would face extreme danger. Many of them have sought refuge in the U.S. after escaping vicious abuse by their governments or communities due to their sexual orientation or gender identity. These deportations, without the required chance to object, plainly violate U.S. law and are unconscionable,” said Malcolm Dort, a co-author of the brief and Senior Counsel for Strategic Initiatives at Lambda Legal.

Immigration Equality

“A U.S. judge found that these refugees would likely be persecuted or tortured if sent home, and the administration responded by sending many of them somewhere else equally dangerous, without a warning and without a hearing,” said Bridget Crawford, a co-author of the brief and Director of Law and Policy at Immigration Equality. “The law is clear that the government may not deport people to countries where they face persecution or torture, and it must give them a fair opportunity to raise that fear first. These safeguards are being ignored. Notice and a meaningful chance to object are required by federal law, by our treaty obligations, and by the Constitution, and for LGBTQ refugees, they are the difference between safety and the threat of imprisonment, violence, or death. We are urging the Supreme Court to ensure that, when a U.S. judge says someone cannot be sent to persecution or torture, that protection means something.”

Oasis Legal Services

“Third-country deportations place LGBTQ+ migrants in grave danger. Oasis has worked with many LGBTQ+ migrants who fled harm in their home countries and tried to find safety in a third country like Mexico, only to suffer brutal persecution. Without a correct outcome in this case, LGBTQ+ immigrants will be sent to third countries where being LGBTQ+ is illegal or where their identities place a target on their backs. They will be sent without community support, without government protection, and at very high risk of being harmed. LGBTQ+ immigrants have the right to a real opportunity to show that they would be persecuted or tortured in another country before the government attempts to send them there,” said Celia Meredith, Staff Attorney at Oasis Legal Services.

Council for Global Equality

“Today, we are raising the voices of people like Michael, a Ghanaian man, who was persecuted and tortured due to his sexual orientation as a gay man,” noted Keifer Buckingham, Managing Director of the Council for Global Equality. “A U.S. judge granted him withholding of removal. But the Trump administration shackled him, put him on a plane without telling him where he was being sent, and flew him to Equatorial Guinea, a country where LGBTQI+ people face high levels of violence and torture. He was then forcibly deported back to Ghana. The Trump administration’s practice of third country removals – including the usage of opaque bilateral agreements with countries that routinely abuse human rights – is the very embodiment of what has been a hateful and inhumane immigration policy over the last two years. We hope the Supreme Court will see this policy for what it is: not only cruel, but illegal.”

Outright International

“LGBTIQ people from all over the world seek refuge in the U.S. when their lives are in danger because they expect to find safety, fairness, and dignity on U.S. shores. Yet the Trump administration, in flagrant violation of international law, is shipping them off to countries that its own human rights reporting has deemed unsafe for sexual and gender minorities. These inhumane policies must be reversed. No one should be deported to a country where they face the risk of arbitrary arrest, ill-treatment, and even death just for being who they are,” said Neela Ghoshal, senior director of law, policy, and research at Outright.

Rainbow Railroad

“The United States has a legal and moral duty not to send people to countries where they will face imminent danger. However, the administration is actively deporting LGBTQI+ people who have a credible fear of persecution or torture to third countries where they have no ties or support, and face precarious, emergency conditions that demand immediate protection,” said Oliver Williams, U.S. Policy & Advocacy Officer at Rainbow Railroad. “The United States must uphold the protection it has already granted and stop the practice of third-country removals.”

Organization for Refuge, Asylum & Migration (ORAM)

“LGBTQ+ people who seek protection in the United States place enormous trust in its laws and institutions. For those who have already been granted protection by an immigration judge, being sent to another potentially dangerous country without a meaningful opportunity to be heard is a profound betrayal of that trust,” said Steve Roth, Executive Director of ORAM – Organization for Refuge, Asylum & Migration. “It also undermines the credibility of the United States and its commitment to protecting people fleeing persecution.”

Stories of Impacted People

Thelma: Thelma, a bisexual woman, fled Ghana after her father threatened to kill her and an armed group attacked her and her girlfriend. After a U.S. immigration judge granted her protection from being returned to Ghana, she was shackled and flown to Cameroon, a country to which she has no connection. She remains in Cameroon with restrictions on her movement and has gone without adequate food or medical care, fearing for her safety and fearing she will be sent back to Ghana. (Amicus brief, p.14-15; 18; 26-28)

Thelma says inclusion in the amicus filing gives voice at the nation’s highest court to her experience: “Going through a third-country removal was one of the hardest experiences of my life, and for a long time, it felt like no one was listening. Knowing that my truth is now being offered to protect others from going through the same pain brings real meaning to what I endured. I am hoping with everything I have that this case achieves justice—not just for me, but for every person seeking safety and a chance to live freely.”

Additional Representative Stories in the Brief:

David, a bisexual man from Cameroon (p. 14)

Michael (a gay man), Samuel (a gay man) and Abina (a lesbian) from Ghana (p. 17-19; 26-28)

Alexandra and Maria, transgender women from Mexico (p. 20-21)

Farah, a gay woman from Morocco (p. 16)

Abdul, a gay man from Togo (p. 22)

What the Case is About

Federal immigration law bars the government from deporting anyone to a country where they are likely to be tortured, or persecuted because of who they are, including their sexual orientation or gender identity. That bar applies to any country, not just a person’s home country. When a U.S. immigration judge finds this risk in a refugee’s home country, the refugee is granted “withholding of removal,” a protection like asylum but weaker: it requires a higher standard of proof, yet offers no path to a green card or citizenship.

Withholding blocks return only to the home country, and prior administrations generally allowed those who received it to remain in the U.S. The Trump administration is instead deporting LGBTQ+ refugees with withholding, along with other noncitizens with final removal orders, to third countries never identified in their immigration proceedings, including to countries it knows are hostile to LGBTQ+ people. Some of those countries have sent refugees back to the very places a U.S. judge said they could not be sent.

The policy allows deportation with as little as six hours’ notice, or none at all if the receiving country has given a blanket “diplomatic assurance” that deportees will not be harmed. Under the Trump administration’s legally defective policy, refugees subject to removal from the U.S. can be deported with minimal or no notice at all to countries that have given “diplomatic assurances” that refugees it receives from the U.S. will not be harmed. In the LGBTQ+ context, such assurances are hollow and absurd. In many countries – with Cameroon, Ghana, South Sudan, Eswatini, Honduras, and El Salvador as just a few examples – criminal laws and brutal social conditions for LGBTQ+ people are well-established. Moreover, many of the countries to which the administration is sending LGBTQ+ people engage in “chain refoulement,” the practice of sending people received from the U.S. back to the countries from which they originally fled. According to Refugees International and Human Rights First, more than 25,000 people have been deported to at least 28 third countries in 2025 and 2026.

Lawsuit Background

Human Rights First, the National Immigration Litigation Alliance (NILA), and the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project (NWIRP) filed the case in March 2025 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, on behalf of a nationwide class. The Supreme Court paused the district court’s early orders in June 2025, allowing these deportations to continue while the case proceeded. In February 2026, the district court struck down the administration’s third-country removal policy, holding that people must receive meaningful notice and a meaningful opportunity to show they fear persecution or torture in a new country before being sent there. In September 2026, the First Circuit largely affirmed. The U.S. government then turned to the U.S. Supreme Court, which again paused the district court’s ruling, allowing third-country deportations to continue while it decides whether the policy violates federal immigration law, the Due Process Clause, and/or the Convention Against Torture. Amicus briefs are due today and oral argument is set for December 9, 2026.

The organizations supporting the amicus brief are committed to advocating for the rights and safety of LGBTQ+ refugees and will continue to monitor the case closely.

text:
HOUSTON, Texas – Federal prosecutors in the Southern District of Texas filed charges against 222 people in a single week, the U.S. Attorney’s Office announced Monday, as part of an ongoing surge in border and immigration enforcement.

Of those charged between Nov. 13–19, 204 are undocumented immigrants. The cases span a range of offenses — from illegal entry to felony reentry and human smuggling — and are part of Operation Take Back America, the Justice Department’s nationwide crackdown on illegal immigration and transnational criminal organizations.

Breaking Down the Numbers

The bulk of the new filings — 163 criminal complaints — involve felony reentry after prior removal, a federal charge that carries serious prison time. Another 33 people face illegal entry charges, and 16 are accused of human smuggling, including eight undocumented immigrants who were themselves being smuggled. Four additional cases involve other immigration-related crimes.

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz’s office noted that many of those charged carry prior felony convictions involving narcotics, violent crime, or prior immigration offenses.

A Convicted Child Sex Abuser Caught Trying to Reenter

Among the newly filed cases, Guatemalan national Alixon Eduardo Lopez-Gonzalez faces illegal reentry charges after authorities removed him on Aug. 3 and then discovered him again near Chapeno just last week. Court documents allege he has a prior conviction for child sexual abuse. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in federal prison.

Two Smugglers Sentenced to Federal Prison

Beyond the new filings, two men were sentenced this week for separate human smuggling operations:

Lucas Gallegos Vasquez, a Mexican national, was sentenced to 151 months in federal prison for running a Laredo stash house where 32 undocumented immigrants were held in extreme heat with little food or water. Authorities also found 30 people — including five minors — crammed into a tractor-trailer’s sleeper compartment. Two individuals were hospitalized; one died.

Javier Zamora received 80 months for transporting an undocumented immigrant for financial gain. Zamora led authorities on a 140-mph chase before his vehicle caught fire. He fled on foot, and when an officer caught up to him, Zamora grabbed the officer’s arm while the officer was holding a firearm. The weapon discharged during the struggle, and the officer was injured.

Jury Convicts Honduran National in Laredo

A federal jury also convicted Arnol Josue Flores, a Honduran national, on charges of conspiring to transport undocumented immigrants for profit. Testimony showed Flores picked up two undocumented immigrants near Hebbronville — one of whom had paid $11,000 to be smuggled into the country. Flores attempted to flee on foot after abandoning his vehicle. He faces up to 10 years in federal prison.

One of the Nation’s Busiest Federal Districts

The Southern District of Texas covers 43 counties, more than 10 million people, and 44,000 square miles, with divisions in Houston, Galveston, Victoria, Corpus Christi, Brownsville, McAllen, and Laredo. The office works alongside federal partners including ICE, Border Patrol, the DEA, FBI, U.S. Marshals Service, and ATF, as well as state and local law enforcement.

text:
Massachusetts is suing the federal government for making civil arrests at courthouses without warrants, which is prohibited under a new state law that went into effect earlier this month.

In a federal lawsuit filed Monday, Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell argues the state has “the sovereign right to both manage its judicial system and determine whether and how to deploy state resources,” reads the complaint for the lawsuit. “Massachusetts has exercised that right to protect fundamental safeguards for the state court system by codifying its interests and protections—the PROTECT Act.”

The state says federal agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement have been violating Massachusetts law “nearly every single day” by conducting civil arrests in Massachusetts state courthouses. The attorney general’s office and state’s trial court say that at least 38 individuals have been arrested in courthouses without judicial warrants since the law went into effect.

“With our lawsuit, we hope to demonstrate that ICE’s policy violates federal law by interfering with Massachusetts’ ability to operate our courts and enforcing our state laws, including the PROTECT Act,” Campbell said at a Monday press conference.

“These unlawful ICE arrests have also created unnecessary fear, making it less likely that defendants, victims and witnesses will appear when summoned for a criminal case. creating serious public safety concerns,” she said.

Gov. Maura Healey voiced her support for the lawsuit in a statement Monday.

“The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe,” the governor wrote. “We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law.”

ICE, the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Campbell says that ICE is relying on a May 2025 directive that permits ICE officials to conduct civil arrests in state courthouses, even if state law prohibits those arrests.

The Department of Homeland Security told GBH News last week that it declines to discuss its enforcement operations specifically. “The Supremacy Clause makes it clear that sanctuary politicians do not control federal law enforcement,” a spokesperson said.

“The ability of law enforcement to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense. It conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already know where a target will be. It is also safer for our officers and the community,” the agency said. “DHS also said it conducts those arrests at courthouses because immigrants have been screened “to not have any weapons.”

At Monday’s press conference, Campbell said the state retains sovereign authority over its judicial system. She said that by “openly violating these restrictions, ICE is unlawfully interfering with the commonwealth’s sovereign authority and unlawfully using state courts and resources to carry out federal immigration enforcement.”

The attorney general also said ICE agents are using state resources to identify and target immigrant individuals appearing in court, such as court schedules, security screenings conducted by state employees.

According to Campbell, survivors of domestic violence have been reluctant to go to courts to seek restraining orders against their abusers due to fear that they might be arrested by ICE when they have to testify in court.

Campbell was flanked by District Attorneys Kevin Hayden and Marian Ryan at Monday’s press conference, along with over a dozen legal and immigration advocates.

Campbell recounted how on November 3, the first day the PROTECT Act went into effect, a defendant was scheduled to appear for a criminal trial in Malden District Court. Instead, ICE arrested the individual, preventing him from appearing on domestic violence charges.

“DA Marian Ryan, who is standing to my right, her team was prepared to proceed with the trial, and the victim was present to testify,” Campbell said. “Instead of appearing, the defendant was detained by ICE, now making it nearly impossible to prosecute that case.”

Ryan was one of several plaintiffs in a 2019 lawsuit against the first Trump administration focused on arrests in and around courthouses. After winning a preliminary injunction that blocked ICE from making those civil arrests, a a federal circuit court ultimately vacated it. Ryan said, this time, the state is better situated to defend its position in court.

“We did not have the PROTECT Act,” Ryan told GBH News. In that case, the Middlesex district attorney said, justices found “that while the state had the right to protect and run their own court system, the court’s policy, which existed — it was a trial court policy at that time, not work of the Legislature — was not sufficient to defeat ICE’s purpose in going to the courthouses.”

“It is our belief now that the structure put in place by the PROTECT Act is sufficient to satisfy the court as to us acting under our 10th Amendment right. So we should prevail there, and it defeats that Supremacy Clause question as well,” the Middlesex district attorney said.

Under the 10th Amendment, states hold any rights and responsibilities that are not explicitly granted to the federal government.

title: Real, Positive Change for Immigrants Will Only Come From Continuing Popular Pressure
description:

There is also the question of who actually trusts the Trump administration to implement legislation if it were to pass.
Real change for immigrants could take place during this Congress, or the next.
text:
Much was made of President Donald Trump’s apparent softening of his hard-line position on immigration during his interview on “60 Minutes“ following the thumping Republicans received in the November midterms.

Speculation abounds: Could the president make an immigration deal with Democrats? Will children of undocumented people who were brought to the US when they were minors—the Dreamers—get permanent status? Or could our lawmakers pass legislation to provide relief in the form of work permits for the million or so farmworkers who do not have legal status?

If we lived in a normal political world, then we would expect some legislative movement on immigration, especially as the midterms sent a clear message that the American public is upset with the Trump administration, including with his handling of immigration.

What should provide hope is not the pundits speculating on the future of immigration reform, or Trump’s musings, but how grassroots groups have stood up for their neighbors.

But political normalcy doesn’t guide the Trump administration, as on immigration, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents continue their statewide surge operation throughout California and brutalize families at airports; the president promoted immigration hard-liner, Stephen Miller, to serve as White House chief of staff; and Border Czar Tom Homan recently boasted about the record number of immigrant arrests this year—the vast majority of whom have no criminal record—and how that number will increase next year.

Considering this reality, we should bear in mind the words of Reverand Fred Shuttlesworth. Describing his approach when advocating for civil rights, he said, “You can’t shame segregation… Rattlesnakes don’t commit suicide; ball teams don’t strike themselves out. You gotta put ‘em out.”

Such clarity should guide immigrant rights groups and their allies in their advocacy work heading into the next Congress. More to the point, we must not rest and trust that a Democrat-majority Congress will lead positive change for immigrants. Instead, we need to continue to grow the mass movement that has been organizing to defend immigrant communities, building from actions in neighborhoods and states, as we force this Congress or the next to pass comprehensive changes to the immigration system.

It’s not that there is a shortage of immigration proposals floating around the halls of Congress.

For instance, there is the Farm Workforce Modernization Act, which has been introduced in multiple past Congresses, and that enjoys bipartisan support. This bill provides work permits to farmworkers and their family members, while also expanding the controversial E-Verify program to all farming operations.

There is also the American Dream and Promise Act, which grants a pathway to citizenship for young people who were under the age of 16 when they came to the United States, many of whom received renewable two-year work permits from the Obama-era DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) executive order.

Then there’s the Dignity Act. This bill provides permanent status for Dreamers, offers a way to legalize the undocumented spouses of US citizens who currently cannot fix their status if they have unauthorized entries into the country, and also makes it possible for everyone else who is undocumented to receive work permits.

This last portion of the bill has been particularly controversial, as the potential beneficiaries who are neither Dreamers nor married to US citizens would receive a renewable work permit that is good for seven years but doesn’t lead to permanent status, and must pay a yearly $1,000 fee while having 1% of their income taken from their paychecks.

All these bills would provide much needed relief for families who have undocumented members. The problem is that most of them deal with one particular group, leaving the others vulnerable to continuing state violence. It’s possible that group by group, different laws could be passed. But the legislative process is slow. If one initiative, say for Dreamers, gains momentum, it will take months or probably a year to get to the president’s desk, leaving little time in the legislative calendar for Congress to take up a bill for others.

There is also the question of who actually trusts the Trump administration to implement legislation if it were to pass. Are we to believe that undocumented people feel safe enough with this government to send it their pertinent documents? If this administration were to receive immigrants’ information, what assurances will there be that it will change people’s statuses instead of sending ICE to arrest them?

Still, I wouldn’t hold my breath waiting for Congress to act and Trump to move any legislation forward.

What makes the odds so low for decent immigration policy coming from the Trump administration, besides the presence of such figures as Homan and Miller, is how much money has been invested in repression.

Specifically, last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, HR 1, dedicated $170 billion for immigration enforcement. ICE is now the highest-funded federal law enforcement agency, with an annual budget around $28 billion annually for the next four years, eclipsing the combined budgets of the FBI, Drug Enforcement Agency, ATF, and US Marshals. This is also more than the annual military budgets of Iran, Turkey, Spain, Mexico, Iran, and at least 23 countries in the list of the top 40 military spenders. A total of $45 billion is also for building new immigration detention centers, including for families. This last amount is a 400% increase when compared with 2025 and exceeds allocation for the entire federal prison system.

Moreover, this is direct handout to the corporations, Geo Group and CoreCivic, which together house approximately 90% of immigrants detained. Both corporations also donated directly to the Trump campaign, or to Trump-affiliated super-PACs.

This money has been locked into the budget and must be spent by 2029, so Democrats coming into Congress cannot defund ICE in upcoming budget debates.

Let’s be clear—taxpayers have paid for a deportation-industrial complex fueled by widespread misinformation that depicts all immigrants as violent criminals. If Miller’s promotion or Homan’s words don’t make you second guess the administration’s true priorities, then the billions dedicated to arresting and detaining undocumented people, regardless of their crimes, should make you aware of what to expect for the next couple years.

In this environment, change will not come from the “top,” but the “bottom,” that is, from the grassroots.

What should provide hope is not the pundits speculating on the future of immigration reform, or Trump’s musings, but how grassroots groups have stood up for their neighbors in neighborhood patrols. People around the country have attended ICE verification meetings with immigrant-led organizations. The city of Minneapolis amid “Operation Metro Surge” held a one-day general strike that shut down the city over how the immigrant community was being mistreated. People who are not immigrants, perhaps for the first time, are actually thinking about the issue and wanting to defend people who are being persecuted.

More mass action will be needed to push for real immigration reform, that is, comprehensive changes to the legal system that guarantee status to all undocumented people, while also creating pathways for future migrants to apply for status without unduly penalizing or persecuting them. We need a new national conversation, and not our current one that is based on overhyped security concerns. A place to start is with how immigrant rights are human rights, and that it’s immoral for native-born citizens, who literally have done nothing to receive their status other than being born here, to stand behind a system that unduly persecutes vulnerable people. We need protests at the scale and regularity of what we saw for months in 2006, when in opposition to HR 4437 (The Sensenbrenner Bill), thousands blocked that anti-immigration legislation from advancing.

Real change for immigrants could take place during this Congress, or the next. Regardless of when, the truth is that meaningful change, and not piecemeal, isolated initiatives, will come from mass political action calling for a system overhaul and a new national conversation on immigrant rights. The Trump administration has muddied the water when it comes to understanding the immigration issue. Immigrant rights groups and their allies best work together to toss it out, beginning with new proposals that do not discriminate, and that put us on solid moral ground.

Much was made of President Donald Trump’s apparent softening of his hard-line position on immigration during his interview on “60 Minutes“ following the thumping Republicans received in the November midterms.

Speculation abounds: Could the president make an immigration deal with Democrats? Will children of undocumented people who were brought to the US when they were minors—the Dreamers—get permanent status? Or could our lawmakers pass legislation to provide relief in the form of work permits for the million or so farmworkers who do not have legal status?

If we lived in a normal political world, then we would expect some legislative movement on immigration, especially as the midterms sent a clear message that the American public is upset with the Trump administration, including with his handling of immigration.

What should provide hope is not the pundits speculating on the future of immigration reform, or Trump’s musings, but how grassroots groups have stood up for their neighbors.

But political normalcy doesn’t guide the Trump administration, as on immigration, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents continue their statewide surge operation throughout California and brutalize families at airports; the president promoted immigration hard-liner, Stephen Miller, to serve as White House chief of staff; and Border Czar Tom Homan recently boasted about the record number of immigrant arrests this year—the vast majority of whom have no criminal record—and how that number will increase next year.

Considering this reality, we should bear in mind the words of Reverand Fred Shuttlesworth. Describing his approach when advocating for civil rights, he said, “You can’t shame segregation… Rattlesnakes don’t commit suicide; ball teams don’t strike themselves out. You gotta put ‘em out.”

Such clarity should guide immigrant rights groups and their allies in their advocacy work heading into the next Congress. More to the point, we must not rest and trust that a Democrat-majority Congress will lead positive change for immigrants. Instead, we need to continue to grow the mass movement that has been organizing to defend immigrant communities, building from actions in neighborhoods and states, as we force this Congress or the next to pass comprehensive changes to the immigration system.

It’s not that there is a shortage of immigration proposals floating around the halls of Congress.

For instance, there is the Farm Workforce Modernization Act, which has been introduced in multiple past Congresses, and that enjoys bipartisan support. This bill provides work permits to farmworkers and their family members, while also expanding the controversial E-Verify program to all farming operations.

There is also the American Dream and Promise Act, which grants a pathway to citizenship for young people who were under the age of 16 when they came to the United States, many of whom received renewable two-year work permits from the Obama-era DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) executive order.

This last portion of the bill has been particularly controversial, as the potential beneficiaries who are neither Dreamers nor married to US citizens would receive a renewable work permit that is good for seven years but doesn’t lead to permanent status, and must pay a yearly $1,000 fee while having 1% of their income taken from their paychecks.

All these bills would provide much needed relief for families who have undocumented members. The problem is that most of them deal with one particular group, leaving the others vulnerable to continuing state violence. It’s possible that group by group, different laws could be passed. But the legislative process is slow. If one initiative, say for Dreamers, gains momentum, it will take months or probably a year to get to the president’s desk, leaving little time in the legislative calendar for Congress to take up a bill for others.

There is also the question of who actually trusts the Trump administration to implement legislation if it were to pass. text:
A chaotic scene unfolded Sunday on 86th Avenue and E Street in East Oakland when about a dozen masked federal immigration agents arrested two young men and used force, including chemical weapons, against community members who were objecting to the agents’ actions.

The violence, recorded by bystanders and shared widely on social media, drew condemnation from Mayor Barbara Lee and others.

“ICE is not wanted in Oakland, the Oakland Police Department does not cooperate with ICE, and I am profoundly grateful to our residents for standing together to protect their neighbors,” said Lee.

ACILEP, the Alameda County Immigration Legal Education Partnership, a county program launched last year in response to the Trump Administration’s escalation of immigration enforcement, confirmed the arrests on social media. Both young men have been released according to the immigrant rights group.

Alejandro Guzman, a neighbor who lives near 86th Avenue, told The Oaklandside yesterday that around 11 a.m., he noticed a masked agent wearing beige and green clothing and tactical gear inside a truck parked on the street. Guzman and another neighbor approached the vehicle and asked the agent if he was ICE. The agent, Guzman said, did not respond. Another neighbor, a teenager, also approached the agent and asked if he was ICE. The youth, Guzman said, wrote on a piece of paper “ICE OUT” and placed it on the truck’s windshield, an action that angered the agent.

Guzman began recording as two federal agents tackled the young man while another agent pepper-sprayed observers who were recording. A third ICE agent shoved another observer to prevent them from recording.

A fourth agent wearing a gas mask and tactical helmet is seen throwing a tear gas canister at observers, then violently shoving and knocking to the ground a person who was recording the agents.

In another video from a different angle, an agent in a tan baseball cap warns a man who is recording video to “get back.” The agent then rushes to grab one of the two people who was violently knocked to the ground and drags them several feet.

As the teenager is being handcuffed, he screams repeatedly, “I am under 17 years old.”

Guzman said he was pepper sprayed and ran into his house to wash his face. As he was inside, he said, an ICE agent driving a black Chevy Tahoe with civilian California license plates clipped the left side of his truck that was parked on 86th Avenue.

“We have lived on this block since 2008, and we have never seen this type of violence,” Guzman said. “All the neighbors talk to one another. Two of them are veterans, and they came out to help and try to reason with the agents, but they didn’t listen. Neighbors are scared to leave their homes.”

Guzman said the two observers who were assaulted by ICE agents had to be taken to the hospital. Michael Hunt, a spokesperson with the Oakland Fire Department, confirmed to The Oaklandside that two women were transported by Falck Ambulance.

Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee released a statement late on Sunday condemning the immigration agents.

“We are witnessing a disturbing and unacceptable surge in aggressive ICE operations,” Lee said. “Federal agents have no business terrorizing our neighborhoods or bringing violence into spaces where Oakland families live and work. My office is working alongside Congresswoman Lateefah Simon, ACILEP, and local partners to actively monitor these developments and defend our community’s rights and demand accountability.”

In early October, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced the launch of “Operation Safe California,” a 45-day surge to arrest immigrants without legal status. Since the operation began, federal agents have arrested at least a dozen people in Oakland, including Sunday’s arrests.

On Nov. 7, ICE agents arrested four people in Oakland, including a man on 81st Avenue, a few blocks away from Sunday’s incident.

The Oaklandside reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, but they did not respond to a request for comment.

A 21-year-old U.S. citizen was detained and later released

Just a few houses down from where the minor was detained, five agents surrounded 21-year-old Saul Hernandez, and two tackled him to the ground, handcuffed him, and put him in the back of an SUV.

The Oaklandside spoke to Hernandez about an hour after his release from the ICE field office at 630 Sansome St. in San Francisco.

Hernandez told The Oaklandside that when he heard federal agents were harassing his neighbors, he ran towards the scene to help. “It’s my community. It’s our people. We should look out, especially in times like this,” Hernandez said. “I was feeling a lot, seeing our people get taken away. It made me want to come out and do something.”

Hernandez said that he was angry seeing his neighbors assaulted. In videos on social media, two agents can be seen tackling him. Hernandez said he hit his forehead on the sidewalk and was not given any medical attention for his injuries while in ICE custody.

“It’s way too much excessive force for just one person who’s completely smaller than the rest of the agents,” Hernandez said.

At no point, he said, did the agents identify themselves to him. “When we were in the car, I would try to talk to them, and they kept telling me to shut up,” he said.

Hernandez told The Oaklandside that before being taken to San Francisco, the agents who arrested him drove to a lot nearby where Walmart used to be on Edgewater Drive near Hegenberger Road. There, he said, around 20-30 agents who participated in the incident on 86th Avenue rendezvoused.

Hernandez said that while the agents debriefed, the young person who was arrested was put in the same car as him.

“He was telling me, ‘Man, I’m only 16-17 years old. I don’t understand why I was arrested. I was just recording,’” Hernandez said.

District 7 councilmember Ken Houston released a statement on social media on Sunday, denouncing the federal agents’ actions.

“This is a residential block where families live, children play, and elders sit on their porches,” Houston wrote. “If these reports are accurate, using chemical agents on this street is reckless.”

Houston said he won’t tolerate the agents’ actions. “No agency can come running wild and rampant in my city, using chemical warfare on our neighbors without notifying the proper local authorities,” he wrote. “That advance notice is my demand. Oakland is a sanctuary city.”

ICE’s San Francisco lockup

At ICE’s Sansome Street facility, Hernandez said, he was first put in what looked like a warehouse. Then he was moved to a different location within the building.

“It was a blue room with a camera in the corner, and they had a bathroom in there too, with a metal bench,” he said. “After that, they kept telling me that they were going to give me the opportunity to make a call later. I never got to make my phone call until I was released.”

Hernandez said that before being released, he had to speak with two Department of Homeland Security officers. A third officer who was in the room when Hernandez was being interrogated escorted him out upon his release.

“The guy who walked me out, he’s all, ‘Here, I can let you use my phone just to make a quick call,’” Hernandez said.

Hernandez said that the entire ordeal was traumatizing.

“I still want to be there for my community and show support. But I think I want to step back for now. They already arrested me once,” Hernandez said. “It was pretty tough, but I thank God I’m home.”

text:
Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

This article is part of The 74’s EDlection 2026 coverage, which takes a look at candidates’ education policies and how they might impact the American education system after the 2026 election.

Normally, post-election prognostication involves sifting through and reading the proverbial tea leaves to divine our new political future. One region may tilt right, but only among older voters, while another state’s new political lean seems to be drifting left due to an influx of young college graduates.

But my goodness, the 2026 midterm results are so heavy, it’s a different sort of project. This time, it’s a little more like sifting through the ashes of a blast crater.

I mean, South Carolina is sending a Democrat to the Senate? I’m old enough to remember when Sen.-elect Annie Andrews’ seat was held by Strom Thurmond, who famously abandoned the party for the Republicans when the Johnson administration got too woke for his liking (by pushing for major civil rights legislation).

What was the (historic) 2026 election for education? Some education analysts have mixed feelings. While many are eager to see some curbs on the Trump administration’s wanton wielding of power, they also worry that the country’s all-but-wholesale repudiation of the Republican Party represents a threat to education reform’s political fortunes.

After a shift this seismic, no prognosticator should be too confident about the details of what comes next, but one thing’s clear: The curbing of the Trump administration will be good for children in the United States.

That ought to be the guiding light here, right? Those of us who measure our involvement in public education in decades, not years, will remember the days when “putting kids’ interests before adults’ hangups” was the reform movement’s North Star — however imperfectly it embodied that ideal from year to year.

That’s how reformers proposed, tested, implemented and adjusted the core elements of their agenda during the first two decades of this century. Tests help measure students’ progress to ensure that they’re on track for mid- and long-term success. Accountability systems linked to those tests — and other educational elements — focus adults’ attention on the public’s academic priorities for our schools.

Public choice programs protect families from being trapped if the schools assigned to them based on their ability to purchase housing are particularly dysfunctional. Finally, public choice programs are maximally beneficial for children when participating schools have flexibility to design campuses that work but strict public accountability for demonstrating improved student outcomes.

Those things are good for kids. Some of them are more popular with Democrats or with Republicans, but none are exclusively the province of either political party. So it’s understandable that reformers might fret that American voters’ firm rejection of Republicans at every level of government could imperil high-quality charter schools or test-based accountability systems for K–12 schools.

And yet, the election results could produce negotiations with Congress that ultimately force the Trump administration to end its lawless, chaotic, violent approach to immigration enforcement. That might not be a classic education reform priority, but it could free tens of thousands of terrified children to go back to school.

Research indicates that the past 18 months of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, funded through several party-line Republican budget bills, have disrupted learning and spiked absenteeism rates, particularly for Latino students in immigrant communities.

And that’s to say nothing of conservatives’ many-fronted attacks on multilingual children’s civil rights, such as White House efforts to reduce the amount of information schools translate for families who do not speak English proficiently, launching a new federal mandate that local Head Start programs teach only in English and more.

Republicans didn’t just spend their two years of unified control of the federal government targeting immigrant families and communities — and the U.S. citizens living among them. They passed an enormous school choice tax credit that appears likely to primarily fuel more public funding to private schools with limited oversight at any regulatory level.

A recent Brookings analysis predicts that the tax credit will produce widespread waste and implementation problems. Research on private choice programs has been largely discouraging, producing mixed academic results and consistent civil rights concerns. Kids may also benefit from new scrutiny of private choice programs at the state level as well, as Democrats won gubernatorial races in Texas, Iowa, and Ohio — three states with robust private choice programs.

Since 2024, Republicans also enacted severe cuts to federal food and health care programs for low-income families. To cover the lost revenue produced by dramatic tax cuts for particularly wealthy Americans, Republicans’ “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” pushed at least one million children off of federal food assistance, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. It also included a series of new federal rules that will likely take away Medicaid coverage from millions of families.

None of this is good for kids. Children do not educationally benefit from increased food insecurity or less reliable, affordable access to health care. No, research is clear that children learn better when they have their basic needs met. This consensus is among the sturdiest in public education research.

And so, no, under this new Congress, federal grants supporting charter schools might not grow. There may be no new progress on the long-stalled project of strengthening the federal role in K–12 education accountability.

But those aren’t the only policies that matter for children’s learning. That is, if Democrats use their new congressional majorities to pressure the administration to end its many campaigns against immigrant families — and U.S. citizens — that will be good for K–12 students the country over. If they use their majorities to force Republicans to restore SNAP and health care benefits to low-income kids, that will improve learning outcomes.

There are countless other ways that the election results could be great for education. It would improve student learning if Congress’ new majority unwinds Republicans’ attacks on Head Start’s quality regulations, but research suggests even more benefits if Democrats pushed even harder — to expand Head Start access.

Or, similarly, English learner students will benefit if Congress disposes of the Trump administration’s English-only crusades — but they’ll benefit far more if it keeps going and invests in growing access to bilingual learning across the country.

Finally, Congress might insist on meaningful oversight of the new federal school choice tax credit — and then go further, reforming it to push more resources to public school choice programs with much firmer grounding in research — and admissions policies that don’t violate students’ civil rights.

Indeed, anxious reformers might pause a moment to reapply their old formula: Right now, reform priorities from 2007 aren’t the only policy ideas that would benefit kids — whatever adults’ 2027–28 political hangups may be.

The views expressed here are Conor P. Williams’s alone, and do not reflect those of his employer or any other affiliated organizations.

text:
Virginia’s masking ban and identification requirements for federal officers likely violate the US Constitution, a federal appeals court ruled in an opinion that also backed the state’s ability to refuse to help enforce immigration laws.

A panel of the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit lifted a preliminary injunction to allow the state to enforce its law dictating terms for local cooperation with federal law enforcement.

The federal government can’t make the state or its localities assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts. Nothing about Virginia’s decision to limit when its agents may do so violates the law, Judge Toby J. Heytens, a Biden appointee, said.

The statute doesn’t require the federal government to do anything or prevent private parties from entering into contracts with it, Heytens said. And it doesn’t violate the contract clause of the Constitution because the agreements allow the state party to unilaterally terminate without cause, and, even if they didn’t, Virginia “would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing new terms for future cooperation,” Heytens said.

The court affirmed, however, a preliminary injunction barring enforcement of a new state law dictating when federal officers may wear facial coverings and requiring them to display visible identification while performing their federal duties.

The same way the US Congress can’t issue orders to the states, the states can’t command the federal government, Heytens said.

A chorus of federal courts across the country have halted the enforcement of similar state laws prohibiting ICE officers from concealing their identities.

DeAndrea Gist Benjamin, also a Biden appointee, joined the decision. Judge Robert B. King, appointed by Bill Clinton, concurred in part and dissented in part.

King said he would have vacated the injunction barring enforcement of Virginia’s mask and identity law.

Laws enacted by a sovereign state “traditionally enjoy a presumption of constitutionality,” and that’s especially true when state’s are acting pursuant to their traditional police powers, he said.

The masking and identify law regulates “only a limited aspect of an officer’s public conduct,” and it doesn’t prohibit or dictate the performance of their duties, King said. The law makes exceptions where masks or anonymity may be necessary for officer safety or the performance of certain operations.

“Those accommodations are significant and they demonstrate that the Commonwealth is not seeking to impede federal law-enforcement functions,” King said.

text:
Los Angeles – In a brief filed in federal court on November 20, children incarcerated at the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, Texas (Dilley) again speak out against the government’s shameful noncompliance with the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA). The brief was filed by Plaintiff co-counsel, the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law, the National Center for Youth Law, and Children’s Rights.

For more than a year and a half, the government has refused to tell children at Dilley about their most basic Flores rights. The Court has repeatedly ruled that children are entitled to the notice necessary to act on them. Yet children aren’t even given a simple list of these rights, let alone opportunities to learn about them from a lawyer in a know-your-rights training. They also are not receiving free phone calls to their attorneys to which the Settlement entitles them.

Families Deliberately Kept in the Dark

Families repeatedly report that the internet and email restrictions at Dilley make it nearly impossible to work on their immigration cases or advocate for themselves, while limited interpretation services exacerbate the challenges. Legal service provider RAICES has offered regular know-your-rights presentations. ICE has refused for over a year to allow such presentations and has not answered a FOIA request asking why.

Over the course of 15 Dilley site visits, Flores counsel interviewed more than 200 families. None recalled learning about their child’s comprehensive Flores rights from ICE or its contractor, CoreCivic. The only “rights” information many families received was a statement from ICE that children cannot be held more than 20 days, on an English-language form that many couldn’t read and weren’t allowed to keep. Since countless children have been held far longer, some for 50, 70, or more than 100 days – this information made no sense to them.

Rather than provide children with notice of their Flores rights, families reported ICE told them misinformation like they “don’t qualify for Flores,” that they had “lost [their] chance [to use it],” or that Flores is “history.” ICE says it meets its obligations with a generic immigration video and a resident handbook, neither of which mentions Flores.

Recent declarations taken from parents and children at the time attorneys met with them, and filed along with plaintiff’s motion, provide a stark contrast to ICE’s claims of compliance with Flores.

“Bluey, just Bluey, the whole time.” This is the only video one family saw.

– W.T.P., 10, detained at Dilley for over a month with their mother and eight-year-old brother. Decl. ¶ 8.

“When we arrived at Dilley, there was an orientation, but I only remember that they told me I would be deported . . . No one has ever mentioned Flores to me or told me that my child and I have any rights related to conditions or release.”

–Y.Z., 36, mother detained at Dilley for 33 days with their seven-year-old daughter; separated from their breastfeeding one-year-old son. Decl. ¶¶ 15, 19.

“The staff has not explained our rights to us. What we learn is from the other people detained with us.”

–M.M.V., 15, detained at Dilley for 36 days with their father. Decl. ¶ 35.

Meanwhile, children continue to suffer. Other signed declarations included in this motion (excerpts can be found below) add to the horrific narrative of abuse and neglect that Flores counsel continue to record at Dilley. Families describe prolonged detention, delayed or denied medical care, lights that never turn off and noise that prevents sleep, food children won’t eat, and water they can’t drink. Without knowledge of their rights or access to an attorney, the pattern of mistreatment continues unabated, in violation of Flores, and of the basic moral principles of respect and dignity that every child and every human deserves.

What counsel are asking the court to order

Plaintiffs have repeatedly raised these violations with the government in correspondence, meetings, mediation sessions, and court filings since May 2025. ICE has made no attempt to address and correct them and instead maintains that no violations exist.

Plaintiffs’ motion therefore asks the Court to give every child and parent: an approved Notice of Rights document within 24 hours of arrival in a language they understand and are allowed to keep, a list of legal service providers and instructions for free calls and emails to attorneys, and a know-your-rights training by qualified providers, with records of compliance to be filed with the court.

Excerpts from declarations made by parents and children confined at Dilley

Unmet medical and mental health care

“My son has regressed so much here. He doesn’t talk anymore. He used to talk before coming here. There is no therapy here for children with autism.” (J.M.O. Decl. ¶¶ 23-25)

“My older son has been biting the inside and outside of his hands due to the stress of being here.” (E.N.P. Decl. ¶ 11)

A child with respiratory issues was denied a breathing apparatus, and a mother with a tumor was denied appropriate care. (D.L.R. Decl. ¶¶ 37, 43)

Prolonged detention

“This is a prison sentence that has no release date.” (M.T. Decl. ¶ 39)

“I am really good at fixing things. I like finding a way to solve hard problems. It’s really hard to be in this place where I am powerless. I don’t think I will ever get over the trauma of being detained by ICE and seeing my mom go down on the airplane. These memories keep replaying in my head.” (S.N.K. Decl. ¶ 23)

Sleep deprivation

“He is also afraid to go to sleep because of the nighttime patrols, but then in the morning, he does not want to wake up.” (X.W. Decl. ¶ 18)

“We suffer a lot because they make us keep the lights on throughout the night.” (Y.P.R. Decl. ¶ 12)

Unsafe and inadequate food and water

“I feel hungry a lot here.” (J.P.R. Decl. ¶ 30)

“I ate chicken at lunchtime, but it looked like it had blood inside it. It made me feel bad right away, and I started vomiting.” (S.N.K. Decl. ¶ 19)

“I had some cornflakes from the cafeteria in my room, and the staff inspected my things, found the cornflakes, and threw them away. I got so upset again, because I only took them to be able to feed my daughter. The people who work here have stone-cold hearts.” (K.O.C Decl. ¶ ¶ 20-21)

Mistreatment by staff

“An officer threatened to hit my seven-year-old the other day.” (D.L.R. Decl. ¶ 34)

An officer responded to a mother’s disclosure that her son has autism by saying, “Oh, so now everyone has autism.” (J.M.O. Decl. ¶ 32)

“When we got to the center in El Paso, my little sister and I saw a paper that called us ‘aliens.’ That made us feel really awful and like there is something wrong with us. They treat us like we are something bad when we are just kids.” (M.A.G.Z. Decl ¶ 24)

Senators call for Inspector General investigation into reports that ICE is concealing the whereabouts of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders, leaving families and attorneys unable to locate them.

Text of Letter (PDF)

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) led 18 of their Senate colleagues in calling on the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Inspector General to investigate reports that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) stopped listing thousands of detainees with final deportation orders in its public Online Detainee Locator System (ODLS), leaving families and attorneys unable to determine where they are being held.

The lawmakers pressed DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari to investigate whether ICE deliberately changed its policy to exclude people with final removal orders from the locator system. The senators asked the Inspector General to determine when the change was made and how many detainees have been affected.

“[T]he Department of Homeland Security (DHS) appears to have made an intentional policy change — without any warning to the public — to exclude people with final removal orders from ODLS,” wrote the senators.

In April 2026, Senator Warren led 32 members of Congress in asking the Inspector General to investigate ICE’s failure to maintain an accurate and timely detainee locator system. In August, the Inspector General acknowledged that the request raised important questions about due process and the well-being of detainees and their families but said the office did not intend to begin an evaluation at that time. The latest reports raise fresh concerns that ICE is not simply failing to update the system, but intentionally preventing certain detainees from appearing in it altogether.

“Without knowing their client’s detention location, attorneys cannot file time-sensitive habeas petitions in the proper venue and cannot intervene to challenge third-country removals. Families and attorneys are now left scrambling to find out where the affected detainees have been taken,” continued the senators.

The lawmakers highlighted that removing individuals’ records while they remain in detention can also increase the risk of serious physical harm, particularly amid growing reports of medical neglect and fatalities in immigration detention facilities.

They pressed DHS Inspector General Cuffari to determine:

Whether ICE has instructed personnel not to provide detainees’ locations to family members or attorneys;

How many detainees have been removed from the ODLS while remaining in custody;

And whether detainees have been transferred, deported, or required medical attention after their records disappeared from the system.

“Erasing detained individuals from a public searchable system eliminates transparency. It can put lives at risk while making it easier for ICE to conceal any harm against people in immigration detention,” continued the senators.

In addition to Warren, Van Hollen, and Luján, the letter was signed by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Richard Durbin (D-Ill.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Tina Smith (D-Minn.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Angus King (I-Maine), Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.).

text:
By Alison Kuznitz

Attorney General Andrea Campbell sued U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Monday and accused the agency’s officers of continuing to make civil arrests at courthouses in violation of a state law that took effect earlier this month.

Immigrant safeguards embedded in the PROTECT Act kicked in on Nov. 3, including a provision that bars ICE agents from making civil immigration arrests at state courthouses without judicial warrants, Campbell’s office said. In the last two and a half weeks, the AG’s office said, ICE has arrested at least 38 people at Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants.

“ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable,” Campbell said. “ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE’s actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved.”

The lawsuit itself extends beyond the state law, and challenges a May 2025 ICE directive that allows for arrests in state courthouses “even when the state prohibits them,” according to Campbell’s office. That policy “was ruled unlawful and vacated by a federal court in California in June 2026, but ICE continues to carry out such arrests,” the office said.

Campbell did not sue to enforce the PROTECT Act against ICE directly, but rather brought claims under the federal Administrative Procedure Act and the 10th Amendment.

Campbell is asking the U.S. District Court in Boston to issue an order vacating the directive and barring civil immigration arrests at state courts unless state law permits them.

“Time and time again, sanctuary politicians in Massachusetts have made the dumbfounding choice to prioritize dangerous criminal illegal aliens rather than their law-abiding American citizens,” acting ICE Boston Field Office Director Joseph Sher, who is named as a defendant in Campbell’s suit, said in an October press release. “While these politicians continue to waste valuable time, energy and resources passing embarrassingly performative legislation such as the Protect Act, [Enforcement and Removal Operations] Boston will continue to proudly protect Massachusetts communities from these dangerous criminals.”

Campbell is holding a press conference to discuss the lawsuit Monday afternoon.

text:
A new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule would unlawfully strip federal housing assistance from mixed-status families, according to a new lawsuit filed by Washington and 22 other plaintiffs.

Under the new rule, any household with at least one member who is not eligible for housing assistance due to their immigration status would be cut off from HUD assistance entirely, even though federal subsidies are already prorated to only include eligible individuals in those households. The change means about 600 mixed-status families in Washington face the prospect of losing their homes or having to split up. The rule is expected to heavily impact children, with HUD’s own analysis estimating that 65% of eligible members of mixed-status families are under the age of 18.

“Because of this unlawful rule, hundreds of Washington families face homelessness,” Attorney General Nick Brown said. “Our office will fight this administration’s cruel attempt to upend federal housing policy so we can keep families in Washington stable and defend the rule of law.”

The rule also imposes a sweeping requirement that all U.S. citizens in federal housing programs undertake additional and potentially burdensome steps to once again establish their eligibility or risk eviction. In Washington, about 82,000 people who have already demonstrated their eligibility would be subject to these new requirements.

Under the new rule, every U.S. citizen would also need to provide their Social Security number and consent to have their citizenship status checked through the federal SAVE database. If SAVE cannot automatically confirm their citizenship, U.S. citizens would have to produce official documents to prove their status, such as an original or certified birth certificate, naturalization certificate, or passport.

In a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Brown and the coalition argue that the rule illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal policy, and clear Congressional intent, allowing mixed-status families to stay together and violates the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding HUD’s authority to enact this arbitrary new restriction.

For nearly 30 years, federal housing programs have provided housing assistance to low-income families even if not every household member is eligible for assistance. Under this system, known as proration, HUD reduces the family’s subsidy so it covers only the eligible household members. Congress codified this protection in 1997, explicitly stating that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them. The new HUD rule eliminates this protection.

Under the administration’s new rule, a family can stay in HUD-assisted housing only if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant. As a result, U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants who live with an ineligible relative will be forced to choose between maintaining their housing and keeping their family together.

Nationwide, HUD estimates that around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, will lose their housing assistance. This includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. The agency also acknowledges that the rule will lead to evictions and displacement, and that many of these families could become homeless.

The coalition asserts that the rule will increase homelessness and shift major costs onto state and local governments. By HUD’s own estimates, sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per person each year.

Brown and the coalition argue that HUD’s new rule exceeds the agency’s authority and violates federal law, which expressly allows prorated assistance for mixed-status families and establishes different documentation requirements for U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants aged 62 and older. They argue that HUD also violated the Administrative Procedure Act by issuing an arbitrary and capricious rule. The coalition is asking the court to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities.

Joining Brown in filing this lawsuit, which is led by the attorneys general of New York, California, and Massachusetts, are the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaiʻi, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Wisconsin, the District of Columbia, and the governor of Pennsylvania.

text:
Five EU countries announced the opening of a migration deportation center in Rwanda as part of an effort to boost removals. While this seems effective, human rights groups criticized the plans, saying that EU countries cannot guarantee that migrants’ human rights would be respected in Rwanda. This event highlights the broader issue of the harmful effects of offshore detention on migrants and asylum seekers. In Australia, an abusive detention policy has been in place since September 2001, sending over 5,000 migrants to Nauru and Manus Island, Papua New Guinea, causing profound harm to men, women, and children seeking refuge, said Annabel Hennessy, an Australian researcher at Human Rights Watch. In the U.S., the current administration has escalated the use of third-country deportations in an attempt to expand the abrasive U.S. immigration law. This issue is significant internationally because offshore detention shifts the responsibility away from the countries who send migrants there, making it difficult to ensure that migrants are treated well.

After World War II, many countries signed international accords to prevent sending refugees back to places where they might be persecuted, but governments still wanted to block the entry of refugees. One of the methods of doing so was by offshoring the detention and processing of asylum seekers. An early example of this was in the early 1990s when the U.S. Coast Guard started intercepting asylum seekers at sea and taking them to the U.S. naval base at Guantanamo, where they were granted fewer rights than they would have on the mainland. Inspired by this model, Australia created its own offshore detention system called the Pacific Solution, sending asylees to Nauru and Manus Island, Papua New Guinea.

The UN Committee Against Torture has condemned Denmark’s recently planned offshore schemes with Rwanda, citing Rwanda’s history of human rights violations. The Supreme Court of the United Kingdom blocked the policy when the UK tried to send asylum seekers to Rwanda for similar reasons.

Existing Responses

Current responses to offshore detention have mainly included public advocacy, for example, the ‘Let them Stay’ campaign in Australia, where protests occurred, and doctors refused to discharge patients when it was unsafe for them to return to detention. Churches proposed invoking the right to sanctuary to prevent asylees from being removed, and states offered support for them too. Because of these efforts, the government reversed its position and allowed 267 asylum seekers to remain in Australia. Legal routes also have helped, with notable cases employing constitutional law, tort law, and international criminal law.

Attempts at systemic change to refugee and asylum policy through the legal route have had limited success. For example, according to Cambridge University Press, the government of Australia has acted to legislate to anticipate the outcome of litigation challenging the legal basis for offshore detention, limited avenues for judicial review, and has restricted the jurisdiction of Australian courts to hear claims concerning offshore detention. All of these factors make it challenging to litigate the underlying policies and seek redress for detainees. There are clear constraints on the law’s ability to drive policy change.

David Scott Fitzgerald, the Theodore E. Gildred Chair in U.S.-Mexican Relations and Professor of Sociology at the University of California, San Diego, shares his thoughts on this. He claims, “The real rationale for countries wishing to offshore the processing and detention of asylum seekers and even long-term immigrants is to create a spectacle of control while hiding individual immigrants in legal black holes.” Under the Trump administration in the U.S., many instances of offshoring have happened extrajudicially, through orders from the Department of Homeland Security and not immigration judges. This suggests that offshore detention policies may serve not only to deter migration but also to create a spectacle of government control. This is a clear undermining of current policy, worsening the issue. Overall, though, the problem seems to persist because offshore detention provides a shifting of the burden to other countries.

For future efforts to succeed, there needs to be a focus on not only changing policy but also ensuring it is actually upheld. Various legal and non-legal strategies have been used to challenge offshore detention, but in the case of the United States, if the rules can be undermined easily, there needs to be an emphasis on accountability. Therefore, the need for a different approach is apparent.

Possible Solutions

For change to occur, policy change is crucial. However, if existing policies aren’t being followed, how would policy change be effective? Therefore, compliance with immigration and asylum policy should be gradually strengthened alongside the introduction of new policy restrictions with stricter standards. Policy reform without effective accountability may reproduce the weaknesses of existing systems.

It is imperative to implement actionable goals to ensure human rights. Legislative oversight could reduce the limited transparency surrounding offshore detention and third-country agreements through mandatory reports, hearings, or investigations and explore violations. Alongside these oversight efforts, reform of the system can begin through gradual, incremental change.

An initial step would be to restrict offshore transfers to centers that can demonstrate adequate human rights protections for migrants and require independent legal review before third-country removals, making it easier to challenge transfers before they occur. While this is happening, offshore detention facilities should be monitored for compliance through regulations with independent inspections and public reports.

When violations occur, there are certain mechanisms through which migrants, lawyers, and organizations can respond. This can include guaranteeing migrants access to legal representation, allowing migrants to challenge unsafe conditions. Additionally, violations can be met with consequences, such as suspending transfers to noncompliant facilities or requiring the transfer of detainees to safe conditions when treatment is not corrected by certain deadlines. Legislation can be introduced to restrict funding for detention centers that have violations until compliance with policy is verified.

Finally, there can be an emphasis on expanding alternatives to detention, such as community-based asylum processing instead of offshore detention.

International organizations can collaborate to ensure practices are being met. Unfortunately, it is highly likely that some national governments will oppose the proposed reform, because it poses a threat to their illusion of control. Governments may even argue that offshore processing is necessary to support migration management or deterrence. However, tying government funding to independently reviewed compliance standards could create financial consequences for violations, reducing reliance on governments voluntarily following regulations.

Overall, this strategy could strengthen accountability by making it more difficult for governments to circumvent existing policies and avoid responsibility for the treatment of migrants and asylum seekers. By combining stronger enforcement mechanisms with gradual policy reform, governments can begin addressing the systemic weaknesses that have allowed offshore detention practices to persist for so long.
