title: ICE: release Dr Lawani and stop the anti-immigrant repression - PSI
description:
“We need more nurses like Dr Lawani.
And the AFT president was clear about the demand we all must make: Dr Ann Lawani “must be freed”.
Dr Lawani holds a valid US work permit, which runs until 2029.
In it, the union describes Dr Ann Lawani as representing “the best of us: a hardworking, dedicated nurse who committed herself fully to her education and profession”.
We therefore demand the immediate and unconditional release of Dr Ann Lawani.
text:
PSI General Secretary Daniel Bertossa expressed PSI’s concern that Dr Lawani, who was on the front line of care during the COVID-19 pandemic and is mentoring a new generation of nurses at a crucial time of health worker shortages, could be treated so unjustly. “We need more nurses like Dr Lawani. The United States should be celebrating her and not hounding her”, he said.

National Nurses United (NNU), a PSI affiliate, has called for her immediate release, pointing out that ICE purposely disappeared her “so as to deny her rights to communication with her family and her right to timely legal representation”. The American Nurses Association and the American Association of Colleges of Nursing have also issued a joint statement expressing their concern and highlighting how such arrests have “effects on nurses, their families, and the patients, students, and communities who rely on them”.

her detention – and disappearance from the ICE database – is a horrifying and despicable situation

Randi Weingarten, president of the PSI-affiliated American Federation of Teachers (AFT), of which Dr Lawani is a member, described her as a “valued mentor and constructive force in her community”, adding that “her detention – and disappearance from the ICE database – is a horrifying and despicable situation”. And the AFT president was clear about the demand we all must make: Dr Ann Lawani “must be freed”.

Dr Lawani, a Nigerian immigrant to the United States, is a professor of nursing. Dr Kabir Ado Sani Minjibir, president of the PSI-affiliated Medical and Health Workers’ Union of Nigeria (MHWUN) and national chairperson of the Nigerian Joint Health Sector Unions (JOHESU), has called for justice for Dr Lawani and respect for migrant health workers. Dr Minjibir, who is also chairperson of the West African Health Sector Unions’ Network (WAHSUN), said that “health workers like Dr Ann Lawani play crucial roles in the United States’ health care system and deserve respect, not humiliation. She must be released from the clutches of ICE immediately.”

The Lagos State council of the National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives (NANNM) has also issued a statement. In the statement, signed by Comrade Christiana Adeboboye, chair of the council, the association stressed that the arrest and detention of Dr Lawani violated the tenets of “human dignity, fundamental rights, fairness and due process”. The statement ended with the association declaring its solidarity with Dr Lawani and issuing a “call on the relevant authorities to act urgently to secure her release and prevent her deportation”.

This case is bizarre on so many levels. Dr Lawani holds a valid US work permit, which runs until 2029. But ICE has never cared for such niceties. It is an authoritarian enforcement arm of a state that has consistently attacked public services and working people, scapegoating immigrants for the failure of the neoliberal policies it pursues.

tens of thousands of working people have been disappeared by the Trump administration’s cruel policies

But fight back we must – against this illegal detention and against the authoritarian right-wing politics it represents. The NNU has launched an online petition, which we urge you to sign. In it, the union describes Dr Ann Lawani as representing “the best of us: a hardworking, dedicated nurse who committed herself fully to her education and profession”. The petition also sets out the broader context, pointing out that “tens of thousands of working people have been disappeared by the Trump administration’s cruel policies”.

Dr Lawani is a model of the public service that members of PSI affiliates in the United States and across the world deliver to keep society running, as nurses, doctors, community health workers, firefighters, sanitation workers and more. Her arrest and detention also reflect right-wing attacks by neoliberal governments on public services and the working class, in the interest of the 1%, using false narratives that present migrants, and the “other” in whatever form, as the problem.

These narratives, which are used to justify ICE and its violence, aim to turn mass anger away from the failure of their system, which puts the profits of a few billionaires above the wellbeing of people and the planet. PSI and our unions are fighting back with the Public Service Fightback campaign. We will defend public services. We will defend the leaders and members of our unions, and the publics we serve. We will fight every inch of the way until we win.

The arrest and continued detention of Dr Ann Lawani is an assault on her, an assault on the fight for universal access to quality public services, and an attempt to shatter our solidarity. It is an attack on us all. It is an attack we must resist. We therefore demand the immediate and unconditional release of Dr Ann Lawani.

title: Stop, Hide, Deport: ICE Scandals Continue; the Latest Involves a Flight Boarding in Seattle

During the confrontation, they assert, several passengers obstructed their work, and one of them, Sofía Hernández, "threw hot coffee" at the ICE members.

text:
A video of an ICE operation, the U.S. immigration agency, at Seattle airport, featuring masked agents dragging two desperate passengers across the boarding ramp of an Alaska Airlines flight, has gone viral. Another scandal, another display of impunity, another action without protocols. The scene is, once again, heartbreaking. A woman screams that they are taking her daughter who has a work permit, while other travelers watch the detention in shock.

The airline stated that it had not received prior notice and described the incident as "distressing." The Immigration and Customs Enforcement has claimed in a statement that its agents were at the airport to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican who "stayed longer than allowed by his visa in violation of our nation's laws." During the confrontation, they assert, several passengers obstructed their work, and one of them, Sofía Hernández, "threw hot coffee" at the ICE members. She was also detained, accused of overstaying her visa.

The main issue with the video is that it does not show an exception, but a pattern. Washington Governor, Democrat Bob Ferguson, has denounced that ICE's tactics are "deeply un-American" and is one of the politicians calling for the agency's abolition. "The video is horrifying and chilling. We need an immigration control and border security system that is effective, ethical, and humane. And ICE is not. It is irreformable," he lamented at a press conference. The governor indicated that his team is now investigating why ICE agents were able to reach the finger, thereby violating a state law he signed in March that limits the use of ski masks and masks by law enforcement members.

Ten months ago, Minneapolis became the epicenter of national outrage after federal agents killed Renée Good and Alex Pretti, two U.S. citizens, during protests against immigration operations. In front of cameras, with hundreds of witnesses. Their deaths sparked protests, investigations, and a political crisis that ultimately led Donald Trump to replace both the Secretary of Homeland Security and the head of the Border Patrol. Since then, media attention has shifted, but scandals have not ceased. On the contrary.

An investigation by the San Francisco Chronicle, published this month, counted at least 62 deaths in ICE custody since January of last year and found that the mortality rate had reached extraordinary levels. According to reports and internal investigations by federal agencies, 23 of the immigrants who died in custody between January 2025 and January 2026 had received poor medical care, especially in centers managed by private companies, particularly GEO Group and CoreCivic.

Associated Press has documented at least 10 suicides of detainees since Donald Trump's return to the White House and found cases of delayed medical and psychological care, systematically ignored warning signs, and vulnerable individuals held in isolation. Or individuals released thousands of miles from their families, without resources or even appropriate clothing to face winter, leading to the deaths of several, including a Haitian immigrant with mental health issues near Pittsburgh.

ABC News has counted at least 21 people shot by federal immigration agents during Trump's second term up to September; eight of whom died, including three U.S. citizens. There are hundreds of documented cases across the country where the Administration has violated court orders during arrests. In many of these cases, the detained individuals had pending asylum requests or other immigration proceedings and none had a final deportation order. In July, an investigation by several media outlets and a report from Human Rights Watch documented allegations of beatings, lack of medical care, and unsanitary conditions at the Camp East Montana facility in Texas.

One of the most striking contributions was published by The Washington Post just two weeks ago. After a hack of a Homeland Security database exposed the data of over 1,500 agents hired since 2005, the newspaper revealed that at least 19 ICE agents had a concerning history. Five of them had been involved in incidents related to excessive use of force. Another five had been sued, and the proceedings ended with financial settlements to the victims. At least six had been fired, lost their badges, or left their positions under threat of dismissal. Among them was an agent from Detroit who shot a fleeing teenager in the back and a New York detective convicted of stealing champagne.

The agency, pressured by the need to hire and deploy agents to meet the White House's demands, has eliminated filters and procedures. Training that used to last months is now done in days or hours. Serious offenses are overlooked. Protocols for action and review are nonexistent. Departments have daily quotas for detainees and use applications designed by Palantir, the company of Peter Thiel, to identify their targets in each neighborhood.

Everything surrounding the detentions breaks with the tradition of civil rights. When ICE detains a person, it is customary for them to be taken to a processing office and then transferred to an immigration detention center. But not necessarily a center close to the arrest location; they can put them on a plane and take them to facilities in other states, distancing them from their families and lawyers. Although the agency's rules stipulate that transfers should be reported and that the person can call upon arriving at the new center, there are thousands of examples where this has not been done. In practice, families can go days or weeks without knowing where the detainees are.

Finding someone is not easy. The system requires precise data, and it is not enough to just call and provide a name. A migration registration number, known as an A-number, the date of birth, and the country of origin are required, and the data enters the system very slowly. For many families, obtaining that number is practically impossible if the person has not been able to call, does not have documents with them, or has not had the opportunity to share it. Since September, this problem has worsened as ICE has stopped showing in the search tool that is theoretically available online certain individuals with final deportation orders and, according to various journalistic investigations, has instructed its agents not to communicate their whereabouts to family members or lawyers over the phone.

Equally serious or worse is when the process ends in deportations to third countries. The Administration's policy, cheered during the elections, was to carry out the largest deportations in history. And it does not matter where. The agreement with El Salvador to send detainees to its prisons became very famous. But there is much more. ICE expels individuals not to their country of origin but to states that agree to accept them through diplomatic agreements, even if they have no nationality, family, ties, or knowledge of the language there.

text:
A video of masked ICE agents arresting a father and his adult daughter inside an Alaska Airlines jet bridge at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning has since gone viral and sparked outrage from both the community and political leaders,

ICE confirmed that on Nov. 21. The agency said both people arrested are originally from Mexico and have overstayed their visas,

PREVIOUS COVERAGE |

Olia Catala, a local immigration attorney, is representing both detainees and confirmed to KOMO News that they're currently being held in the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.

Ricardo and Sofia, who are father and daughter, came to the U.S. legally in 2015 with tourist visas, according to Catala. A person can typically stay in the U.S. for up to six months under a tourist visa.

Catala said Ricardo has a pending asylum application, and Sofia was originally listed as a derivative asylee on her father's application. Since then, Sofia has reportedly married a U.S. citizen and is in the process of obtaining a Green Card, Catala confirmed.

Catala alleges both of her clients have been allowed to stay in the U.S. legally because they have pending asylum, which is also how they have had work permits continuously renewed.

"Technically, ICE can arrest somebody in that circumstance and place them in removal proceedings, but generally speaking, if they have a pending application that puts them in this toll status, ICE hasn't gone after them," said Adam Boyd.

Boyd is also a local immigration and removal defense attorney, and he currently serves as chair of the Washington state chapter of the American Immigration Lawyers Association. Boyd is not involved in Sofia and Ricardo's case.

He said ICE arrests of non-citizens with pending immigration status and no criminal history, like Sofia and Ricardo, have allegedly become more common under the Trump administration. Boyd also confirmed that it's typical for an asylum application to remain pending for several years due to court backlog and the lack of a local office in Washington.

"An application filed in the Pacific Northwest, it's not unusual that it would be pending for 12 years before you get an interview on that application," he said as an example.

SEE ALSO |

ICE said in a statement shared Saturday that Sofia will also be charged with assaulting a federal officer because she "hurled hot coffee on the officers." Catala denied that the coffee was intentionally thrown.

She, and at least one traveler who witnessed and recorded the arrests, claimed the coffee was knocked out of someone's hands by agents after they "lunged" at Ricardo.

"[The officers] took the father to the ground and knocked the coffee out of the family member's hands, threw coffee, and that put coffee onto other passengers," said John Gaedeke, who was in the jet bridge when the arrests happened Saturday.

Regardless, Boyd explained an immigration judge is likely to take ICE's word for what happened between Sofia and the arresting officers, which he said will have implications for her potential release from custody.

"If it's written in a report that she assaulted the officers, it's going to be a serious, negative factor," Boyd continued, "and it might actually lead to her being denied bond."

Catala maintains that neither Sofia nor Ricardo has any sort of criminal history or prior arrests in the U.S. She said she will fight to have them both released from ICE custody on bond.

"This is happening way too often," she said over the phone. "Detention centers are filled with people who have no criminal records and are picked up this way."

KOMO News has reached out to ICE for confirmation of Sofia and Ricardo's lack of criminal history, as well as to Tacoma Immigration Court to inquire about scheduled court proceedings.

title: Judge fast-tracks NJ challenge to ICE's Roxbury detention center contract
description:
State officials say the federal government is violating a court order by moving ahead with plans for the facility before completing an environmental review.
New Jersey attorneys contend that the contract effectively commits the federal government to building the detention center before the environmental review is completed, undermining the purpose of the judge’s order.
In a Nov. 20 filing, Justice Department attorney Krystal-Rose Perez said the contract expressly prohibits renovations to house immigrant detainees until the environmental review is completed.
She argued that the state had failed to identify any contract provision showing that ICE had authorized construction in violation of the court order.
Federal officials have since confirmed that ICE intends to pursue some level of detention capacity at the warehouse, subject to environmental review and the court order.
text:
State officials say the federal government is violating a court order by moving ahead with plans for the facility before completing an environmental review.

A federal judge has agreed to expedite proceedings in New Jersey’s challenge to a federal contract to turn a vacant Roxbury warehouse into an immigrant detention center, setting up a dispute with the Trump administration over whether there is any urgency in resolving the matter.

At the center of the dispute is a contract that could be worth nearly $1 billion over five years. The federal government has initially committed $31.8 million, but New Jersey officials argue that moving forward with the contract before completing a required environmental review violates a court order issued in May.

U.S. District Judge Jamel K. Semper approved an expedited filing schedule Friday, Nov. 20, requiring New Jersey to file a motion to enforce his earlier order by Monday, Nov. 23. Federal attorneys have until Dec. 2 to respond, and the state has until Dec. 7 to reply.

The Justice Department asked Semper to reconsider the accelerated schedule, arguing that the contract does not authorize renovations prohibited by the May order and that the state’s concerns do not warrant urgent court intervention.

New Jersey attorneys contend that the contract effectively commits the federal government to building the detention center before the environmental review is completed, undermining the purpose of the judge’s order.

“Defendants have already committed — in writing and financially — to the renovations before actually undertaking the required environmental assessment,” Shankar Duraiswamy of the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office wrote in court papers.

“At a minimum, defendants’ actions raise significant concerns that merit this court’s prompt attention and an expedited briefing schedule,” he wrote.

The contract, awarded Nov. 5 to a Tennessee-based company, calls for maintaining the Route 46 property, designing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s preferred plan for converting the warehouse into a detention center, and conducting the environmental review.

The initial $31.8 million commitment is part of a contract with options that could bring its total value to nearly $1 billion over five years.

Duraiswamy argued that only $650,000 of the initial contract is allocated to the environmental assessment. He also pointed to a provision allowing “interior construction or reconfiguration of administrative and office space while environmental review is ongoing.”

“It is hard to fathom that defendants are paying more than $30 million for just a few months of site maintenance and the preparation of design documents,” he wrote.

Under Semper’s May 12 order, federal immigration authorities can perform basic security and maintenance work at the property, but cannot proceed with converting it into a detention center until the required environmental assessment is completed.

New Jersey officials argue that the order was intended to preserve the status quo, giving the state and local officials an opportunity to review the environmental findings and potentially challenge the project before the federal government commits to construction.

“The purpose of the May 12 order was to freeze the status quo to allow for a genuine environmental assessment — and, if necessary, litigation over its findings and further steps — before defendants committed to constructing a facility that will impose severe harms on local infrastructure, public health, and the environment,” Duraiswamy wrote.

Federal attorneys dispute the state’s interpretation.

In a Nov. 20 filing, Justice Department attorney Krystal-Rose Perez said the contract expressly prohibits renovations to house immigrant detainees until the environmental review is completed. She argued that the state had failed to identify any contract provision showing that ICE had authorized construction in violation of the court order.

“Plaintiffs still fail to provide any provision of the contract evidencing a supposed violation of the May 12 order,” Perez wrote. “Instead, plaintiffs rely only on their own disbelief — and apparent misunderstanding of contract costs — to take aim at the maintenance and design tasks.”

Perez said the only work currently authorized under the contract involves environmental compliance, maintenance, and design. The federal government has not committed funds to renovations that would house detainees, she said.

She also argued that New Jersey’s anticipated motion to enforce the order was unnecessary and did not warrant shortening the federal government’s response time by five days, particularly during the Thanksgiving holiday.

The latest filings are part of a months-long legal battle over the federal government’s plans for the Roxbury warehouse, which could eventually house between 500 and 1,500 immigrant detainees.

The Trump administration purchased the Route 46 property in February for $129.3 million. New Jersey officials sued in March, alleging that ICE had failed to comply with federal environmental laws and requirements to consult with state and local governments before moving ahead with the project.

After Semper issued his May order restricting activity at the property, federal attorneys initially said the Department of Homeland Security had abandoned plans to convert the warehouse into a detention facility. Two weeks later, the agency changed course, saying no final decision had been made.

Federal officials have since confirmed that ICE intends to pursue some level of detention capacity at the warehouse, subject to environmental review and the court order.

The property has drawn scrutiny over ICE’s use of the site. Immigration authorities acknowledged that agents brought more than a dozen immigrants to the warehouse on two occasions in September following enforcement operations in Dover and Ledgewood. Officials said the activity stopped after the Newark field office director instructed agents to end the practice.

title: As the Trump administration puts ankle monitors on more immigrants, it's taking ... - WBEZ Chicago
description:
Lately, Liz has been jolted awake at night in a panic when her ankle monitor starts to vibrate.
Her husband was taken into immigration custody while Liz was fitted with an ankle monitor and released with her 15-year-old daughter.
So far this year, ICE’s Chicago field office — which oversees Illinois, Indiana, Wisconsin, Missouri, Kentucky, and Kansas — has issued nearly 3,800 ankle monitors — a nearly 40% jump since 2024.

Human rights advocates argue that the federal ankle monitor policy is not necessary and is driven by cruelty and the profits the companies who supply the ankle monitors are making.
text:
Lately, Liz has been jolted awake at night in a panic when her ankle monitor starts to vibrate. The buzzing reminds her of her greatest fear: that immigration agents will barge into her small apartment on Chicago’s North Side and take her away to a detention center.

“ICE agents told me the monitor would vibrate if it’s broken or tampered with,” she says crying. “ ‘We’ll look for you right away,’ ” she says they told her, “ ‘because we know where to find you.’ ”

The Guatemalan asylum-seeker has been living in a constant state of anxiety since she, her husband and daughter were asked to show up for an unexpected immigration check-in last August. Her husband was taken into immigration custody while Liz was fitted with an ankle monitor and released with her 15-year-old daughter. Neither she nor her husband have criminal records.

WBEZ is not using their full names because they fear government retaliation.

“I asked the immigration agents, ‘Why? Did we do something wrong?’ ” Liz says in her native Spanish, adding that since the family arrived in the United States in 2024 from Guatemala they’ve been trying to follow every step of their asylum application process by the book.

Like Liz, more than 53,000 noncitizens nationwide in 2026 have been fitted with ankle monitors under the Department of Homeland Security’s Alternatives to Detention program, according to government data. That number has more than tripled since 2024 as the Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement. It’s the same trend locally, a WBEZ/Sun-Times analysis found. So far this year, ICE’s Chicago field office — which oversees Illinois, Indiana, Wisconsin, Missouri, Kentucky, and Kansas — has issued nearly 3,800 ankle monitors — a nearly 40% jump since 2024.

The surge has raised concerns among immigration advocates over the mental health toll they say the constant surveillance takes on those who wear the ankle device and pose no risk. Advocates argue the use of ankle monitors was supposed to be an alternative to detention but as more people have been fitted with them, detentions have also increased.

“We have seen so many people across the country who have been complying with their immigration cases, who have families, who have jobs, who have strong community ties, no significant criminal history, going to their regular appointments and suddenly getting shackled with ankle monitoring,” says Lauren Hodges, senior attorney with Amica Center for Human Rights, a legal advocacy group.

Advocates like Hodges point out that the upward trend began soon after an internal Trump administration directive last year ordering immigration agents to fit noncitizens with ankle monitors “whenever possible.”

Her organization filed a class action lawsuit that accuses the Trump administration of requiring noncitizens to wear an ankle or wrist monitor without providing justification for why such “harmful and invasive” monitoriing is warranted. The lawsuit says people fitted with the devices have experienced health problems as result, such as high blood pressure, as well as anxiety and depression.

The Department of Homeland Security did not answer specific questions about its increased use of ankle monitors or any other questions about this tracking device. In a statement, the agency defended the ATD program as a critical tool to ensure “compliance with release conditions, and regular check-ins.”

The agency says people without a flight risk or criminal history are enrolled because it is the most “cost-efficient way to ensure compliance with their immigration proceedings.”

Effects on mental health

Alternatives to Detention was started more than 20 years ago as a way to keep track of immigrants who were released under supervision while facing deportation.

But advocates say the continual surveillance is just a different form of detention.

When the Trump administration stripped Haitians of their Temporary Protected Status in June — which allowed hundreds of thousands of immigrants fleeing natural disasters or political conflict back home to live and work in the U.S. temporarily — many were later fitted with ankle monitors. Among them was Pierre Damas Bel, a college student and star soccer player. News reports say he struggled deeply with the humiliation of the device, even sharing his frustrations on social media before taking his own life.

Liz and her family have also struggled with shame and anxiety around the device. At that August check-in, Liz says immigration officials openly debated putting an ankle monitor on her 15-year-old daughter, even though federal guidelines restrict ICE from placing tracking devices on minors.

Overhearing the agents, the high schooler, who plays flag football, began sobbing. She worried about being bullied at school or perceived as a criminal.

“When I saw her little face and she started crying, she said to me, ‘Mommy, I won’t be able to play anymore.’”

Agents ultimately let the teen go without one.

Since then, Liz says the shame of wearing an ankle monitor has been devastating. Strapped tightly to her leg, the device is bulky and uncomfortable.

“When I go to church, I like to wear a skirt or a dress, and now I can’t,” she says. “I have to wear a long dress so people don’t stare at me. It’s embarrassing.”

“We’re making the act of being an immigrant a criminal state,” says Jennifer Babaie, associate director of the Adult Detention Project at the National Immigrant Justice Center. “The majority of the people being arrested are folks that are applying or [are] otherwise in a legal status ... now you’re on an ankle monitor, and you’re suddenly in a completely different category. “

Not only are more people wearing ankle monitors, but they are wearing them for longer.

ICE has increasingly imposed GPS ankle monitors on immigrants even after federal judges have ordered they be released from custody because the government has failed to justify the detention, Anthony Enriquez, vice president of U.S. advocacy and litigation at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said during a recent panel led by data journalist Austin Kocher.

Human rights advocates argue that the federal ankle monitor policy is not necessary and is driven by cruelty and the profits the companies who supply the ankle monitors are making. The cost of the technology rose from roughly $25,500 per day in 2022 to more than $145,000 in 2026.

Constant anxiety the monitor won’t work

Liz says her family has always been under some form of federal surveillance. Her husband was fitted with an ankle monitor when he first arrived in the United States in 2024. Still, the family managed to find work and build a life in Chicago after fleeing violence and street crime in Guatemala. He worked as a scrap metal collector, and she cleaned homes.

Now, Liz is trying to hold the family together on her own.

But she’s struggling.

In late October, Liz received an unexpected message ordering her to report for an immigration check-in at the same building where her husband was arrested. She worried agents would accuse her of tampering with her ankle monitor and take her into custody.

“I’m coming here prepared for anything, because I don’t know what could happen to me inside,” she says.

On the morning of her appointment, Liz’s attorney could not attend, so she arranged for a pro bono lawyer to accompany her. Before heading to the check in Liz spoke with relatives about the possibility that she might not return. She says her 15-year-old daughter was crying as she walked out the door.

But this time that appointment went OK.

A technical glitch had caused her ankle monitor to stop sending location data to ICE, triggering the urgent check-in to verify she had not cut it off. Officials adjusted the device and told her she must wear it for a year and a half of full compliance before she can be moved to a phone-based check-in app.

“I think the fear is also that if you don’t do everything perfectly, even with all these barriers, that something’s going to happen to you,” says Gabriela Nicolau, the pro bono attorney who accompanied Liz.

Outside the federal building, Liz says she felt relieved — for the moment. Maybe this time, she got lucky, or bringing an attorney made a difference.

But that relief is temporary. The tracker — and the anxiety and fear it brings — isn’t going anywhere.

text:
A group of Democratic lawmakers has introduced legislation that would allow certain immigrants facing deportation to obtain green cards after spending at least a decade in the United States under removal orders.

The Protect Our Neighbors Act—which Democratic Representatives from California Lateefah Simon, Zoe Lofgren, John Garamendi and Juan Vargas introduced on Thursday—would allow the attorney general or homeland security secretary to cancel certain removal orders and adjust qualifying immigrants to lawful permanent resident status.

Since taking office in 2025, the Trump administration has tightened lawful pathways to immigration, imposing new restrictions and greater scrutiny on some people seeking green cards and other legal status in the United States.

Read More on News

Lofgren, a senior member of the House Judiciary Committee and a former immigration lawyer, said in a news release that the legislation "provides long-term residents who have built their lives here with a fair opportunity to resolve outdated removal orders and earn lawful permanent status."

Newsweek has contacted Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Lofgren's office for comment via email.

What Would Protect Our Neighbors Act Do?

The bill would make final removal orders expire after 10 years. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) could ask an immigration judge to renew an order, but it would have to justify the delay and show that renewal was in the public interest.

Under the green card provision, eligibility would be limited to immigrants whose final removal, exclusion or deportation orders were based only on certain immigration violations specified in the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Migrants would have to remain in the country for at least 10 years after the removal order and comply with an order of supervision or other conditional release without absconding.

The measure would exclude immigrants who fall under several grounds of inadmissibility listed in federal immigration law, including specified criminal and national security grounds.

Applicants seeking permanent residency under the measure would have to provide a certified copy of their most recent federal income tax return. The bill would require DHS to charge a single application fee of no more than $1,200.

The proposal's separate 10-year expiration provision would allow an immigrant whose final removal order has expired and not been renewed to petition U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for any lawful status for which the person is eligible. To qualify, the individual would have to have been continuously physically present in the country for at least 10 years and not have been convicted of a crime carrying a possible sentence of more than one year.

An expired removal order could not be renewed while such a petition was pending.

A Congressional Research Service report citing ICE data estimated that 1.6 million people on ICE's non-detained docket had final orders of removal as of February 26. A final removal order does not necessarily mean a person will be deported immediately, as removal can be delayed or suspended.

What Prompted Protect Our Neighbors Act?

In a news release announcing the bill, lawmakers cited the deportation of 73-year-old Harjit Kaur as an example of why the legislation was necessary.

The Sikh grandmother, who had lived in California for more than 30 years, was deported to India in September 2025 after being detained during a routine immigration check-in.

Simon said the bill "would provide people, like Ms. Kaur who worked in my district for decades, with a fair opportunity to move beyond a final order of removal and continue building futures here in the U.S where they have made their homes and families."

Kaur's family said in the news release: "Harjit was a pillar to our family and our community. She spent over 30 years in the United States, raising her children and later her grandchildren, and became a grandmother figure to our whole community."

The Trump administration has pursued a sweeping immigration enforcement campaign that has included large-scale deportations. ICE deported 483,200 people and made more than 491,000 arrests in fiscal year 2026, according to DHS data.

The legislation faces steep odds of passing during Congress' lame-duck session, where Republicans still control both chambers. Republicans hold 218 House seats, while the Senate Republican conference has 53 seats. However, the political landscape is set to change in January, after Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterm elections.

Democrats have secured at least 258 House seats and a 56-44 Senate majority in the new Congress. Still, any legislation passed by the new Democratic-controlled Congress would face President Donald Trump, who retains veto power.

Trump has softened some of his immigration rhetoric since Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterms, acknowledging in an interview with CBS News that his deportation policy may have been "too tough" and expressing openness to a deal with Democrats for some long-term immigrants. He subsequently said his administration's policy remained "very strong" and ruled out any agreement that would amount to amnesty.

title: 'We took turns to sleep': Detainees describe overcrowding at Whipple - Sahan Journal
description:
When Bounpama Vilailath was taken to a Whipple holding room by ICE on Jan. 21, he was the fifth person in the room.
ICE’s own hold facility standards mandate that: “Each single-occupant hold room shall contain a minimum of 37 square feet.
In comparison, ICE held 364 detainees on Jan. 10, 2026, at Whipple, three days following Good’s fatal shooting, Sahan’s analysis shows.
As a holding facility, Whipple does not have resources to provide meals.
Still waiting to help Haven Watch was formed during Metro Surge to help Whipple detainees get home.
text:
Every day for the last nine months, Myriam Dickinson has sat opposite the gates of the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building on a folding chair.

“¿Necesita ayuda?” (“Need help?”), she yells out to people walking out of the building that houses the regional Immigration and Customs Enforcement headquarters, immigration court, and a holding facility for detainees.

A volunteer with Haven Watch, Dickinson is one of the few Spanish speakers who waits outside Whipple to help people with water, food, phone calls to their families, visits to the doctor, plushies to bring their kids and a ride home.

“Their faces light up when they hear someone speak their language, offering help,” said Dickinson, who is from Chile.

At the peak of Operation Metro Surge, hundreds of detainees passed through the Whipple Building each week. They were crowded into cells meant to hold a couple dozen people, shackled for extended periods, forced to sleep upright or on cold concrete floors, given limited food and water and minimal medical care.

The facility was the site of 911 calls, and Haven Watch volunteers say they helped multiple detainees who were rushed to the hospital upon their release.

A Sahan Journal investigation has revealed that the conditions at the holding facility violated ICE’s own standards for room capacity and the length of stay.

Rooms meant to hold 30 people at most were crowded with as many as 60 or more at the height of Metro Surge. And at a facility meant to hold detainees no more than 12 hours, some were held for weeks — one teenage boy for 179 days.

“They weren’t treated like humans,” said Haven Watch chief of staff Sarah Haraldson, who has helped dozens of detainees in recent months.

A facility not built for Operation Metro Surge

Between Dec. 1, 2025, and Aug. 5, 2026, ICE detained 5,687 men, women and children at the Whipple Building, according to ICE data obtained by the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by Sahan Journal. More than 1,600 of these detainees were held at Whipple multiple times while in ICE custody.

During Operation Metro Surge, ICE also held detainees for days at Whipple — a facility meant to hold people for processing for no longer than 12 hours before they are transferred to county jails or bigger detention centers across the country.

U.S. Rep. Kelly Morrison, D-Minn., who has conducted multiple oversight visits, said the conditions she witnessed were inhumane.

“My overwhelming initial reaction each time I was in there, and I was in there three times, was just the inhumanity and really what felt like purposeful dehumanization of people,” she told Sahan Journal.

U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn, who also made oversight visits to Whipple, said the hold facility was not set up for extended detentions.

“They do not have medical staff, a kitchen, or adequate space and amenities for stays longer than a few hours; that underscores why ICE’s use of the facility during Operation Metro Surge was so egregious,” she said in written responses to Sahan Journal.

ICE did not respond to requests for comment on the overcrowded rooms, prolonged stays, lack of sufficient food and drinking water, as well as the sanitary conditions inside the rooms, as well as the minor who was reportedly held at Whipple for 179 days.

‘We took turns to sleep’

Freddy, 41, from El Salvador, was one of more than 5,000 male detainees who passed through the Whipple Building between Dec. 1, 2025, and August 2026. He was arrested by ICE on his way home from work in Brooklyn Center on Jan. 8, the day after Renee Good was fatally shot by ICE agent Jonathan Ross.

Freddy, who is using a pseudonym because he has an active immigration case and fears retaliation for speaking up, was taken to the first floor of the Whipple building, where the holding rooms are. He told the officers who processed him that he has a work permit, no prior deportation order or criminal history, a U-visa — a temporary visa for victims of qualifying crimes who have suffered mental or physical abuse — and has an active asylum case.

Freddy was detained for five days at Whipple before being transferred to the Freeborn County Jail for almost a month. He spent those five days thinking about his family and four children.

He was one of the over 1,400 people held at Whipple during the week when it was most crowded and was put in a room with about 60 other male detainees, he said.

According to ICE’s 2025 standards for holding facilities, the maximum number of detainees for a medium-sized holding room (330 square feet) is 30 people. Sahan Journal analyzed ICE’s standards and referenced it against Freddy’s observations and those of former ICE deportation officer Eric O’Denius to illustrate what conditions may have been like in Freddy’s holding room in Whipple.

The holding room was “very cramped,” Freddy told Sahan Journal in Spanish. “We took turns to sleep. I organized them because I was organizing the room where we were. I told them that we were going to sleep for three hours, some standing and some lying down so that we could rest.”

“Nobody wanted to move because [detainees] were coming in and it was becoming overcrowded, and coping with it each person then took care of their space because otherwise they would be left without space,” Freddy said.

When Bounpama Vilailath was taken to a Whipple holding room by ICE on Jan. 21, he was the fifth person in the room. By night time, there were 38 people, and the next day, there were about 54 people by noon. That day, Vilailath was put on a flight to El Paso, Texas. He was deported to Laos on March 25.

In the holding room at Whipple, Vilailath said he started counting the number of people because he “was stunned by the overcrowding and decided to keep a count to document my detention.” According to his estimate, his room was about 15 square feet and was meant for no more than 18 detainees.

Vilailath had a pending final removal order from the early 2000s and had also pleaded guilty to drug trafficking charges in 2008. He knew his removal was imminent.

Throughout his long history of incarceration, Vilailath, who now lives in Laos, said he had been in about three dozen holding cells, including at youth, county, state and federal facilities, but none compared to what he experienced at Whipple.

“The Whipple holding [room] was the worst for me because it was overcrowded, and everyone remained shackled at the ankles for the entire duration of our stay there,” he said in written responses.

His room was also too crowded for anyone to lie down and rest.

“People were sleeping all over the place, mainly on the floor but also on the benches. They slept in various positions depending on the space available, including lying down on the concrete, sitting upright against the wall, or crouching over the benches. It was challenging to sleep, especially being shackled. Many people [slept] a couple of hours. I got only 30 minutes, even though I was exhausted and worried about my wife, young adult daughters, and newborn, who were all present when ICE came to capture me.”

Sahan’s reporting points to unprecedented levels of overcrowding and inhumane conditions inside the holding rooms in the building during the peak months of the surge activity.

ICE’s own hold facility standards mandate that: “Each single-occupant hold room shall contain a minimum of 37 square feet. Multiple-occupant hold rooms shall provide an additional seven square feet of unencumbered space for each additional detainee.”

O’Denius, the former ICE officer who now works as a paralegal, was present at the facility when it opened in 2014. He also served as an inspection officer making sure the hold facility complied with ICE standards.

O’Denius said the facility has 22 rooms of different sizes, with only 15 of them equipped with a toilet, sink and running water and capable of holding detainees.

“Before the surge, the most people they’d hold at once was 50 or 60 people between all those hold areas,” O’Denius said.

In comparison, ICE held 364 detainees on Jan. 10, 2026, at Whipple, three days following Good’s fatal shooting, Sahan’s analysis shows.

That month, ICE held an average of 163 detainees daily, followed by 69 during February. This number was a spike from the average of 48 detainees held during December.

Those numbers shocked O’Denius. “A couple times I remember in my career we were kind of close to pushing 100, and it was bad at 100,” he recalled, referring to the number of detainees in Whipple holding rooms. “I can’t even imagine 300. It becomes a physics problem at that point.”

‘I cried the whole time’

Rosa, a 28-year-old Venezuelan refugee awaiting her green card, showed up at Whipple for what she thought was a routine immigration check-in on Jan. 21. Instead, she ended up inside one of the rooms before being flown to El Paso, Texas, within hours before being returned to Whipple. She ended up being held there for five more days.

Rosa also asked to use a pseudonym for safety reasons and due to a fear of retaliation.

Rosa’s room wasn’t as crowded as Freddy’s. Women are held in separate rooms from men at the Whipple Building and a smaller number were detained — 617 between Dec. 1, 2025, and August 2026.

But the conditions of her room were bad nonetheless, Rosa said.

“While I was there, a person never came to clean, not even the bathrooms,” she said in Spanish. She had little to no privacy to use the bathroom, adding that “the windows [into the room] were glass, and whoever passed by there would see you.”

There were no showers. No hygiene products. Not even toothbrushes to brush her teeth for five days.

She slept on the cold concrete floor of the room which she shared with six other women, all from Latin America. “I cried the whole time,” she told Sahan Journal in an earlier interview.

Rosa, Freddy and Vilailath say that the latrines in their rooms were clogged and gave off a foul smell, and they had little privacy to use it.

“There was one roll of toilet paper, and the officers hardly brought any. I think only one person used the toilet. No privacy, other than the toilet being in its own corner with a concrete wall in front of it and a stall on the entrance side that came up to chest level when sitting. Half of the detainees who sat on that side of the holding tank could see you using the restroom. Everyone was probably in shock, like me, over their detention, so no one else used the toilet except to urinate. There was no soap to properly clean our hands afterward,” Vilailath said.

The sink with the running water was attached to the toilet, and detainees were given a cup to drink from that sink. “They didn’t give you bottled water,” Rosa said. “You had to drink water from the one that was connected — well, there was something like a sink, and the water came out right there, and the water was horrible.”

Extended stays

Sahan’s analysis also shows that over half the detainees held in January and February were held in Whipple for far longer than 12 hours.

Volunteers from Haven Watch said they helped multiple detainees who were held at Whipple for far longer than 12 hours, like Freddy — who was held for a week — and Rosa.

“They were keeping people for so long, I thought they had beds in there,” Jack Lynch, a volunteer with Haven Watch, told Sahan Journal in October.

This, too, is in violation of ICE’s standards.

“An individual may not be confined in a facility’s hold room for more than 12 hours,” a 2025 ICE standards bulletin reads. “Hold rooms are used for detention of individuals awaiting removal, transfer, EOIR hearings, medical treatment, intra-facility movement, or other processing into or out of a facility.”

ICE data shows that in December 2025, 63 of the 1,023 detainees were held for over 12 hours. In January, that number increased eightfold — as many as 52% of the 2,953 detainees held at Whipple ended up staying there for longer than 12 hours; in February, too, half the 895 detainees stayed at Whipple for over 12 hours.

More than a third of all detainees at Whipple between Dec. 1, 2025, and August 2026 were held there for over 12 hours.

‘You could always hear children crying’

“In the rooms next to us there were children because you could always hear some children crying when they arrested them,” Rosa said.

ICE’s standards also mandate that unaccompanied minors (persons under 18) and parents or legal guardians accompanied by minor children not be placed in hold rooms, “unless they have shown or threatened violent behavior, have a history of criminal activity, or have given staff reasonable grounds to expect an escape attempt.”

According to ICE records, 66 minors were held at Whipple between December and August. That number excludes 11 people who may have turned 18 at the time of their detention. Almost all minors were held there during Operation Metro Surge, with only one held there in June.

The longest detention recorded at Whipple is 180 days of a male individual from Ecuador who was 16 at the time of his detention.

Medical neglect

In the nine months she has worked with Haven Watch, Haraldson has come across multiple detainees who have complained of injuries and medical neglect. But she remembers one person specifically — a Hispanic woman whom Haraldson and other volunteers drove home after she was released from Whipple.

“She said she was shackled tightly around her stomach [at Whipple],” Haraldson said. The woman said she was detained for weeks, but Haraldson was not sure if she was at Whipple for that entire period.

Dickinson said Haven Watch volunteers have taken multiple detainees to hospitals after their release.

At Whipple, Rosa did not have her diabetes medication for the duration of her stay. “There was never a doctor. I suppose that if someone got sick, they had to take them to some clinic or something, but there was never a doctor,” she said.

Morrison said that the lack of medical care “was very noteworthy to me as a doctor.”

“There were no protocols in place when I was there, and they kept justifying that by saying ‘This is not a detention center.’ The one screen that they used before they put people on planes to send them to Texas was to ask them if they had a cough. So there was no medical care whatsoever.”

She added that during one of her visits to the facility, the officers told her 911 had been calls made from the facility, but did not share any further details.

“They wouldn’t tell me how many, or what the outcomes of those were, and also why people required a 911 call. Was it something about the way that they were taken in that caused the need for a 911 call? They weren’t able to answer any of those questions.”

Morrison said during her most recent oversight visit, in February, there was a public health nurse present at the facility for eight hours a day.

Vilailath, however, did not see any medical staff present at the holding facility. He said that several detainees spoke with ICE officers about their medications or voiced concerns regarding their health, “but nothing happened for most of them.”

One man was allowed to have his wife bring his inhaler, which he received a few hours later. One Afghan man had serious health issues and was briefly taken outside of the holding tank to speak with someone, Vilailath said.

“It may have been for a phone call with a doctor or nurse, or possibly a translator since he did not speak English. Throughout our time together in Whipple and on the way to El Paso, he remained in distress,” he said.

The neglect extended to the food detainees were given. As a holding facility, Whipple does not have resources to provide meals.

Freddy and Rosa said that once a day, they were given snacks like cold sandwiches, cookies and sometimes, water.

“Everyone got sick,” Freddy said. “The majority got sick because maybe they had [the food] refrigerated, because it arrived almost frozen.”

Haraldson said that after being released, detainees would ask for water, a blanket or other coverings during the winter months, and warm food. She said Haven Watch had warm tamales and beverages waiting in volunteers’ cars.

Lasting effects

For about two weeks after she was released, Rosa said she suffered from back pain and swollen knees due to sleeping on the concrete floor and being shackled all the time. Months after her release, she continues to fear immigration enforcement, not only for herself but also her 7-year-old son after she saw children being at Whipple. “Every time I go outside, I carry that fear with me all the time. I haven’t gotten over it yet,” she said.

Freddy, too, continues to live in fear of being re-detained. “That is a trauma no man can get over. When I slept alone, I would dream that ICE was shooting at me and arresting me,” he said.

The impact of his detention is more than just psychological. While at Freeborn, Freddy said he signed over the custody of his youngest children — 5- and 2-year-old U.S. citizens — to his girlfriend.

His girlfriend, who is Thai, and the kids now live in Thailand and don’t plan to come back to the U.S. until the end of the current administration, he said.

‘He couldn’t even cross the door’

Starting in May, Whipple became a passthrough for many of those who were released, and then immediately redetained. Between Dec. 1, 2025, and Aug. 5, 2026, 27 people were released and detained again, according to ICE data.

Minneapolis attorney Daniel Suitor started noticing rearrests at Whipple after detainees were released by a court order. In September, a judge ordered one of Suitor’s clients, Alejandro, to be released immediately after ruling that his detention was unlawful. On Sept. 25, he was brought back to Whipple for a few hours from a county jail.

ICE escorted him through the building, took him out of the front door, and directly into the arms of four to five ICE agents who were waiting outside. “And they claim that that is a relief,” Suitor said. “They claim that they have fulfilled the judge’s order by releasing the client.”

In early October, Dickinson was waiting for a man who was set to be released from Whipple so she could offer him a ride home. That man was given his belongings in a plastic bag, as released detainees often are, and let go through the garage.

“He couldn’t even cross the door before he was taken back in,” she said.

In another case, on Oct. 2, attorney Danielle Oxendine Molliver received a hysterical call from the wife of one of her clients, Yader Cortez, who was rearrested after he was processed for release.

“This isn’t a new practice. We’ve been doing it since May,” an officer told her.

Suitor said the redetentions appear to be where the detainee has an ongoing removal case. “ICE just didn’t want to let go of anyone who they could still potentially deport,” he said.

The Advocates for Human Rights has sued DHS for not allowing access to their clients held at Whipple through mandated, private phone calls and visits.

Still waiting to help

Haven Watch was formed during Metro Surge to help Whipple detainees get home. The volunteer-led organization has helped 600 people in the last 11 months and has expanded its services to legal aid, mental health care, help for those self-deporting and more.

Dickinson says the number of people released daily has dropped from nine to 10 a day to just three or four a week now. Still, she keeps watch.

She remembers the day when she decided to carry her ID in her phone case to prove her citizenship. “I cried that day,” she said. “I’ve been here for 32 years.”

On a day in mid-October, she shuffled between working from her car in Whipple’s parking lot, sending people money for their rent, groceries, medical bills, and self-deportation flights and to the entrance gate whenever someone was released.

“I spent a whole summer here; The leaves are changing,” she said.

She doesn’t anticipate a day anytime soon when she won’t have to sit in front of the building, waiting for someone who might need her help.

Sahan Journal intern Nicolas Scibelli contributed to this story.

title: Joel Platt: Liberty by Nobody? Immigration Bail and Government by Regulation

Importantly, clause 9(7), added during the Bill’s passage, expressly makes whether proceedings are being expedited following a ministerial request a factor in the immigration bail decision.

text:
Decisions about liberty should have a clear owner. Hannah Arendt’s concept of the “rule by Nobody” captures the difficulty of locating responsibility within complex systems of administrative government. The Immigration and Asylum Bill (the Bill)* would move certain bail decisions (cl 1(2)(b)) to a new non-judicial body, the Independent Immigration Appeals Authority (IIAA), whose timetable and bail factors ministers can influence, and whose decisions can be challenged only through narrowed routes. This post argues that the Bill’s surrounding architecture—arrangements as to who appoints and allocates adjudicators, sets the timetable, serves the claim notice, writes the procedure rules, and hears challenges—disperses responsibility for a decision to keep someone detained so widely between Parliament, the Secretary of State, the IIAA’s officers and its adjudicators, that no one clearly owns it.

In a previous post on this blog, Joanna Bell has highlighted how the Bill risks weakening the institutional independence of the IIAA by giving the Home Secretary significant influence over its leadership, resources, and operation. This post builds on that analysis by examining a related but distinct constitutional concern: how the Minister’s power to determine the institutional and procedural conditions under which decisions affecting liberty are made may obscure accountability for the resulting decisions, even where individual adjudicators formally exercise their functions independently.

The Rule by Nobody

Arendt’s (1970, p. 38) “rule by Nobody” alludes to how many agents of the state performing their duties in their individual bureaus operate collectively to govern, but ultimately the ‘intricate system of bureaus’ obscures channels of accountability. Individual ‘decision-makers’ do not make decisions for which they are ultimately responsible; they merely ‘process’ an arrangement predetermined by another bureau that itself may defer to the (statistical) output of another. This labyrinthine system ultimately leaves the aggrieved with nobody left to answer because no individual(s) may truly be held responsible for a decision. It is not the absence of governance: the peril is in the structure of governance.

Two ideas need to be separated. Decisional independence means that the adjudicator deciding a bail application is free from interference in that case. Institutional accountability means that someone can be asked to answer for the arrangements within which the decision is made: who allocates the case, how quickly it must be decided, and which factors the law tells the adjudicator to weigh. The first can exist without the second. The Bill contains safeguards aimed at the former. Ministers of the Crown must not seek to influence particular decisions through special access to adjudicators (cl 1(6)). The IIAA also decides whether to approve ministerial requests to expedite individual bail applications (cl 9(2)–(3)). These protections matter, but independence at the point of final decision does not necessarily ensure accountability for the decision itself, given the arrangements within which the decision is made. An adjudicator may exercise their function independently, yet the outcome may be shaped by arrangements that distribute responsibility for it across several actors.

The distinction is particularly important in the context of detention. Article 5(4) of the European Convention on Human Rights requires a ‘court’ with the power to decide speedily whether detention is lawful and to order release. In Chahal v UK (1996), the Strasbourg Court distinguished this guarantee from Article 13 of the ECHR, which requires only a remedy before a ‘national authority’ and need not involve a judicial body (§§126, 130, 152). The Home Office’s original human rights memorandum addresses the IIAA’s independence under Article 13 (30 June 2026, paras 11–15). A supplementary memorandum (12 October 2026) considers the implications of subsequent Government amendments for adjudicator independence under Article 13 (paras 11–16). Neither, however, specifically addresses Article 5(4). The requirement that a body must itself have the power to decide is pertinent here. Article 5(4) demands more than a formally available avenue of challenge: it requires an effective decision on liberty by a body that can be held to account for deciding. The question, therefore, is whether the Bill’s institutional arrangements provide sufficiently clear lines of responsibility for the decisions that determine whether someone remains detained.

Who appoints and allocates the decision-makers?

The IIAA would take over certain immigration bail applications from the First-tier Tribunal (cl 1(2)(b), (3); Sch 1, paras 13–14). Adjudicators exercise that function (cl 3(1)), but they are appointed by the Chief Executive (cl 2(5)). Senior adjudicators must be legally qualified with two years practice, or equivalent in the Chief Executive’s opinion; clause 2 states no equivalent requirement for executive adjudicators (cl 2(9)).

The Chief Appeals Officer allocates cases and oversees decision quality (cl 3(3)(a), (c)), and may delegate these functions to a senior adjudicator (cl 3(4)). The Home Office maintains that the Chief Appeals Officer cannot intervene in individual decisions (Explanatory Notes to the Bill as introduced (EN), para 68). That may protect adjudicative independence, but it does not remove the Officer’s influence over the conditions in which decisions are made. By allocating cases, the Officer decides who hears each bail application, and whether the decision-maker is legally qualified. By overseeing decision quality, the Officer helps set the standards by which adjudicators’ work is judged. Neither involves intervening in an individual decision, but both shape the context in which it is taken.

The Secretary of State also has a significant role in the IIAA’s institutional composition. The Secretary of State appoints the Chair, the Professional Standards Officer, and the first Chief Executive and Chief Appeals Officer (cl 2(2), (3)). The Chair and Professional Standards Officer as non-executive members may be removed where the Secretary of State is satisfied that specified grounds exist; the Secretary of State may also attach conditions to financial assistance provided to the IIAA (Sch 2, paras 3(3), 12(2)). These powers do not establish ministerial control over individual bail decisions, but they give the Secretary of State significant influence over the composition, tenure, and resources of the body responsible for making them.

Who controls the timetable and procedures?

The Secretary of State has further powers over how and when the IIAA operates. By regulations, the Secretary of State sets the time period within which the IIAA must decide a bail application (cl 8(1)(a)). The Secretary of State can also ask the IIAA to decide a bail application by a specified date, on a public-interest test the Bill does not define, which the IIAA may decline only if compliance is impracticable or contrary to the interests of justice (cl 9(1)–(3)); the process for such requests is set by regulations (cl 9(4)). The Bill prescribes no minimum period within which the IIAA must be required to determine an individual case under an expedition request.

Importantly, clause 9(7), added during the Bill’s passage, expressly makes whether proceedings are being expedited following a ministerial request a factor in the immigration bail decision. The ministerial request therefore has implications beyond the pace of proceedings: once approved, expedition becomes a statutory consideration in the subsequent assessment of liberty, potentially weighing against the applicant’s release. The Secretary of State sets the framework and initiates the request; the IIAA decides whether to approve it; and the adjudicator must subsequently take the expedition into account. Responsibility for the resulting decision is consequently distributed across different institutional actors, even though the IIAA formally decides whether to approve an application.

Arendt (1951, ch. 7) tied bureaucratic rule to government by decree, in which administrative orders displace stable law and those who issue them stay removed from accountability. This focus on administrative control can be seen in the Bill. The Bill leaves several important aspects of the IIAA’s operation to secondary legislation and procedural instruments, rather than fixing them in primary legislation. These include the time period for deciding bail applications (cl 8), the procedure for expedition requests (cl 9(4)), additional claim-notice requirements (cl 13(4)), transitional arrangements determining the forum for specified cases (cl 19(1)), and the IIAA’s Procedure Rules (cl 4). The relevant statutory instruments are subject to the negative rather than affirmative resolution procedure (cl 58(5)). Regulations under these provisions are subject only to the negative procedure (cl 58(5)): a minister makes them without Parliament’s prior approval, and they stand unless either House votes to annul them. Parliament cannot amend them through this procedure, so its role is limited to a possible veto after the fact. Moreover, the Procedure Rules are made by a Board within the IIAA, without requiring prior approval by a minister or external body (cl 5(1); EN para 72). The arrangements governing bail decisions can therefore be altered without further primary legislation and, in the case of the Procedure Rules, without any prior external approval.

The Government presents statutory timeframes as promoting prompt bail decisions (Home Office original human rights memorandum, para 14(b)). Speedy decisions on liberty are, of course, defensible; my objection concerns the form of control. A minister can set the time limit and request expedition case by case on an undefined public-interest test, while the reporting that would show how often this happens depends on regulations made by the same minister (cls 8(6), 9(5)). This is administration through adjustable instruments, justified by efficiency, the pattern Arendt contrasted with law. The IIAA formally approves or declines each request (cl 9(2)–(3)), but that division is the point: a detained person’s timetable can be shaped by a ministerial request, approved by the IIAA, under regulations that can themselves be changed without affirmative parliamentary approval. No single actor clearly owns the choice to expedite a decision about liberty.

The late-claims provisions provide a further illustration of how these arrangements can shape decisions affecting liberty. The Secretary of State or an immigration officer serves the claim notice and sets the deadline whose expiry, followed by late immigration information while detained or after notice of departure details, triggers the late-claims process (cls 13(1), (3)(a), 14(1), (4)). Under clause 14(3), whether the process applies, or is likely to apply, then becomes a factor in the bail decision. Clause 14(2), originally clause 12(2), also requires those exercising IIAA case-management functions to ensure, so far as reasonably practicable, that proceedings subject to the late-claims process are prioritised over other appeal proceedings. A House of Commons Public Bill Committee also added clause 15 (Government new clause 3, agreed on 27 October), under which late information and evidence may damage an appellant’s credibility, subject to the adjudicator’s ability to reduce or disapply these consequences where there are good reasons (cl 15(2)–(5)). The adjudicator must explain how these provisions have affected the decision (cl 15(6)). The late-claims process therefore extends beyond the prioritisation of proceedings: it can affect the assessment of credibility and, in turn, the determination of liberty.

Who can challenge and scrutinise the decision?

The question of accountability also depends on the extent to which decisions and the arrangements shaping them can be challenged. IIAA bail decisions may be questioned through a single internal review, limited to errors of law (cl 6(1)–(5)), or an appeal to the Upper Tribunal on a point of law with permission (cl 7(1)–(3)). This represents a gain in one respect: certain First-tier Tribunal decisions under paragraphs 1, 5, 6, and 10(12)–(13) of Schedule 10 to the Immigration Act 2016 are excluded decisions, with no appeal to the Upper Tribunal (Appeals (Excluded Decisions) Order 2009, art 2(b)). However, the Upper Tribunal’s refusal of permission is final (cl 7(3)), and judicial review is excluded in relation to IIAA decisions (cl 1(8)), including on case-management grounds (EN, para 60). The Bill does not say explicitly whether case-management decisions, such as approval of an expedition request, can be appealed. While challenge is not removed, it is narrowed and channelled. With judicial review excluded, there are few points at which a detainee might obtain a meaningful answer about the institutional decisions shaping their bail application.

The Bill does provide for institutional oversight. The Chief Executive may make representations to the Secretary of State, which must be laid before Parliament (cl 3(7)). The Chief Inspector must report annually on the IIAA, and the Chief Executive must respond; and both the report and response must be laid before Parliament. The Secretary of State may omit material on national-security or individual-safety grounds (cl 17, inserting UK Borders Act 2007, s 50A). However, the Public Bill Committee rejected a proposed new clause that would have required quarterly publication of detailed IIAA statistics, including appeal volumes and outcomes, legal representation rates, the number of appeals awaiting processing, and the number and outcomes of internal reviews (new clause 28; Division 57, 3 November 2026). The Bill thus retains annual inspection and reporting rather than the proposed quarterly data regime.

The amended Bill also adds a provision empowering the Secretary of State to take steps to increase the general availability of qualified IIAA advice and representation (cl 12). Schedule 3 mandates the Procedure Rules to require a person initiating an appeal or bail application to state whether they have had, or wish to obtain, qualified advice and representation; the IIAA must then provide information about how to obtain it. These are relevant safeguards, but they do not themselves resolve the question of who is institutionally accountable for a decision that results in someone remaining detained.

None of this is to suggest that the safeguards are insincere or that adjudicators will act in bad faith. Nor is the argument that the Secretary of State, Chief Executive or Chief Appeals Officer can dictate the outcome of an individual bail application. The Bill expressly seeks to protect adjudicators from such interference. Rather, the problem is that the independence of individual decision-makers does not necessarily ensure accountability for the decision to keep someone detained.

An adjudicator might say that Parliament made late-claims status relevant to the bail decision, that time limits are set by regulations, and that cases are allocated by someone else (cls 3(3)(a), 8(1)(a), 14(3)). The Chief Appeals Officer might say they cannot intervene in individual decisions (EN para 68). The Secretary of State might say that the IIAA is independent, that ministers must not influence particular decisions (cl 1(6)), and that the decision whether to expedite belongs to the IIAA (EN para 83). Parliament might say that procedural rules belong to a Board within the IIAA (cl 4(3)). Each answer is true. Together, however, they leave unclear who is ultimately responsible for the outcome.

Conclusion

The constitutional peril identified by Arendt’s notion of the ‘rule by Nobody’ is that power can be exercised through an intricate administrative system in which responsibility for its consequences becomes difficult to locate. The Bill risks creating precisely this arrangement in the exercise of the state’s power to deprive individuals of their liberty. An adjudicator may exercise their function independently, yet the outcome of a bail decision may be shaped by allocation decisions, procedural rules, statutory requirements, and ministerial requests for expedition, for which responsibility is distributed across several actors, leaving no clear point of accountability. This leaves the law in a state where there is potentially rule by nobody, or perhaps even no rules at all.

* A House of Commons Public Bill Committee completed line-by-line scrutiny on 3 November 2026. The current text is Bill 153.
