text:
Lately, Liz has been jolted awake at night in a panic when her ankle monitor starts to vibrate. The buzzing reminds her of her greatest fear: that immigration agents will barge into her small apartment on Chicago’s North Side and take her away to a detention center.

“ICE agents told me the monitor would vibrate if it’s broken or tampered with,” she says crying. “ ‘We’ll look for you right away,’ ” she says they told her, “ ‘because we know where to find you.’ ”

The Guatemalan asylum-seeker has been living in a constant state of anxiety since she, her husband and daughter were asked to show up for an unexpected immigration check-in last August. Her husband was taken into immigration custody while Liz was fitted with an ankle monitor and released with her 15-year-old daughter. Neither she nor her husband have criminal records.

WBEZ is not using their full names because they fear government retaliation.

“I asked the immigration agents, ‘Why? Did we do something wrong?’ ” Liz says in her native Spanish, adding that since the family arrived in the United States in 2024 from Guatemala they’ve been trying to follow every step of their asylum application process by the book.

Like Liz, more than 53,000 noncitizens nationwide in 2026 have been fitted with ankle monitors under the Department of Homeland Security’s Alternatives to Detention program, according to government data. That number has more than tripled since 2024 as the Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement. It’s the same trend locally, a WBEZ/Sun-Times analysis found. So far this year, ICE’s Chicago field office — which oversees Illinois, Indiana, Wisconsin, Missouri, Kentucky, and Kansas — has issued nearly 3,800 ankle monitors — a nearly 40% jump since 2024.

The surge has raised concerns among immigration advocates over the mental health toll they say the constant surveillance takes on those who wear the ankle device and pose no risk. Advocates argue the use of ankle monitors was supposed to be an alternative to detention but as more people have been fitted with them, detentions have also increased.

“We have seen so many people across the country who have been complying with their immigration cases, who have families, who have jobs, who have strong community ties, no significant criminal history, going to their regular appointments and suddenly getting shackled with ankle monitoring,” says Lauren Hodges, senior attorney with Amica Center for Human Rights, a legal advocacy group.

Advocates like Hodges point out that the upward trend began soon after an internal Trump administration directive last year ordering immigration agents to fit noncitizens with ankle monitors “whenever possible.”

Her organization filed a class action lawsuit that accuses the Trump administration of requiring noncitizens to wear an ankle or wrist monitor without providing justification for why such “harmful and invasive” monitoriing is warranted. The lawsuit says people fitted with the devices have experienced health problems as result, such as high blood pressure, as well as anxiety and depression.

The Department of Homeland Security did not answer specific questions about its increased use of ankle monitors or any other questions about this tracking device. In a statement, the agency defended the ATD program as a critical tool to ensure “compliance with release conditions, and regular check-ins.”

The agency says people without a flight risk or criminal history are enrolled because it is the most “cost-efficient way to ensure compliance with their immigration proceedings.”

Effects on mental health

Alternatives to Detention was started more than 20 years ago as a way to keep track of immigrants who were released under supervision while facing deportation.

But advocates say the continual surveillance is just a different form of detention.

When the Trump administration stripped Haitians of their Temporary Protected Status in June — which allowed hundreds of thousands of immigrants fleeing natural disasters or political conflict back home to live and work in the U.S. temporarily — many were later fitted with ankle monitors. Among them was Pierre Damas Bel, a college student and star soccer player. News reports say he struggled deeply with the humiliation of the device, even sharing his frustrations on social media before taking his own life.

Liz and her family have also struggled with shame and anxiety around the device. At that August check-in, Liz says immigration officials openly debated putting an ankle monitor on her 15-year-old daughter, even though federal guidelines restrict ICE from placing tracking devices on minors.

Overhearing the agents, the high schooler, who plays flag football, began sobbing. She worried about being bullied at school or perceived as a criminal.

“When I saw her little face and she started crying, she said to me, ‘Mommy, I won’t be able to play anymore.’”

Agents ultimately let the teen go without one.

Since then, Liz says the shame of wearing an ankle monitor has been devastating. Strapped tightly to her leg, the device is bulky and uncomfortable.

“When I go to church, I like to wear a skirt or a dress, and now I can’t,” she says. “I have to wear a long dress so people don’t stare at me. It’s embarrassing.”

“We’re making the act of being an immigrant a criminal state,” says Jennifer Babaie, associate director of the Adult Detention Project at the National Immigrant Justice Center. “The majority of the people being arrested are folks that are applying or [are] otherwise in a legal status ... now you’re on an ankle monitor, and you’re suddenly in a completely different category. “

Not only are more people wearing ankle monitors, but they are wearing them for longer.

ICE has increasingly imposed GPS ankle monitors on immigrants even after federal judges have ordered they be released from custody because the government has failed to justify the detention, Anthony Enriquez, vice president of U.S. advocacy and litigation at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said during a recent panel led by data journalist Austin Kocher.

Human rights advocates argue that the federal ankle monitor policy is not necessary and is driven by cruelty and the profits the companies who supply the ankle monitors are making. The cost of the technology rose from roughly $25,500 per day in 2022 to more than $145,000 in 2026.

Constant anxiety the monitor won’t work

Liz says her family has always been under some form of federal surveillance. Her husband was fitted with an ankle monitor when he first arrived in the United States in 2024. Still, the family managed to find work and build a life in Chicago after fleeing violence and street crime in Guatemala. He worked as a scrap metal collector, and she cleaned homes.

Now, Liz is trying to hold the family together on her own.

But she’s struggling.

In late October, Liz received an unexpected message ordering her to report for an immigration check-in at the same building where her husband was arrested. She worried agents would accuse her of tampering with her ankle monitor and take her into custody.

“I’m coming here prepared for anything, because I don’t know what could happen to me inside,” she says.

On the morning of her appointment, Liz’s attorney could not attend, so she arranged for a pro bono lawyer to accompany her. Before heading to the check in Liz spoke with relatives about the possibility that she might not return. She says her 15-year-old daughter was crying as she walked out the door.

But this time that appointment went OK.

A technical glitch had caused her ankle monitor to stop sending location data to ICE, triggering the urgent check-in to verify she had not cut it off. Officials adjusted the device and told her she must wear it for a year and a half of full compliance before she can be moved to a phone-based check-in app.

“I think the fear is also that if you don’t do everything perfectly, even with all these barriers, that something’s going to happen to you,” says Gabriela Nicolau, the pro bono attorney who accompanied Liz.

Outside the federal building, Liz says she felt relieved — for the moment. Maybe this time, she got lucky, or bringing an attorney made a difference.

But that relief is temporary. The tracker — and the anxiety and fear it brings — isn’t going anywhere.

text:
Emma V.F. is among the legion of photographers, videographers and other journalists who have chronicled the human drama unfolding in New York City’s main immigration court, located in the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building, where masked federal agents have plied the halls for more than a year arresting immigrants leaving court hearings.

V.F. filmed scores of arrests at the sprawling government complex at 26 Federal Plaza in Lower Manhattan, where a federal judge later temporarily barred U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from making routine civil immigration arrests. She also captured something rarer still: the small talk among the omnipresent ICE agents at the facility.

Her new documentary short, “Water Cooler,” splices together snippets of the mundane, day-to-day chatter among the agents and airs them alongside footage of some of the many immigrants being arrested in the hallways and thereafter being sent off to ICE detention centers. V.F calls the film an exploration of the “banality of evil."

The compilation provides a rare airing of the personal musings of agents — all recorded in a public place — as they execute what President Donald Trump has billed as the largest mass deportation effort in the nation’s history.

The documentary had its New York City premiere at the festival DOC NYC earlier this month, and will be screened again at DCTV’s Firehouse Cinema in Manhattan on Dec. 2 at 7 p.m.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, in a statement referred to the filmmaker as an "activist" and said her work "smears ICE."

V.F. expressed a different view in an interview with Gothamist. Here is a transcript of the conversation, edited for length and clarity:

What were your main impressions from watching and recording ICE agents for weeks?

V.F.: From literally the first day I went just to observe without my camera, I was really struck by the fact that the agents were just standing around having these very mundane conversations that felt to me very indifferent about what they were doing, what they were there to do. And the fact that they were having these very openly right next to all the journalists, that really surprised me, and was not something I knew about from just being a viewer and reader of the news.

So, right away I thought, if I can capture elements of this, there's something there, this kind of banality-of-evil theme that feels really interesting and important to memorialize in some way. It feels like this dark history is happening in these very kind of claustrophobic hallways. So that was my goal.

The thing that struck me was this complete lack of acknowledgement on the part of the ICE agents of what they were there to do, until they were arresting someone. Like, you wouldn't know from their conversations that they were tearing families apart and potentially ruining lives. Just this ability that they have to have these very water cooler conversations, very kind of like standard small talk, felt really eerie and upsetting to me.

How did you make sense of that discrepancy between their conversations and the arrests they were making?

On a human level, I don't know that I have. I think that's why I wanted to make the film in this way. I don't know how to grapple with that as a human being, that people can be this heartless.

I think as a filmmaker, it really immediately felt clear to me, especially because of, I should say, references like “The Zone of Interest” (a historical drama) that had come out a few years before, about the banality of evil during the Holocaust. It felt clear to me that this was something that could be compelling if edited the right way. And so I really embraced juxtaposing these very kind of normal, quiet conversations with these scenes of state violence to try to make that point.

Did any particular scenes stand out to you, when you were there observing and filming?

I think the conversation that cemented for me that I was making a short film and that there was something noteworthy going on was the conversation where this female supervisor is talking about how she always gets broken appliances. Her appliances are always broken when she orders the things online. And she kind of flippantly says that she has PTSD from that. And that was very early on in the filming process that that conversation happened.

So I think it was both the combination of the fact that it happened at all, that she said this very ironic thing, when she is in fact inflicting trauma on people as an agent of the government — it boggled my mind, it still does — and also the fact that she said it knowing I was feet away from her recording. I wonder if that was a bit of a trolling me moment. But either way, I think it shows the true colors very clearly and is a part of the film that the audience holds onto as well.

What was your dynamic with the ICE agents? Were they aware you were filming them?

I know for a fact that they knew I was filming them because I actually filmed them talking about me at one point. There's a shot at the very end of the film where there are five agents standing kind of far away from me in a hallway, and they all turn and look at me at once, and that's because they're saying, "Oh, homegirl's still recording us. What do you think she does with this footage? Do you think she just goes home and watches us?" And they're like making jokes about the fact that I'm filming. And then they actually joke about harming me in some way. I don't know exactly what they said, but they start talking about how, like, "Why don't you just go over there and by the time the investigation's over you'll be long gone."

So I know that they knew I was filming and I know they didn't appreciate it. But I think they also knew I was well within my rights. Anyone can film ICE agents on the job in a public place. So I always tried to be respectful and safe, but I knew that I was well within my journalistic and filmmaking rights to be doing that.

What do you hope audiences take away from the film?

I guess my answer has changed a little since the Blue Wave. I've always hoped that people would feel invigorated to either call for abolishing ICE, or learn how to be a volunteer or learn know-your-rights trainings, like any of these things that are kind of the obvious impact of storytelling about ICE from this point of view.

But I think especially now in this moment when so many people on the left are rightfully very excited and very happy, I think I feel like it's a really valuable film to remind people, ICE is part of the executive branch and that hasn't changed, and if anything, we've seen the president elevate Stephen Miller to White House Chief of Staff, and Stephen Miller has been one of the key policymakers in all this. So I think, I hope that the film will remind everyone who shares these values to really stay vigilant and stay calling for change and decency and humanism.

text:
The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.

Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.

The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.

Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.

Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.

Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.

Morales García’s attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation.

But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García’s lawsuit said.

The Trump administration denied Morales García’s assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García “was permitted entry” back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed “information concerning plaintiff’s place of birth”.

“Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune.

Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García’s, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy.

Texas’s public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program.

The judge presiding over Morales García’s lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration’s request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants.

An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump’s second presidency.

Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny.

title: Migration hubs are not limited to Europe: why the 'Rwanda Plan' is not working - Voxeurop
description:

“We are very concerned about this announcement, particularly given Rwanda’s human rights record as a potential partner country,” she adds.

text:
Monday 16 November marked a turning point in European migration policy; five European Union countries agreed with Rwanda to set up a so-called “return centre” asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected within the bloc. This will be the first “return hubs” spearheaded by Austria, Germany, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands. For the so-called “Implementers’ Group”, the project is necessary to “regain control”, according to Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s Prime Minister.

For Christian Stocker, leader of the Austrian People’s Party (ÖVP), it is a milestone: “It is a truly historic paradigm shift in migration policy”.

The “Rwanda Plan”, however, has been a point of contention in several countries for years. It was already controversial when Denmark first proposed it. Now, its four other allies have drawn on that Danish initiative to set up return hubs in the African country.

In 2021, the government signed wide-ranging bilateral agreements with Rwanda, and the Danish Parliament passed a law to pave the way for outsourcing. A year later, Denmark and Rwanda signed a Joint Statement on Bilateral Cooperation. In January 2023, however, Denmark announced that it was suspending the plan and would instead work in collaboration with other EU Member States.

“I have been isolated, and people regarded our plans as wrong, un-European and un-Social Democratic – not to mention other terms that have been used to describe me”, Mette Frederiksen told the Danish newspaper Berlingske in June 2026. “Now an absolute majority of my colleagues are on my side and believe that too many people have come to Europe, and that the consequences are too great.”

The concept is underpinned by new European return legislation, which replaces the 2008 Return Directive and allows Member States to enter into agreements with third countries to establish return hubs. The proposal was presented by the European Commission in March 2025, received the European Parliament’s approval in June 2026 and was finally adopted by the Council on 1 October 2026. Spain was the only country to vote against it. The remaining 25 Member States voted in favour, except for Belgium, which abstained.

The proposal of the “Implementers” Group’ is inspired by similar plans that have failed. In every case, putting those ideas into practice proved costly. For example, Israel transferred Eritrean and Sudanese migrants to Rwanda. Asylum seekers were also sent from Libya to the East African country only to be returned again. Then there is the most high-profile case: the UK’s failed attempt at a return agreement, which ended with a cancelled flight and expenditure of over £290 million (€350 million), without sending a single asylum seeker to Rwanda.

“Open” doors and the right to residency

The proponents of the “Rwanda plan” argue that outsourcing would act as a deterrent and claim that the planned facilities in Rwanda would be “open”; in other words, asylum seekers would be allowed to enter and leave, as revealed by Greece’s Minister for Migration and Asylum, Thanos Plevris, during an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1.

For its part, the Dutch government has confirmed that people transferred to Rwanda will have the right to residence, as well as access to the labour market and healthcare, according to an official statement of 16 November. According to diplomatic sources consulted by Der Standard, the pilot project would begin with around 100 people, some 20 from each of the five participating countries.

Migration policy experts, however, doubt its deterrent effect and question the consequences of uprooting people by sending them to a country with which they have no ties, as well as the difficulty in monitoring human rights compliance in Rwanda.

“At Amnesty International, we have been highly critical of the concept of return centres ever since it was introduced into European legislation on returns,” Adriana Tidona, a researcher on European migration at Amnesty International, told ElConfidencial. Tidona explains that such centres “cannot be implemented in a way that respects human rights”. “We are very concerned about this announcement, particularly given Rwanda’s human rights record as a potential partner country,” she adds.

The UK’s failed attempt at a return agreement […] ended with a cancelled flight and expenditure of over €350 million, without sending a single asylum seeker to Rwanda

In Austria, some prominent figures within the Austrian People’s Party have been critical of the announcement, such as the veteran MP and former Secretary General of the ÖVP, Ferry Maier, who, in an interview with Der Standard the day after the announcement, stated: “I find it surprising that there are actually so many ministers at EU level willing to participate in a scheme of this kind.”

“This is nothing more than a publicity stunt”, that “serves absolutely no purpose, as experience should already have taught us”. He added that “it does, however, cost a great deal of money that is being thrown away”.

Modern infrastructure in an authoritarian country

Rwanda has rejected criticisms of the plan. “It is easy for some organisations to simply criticise without proposing any alternatives,” said Rwanda’s Minister of the Interior, Vincent Biruta.

Biruta insists that the African country is well-suited to receiving asylum seekers rejected in Europe, despite its past. Three decades after the genocide by Hutus against the Tutsis, Rwanda is today a country with modern infrastructure under an authoritarian regime.

The announcement of the return centres comes two and a half weeks after the United States imposed sanctions on Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence, on 28 October, for its alleged military and logistical support to the M23 rebel group, which operates in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In March, Washington had already sanctioned the Rwandan army for the same reason.

“Rwanda is a terrible choice,” Judith Sunderland, Senior Associate Director in the Refugee and Migrant Rights division at Human Rights Watch (HRW), tells ElConfidencial emphatically. “Rwanda’s human rights record is deplorable,” she continues, pointing out that the country “is responsible for serious abuses and war crimes in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and engages in transnational repression”.

According to the expert, “by choosing Rwanda, these five EU member states have completely disregarded their obligations set out in the European Return Order to enter into such agreements only with countries that respect human rights”.

When Israel sent Eritreans to Rwanda

This latest proposed plan is similar to the one Italy once sought to implement with Albania, which cost hundreds of millions of Euros, but Israel was among the first to seek to implement it.

Between 2006 and 2012, thousands of Eritrean and Sudanese people fled indefinite compulsory military service, as well as arbitrary detention in Eritrea and political violence in Sudan. A large number of them managed to reach the Israeli border on a perilous journey through the Sinai Desert, where cases of abduction, torture and extortion were documented.

By 2012, there were some 37,000 Eritreans and 14,000 Sudanese in Israel, according to estimates by Human Rights Watch, who were unable to return to their home countries. Sudanese criminal law makes it a criminal offence, punishable by up to ten years’ imprisonment, for its citizens to visit Israel. If [we] cannot deport them, “let’s imprison them to make their lives miserable”, said the then Israeli Interior Minister Eli Yishai in an interview published in August 2012.

Israel then reached a secret agreement with Rwanda. Unmarried Eritrean or Sudanese men whose asylum applications in Israel had been rejected were given three options: to return to their home country, to be imprisoned indefinitely in an immigration detention centre, or to accept $3,500 and a one-way ticket to Rwanda, as revealed by Amnesty International.

Bahabelom Mengesha, a 36-year-old Eritrean, chose Rwanda because he could neither return to his home country nor did he believe he deserved to be imprisoned, as he told the BBC. Some 4,000 people were sent from Israel to Rwanda between 2014 and 2017. The programme was suspended in 2018 following allegations of human rights violations.

The UK’s £290 million experiment

The “Rwanda Plan” already seemed like a far-fetched idea when, less than five years ago, then Prime Minister, Boris Johnson, announced that anyone who had entered the UK illegally from 1 January onwards “may be transferred to Rwanda”. “The agreement we have reached has no limit, and Rwanda will have the capacity to resettle tens of thousands of people over the coming years,” he stated.

Shortly afterwards, in June 2022, a Boeing 767 was ready to take off from the British military base at Boscombe Down bound for Rwanda. At the last minute, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim order preventing the removal of one of the Iraqi asylum seekers. In a frantic few minutes, lawyers secured injunctions for the other passengers and the flight was cancelled minutes before take-off.

“That agreement was ultimately declared unlawful, precisely because it was deemed not to meet the necessary safeguards and to pose risks in relation to the principle of non-refoulement,” explains Adriana Tidona. The choice of Rwanda is worrying, she continues, “both because of the human rights risks in the country itself and because of the issues relating to the principle of non-refoulement that already arose in the agreement between the UK and Rwanda”.

The British government then negotiated a new agreement with the African country and introduced legislation declaring Rwanda a “safe country”. In the two years the agreement was in force, only four people — who had volunteered, according to the British government — were sent to Rwanda. Following the victory of Keir Starmer’s Labour Party in July 2024, the UK withdrew from the agreement.

The move proved costly for Johnson. The UK paid out £290 million (around €350 million) between 2022 and 2024, according to official figures, without having transferred a single asylum seeker under the programme. “That is the sum paid for the preparations for the agreement,” Tidona explains. Had the programme gone ahead, the figure would have been higher.

Following the cancellation of the agreement, Rwanda claimed that it was owed a further €100 million corresponding to two outstanding annual payments, which the UK ultimately did not have to pay, following a ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in June 2026.

Between 2018 and 2025, 2,760 evacuations from Libya to Rwanda were also carried out under a protection programme led by UNHCR. Of these, more than 2,100 were subsequently resettled in third countries, mainly in Europe and Canada.

$7 million for 250 migrants

Although no estimate of the project’s cost has been made public, there is another similar precedent involving the United States. In June 2025, Rwanda signed an agreement with the United States to accept up to 250 migrants deported from US territory, in exchange for an advance payment of $7.5 million (around €6.8 million), according to the Rwandan government spokesperson, Yolande Makolo, as quoted by Human Rights Watch.

The United States transferred 23 people to Rwanda on four flights in 2025, from countries as wide-ranging as Cambodia, Kazakhstan, Jamaica and Ethiopia, according to Third Country Deportation Watch.

There are “Iranians in Panama, Laotians in Eswatini, Venezuelans in Liberia” and as many as 25,000 people who have been transferred since President Trump took office in 2025. Trump has signed bilateral agreements with 35 countries for deportations, as detailed in an investigation by Forbidden Stories.

Adriana Tidona acknowledges that this has been a trend in recent years, “although I would say it has accelerated over the last two year”, she points out, as demonstrated by the comprehensive reform of the European rules on return, which “aims to act as an absolute deterrent to migratory movements”.

She questions the fact that, rather than investing in systems that “prioritise the dignified management of migration within European territory, the externalisation agenda has gained considerable momentum in Europe”.

Tidona points out that, although return centres are “a very new form of externalisation”, they are not the only ones. In terms of border control, Europe has promoted cooperation with countries such as Libya, Egypt, Tunisia, Turkey and Albania at various levels, both at EU level and at the level of the Member States themselves, “despite the suffering this causes people”, she concludes.

📰 Original article on El Confidencial.

🤝 This article was produced as part of the collaborative project PULSE. Contributors included Kim Son Hoang and Flora Lory (Der Standard, Austria) and Emilie Ewald (Føljeton, Denmark).

title: As Syria-EU talks progress, diplomats fear focus will be on repatriation - Al Jazeera

Al Jazeera reached out to the paper’s author, but she was unavailable for comment.

text:
Officials from Syria and the European Union are working on a deal to normalise relations after a 15-year suspension. But current and former European diplomats have told Al Jazeera they fear that growing right-wing sentiment in Europe could see efforts to repatriate Syrians and immigration being prioritised over other key issues, such as human rights.

Syrian and EU officials hope that a deal with the new government will lead to stronger trade and political relations, after a suspension following then-President Bashar al-Assad’s brutal crackdown on protesters in 2011.

list 2 of 3Syria’s restrained approach to Israel carries risks

list 3 of 3EU agrees to resurrect cooperation deal with Syria

end of list

With al-Assad’s regime overthrown and a government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa seeking closer relations with Europe, there is an opportunity for diplomatic and trade relations to resume.

“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible,” Kaja Kallas, vice president of the European Commission, said in a statement on November 16. “Syria needs investment and a successful transition.”

Analysts and diplomats told Al Jazeera that Syria’s priority in the talks was the removal of lingering EU sanctions. Brussels is largely focused on the repatriation of Syrians, with more than a million fleeing to Europe during the Syrian war between 2011 and 2024. But they added that these issues must be managed carefully to avoid piling pressure on Syria as it continues to rebuild after the war and decades of dictatorship.

“The migration issue is a big issue in Europe today,” Iyad Jaber, the Damascus-based head of Middle East at Timios & Co and former French diplomat of Syrian origin, told Al Jazeera. “Especially with right-wing and far-right wing [parties] taking more political space, it is moving political speech on migration.”

Deepening agreement

The first cooperation agreement between Europe and Syria was signed in 1978 by the EU’s predecessor, the European Economic Community (EEC), when Hafez al-Assad was Syria’s president. The agreement was focused on the economic and social development of Syria and a deepening of ties between the two parties.

In 2008, the EU-Syria Association Agreement was proposed but never signed by either side, largely due to concerns over the Assad government’s record on human rights. In 2011, when the government brutally repressed a popular uprising, the EU suspended ties with Syria.

During that time, the EU moved its diplomatic mission to Beirut and imposed sanctions on the Assad regime, freezing its assets and imposing travel bans on key officials.

Since the overthrow of the Assad regime, the EU has aimed to revive relations with the country. It lifted all economic sanctions on Syria last year, though some dual-use export controls and state institutions remain sanctioned.

In January, Brussels announced a two-year funding package of 620 million euros ($680m) for Syria and in May the EU held its first high-level political dialogue with Syria, which aimed to revive bilateral relations.

The EU’s diplomatic service prepared a discussion paper outlining the normalisation efforts. Al Jazeera reached out to the paper’s author, but she was unavailable for comment.

Kallas said diplomats are now working through technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create frameworks for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.

Many European nations have been exploring reopening embassies or missions in Syria, diplomats told Al Jazeera, while Syrian and EU officials continue talks on normalisation and sanctions removal.

Sally Shobat, Syria’s European Affairs Directorate at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, met Jonas Jonsson, head of the Middle East and North Africa Division at the European External Action Service, on Saturday, after earlier holding bilateral meetings with French, Cypriot and Belgian diplomatic officials.

Priorities

Since the fall of the Assad government, Syria’s new government has worked to revive suspended relations and remove sanctions imposed on its predecessor. Many of the penalties have now been removed and relations with many countries, notably members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the United States, have also improved.

EU-Syrian relations may be moving in a positive direction, but experts said there are still many legal and technical obstacles to full normalisation.

“Every country has their own foreign policy,” Zakaria al-Shmaly, a nonresident fellow at TIMEP focusing on EU-Syria relations, told Al Jazeera.

Still, Syria has tried to prove its importance to Europe in security matters, particularly in the fight against ISIL (ISIS) and as an energy transit point following global disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Europe needs Syria as much as Syria needs Europe,” President al-Sharaa said in Nicosia in April, after an informal meeting between Syria and EU officials.

In April, al-Sharaa proposed the Four Seas and Nine Corridors Initiative, a proposed transatlantic framework connecting the Gulf, Caspian Sea, Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea via a Syria-Turkiye pipeline and transit corridor. The proposal bypasses the Strait of Hormuz for a land pipeline through Syria, following disruptions to shipping because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February.

“Every power is using Syria to undermine Iran,” al-Shmaly said.

Another key point of discussion between the EU and Syria as normalisation talks continue will be trade. Experts said Brussels will likely try to open the Syrian market to EU products, which could benefit Syrian consumers by lowering costs on certain items. However, Syrian negotiators must also consider what kind of things Syrian companies can export to the EU.

“There are not a lot of Syrian exports,” Jaber told Al Jazeera. “They are mostly agricultural and some pharmaceutical, but there are not a lot of exports and this is what the Syrians need to be careful about; otherwise, they will open the market to a lot of European products while still facing barriers and tariffs on what they can export.”

Jaber said there is also room for EU-Syrian coordination on the issue of Assad regime assets, which could be worth tens of billions of dollars and “hidden in several parts of Europe”.

Returns

In the months following a change in government in Damascus, some European states paused asylum claims for Syrians, citing that the dangers from the war and former regime were over.

Migration and the presence of refugees have been a major political issue in Europe for over a decade, particularly as a number of countries experienced a growth in far-right parties or movements.

In her comments on November 16, Kallas addressed the future of human rights in Syria and decisions taken by the Assad regime. “Everybody said that we need to engage with Syria because if we don’t engage, then this vacuum will be filled by other players,” Kallas said. “We should have clear conditionality regarding human rights. We should have also the nonrecognition of occupied Ukrainian, Georgian territories that they have recognised under Assad’s regime.”

In recent years, al-Shmaly claimed that even governments on the political centre-ground had adopted increasingly extreme policies on immigration.

Current and former European diplomats told Al Jazeera they were concerned that Europe would overly focus on repatriation in any deal with Syria, leaving human rights and other important issues by the wayside.

“Structurally, we have a rising number of member states in the EU that are led by right-wing populists who see no interest in engaging in all of Syria’s complexity and challenges,” a former European diplomat, who requested to speak on background, told Al Jazeera.

“We tend to see Syria only through the very limited lens of migration and we also wrongly perceive Syrian refugees as a burden rather than an opportunity despite the fact that the overwhelming majority of Syrian refugees have very positively contributed to the European economy and culture.”

Since the fall of the Assad government, about one million Syrians have returned home, most from neighbouring countries such as Lebanon, Turkiye and Jordan. But experts said Europe must strike a delicate balance on migration due to the slow process of rebuilding the country after years of dictatorship and war.

“As the European Union deepens ties with Syria, returns cannot become the price of that relationship,” Tariq Azeez, the International Rescue Committee’s policy, advocacy and communications coordinator, told Al Jazeera.

“Our research shows the reality many Syrians are returning to: missing services, damaged housing and conditions worse than expected, and competition over scarce resources driving tension within communities. Accelerating returns, therefore, without investing in services for everyone, returnees and those who never left alike, risks fuelling exactly the instability Europe says it wants to prevent.”

title: Asylum Work Permit, No Status: A 30-Year Conundrum - Immigration Analytics
description:
Congress has treated the asylum work permit as a backlog-control tool since 1994, and has never paired it with status.
What the law says about the asylum work permit The rule is a single sentence in the Immigration and Nationality Act.
Before 1994: work came with filing For most of the 1980s and early 1990s, work authorization and asylum moved together.
From 1980, the government could grant a work permit to anyone who filed a “non-frivolous” asylum application.
They frame the work permit as the incentive behind weak claims, not as a benefit that should come with status.
text:
Asylum seekers and cancellation applicants can hold valid work permits for years without ever having lawful status. The record shows that was a choice made in 1994, and Congress has not revisited it since.

A Princeton doctoral student, a UC Berkeley student and a pair of performers in Phoenix were all arrested by ICE at airports this fall while holding valid work permits. Each had a pending asylum case. DHS’s response has been the same every time: work authorization “does not grant legal status.” That is an accurate statement of the law. It also raises a question many readers have asked since: how can the government authorize someone to work for years without giving them any status at all? The answer is in the statute and the record behind it. Congress has treated the asylum work permit as a backlog-control tool since 1994, and has never paired it with status.

What the law says about the asylum work permit

The rule is a single sentence in the Immigration and Nationality Act. Section 208(d)(2) states that “an applicant for asylum is not entitled to employment authorization, but such authorization may be provided under regulation by the Attorney General.” It adds that an applicant “shall not be granted such authorization prior to 180 days after the date of filing.”

The statute makes the work permit a discretionary benefit rather than a right, and leaves the details to regulation. Under the current rule, 8 C.F.R. 208.7, an applicant may apply once the asylum case has been pending 150 days, and no permit may be granted before day 180. The statute never addresses status.

Before 1994: work came with filing

For most of the 1980s and early 1990s, work authorization and asylum moved together. From 1980, the government could grant a work permit to anyone who filed a “non-frivolous” asylum application. From 1990, applicants could file for asylum and a work permit at the same time, according to a 2013 Human Rights Watch history of the rules.

The system buckled under volume. More than 150,000 asylum applications were filed in fiscal year 1993, and the backlog reached 340,000.

1994: Congress names the problem

Congress responded in the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994.

The findings. In Section 130010, the Senate found that delays had fueled “an abuse of the asylum laws by fraudulent applicants whose primary interest is obtaining work authority in the United States while their claim languishes in the backlogged asylum processing system.” It called for “a comprehensive revision of our asylum law and procedures.”

The statute. Section 130005(b) added a new subsection to INA 208: “An applicant for asylum is not entitled to employment authorization except as may be provided by regulation in the discretion of the Attorney General.”

The regulation. The Clinton administration’s final rule of Dec. 5, 1994, separated work authorization from filing. Applicants had to wait 150 days before applying, and no permit could issue before day 180.

The Senate’s findings are the closest thing in the record to an explanation of congressional thinking. They frame the work permit as the incentive behind weak claims, not as a benefit that should come with status. Nothing in them addresses what an applicant waiting years for a decision should be.

1996: the 180-day bar becomes law

Two years later, the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act moved the 1994 language to its current place, Section 208(d)(2), and wrote the 180-day minimum into the statute. Human Rights Watch describes IIRIRA as codifying the 1994 regulations. The same law required asylum cases to be decided within 180 days, absent exceptional circumstances.

That deadline is now far out of reach. In its February 2026 proposal, DHS said the affirmative asylum backlog had tripled to more than 1 million cases by the end of fiscal 2023. The rules assumed a short wait. Applicants now wait years, many of them holding a renewable work permit the entire time.

Cancellation of removal: a work permit by regulation alone

Cancellation applicants are on even thinner ground. The statute that creates cancellation, INA 240A, says nothing about work authorization. The permit comes from regulation alone: category (c)(10) of 8 C.F.R. 274a.12. That category dates to the 1987 rules that followed the 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act, when it covered applicants for suspension of deportation, the relief cancellation replaced. After IIRIRA, a 1997 rule extended it to cancellation applicants. A permit is available once an application has been properly filed with the immigration court.

Winning is much harder. A non-permanent resident must show:

10 years of continuous physical presence;

good moral character;

no disqualifying convictions;

“exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” to a U.S.-citizen or green card holder spouse, parent or child.

The Board of Immigration Appeals has read that hardship standard to require harm “substantially beyond” what ordinarily follows a family member’s deportation. The law also caps grants at 4,000 a year. Applicants can hold work permits for years while their cases wait for one of those slots.

How a typical case unfolds

For a person who overstays a visa and applies for asylum, the usual path looks like this:

Filing. The person files an asylum application with USCIS and, after the waiting period, applies for a work permit.

Referral. If USCIS does not grant the case, it refers it to immigration court with a Notice to Appear. Since July, a DHS rule allows many referrals without an interview at all.

Court. The applicant renews the asylum claim before an immigration judge, and if eligible, may also seek cancellation as an alternative.

Arrest, if it happens. Most people in this posture are never arrested. They attend hearings and keep working. When ICE does arrest someone, as in this fall’s airport cases, the path runs through a bond hearing under INA 236(a), and the case continues whether or not the person is released.

Congress knows how to protect status when it wants to

Other programs go further:

Temporary Protected Status. INA 244(d)(4) bars detaining a TPS holder “on the basis of the alien’s immigration status.”

Granted asylum. Under INA 208(c)(1)(B), asylees are authorized to work as part of their status, and have a path to a green card.

U visas. INA 214(p)(6) allows work permits for petitioners whose pending cases are found bona fide.

For pending asylum applicants, the main protection Congress wrote in concerns the future, not the present. Under INA 212(a)(9)(B)(iii)(II), time spent with a bona fide asylum application pending does not count as unlawful presence, unless the applicant works without authorization. That keeps the three- and 10-year reentry bars from building. It does not stop an arrest.

The bills: timing, terminations and detention, not status

Bills on asylum work permits have pulled in opposite directions, but none would bar detaining an applicant who holds one:

Faster permits (2023): the Asylum Seeker Work Authorization Act, from Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), would require work authorization 30 days after filing. It applies only to applicants “not in detention,” excluding detained applicants rather than protecting them. The ASPIRE Act, backed by Rep. Dan Goldman and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, also proposed 30 days.

Tighter permits and more detention (2023 and 2026): H.R. 2, the Secure the Border Act, passed the House in 2023. It would have limited asylum work permits to six-month terms and expanded mandatory detention. In 2026, House Republicans introduced the Permanent Trump Secure Border Act, H.R. 9199, and H.R. 9773 to carry that approach forward.

Fees (2025): the reconciliation law added fees for asylum applicants’ initial and renewal work permits.

A status, but broader (2025): the Dignity Act, H.R. 4393, from Reps. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) and Veronica Escobar (D-Texas), would create a renewable seven-year “Dignity status.” It would come with work authorization, travel permission and protection from removal for undocumented people present since Dec. 31, 2020, in exchange for a $1,000 initial payment, $7,000 in restitution and other conditions. It does not single out asylum or cancellation applicants, but many of them would likely meet its presence date.

The administration’s February 2026 proposal goes further in the restrictive direction. It would restore a 365-day wait and pause new permits whenever affirmative asylum processing averages more than 180 days. DHS said the backlog “serves as a magnet pulling aliens into the U.S. illegally.” Comments closed April 24, and no final rule has been published.

Both sides argue about the work permit in economic terms. Supporters of longer waits see it as the draw behind meritless claims, echoing the Senate’s 1994 findings. Supporters of shorter waits see it as the way applicants support themselves rather than relying on public aid. Neither side has proposed that years of authorized work should, by itself, carry any protection from detention.

Why it matters now

The result is a population the law recognizes in pieces. These applicants have Social Security numbers, employers, tax records and court dates, and their unlawful presence often isn’t counting. Yet any of them can be arrested at an airport gate.

Congress showed with TPS that it can write a no-detention rule into a status. Whether it will consider something similar for asylum and cancellation applicants, or for the larger group the Dignity Act targets, is an open question. With asylum backlogs above a million cases and decisions years away, the question Congress set aside in 1994 now reaches far more people.

text:
Changes to the PERM labor certification process are on the horizon.

On Oct. 23, 2026, the White House’s Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) cleared a Department of Labor (DOL) proposal (RIN 1205-AC29) to modernize the PERM labor certification process. Public release of a proposed rule may be on the horizon; followed by a notice-and-comment period as well as issuance of a final rule that will put any changes into effect.

The PERM labor certification process is a key method for employers to sponsor foreign national workers for employment-based green cards. The PERM process has not received a significant update since 2004. Thus, stakeholders can expect the proposal to contain updates to required and acceptable methods of recruitment to better reflect how employers currently recruit and hire talent.

However, the DOL has stated that the proposal will also contain additional enforcement-related updates, including:

Raising the minimum standards for recruiting qualified U.S. workers;

Strengthening safeguards for U.S. workers affected by layoffs; and

Improving employer compliance with non-discriminatory recruitment and hiring practices and record retention requirements.

This development comes amid broader efforts by the DOL and the Department of Justice to identify and prosecute large tech companies and other employers that they allege failed to follow established PERM guidelines.

Although there are no immediate changes, employers should anticipate that the PERM process will soon require:

More demanding recruitment;

Closer scrutiny of any recent layoffs; and

Heavier recordkeeping obligations.

Employers should review their internal processes to ensure compliance and that current PERM recruitment efforts mirror their general recruitment efforts.

text:
EU countries’ plans to send failed asylum-seekers to Rwanda risk fueling violent conflict and forced migration in Africa, according to the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Rwanda stands accused of supporting rebel forces that have taken control of large areas of eastern Congo, resulting in thousands of deaths and hundreds of thousands being displaced, the United Nations has said.

Kinshasa fears the new migration plan will allow Rwanda to funnel European money to the rebels and “divert attention from [the country’s] destabilizing role in the Great Lakes region,” according to Congo’s Foreign Affairs Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner.

“It is puzzling to see that a country that is at the heart, not just of instability, not just of conflict, but also of displacement and forced migration, is perceived to be a safe haven and … a credible partner to uphold international law,” Wagner told POLITICO.

“The issue here is that we have [EU] countries that have the means, the access, [and] the capacity to know better, making an informed choice to look the other way,” Wagner added, telling EU countries to “go back to their notes” and rethink the choice of partner.

The government of Rwanda did not respond to a request for comment.

Last week, five countries — Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands — announced they will set up a deportation hub in Rwanda. While talks are ongoing, the five countries plan to start sending people to Rwanda in 2027. It’s part of a broader push by the bloc to gain greater control over who enters the EU — and who gets to stay.

EU legislation approved earlier this year allows countries to negotiate such deals, as long as they safeguard fundamental rights. The announcement led to an outcry from rights groups, which warned that Kigali’s human rights record should disqualify it from such a partnership.

Rwanda, besides having “a well-established record of repressing dissent,” also “provides critical support to and exercises overall control over the M23 armed group in eastern Congo,” NGO Human Rights Watch said this week.

M23 occupies large swathes of North and South Kivu provinces in eastern Congo, having ramped up hostilities in early 2025 with a major offensive to capture Goma, the capital of North Kivu. The violence has displaced hundreds of thousands and the fighting around Goma alone left thousands dead. “Rapes, gang rapes, violent assaults and killings of civilians are a common feature of M23’s modus operandi,” U.N experts said.

Kigali has repeatedly denied supporting the rebels, but the U.S., U.N. and EU have all called on Rwanda and its army to halt support for M23 and withdraw troops from Congo. Last month, the U.S. announced sanctions on Rwanda’s defense ministry and a financial institution over support for the armed group.

Because of the U.S. sanctions, “there is a need for currency to come into the country. And it’s very convenient that the [EU countries] will be filling that gap,” Wagner said. “Why invest in a country that is violating the territorial integrity of another country?”

“Our cooperation with Rwanda to establish a return hub has no bearing on the German government’s position regarding the conflict in eastern Congo,” said Christina Lewinsky, a spokesperson for German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt.

Denmark’s foreign affairs ministry said the country’s “position on the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains unchanged,” and pointed to a statement dated Oct. 30 by the International Contact Group for the Great Lakes region (of which Denmark is a member) calling for a “lasting and peaceful resolution” to the conflict.

Governments of Austria, Greece and the Netherlands didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Denmark and Greece are both non-permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, which in a resolution last year demanded that Rwanda’s defense forces stop supporting M23, and also called on Congo’s military forces to halt support for armed groups.

Announcing the partnership with Rwanda, ministers from the five EU countries repeatedly stressed that the protection of people sent to the country would remain a key priority and that the hub would be in line with EU and international law. Rwanda, they said, “has established itself as a reliable and responsible partner in addressing the global challenges of migration and forced displacement.”

Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta took a similar line at a migration conference in Vienna last week. “Human rights in Rwanda are respected and granted to everyone and specifically to refugees who choose to come to our country,” he said, hitting back at protests by NGOs against the return hub deal. He stressed that his country already hosts thousands of refugees, including from Congo and Burundi.

Congo’s Wagner said her country houses thousands of Rwandan refugees who “have not felt safe to return,” adding that those numbers “dwarf the number of refugees that are hosted by Rwanda.”

text:
The Ministry of Defence’s latest guidance on the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), updated on 16 November 2026, sets out a much more detailed framework for Category 4. It now explains what a ‘substantive and positive contribution’ to the UK government’s national security objectives requires, a question central to several recent judicial review challenges.

As ARAP closed to new principal applications on 1 July 2025, the changes matter most to pending applicants and those seeking a review of a refusal. This briefing looks at the new Category 4 framework, then summarises the other changes made to the guidance this year.

Category 4: a more detailed and nuanced framework

The Immigration Rules themselves are unchanged. Paragraph ARAP 3.6 of Appendix ARAP provides that a person meets the eligibility requirement ‘if conditions 1 and 2 and one or both of conditions 3 and 4 applies’.

The person must, on or after 1 October 2001, have been directly employed by, contracted to provide goods or services to, or worked alongside (in partnership with or closely supporting and assisting) a UK government department in Afghanistan (Condition 1). In that work, they must have made a substantive and positive contribution to the UK government’s military or national security objectives with respect to Afghanistan, which include counter-terrorism, counter-narcotics and anti-corruption (Condition 2).

In addition, because of that work, they must be or have been at an elevated risk of targeted attacks and at high risk of death or serious injury (Condition 3), and/or hold information whose disclosure would give rise to or aggravate a specific threat to a UK government department or its interests (Condition 4).

What has changed is the guidance on Condition 2. Previously, Category 4 cases involving the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office were assessed under its unpublished operational guidance (in place from 20 June 2023 to 12 March 2026), while the published guidance largely reproduced the Rules. The latest version explains in detail what a ‘substantive and positive contribution’ requires, defining it as one that is:

important, serious and substantial;

the applicant’s own personal contribution; and

one which directly, materially and significantly contributed towards the achievement of the UK government’s national security objectives with respect to Afghanistan.

National security objectives are those ‘intended to promote the security of the United Kingdom and its people’. They are not limited to counter-terrorism, counter-narcotics and anti-corruption; nor need the work have been undertaken specifically to further such an objective. However, it is not enough that an activity furthered such an objective: the applicant’s own contribution must be substantive and positive.

In assessing this, the following factors are considered:

which national security objective(s) the work contributed towards;

how significant the activity was to furthering those objectives;

whether there was a direct link between the applicant’s own actions and those objectives, rather than mere association;

what the applicant personally did;

the impact of the applicant’s personal contribution; and

whether the contribution was routine or mundane, or required specialist skill, knowledge or other qualities.

No single factor is determinative. The evidence is considered as a whole and the onus is on the applicant. A routine or mundane role, even one conducted under dangerous conditions, is unlikely to meet the criteria.

The CHD challenge

The new Category 4 guidance follows a series of judicial review challenges concerning the interpretation of Category 4, most notably CHD v Secretary of State for Defence [2026] EWHC 566 (Admin). See our write-up of that case here.

The claimant in CHD worked on a UK-funded rule of law programme in Afghanistan. During the proceedings, the government disclosed the Foreign Office’s unpublished operational guidance used in Category 4 assessments. Shortly afterwards, the decision and guidance were withdrawn, although Mr Justice Saini gave judgment because the issues raised were capable of affecting other ARAP applicants.

The revised guidance now includes detailed explanations of concepts that featured prominently in CHD, including personal contribution, operational impact and the distinction between direct and supporting roles. It also makes clear that the examples of national security objectives contained in the Immigration Rules are not exhaustive and that qualifying contributions may extend beyond counter-terrorism, counter-narcotics and anti-corruption work.

Other changes to the guidance this year

The Category 4 changes follow earlier amendments made from 28 April 2026 when a written ministerial statement announced the end of in-country assisted evacuation from Afghanistan and the enforcement of relocation time limits. We covered those changes in more detail here.

The deadline for responding to Ministry of Defence information requests has been cut from 42 days to 14. Failure to respond will result in rejection unless exceptional circumstances apply, which may be difficult for applicants who are displaced, in hiding or without documents.

Eligible Afghan citizens and their immediate family members have 12 months from their eligibility letter (or from 28 April 2026, for earlier letters) to travel to a third country and enrol biometrics at a visa application centre. Otherwise, the Ministry of Defence ‘will not make a UK entry clearance application’ and the person ‘will not be able to relocate to the UK under ARAP’. The guidance says this ‘will be rigorously enforced, unless exceptional circumstances apply’, a term it does not define. The ministerial statement set a December 2028 backstop for entry clearance applications, subject to exceptional circumstances.

For decisions from 28 April 2026, a review must be sought within 28 calendar days of receipt of the outcome letter, rather than 90, unless compelling circumstances prevented the applicant from meeting the deadline. The guidance does not repeat the compelling circumstances exception for additional family member reviews.

The Ministry of Defence has also published a fraud and false representation policy and a withdrawal of eligibility policy, and the Home Office caseworker guidance also has new sections on assessing fraud and withdrawing eligibility.

Applicants who do not provide truthful and sufficient evidence may see their application refused or withdrawn on eligibility, and false information about family members may also lead to withdrawal of the principal’s own offer. An offer will also be withdrawn if the applicant stops responding for 12 months before relocation.

Comment

The latest guidance does not formally change the eligibility criteria under ARAP. Its importance is practical: a more detailed Category 4 framework, alongside the tighter deadlines, a strict relocation timetable and more emphasis on compliance and withdrawal.

Taken together, the changes indicate that the Ministry of Defence is focused on closing ARAP. According to the 28 April 2026 ministerial statement, the government aims to make all remaining eligibility decisions by spring 2027, with a December 2028 backstop for relocations. It cited evidence of successful self-moves, a reassessment of risk and value for money, though it has not published those assessments. Clear timescales may also give applicants greater certainty.

At the same time, the timetable places significant demands on applicants. Those found eligible have shown a high and imminent risk to life, yet some may be in hiding or lack the documents or funds to leave Afghanistan unaided.

The key question is how flexibly the Ministry of Defence applies its exceptions. Decisions under the new deadlines are likely to raise issues of procedural fairness and rationality, particularly while ‘exceptional circumstances’ remains undefined.

text:
A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

“They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people,” Catala said of the father and daughter. “She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it’s just heartbreaking.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa "in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia's husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

“When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said.

“It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on.”

“They just lunged forward. They didn’t identify themselves and then sort of hit this family from behind,” John Gaedeke, who was in line waiting to board the flight and filmed part of the confrontation on his cellphone, said of the officers.

Gaedeke said passengers on the jet bridge were screaming or crying “because it was just so emotional, and just to see the pain and anguish and then the speed and violence with which it happened.”

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.
