title: I Fear Victory Without Principle - Liberal Currents
description:
In 1994, 59 percent of California voters voted yes on Proposition 187.
Proposition 187 would have banned children whose parents could not prove they entered the country lawfully from public schools, Plyler v. Doe (which expressly prohibited such exclusions) be damned.
Not only did Proposition 187 pass by a wide margin (59 to 41), it was widely credited with having helped Pete Wilson, the incumbent Republican governor and one of Proposition 187’s biggest boosters, win reelection.
California has elected exactly one Republican governor since 1994: Arnold Schwarzenegger, who unseated Gray Davis in a 2003 recall precipitated by the state’s energy crisis.
What they will not do, what seemingly eternally blue California has failed to do, is find the lives of those others worthy of our investment.
text:
In 1994, 59 percent of California voters voted yes on Proposition 187. That ballot measure, entitled “Save Our State,” made it illegal for “illegal aliens” to access public services of any kind, including non-emergency health care. Proposition 187 would have banned children whose parents could not prove they entered the country lawfully from public schools, Plyler v. Doe (which expressly prohibited such exclusions) be damned. Proposition 187 required every police officer in the state to investigate the immigration status of all arrestees and report any unlawful immigrants to both California’s Attorney General and the Immigration and Naturalization Service (the agency responsible for internal immigration enforcement before Bush-era legislation created the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement).

Not only did Proposition 187 pass by a wide margin (59 to 41), it was widely credited with having helped Pete Wilson, the incumbent Republican governor and one of Proposition 187’s biggest boosters, win reelection. Wilson ran ads with footage of people running through the gates at a border crossing, bemoaning the federal government’s lack of enforcement.

Proposition 187 was, fortunately, never implemented; a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction preventing the state from applying its provisions shortly after it passed (but not in time to save Julio Cano, who died after his parents declined to seek medical care because they feared deportation). Various civil rights groups, including the ACLU and MALDEF, challenged the law on the grounds that it violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s equal protection guarantee and interfered with the federal government’s authority over immigration. (That latter argument proved convincing to the U.S. Supreme Court in striking down much of Arizona’s 2010 SB 1070, another anti-immigration measure. A good reminder, to those of us who wrap ourselves in the bear flag and root for California in its ongoing battles against Trump’s immigration enforcement, that federalism is a fickle friend.) The Ninth Circuit upheld a district court decision enjoining the law, and California elected a Democrat, Gray Davis, in 1998, and he declined to pursue any further appeals, allowing the “Save Our State” initiative to die a quiet, and ignominious, death.

California has elected exactly one Republican governor since 1994: Arnold Schwarzenegger, who unseated Gray Davis in a 2003 recall precipitated by the state’s energy crisis. The last election in which California Republicans won statewide office was 2006, when Schwarzenegger was reelected, along with state insurance commissioner Steven Poizner.

In November 2016, a minority of the American electorate distributed across various states in such a manner as to create an electoral college majority elected Donald J. Trump president. Like Pete Wilson before him, Trump ran on an explicitly anti-immigrant platform, invoking images of contagion and invasion. Eleven months later, in October 2017, the California legislature enacted SB 54, the California Values Act, prohibiting police and sheriffs from inquiring into arrestees’ immigration status (although jails and prisons were allowed to, and still do, release immigrants directly to ICE upon completion of their sentences). A California law enacted in 2016 extended Medi-Cal (the state’s implementation of Medicaid, i.e., the partially federally-funded health insurance program for low-income people) to undocumented immigrant children in low-income families. The state expanded coverage to low-income undocumented immigrant young adults in 2020, to low-income undocumented immigrant adults over 50 in 2022, and to low-income adults, of any immigration status, in 2024. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024 with an outright plurality of votes cast, California had not just repudiated Proposition 187; now, protecting immigrants had become a “California value.”

It is not wrong to read this summary history, to look at the “blue tsunami” of November 3, and think: Trump was our national Prop 187. Despite what you or I may have feared in November 2024, there is no permanent pro-fascism plurality among the American electorate, no mass appetite for sustained anti-immigrant violence or repression. We were never staring down our own 1933, the cannibalization of society by the dark forces of violent white supremacy through the enthusiastic participation or tacit consent of our fellow citizens. We were just metabolizing another phase of demographic transformation. The U.S. has always been anti-immigrant, until it wasn’t; whiteness has proven a surprisingly capacious category, able to absorb the Irish and the Italians and the Jews—after the requisite period of social exclusion and stochastic violence.

The elections of 2016 and 2024, perhaps, were the last spasm of this opposition to the new complexion of the U.S. social body, the final gasp of this generation’s Know Nothings. The white voters who used terms like invasion either succumbed to the demographic wave they feared at the ballot box (California’s electorate was 8% Latino in 1994, 29% in 2024) or realized their racialized and economic status were not actually as threatened by cultural, linguistic, or racial diversity as they had been led to believe.

In this story, 2024 was the high point of white resentment (at least against immigration) and of the Republican Party in its current ideological formation. The blue arrows will become blue areas, the feckless representatives who hitched their elephants to Trump will be definitively discredited, perhaps we’ll even get a Centrist and a Left party, a blue split into purple and cerulean. Or perhaps the presidency will, like the California governorship, become the fiefdom of the most successful Democratic party-climber, and one-party rule will neither be dictatorial nor extremist so much as uninspiring. We (or rather, some significant subset of “we”) will have survived the worst of the reaction. We’ll have immigration itself to thank for this, as well as the basic humanity of voters who liked fascism well enough in the abstract but not when it happened to people they know, and liberalism (in many of that term’s meanings) will have triumphed.

Except. California was very much a part of the blue wave; aided by the state’s revenge gerrymander, Democrats took all but four house seats of the state’s fifty-two. The Republican Party of California is defunct. But when asked to weigh in directly on the state’s policies, the voters of California, apparently, did not share Democratic candidates’ anti-billionaire sentiment. Proposition 40, which would have imposed a one-time tax on billionaires, has failed to secure the requisite 50% of the vote. Perhaps even more surprising, Proposition 42, which would prohibit many wealth taxes, has passed. Some part of this is no doubt the fault of Gavin Newsom, who publicly opposed Proposition 40 and supported Proposition 42. But it also seems utterly inexplicable in a moment in which, if you’re an online lefty, you’re told that expropriating billionaires is the necessary and sufficient condition for a 1,000-year-reign of the Democratic Party.

Those of us familiar with California politics are familiar with tax revolts. We have been living in the wreckage (and caught in the occasional flare-ups) for almost half a century of what is arguably the country’s most dramatic repudiation of giving the government money with which to do things: Proposition 13. Among its many other provisions (including a requirement that new taxes pass the state legislature by a two-thirds majority), Proposition 13 limits property taxes to no more than 1% of assessed value and limits the increase in assessed value on property from year to year to 2%. Proposition 13 is why a 35-year-old may pay five, six, ten times as much in property taxes on their house as their 65-year-old neighbor. Proposition 13 is why California dropped from fifth to forty-seventh in the U.S. for per-pupil funding in K-12 schools. And Proposition 13 is why California’s budget fluctuates wildly based on personal income tax receipts. (A related measure, the Gann Limit, approved the year after Proposition 13, prevents state elected officials from mitigating these swings through budget surpluses, although voters have modified that slightly via Proposition 2 this year.) And yes, given the opportunity, Californians declined to exclude commercial property from Proposition 13’s protections as recently as 2020.

But enacting self-destructive tax measures out of a misguided impulse to protect little old ladies from being taxed out of their modest (but also million-dollar) homes is one thing. Refusing to tax billionaires is quite another. And even if you credit (which I don’t) the argument that taxing billionaires is fine but this specific measure is poorly designed, how could that concern with exactitude justify prohibiting wealth taxes in the future, however designed and targeted? What Proposition 42 specifically prohibits is the taxation of value increases before those increases are realized; if it passes, California can tax capital gains when investors cash out, but not the increase in stock value before those stocks are sold. The fundamental mechanism of ultra-wealthy spending is to utilize endless zero-interest loans in lieu of spending as a means of avoiding taxes. If you want to get at the super-rich, you have to tax unrealized gains, because the super-rich have found One Weird Trick for living off that exorbitant wealth without ever actually realizing it. Only sixty-two percent of Americans have any money in the stock market. Who the heck did “yes” voters on Proposition 42 think they were protecting?

But whatever voters’ appetite might be for taxing billionaires, specifically, Proposition 40 was not merely an anti-oligarchy measure. Rather, Proposition 40 was needed because without it, California is facing a $100 billion funding shortfall as a result of Republican federal health care funding cuts. Beginning January 1 of this year, undocumented adult immigrants are no longer eligible for public health insurance if they have not already enrolled. Next year those who have been enrolled will start having to pay for that insurance. In 2025, all but two Democratic state lawmakers voted to cut medical coverage for Californians without “Satisfactory Immigration Status.” By voting down Proposition 40, California voters have deprived the state of funding that would have restored health insurance coverage (or prevented cutting health insurance coverage) for undocumented immigrants.

If California, under Trump I, took great pride in its refutation of Trump’s anti-immigration rhetoric by extending the state’s social services to those immigrants Trump most wanted to harm and deport, under Trump II, the state and its voters have effectively cut off those same immigrants from public services not through the explicit racism of categorical denial but the backdoor deprivation of budget cuts.

In November’s watershed election, the top issue was, well, the usual: “the economy.” After that though, voters identified “the state of democracy” and “government corruption” as the biggest concerns, at least according to the BBC.

Viewing the state of democracy as imbricated with government corruption is, perhaps, quintessentially American. American voters were unimpressed by Trump’s promises of $5,000 checks after the midterm if Republicans prevailed. As Eric Nelson has extensively documented, the Founders were not solely concerned with executive tyranny, that is to say, a President seizing authority from the legislative branch; they were worried that the interests of the rulers would diverge from those of the ruled. Parliament could be as tyrannical as King George III, and Washington et al. saw the King as a potential bulwark against the depredations of Britain’s elected representatives. As Alexander Hamilton put it in The Farmer Refuted:

“The authority of the British Parliament over America, would, in all probability, be a more intolerable and excessive species of despotism than an absolute monarchy. The power of an absolute prince is not temporary, but perpetual. He is under no temptation to purchase the favour of one part of his dominions, at the expence of another; but, it is his interest to treat them all, upon the same footing. Very different is the case with regard to the Parliament…”

And Thomas Jefferson, writing in July 1774 against the King’s practice of vetoing colonial legislation (one of the “injuries and usurpations” listed in the Declaration of Independence), nevertheless reaffirmed that it was in “the great office of his majesty, to resume the exercise of his negative power, and to prevent the passage of laws by any one legislature of the empire,” that is, Parliament, “which might bear injuriously on the rights and interests of another,” that is, the colonies.

According to Nelson, this view of the king as a potential protector of the colonists as against the self-interested metropolitan Parliament was almost unilaterally bested by the publication of Thomas Paine’s Common Sense. Paine made the case that monarchy led inevitably to corruption and, with it, the loss of self-determination, as a king could buy off political opponents, draft people and tax property to build a personal army, or simply live off the public fisc while spending yet more on wars. The king was the source of corruption in the English constitutional order; his power derived from “being the giver of places and pensions,” and though he “hath little more to do than make war and give away places,” with these powers the king could “empoverish the nation and set it together by the ears.” Patriotism consisted not just in independence from a Parliament looking to extract resources from the colonies for the benefits of its electorate, but the repudiation of self-interested rule altogether, which necessarily entailed the overthrow of the inherently self-interested monarchy.

Originalism is bunk. But also if one is to go looking for a distinctively American political theory dating back to the Revolutionary War and the drafting of the Constitution and all that, one could do worse than to identify opposition to the use of government as a vehicle for economic self-interest by those in power as the canonical and distinctively American political value. Concern with political power as a means of economic exploitation explains colonists’ willingness to invoke King George III as a protector and ally against Parliament, the Boston Tea Party, and the battles over a federal bank (and with it a decent chunk of the central conflict of Act II of Hamilton). If voters cast their ballot with the sense that Trump’s disregard of Congress in crafting his tariff policy and his use of that policy to extract personal gifts from various heads of state were related, well, it may be that they half-remembered high school civics readings in doing so.

Here, however, is the rub. Opposition to the use of government as a means of self-enrichment easily curdles into opposition to government as such, even (maybe especially) when that government is serving as a means of redistribution or just reallocating resources from the private to the public. Heather McGhee has argued that the refusal to pay taxes is not in fact separable from racism, and is instead the self-sabotage of those incapable of sharing with those who do not share their identity, rather than out of a colorblind opposition to taxes as such. But while that argument may have a great deal of force in many other contexts, it does not quite explain California, or at least, not completely.

We are a state of multi-million dollar homes, taxed at a fraction of their market value, with signs reading “In this house we believe…” and asserting all are welcome. Perhaps this is simply hypocrisy, and we are not as embracing of diversity as our posters or legislators claim. But whether we are lying, uninformed, or misguided, California’s decidedly anti-Republican and anti-tax status quo is a harbinger for an electorally ascendant Democratic party across the country as a whole, and must be confronted.

If 2024 was the country’s Prop 187 election (and I hope it was), then the failure of Proposition 40 and passage of Proposition 42 offer a less optimistic preview, one I hope the new class of elected Representatives and Senators will study. I agree with those who believe the most urgent priorities for elected Democrats are about restoring little-d democracy: SCOTUS reform is the necessary precondition to ensure any laws passed are allowed to go into operation. After that: get ICE agents off our streets (unmasking them and marking their vans are woefully insufficient) and reverse Trump’s unlawful and unilateral actions, from tariffs to Iran to the blockade of Cuba and the murder of fishermen in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.

There is no shortage of people who will argue that Democrats should prioritize hearings or healthcare, SCOTUS or executive branch impeachments. Largely unmentioned, though, is the Trump administration action with the highest death toll. I fear that the most consequential of all of Trump’s tyrannical actions will not be a priority, and will go unrepaired and unpunished: DOGE’s rapid unscheduled disassembly of USAID in a shockingly short period in January and February 2025. The aftershocks of the literal ransacking will be felt for generations. A Lancet study concluded that unless USAID funding is restored, fourteen million people will die by 2030 who would have been alive had Elon Musk not stormed into that DC office building with his gang of execrable college dropouts. Perhaps I am wrong (I hope I am wrong) but I have little hope that Democrats who are “laser-focused” on affordability for Americans will expend political capital (or hearing time, or votes) on somehow restoring funding and personnel to the most inaccessible, resource-deprived places in the globe.

Americans, like Californians, will repudiate the explicit denigration of the lives and dignity of non-members, of outsiders, of others. What they will not do, what seemingly eternally blue California has failed to do, is find the lives of those others worthy of our investment. We will not turn away undocumented immigrants because they lack papers, but we’ll turn them away for (our) lack of funds.

There is so very much to be hopeful about after last Tuesday, so much of it the product of quiet, persistent organizing from within deeply gerrymandered and hostile state political systems. When he is sworn in next year, Scott Colom will be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction. The purpose of this warning is not to minimize these accomplishments, but to urge the newly empowered elected officials to spend the political capital to be worthy of those efforts. Out here in California, however, I am wary that the plurality of voters who rejected “corruption” will fail to distinguish between a ballroom and USAID, and only see that the money is going to strangers, that those who cast a vote for “democracy” will also not be willing to pay for its infrastructure. But I am more worried that an ascendant Democratic Party will, rather than embark on the hard work of political education as to the need for this collective contribution, continue to treat citizens like mere consumers.

This election was harm reduction. And perhaps, as my more anarchist-inclined friends would say, that’s all voting can ever be. But I’ll continue to believe that the real victory will come if and when our elected officials can commit to, and convince voters of, the government’s capacity to protect the most vulnerable among us, not just to refrain from murdering them. One day, maybe, voting will cease to be a defensive maneuver against our neighbors’ worst impulses and instead become a debate about how best to use our collective power and resources to secure their well-being. California, despite its decade-old deep blue hue, is not there yet. Instead, California offers the national Democratic Party a warning: If you believe in a multi-racial democracy and if you believe in protecting human dignity, well, you’re going to have to convince people to pay for it. And if you don’t, or if you can’t, well, we’ll all drown together in an empty blue ocean.

text:
The Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in Batavia, New York, where Ukrainian nationals involved in federal immigration detention proceedings have been held.

Attorney Elena Dvoinik at the U.S. District Court for the Western District of New York, where she represents clients in federal immigration detention and habeas corpus proceedings.

New federal habeas petition filed for Ukrainian truck driver; three earlier ICE detention cases see developments involving bond, custody, and missing property.

U4U parole and re-parole questions remain important in these cases. We review each client's immigration records and the legal grounds for detention individually.”

— Elena Dvoinik, Attorney at Law

BUFFALO, NY, UNITED STATES, November 23, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- New York attorney Elena Dvoinik has filed a federal habeas corpus petition on behalf of a 22-year-old Ukrainian truck driver arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on November 18, 2026.

The filing is among several recent developments involving four Ukrainian nationals who entered the United States through the Uniting for Ukraine (U4U) humanitarian parole program. The other developments include a $10,000 immigration bond order, continued detention of a Ukrainian humanitarian volunteer, and an unresolved complaint concerning personal property not returned following immigration detention.

Oleksandr Sovenko: Federal Habeas Petition Filed November 20

Oleksandr Sovenko, 22, left Ukraine with his family following Russia's invasion. He plans to pursue university studies in biochemistry and worked as a commercial truck driver in the United States to save money for his education.

Sovenko entered the United States under the U4U program on April 10, 2024, established a residence in New Jersey, and obtained employment authorization valid through August 2027.

On November 18, 2026, ICE officers arrested him at a truck stop in New York State. According to Sovenko, officers did not present an arrest warrant. The federal petition states that he has no criminal history.

A video reportedly showing the arrest was shared on Instagram.

https://www.instagram.com/reels/Df5Fyo6Rixw/

Sovenko's mother, Svitlana Sovenko, currently resides in Germany. After viewing the video and being unable to contact her son, she submitted a welfare inquiry to local law enforcement on November 19, requesting information about his location and safety.

On November 20, Dvoinik filed an emergency petition for a writ of habeas corpus in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of New York.

The petition, Sovenko v. Ball et al., Case No. 1:26-cv-02725, requests judicial review of the statutory grounds for his arrest and detention, disclosure of relevant government records, and clarification of his immigration custody classification.

The petition also addresses Sovenko's reported renewed humanitarian parole. Counsel had not independently obtained the renewal approval notice at the time of filing.

The requested relief includes release if the detention is determined to be unlawful or, alternatively, an individualized custody hearing.

According to the petition, Sovenko is detained at the Buffalo Service Processing Center in Batavia, New York.

Igor Labunskyi: Property Complaint Remains Unresolved

Igor Labunskyi, who was released from immigration detention after a $25,000 bond was posted, remains subject to ICE electronic monitoring.

Labunskyi reports that his mobile phones, identification documents, jewelry, and other personal belongings were not returned following his detention and transfer to the Jackson Parish detention facility in Louisiana.

A complaint regarding the missing property was submitted to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General (OIG).

According to counsel, as of November 22, 2026, no substantive response to the complaint has been received, and the reported missing property has not been returned.

Labunskyi is seeking financial assistance following his detention and has established a GoFundMe campaign to receive contributions.

His fundraising campaign is available at:

Igor Labunskyi — GoFundMe

Vitaliy Stavnisty: Federal Habeas Proceedings Continue

Vitaliy Stavnisty, 59, a Ukrainian humanitarian volunteer whose activities were described in earlier coverage, remains detained at the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in Batavia, New York.

According to documentation reviewed by counsel, Stavnisty's humanitarian parole is valid through May 2028.

His detention is the subject of a federal habeas proceeding, Stavnisty v. Ball et al., Case No. 1:26-cv-02482-JLS, pending before U.S. District Judge John L. Sinatra Jr. in the Western District of New York.

Counsel has also raised concerns regarding Stavnisty's medical condition and the availability of appropriate medical care during detention.

Roman Serdiuk: Immigration Judge Orders Release on $10,000 Bond

Roman Serdiuk, a Ukrainian international seaman from Mariupol, received a new immigration court custody determination on November 19, 2026.

His detention had been challenged in federal court in Serdiuk v. Ball et al., Case No. 1:26-cv-02567-LJV, before U.S. District Judge Lawrence J. Vilardo.

Following federal court proceedings, Immigration Judge Alexander Rubin conducted a custody redetermination hearing and ordered Serdiuk's release upon payment of a $10,000 immigration bond.

The decision followed an earlier immigration court determination that jurisdiction to grant bond was unavailable.

The U.S. Attorney's Office subsequently notified the federal district court of the November 19 bond order.

Background: November 8 Announcement

The developments involving Labunskyi, Stavnisty, and Serdiuk follow a November 8, 2026, announcement titled New York Attorney Challenges ICE Detention of Three Ukrainian Humanitarian Parolees.

The earlier announcement was also covered by Hoodline in its November 8 article, Buffalo ICE Detention of Three Ukrainian Parolees Sparks Urgent Legal Fight.

The present update addresses developments occurring after that announcement and introduces the federal habeas proceeding filed on behalf of Oleksandr Sovenko.

Statement from Counsel

"Each case involves different facts, immigration records, and custody proceedings," said Elena Dvoinik, Attorney at Law.

"The November 20 petition seeks judicial review of Oleksandr Sovenko's detention. Vitaliy Stavnisty's habeas proceeding remains pending, and Roman Serdiuk received a new bond order on November 19."

"Separately, Igor Labunskyi continues to seek the return of personal property he reports was not returned following detention. His complaint to the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General remains without a substantive response, and he has established a fundraising campaign."

The pending proceedings remain subject to further judicial and administrative action.

text:
Officials from Syria and the European Union are working on a deal to normalise relations after a 15-year suspension. But current and former European diplomats have told Al Jazeera they fear that growing right-wing sentiment in Europe could see efforts to repatriate Syrians and immigration being prioritised over other key issues, such as human rights.

Syrian and EU officials hope that a deal with the new government will lead to stronger trade and political relations, after a suspension following then-President Bashar al-Assad’s brutal crackdown on protesters in 2011.

list 3 of 3EU agrees to resurrect cooperation deal with Syria

end of list

With al-Assad’s regime overthrown and a government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa seeking closer relations with Europe, there is an opportunity for diplomatic and trade relations to resume.

“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible,” Kaja Kallas, vice president of the European Commission, said in a statement on November 16. “Syria needs investment and a successful transition.”

Analysts and diplomats told Al Jazeera that Syria’s priority in the talks was the removal of lingering EU sanctions. Brussels is largely focused on the repatriation of Syrians, with more than a million fleeing to Europe during the Syrian war between 2011 and 2024. But they added that these issues must be managed carefully to avoid piling pressure on Syria as it continues to rebuild after the war and decades of dictatorship.

“The migration issue is a big issue in Europe today,” Iyad Jaber, the Damascus-based head of Middle East at Timios & Co and former French diplomat of Syrian origin, told Al Jazeera. “Especially with right-wing and far-right wing [parties] taking more political space, it is moving political speech on migration.”

Deepening agreement

The first cooperation agreement between Europe and Syria was signed in 1978 by the EU’s predecessor, the European Economic Community (EEC), when Hafez al-Assad was Syria’s president. The agreement was focused on the economic and social development of Syria and a deepening of ties between the two parties.

In 2008, the EU-Syria Association Agreement was proposed but never signed by either side, largely due to concerns over the Assad government’s record on human rights. In 2011, when the government brutally repressed a popular uprising, the EU suspended ties with Syria.

During that time, the EU moved its diplomatic mission to Beirut and imposed sanctions on the Assad regime, freezing its assets and imposing travel bans on key officials.

Since the overthrow of the Assad regime, the EU has aimed to revive relations with the country. It lifted all economic sanctions on Syria last year, though some dual-use export controls and state institutions remain sanctioned.

In January, Brussels announced a two-year funding package of 620 million euros ($680m) for Syria and in May the EU held its first high-level political dialogue with Syria, which aimed to revive bilateral relations.

The EU’s diplomatic service prepared a discussion paper outlining the normalisation efforts. Al Jazeera reached out to the paper’s author, but she was unavailable for comment.

Kallas said diplomats are now working through technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create frameworks for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.

Many European nations have been exploring reopening embassies or missions in Syria, diplomats told Al Jazeera, while Syrian and EU officials continue talks on normalisation and sanctions removal.

Sally Shobat, Syria’s European Affairs Directorate at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, met Jonas Jonsson, head of the Middle East and North Africa Division at the European External Action Service, on Saturday, after earlier holding bilateral meetings with French, Cypriot and Belgian diplomatic officials.

Priorities

Since the fall of the Assad government, Syria’s new government has worked to revive suspended relations and remove sanctions imposed on its predecessor. Many of the penalties have now been removed and relations with many countries, notably members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the United States, have also improved.

EU-Syrian relations may be moving in a positive direction, but experts said there are still many legal and technical obstacles to full normalisation.

“Every country has their own foreign policy,” Zakaria al-Shmaly, a nonresident fellow at TIMEP focusing on EU-Syria relations, told Al Jazeera.

Still, Syria has tried to prove its importance to Europe in security matters, particularly in the fight against ISIL (ISIS) and as an energy transit point following global disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Europe needs Syria as much as Syria needs Europe,” President al-Sharaa said in Nicosia in April, after an informal meeting between Syria and EU officials.

In April, al-Sharaa proposed the Four Seas and Nine Corridors Initiative, a proposed transatlantic framework connecting the Gulf, Caspian Sea, Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea via a Syria-Turkiye pipeline and transit corridor. The proposal bypasses the Strait of Hormuz for a land pipeline through Syria, following disruptions to shipping because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February.

“Every power is using Syria to undermine Iran,” al-Shmaly said.

Another key point of discussion between the EU and Syria as normalisation talks continue will be trade. Experts said Brussels will likely try to open the Syrian market to EU products, which could benefit Syrian consumers by lowering costs on certain items. However, Syrian negotiators must also consider what kind of things Syrian companies can export to the EU.

“There are not a lot of Syrian exports,” Jaber told Al Jazeera. “They are mostly agricultural and some pharmaceutical, but there are not a lot of exports and this is what the Syrians need to be careful about; otherwise, they will open the market to a lot of European products while still facing barriers and tariffs on what they can export.”

Jaber said there is also room for EU-Syrian coordination on the issue of Assad regime assets, which could be worth tens of billions of dollars and “hidden in several parts of Europe”.

Returns

In the months following a change in government in Damascus, some European states paused asylum claims for Syrians, citing that the dangers from the war and former regime were over.

Migration and the presence of refugees have been a major political issue in Europe for over a decade, particularly as a number of countries experienced a growth in far-right parties or movements.

In her comments on November 16, Kallas addressed the future of human rights in Syria and decisions taken by the Assad regime. “Everybody said that we need to engage with Syria because if we don’t engage, then this vacuum will be filled by other players,” Kallas said. “We should have clear conditionality regarding human rights. We should have also the nonrecognition of occupied Ukrainian, Georgian territories that they have recognised under Assad’s regime.”

In recent years, al-Shmaly claimed that even governments on the political centre-ground had adopted increasingly extreme policies on immigration.

Current and former European diplomats told Al Jazeera they were concerned that Europe would overly focus on repatriation in any deal with Syria, leaving human rights and other important issues by the wayside.

“Structurally, we have a rising number of member states in the EU that are led by right-wing populists who see no interest in engaging in all of Syria’s complexity and challenges,” a former European diplomat, who requested to speak on background, told Al Jazeera.

“We tend to see Syria only through the very limited lens of migration and we also wrongly perceive Syrian refugees as a burden rather than an opportunity despite the fact that the overwhelming majority of Syrian refugees have very positively contributed to the European economy and culture.”

Since the fall of the Assad government, about one million Syrians have returned home, most from neighbouring countries such as Lebanon, Turkiye and Jordan. But experts said Europe must strike a delicate balance on migration due to the slow process of rebuilding the country after years of dictatorship and war.

“As the European Union deepens ties with Syria, returns cannot become the price of that relationship,” Tariq Azeez, the International Rescue Committee’s policy, advocacy and communications coordinator, told Al Jazeera.

“Our research shows the reality many Syrians are returning to: missing services, damaged housing and conditions worse than expected, and competition over scarce resources driving tension within communities. Accelerating returns, therefore, without investing in services for everyone, returnees and those who never left alike, risks fuelling exactly the instability Europe says it wants to prevent.”

title: ICE arrests — Korean Woman Sues After Warrantless Detention in LA - The Korea Daily
description:
A Korean woman who applied for permanent residency was arrested without a warrant by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and later released by court order.

text:
A Korean woman who applied for permanent residency was arrested without a warrant by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and later released by court order. Amid a series of aggressive ICE crackdowns—including agents forcibly dragging passengers from a plane at another airport and smashing a car window to detain a man in front of an LA-area police station—controversy over human rights violations is growing.

According to attorney Ji-il Kang of Torrance on the 20th, a Korean national identified as Mrs. Lee went to LAX last month on the 10th with her husband to move to Texas, where she was apprehended by ICE and placed in the Adelanto Immigration Detention Facility.

Mrs. Lee entered the U.S. in 2021 under the Visa Waiver Program (VWP) and had overstayed the 90-day permitted period. Afterward, she married a U.S. citizen in August of this year and filed a Form I-130 (Petition for Alien Relative) and Form I-485 (Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status) in early September.

Kang filed a habeas corpus petition in federal court, stating that ICE arrested Mrs. Lee without prior notice or a warrant, and that a warrant and deportation order were issued only the day after her arrest.

Recognizing the violation of due process, the court ordered her release on the 4th. The ruling stipulated that any re-detention requires at least two days’ written notice and an immigration court hearing. Mrs. Lee is currently undergoing green card processing, but her deportation order remains valid.

On the morning of the 21st, at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, masked ICE agents entered the jet bridge of Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 bound for LA and arrested two passengers.

Footage released to the public showed a weeping woman being dragged away by masked ICE agents. Passengers who witnessed the incident protested strongly. ICE claimed that both arrested individuals were Mexican nationals who had overstayed their visas, and alleged that one of them threw hot coffee at agents during the arrest.

The disturbance delayed the flight’s departure by about three hours. Alaska Airlines stated that it was not given advance notice of the enforcement action and is reviewing whether the procedures were appropriate. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson also criticized the arrest method and launched an investigation into the circumstances.

One day prior, on the 20th, ICE agents used a baton to smash the rear window of a vehicle and pulled a man out to arrest him in the parking lot of the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department’s Santa Clarita Valley Station.

Testimony emerged that during the incident, the car’s driver and immigrant rights advocates at the scene were sprayed with pepper spray by ICE agents. The Sheriff’s Department stated it was not involved in the arrest, and the man’s identity and reasons for detention have not been made public.

Enforcement actions are also continuing throughout the Los Angeles Koreatown area. LA Public Press reported that at least 36 immigrant arrest cases were reported in Los Angeles County between the 12th and 19th. This data was compiled from tips provided by residents and local organizations and does not represent official ICE statistics.

On the 16th, one person was arrested in the parking lot of a Starbucks near 3rd Street and Alvarado Street in Koreatown. Enforcement cases were also confirmed in Gardena and Van Nuys.

Amid ongoing concerns regarding aggressive arrest tactics and the treatment of detainees, there are also moves in Congress to strengthen oversight of ICE. On the 19th, U.S. Senator Andy Kim (D-NJ) introduced a bill requiring ICE to notify Congress within 72 hours of any death occurring in immigration detention facilities or during arrest and transport, and to release a related report within 30 days.

The U.S. Attorney's Office in Mobile will appeal a ruling by Chief U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Beaverstock in a lawsuit against immigration agents brought by Leo Garcia Venegas, a Baldwin County construction worker. Beaverstock conditionally certified the complaint as a class action and ordered federal officers to stop enforcing three immigration policies that Venegas challenged.

Why it matters

The ruling bears on how Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents may conduct operations and whether policies challenged in court remain in effect. The government maintains that the policies cited in the lawsuit do not exist, leaving the scope of the order contested for Alabama residents and others affected by enforcement at construction sites.

Judge Beaverstock ordered three challenged policies stopped in September and issued a temporary stay without a formal preliminary injunction. The government has appealed to the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlanta, and the court has not yet ruled on whether the order's terms are clear enough to enforce.

The players

Jeffrey Beaverstock

Beaverstock is the Chief U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of Alabama, who presides over the case and issued the ruling and class certification.

Tom Homan

Homan serves as the Trump administration's border czar and is a named defendant in the lawsuit brought by Leo Garcia Venegas.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement

ICE is the federal agency responsible for immigration enforcement within the United States, whose agents are accused in the lawsuit of violating constitutional rights during raids.

U.S. Attorney's Office in Mobile

The Mobile office of the U.S. Attorney represents the federal government in the case and will file the appeal to the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

The details

Venegas sued border czar Tom Homan and other federal officials last year, alleging that ICE agents unlawfully detained him in two immigration raids at Baldwin County construction sites and refused to accept his STAR ID despite his U.S. birth. Earlier this year, Beaverstock ruled that ICE agents have adopted policies that likely violate the Constitution, and last week he denied a request by the U.S. Attorney's Office in Mobile to clarify the ruling. The government argued that the order's indefinite scope leaves it unable to guard against a future contempt motion or to give agents adequate guidance.

Timeline

Last year: Venegas sued Tom Homan and other federal officials.

Earlier this year: Beaverstock ruled that ICE policies likely violate the Constitution.

September: Beaverstock ordered federal officers to stop enforcing three challenged policies.

Last week: Beaverstock denied the government's request to clarify his ruling.

November 23, 2026: The government announced it will appeal the ruling.

Legal Context

The case tests whether federal courts can restrain ICE enforcement practices through class-wide relief, extending constitutional scrutiny of immigration raids beyond individual plaintiffs. The government's dispute that the cited policies exist adds a question of how courts enforce orders against practices the executive branch denies having.

Residents of Alabama who work at construction sites or who carry identification such as a STAR ID may be affected by how federal agents are permitted to conduct immigration stops. The outcome of the appeal will determine whether the three challenged policies remain stopped while the case proceeds.

The takeaway

Court orders restricting federal enforcement practices depend on clear terms that agents can follow, and disputes over scope can determine whether those orders have practical effect on the ground. Readers following immigration enforcement in Alabama should watch the appeal and any further clarification from the district court.

What happens next

The government's appeal will be heard by the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlanta, and the district court has yet to rule on the clarification request's broader effect on the injunction.

text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - The U.S. Attorney’s Office will ask an appeals court to overturn a judge’s ruling in a lawsuit alleging that immigration agents have violated the Constitution, according to a filing in U.S. District Court.

Chief U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Beaverstock earlier this year ruled that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have adopted policies that likely violate the Constitution. He also conditionally granted a request by attorneys for plaintiff Leo Garcia Venegas, a construction worker in Baldwin County, to certify the civil complaint as a class action lawsuit.

The judge last week turned down a request by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Mobile to “clarify” his ruling by more clearly identifying which policies are unconstitutional and more clearly defining who belongs to the class represented in the lawsuit.

Venegas last year sued border czar Tom Homan and other federal officials, alleging that ICE agents violated his rights in a pair of immigration raids at construction sites in Baldwin County, where he was working. Venegas was born in the United States, but he alleged in the lawsuit that agents unlawfully detained him and refused to accept his STAR ID.

In September, Beaverstock ordered federal law enforcement officers to stop enforcing three immigration policies that Venegas challenged. Although the judge declined to issue a formal preliminary injunction, he issued a temporary “stay” of the policies, which he characterized as “less drastic.”

But a lawyer for the U.S. Attorney’s Office argued that the judge’s ruling was a “de facto injunction,” nonetheless.

“Its indefinite scope leaves the United States unable to guard sufficiently against the prospect of a future contempt motion,” he wrote. “The United States maintains other objections to any preliminary relief, but the Court should—at a minimum—clarify the scope of its ruling.”

The government maintains that the policies cited in the lawsuit do not exist. The court filing argued that the order does not give clear guidance on when agents may enter construction sites.

“Without clear terms, the United States cannot determine the effect of the injunction, provide adequate guidance to its agents, or fully assess the impact of the ruling for any potential appeal,” the filing states. “Accordingly, the United States moves for clarification of the Court’s ruling.”

The incoming House Speaker also said that immigration and affordability will be major priorities for the next Congress.
Trump Prepares to Fight Despite his recent comments about compromise, President Trump has also taken steps that suggest he intends to be confrontational on issues he won’t compromise on.

text:
In the wake of the Republicans’ sweeping defeats in the November 3 midterm elections, President Donald Trump is signaling that he is willing to compromise with the Democrats while also fighting them on some of his biggest policy promises.

The administration is set for two years of confrontation, with many Democrats promising to cause as many problems for the Republicans as possible in the form of investigations and subpoenas.

But in recent days, President Trump has told several news outlets that major agreements could still be made on healthcare and immigration, and he even shared a Democratic proposal for universal healthcare bearing his name.

Trump, however, continues to promise to veto legislation passed by the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress that he doesn’t support.

He has also appointed hardliners to senior positions within his administration and has warned that working with the next Senate majority leader could be difficult.

On Sunday, November 22, USA TODAY columnist Tim Swarens argued that the president’s priorities are all wrong, and that the “shellacking” his party received in the midterms should have shown him that the American people want him to change course. But is that really the case?

Trump Offers Dems Major Deals

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Friday, November 20, President Trump suggested that the incoming Democratic majority could actually present an opportunity to negotiate legislation that Republicans struggled to pass when they had a slim majority in Congress.

He identified healthcare and immigration as two areas for potential cooperation, and said that some prominent Democrats had already contacted him about reaching agreements.

President Trump said he could work with Democrats on other areas, including incentivizing movie production in the United States—which is increasingly moving overseas—and providing financial assistance for college students.

On Saturday, November 21, President Trump also shared a post by Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed advocating for a universal healthcare program branded as “TrumpCare.”

Trump, it seems, is willing to work with Democrats — but that doesn’t mean he won’t also fight.

It certainly doesn’t mean that American voters have completely abandoned their support for his biggest policy pledges, including securing the border.

Some Democrats Are Seemingly Open to Negotiations

While the progressive wing of the Democratic Party has been generally combative since the party’s midterm victories, some Democrats appear willing to negotiate.

Speaking on CBS News’ Face the Nation on Sunday, November 22, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said that there were several areas where Democrats could potentially work with President Trump.

Jeffries singled out lowering the Medicare eligibility age and expanding coverage for hearing services and dental as examples.

“Let’s see what’s possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare,” he said.

The incoming House Speaker also said that immigration and affordability will be major priorities for the next Congress.

However, Democrats ultimately have their own legislative ambitions that President Trump won’t necessarily support, including their plans to remove Trump’s tariffs and force the president to end the war with Iran without a negotiated agreement or without ending the country’s nuclear program.

Trump Prepares to Fight

Despite his recent comments about compromise, President Trump has also taken steps that suggest he intends to be confrontational on issues he won’t compromise on.

The appointment of Stephen Miller, a known hardliner on immigration and other core MAGA issues, as White House chief of staff is a good example of that.

Miller was one of the primary architects behind the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown and is widely seen as being particularly aggressive toward Democrats — but not without good cause.

House Republicans have also elected Jim Jordan as their new minority leader, choosing a longtime ally of the president who himself has promised to challenge incoming Democrat-led investigations.

President Trump has also warned that he intends to use his veto power against legislation he opposes—which is, in one way, confrontation, but also a tactic he has identified as a way to force Democrats to negotiate.

On Sunday, the president also warned that cooperating with Senator Chuck Schumer would be particularly difficult if he becomes the next Senate majority leader.

Do Americans Want Compromise or Confrontation?

Recent polling suggests that Americans do want cooperation, although voters disagree about the extent to which political leaders should compromise.

A Reuters/Ipsos survey published on November 10 found that 81% of Americans considered it important for President Trump to work with Democratic leaders. 74% said they want Democrats to work with the president.

A Pew Research Center survey also found that 72% of Democrats want their leaders to stand up to President Trump. 53% of Republicans said they preferred compromise.

The challenge for the two parties now will be balancing those expectations.

Tenants and housing advocates in four states have filed a class-action lawsuit asking a Boston-based federal court to stop the Trump administration from cutting housing benefits for tens of thousands of immigrants living across the United States.

According to The New York Times, the federal government has long allowed households with mixed immigration statuses—meaning those that include citizens or legal residents alongside undocumented people—to live in subsidized housing. An estimated 80,000 people throughout the country live in so-called mixed-status households, including 35,000 children, most of whom are U.S. citizens.

Earlier this month, however, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development finalized a rule that would make mixed-status households ineligible for housing assistance. The rule is expected to take effect in December.

Agency secretary Scott Turner said in a statement that the revised policy was put into place to prevent “illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens” from “exploiting” government programs.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts, claims that the rule violates both federal law and the Constitution. If allowed to take action, the plaintiffs say, it could lead to the displacement or separation of thousands of families across the country.

Lucy Newman, a Legal Aid Society attorney who helped file the lawsuit, described the rule as “unlawful and inhumane.”

“Simply put, this rule is both unlawful and inhumane,” Newman said in a media statement. “It targets immigrant communities with no regard for the devastating consequences of forcing children from their homes, separating families, and increasing homelessness.”

In response to the lawsuit, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner said that the rule simply “implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”

“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” Turner said. “This change represents a reallocation of $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

The Massachusetts case is one of several lawsuits already filed against the rule.

Earlier in November, a Los Angeles-based nonprofit, Public Counsel, took the Trump administration to court over the same policy.

“You’re gonna have more demands for shelters and other services, and that’s going to impact not just the families that are displaced but everybody else who relies on those services,” Public Counsel attorney Amanda Mangaser Savage told The Los Angeles Times.

text:
Korea's rights watchdog said Monday it recommended that an immigration detention center minimize restrictions on detainees' freedom of communication, after it found that a facility violated a detainee's right to pursue happiness by not allowing a video call with a dying father.

The National Human Rights Commission of Korea, which made the recommendation last week, called on the center to guarantee that detainees can use their personal mobile phones to the extent necessary in urgent and serious humanitarian cases, such as when a family member is critically ill or dying.

The complainant, a foreign national held at the center, brought the case to the commission in November 2025. The detainee claimed that they were refused after asking staff for permission to use a personal mobile phone to see their critically ill father one last time over a video call. The father died that day, and the complainant said the refusal deprived them of the most basic human right to pursue happiness.

The center said it had never received the request and would have considered necessary measures if it had. It added that it had allowed other detainees who lost their fathers while in custody to use their phones.

Although no material directly verified the detainee's request to use a phone, the commission concluded that the records or staff members' recollection of the incident may be inaccurate, and accepted as fact that the complainant had asked for a video call with the father.

It based its finding on the fact that the father died on the day the request was made, records show the complainant sought counseling that same day and the detention center had to correct its initial response to the commission after mistaking another person's file for the complainant's.

The commission stressed that the chance to see a dying family member one last time, say goodbye and mourn the deceased is a significant personal interest that is hard to regain once missed.

It added that the complainant lost that chance with their father because they could not use a phone despite asking, a violation of the right to pursue happiness guaranteed under Article 10 of the Constitution.

text:
On November 24 at 1 p.m., Chloe Freeman, a 29-year-old Ann Arbor registered nurse, is scheduled to appear for a preliminary examination in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan. Her “crime”: on the night of May 28, 2026, she refused to hand a wounded immigrant worker over to the Border Patrol.

For this act of human compassion and working-class solidarity, the Trump administration is seeking to send her to federal prison for up to a year on a misdemeanor charge of “instigating or assisting escape.”

According to the government’s own criminal complaint, Border Patrol agents were conducting a “targeted immigration enforcement operation” in Ann Arbor against a Mexican worker identified only by the initials “OBP.” According to the government, the man fled when agents approached, “tripped over a curb” and struck his face on the pavement. The bleeding man was taken by ambulance to Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital, where he underwent a CT scan. At approximately 11:30 p.m., Freeman entered the CT room, removed his IV and escorted him out through the ambulance bay doors. He has not been located since.

The government’s account of a man who merely “tripped and fell” is not credible. It comes from a paramilitary force notorious for its use of violence. Workers across the country have rightly asked: Does anyone believe that a man fleeing armed agents in the middle of the night simply stumbled over a curb?

And what awaited the worker had Freeman not acted? In the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, through June 4, 2026, 52 people died in ICE custody, according to Human Rights Watch, and the toll has continued to rise. The man Freeman helped was not being taken to safety. He was being taken to a concentration camp.

What is on trial in Detroit is not a criminal act. It is the right of a nurse to treat her patient as a human being rather than as the property of the immigration police. It is the right of every worker to refuse to serve as an instrument of the deportation machine.

Freeman’s prosecution is political persecution directed against all workers and youth. Its purpose is to terrorize every worker who would defend an immigrant from police-state operations. It is part of a bipartisan assault on democratic rights, in which the fascistic Trump administration builds on the foundations laid by the Democrats. Here at the University of Michigan, it was Democratic Attorney General Dana Nessel who brought criminal charges against 11 participants in the 2024 Gaza solidarity encampment, at the request of the university’s Board of Regents.

On October 30, the same US Attorney’s Office that is prosecuting Freeman unsealed a superseding indictment expanding its federal conspiracy frame-up of anti-genocide protesters at the university from eight defendants to 12, the “U-Mich Twelve.” US Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon Jr. prosecutes Chloe Freeman for refusing to serve as a jailer and prosecutes students and former students for the “crime” of opposing a genocide.

The same state is also waging a witch-hunt against Chinese researchers on this campus. On March 18 of this year, Homeland Security agents questioned 31-year-old postdoctoral researcher Danhao Wang at his Ann Arbor home. The following night, he took his own life, jumping from the G.G. Brown Laboratory on North Campus. His death came amid the prosecution of five Chinese researchers at the university on charges of smuggling harmless biological materials, a revival of the “China Initiative.”

A week later, Interim President Domenico Grasso boasted to a House committee that the university had acted “swiftly and decisively,” “promptly terminating student and work visas, and severing all ties with those individuals.” The anti-immigrant offensive that hunts a Mexican worker in Ann Arbor is the same offensive that whips up xenophobia against Chinese scientists in the drive toward war.

The federal charge is not the only weapon the capitalist state can wield. The Michigan Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA) holds Freeman’s nursing license. As of this writing, LARA has taken no action against it, but the threat is real. A conviction, or simply the political pressure generated by the prosecution, could be used to strip her of the right to practice.

The same apparatus that disciplines nurses for speaking out about unsafe staffing can be turned against any healthcare worker who refuses to collaborate with ICE. Workers and youth must make clear now that any move by LARA to sanction Freeman, or any other worker who refuses to serve as a jailer, will meet organized opposition.

The working-class response to the Trump administration’s attack on Freeman has been significant. More than $55,000 has been raised for her defense through more than 1,300 donations, accompanied by messages of solidarity from nurses and workers across the country. In October, Will Lehman, the Mack Trucks worker and socialist then running for president of the United Auto Workers, called on workers and youth to demand that all charges against Freeman be dropped. Students here at the University of Michigan have spoken out, drawing the connection between the assault on immigrants and the broader attack on democratic rights.

Not one prominent Democrat has said a word in Freeman’s defense. This includes those who are members of or are supported by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)—such as Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib and Abdul El-Sayed. No trade union, including the unions of healthcare workers and the American Federation of Teachers locals on the Ann Arbor campus, has declared its support.

This silence is no accident. The Democratic Party helped build and fund the deportation machine and has maneuvered with Trump and the Republicans to expand funding for ICE and the Border Patrol while placing no restrictions on their operations. The union apparatuses, integrated into the corporations and the state, have no interest in mobilizing workers or defending democratic rights. Their function is to contain and dissipate the anger expressed in the outpouring of support for Freeman.

The working class is international. The immigrant worker Freeman aided is not a foreigner to be expelled but a fellow worker, exploited by the same corporations and hunted by the same state. The borders that divide workers are the borders of the capitalist nation-state. The defense of Chloe Freeman is inseparable from the defense of every immigrant worker, and from the fight against the entire system of capitalist exploitation and imperialist war that requires a deportation Gestapo to function.

The IYSSE at the University of Michigan calls on students, nurses and all workers to take up this fight in an organized and collective form. We call for building rank-and-file committees, independent of the big-business parties and the trade union bureaucracy, in every hospital, workplace and neighborhood. The support for Freeman must not remain a matter of individual donations and online messages. It must become a political movement.

text:
The National Human Rights Commission of Korea has ruled that preventing a foreign national from saying goodbye to his dying father over a video call, because of restrictions on mobile phone use at an immigration detention center, violated his “right to pursue happiness.”

The Commission said on November 23 that it had recommended that the director of the immigration detention center ensure detained foreign nationals can use mobile phones when urgent circumstances arise, such as a family member becoming critically ill or dying. Immigration detention centers are facilities under the Ministry of Justice that temporarily hold foreign nationals subject to deportation.

In early 2025, while being held at an immigration detention center, the petitioner learned that his father was critically ill. He asked a staff member to use a mobile phone for a video call so he could see his father one last time, but permission was denied. His father died that day, and the petitioner was unable even to say goodbye. In November 2025, he filed a complaint with the Commission.

The immigration detention center initially responded that it had allowed the petitioner to use a mobile phone. It later reversed its position, saying it had confused his case with that of another detained foreign national and that he had never requested to use a phone. However, after considering the fact that the petitioner’s father had died, the existence of a record showing that he had sought counseling at the center at the time, and the center’s reversal of its initial response, the Commission found the petitioner’s account to be credible.

The Commission determined that being able to see a family member one last time and say goodbye is an important right directly connected to human dignity and family relationships. It noted in particular that, because detained foreign nationals often have family members living overseas, video calls may be the only practical way for them to stay connected with their families.

The Commission said, “The opportunity to say a final goodbye following a family member’s death is a right that cannot be restored after the fact once the moment has passed. Restrictions on freedom of communication should be kept to a minimum, and mobile phone use should be permitted to the extent necessary after considering each individual’s circumstances.”

The air traffic control tower is seen in the distance as Alaska Airlines planes sit at the gates at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Nov. 6, 2025, in SeaTac, Wash.

A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle , causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

“They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people,” Catala said of the father and daughter. “She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it’s just heartbreaking.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa "in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia's husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

“When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said.

“It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on.”

“They just lunged forward. They didn’t identify themselves and then sort of hit this family from behind,” John Gaedeke, who was in line waiting to board the flight and filmed part of the confrontation on his cellphone, said of the officers.

Gaedeke said passengers on the jet bridge were screaming or crying “because it was just so emotional, and just to see the pain and anguish and then the speed and violence with which it happened.”

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.

People familiar with immigration networks in US said the decline could partly be linked to stricter enforcement and faster deportations. Earlier, minors were allegedly used as ‘green card bringers’ to help parents or relatives strengthen their chances of obtaining legal status. This practice is reportedly becoming less common as authorities swiftly deport those caught.

text:
A United States federal appeals court has put a hold on a ruling that required the Trump administration to return a Nicaraguan immigrant from the Central African Republic, adding another legal twist that complicates the prospects for Cubans hoping the courts will pave the way for their return from the same African nation.

The decision, handed down on Thursday, November 19, by the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals, was reported by CBS Minnesota and FOX 9.

The court agreed to the government's request to temporarily halt the return of Kenis Adalberto López González, a Nicaraguan national deported to Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, in August.

This ruling pauses an order issued on October 30 by federal judge Jeffrey M. Bryan of the Minnesota District Court. Judge Bryan had determined that the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) likely violated its own regulations when it re-arrested and subsequently deported the immigrant.

The Trump Administration's Legal Maneuver

Judge Bryan's order had required the U.S. government to arrange and pay for López’s return, allow him back into the U.S., and reinstate his previous immigration supervision conditions. However, the Trump administration appealed the ruling and succeeded in suspending its execution while legal proceedings continue.

This means that, for now, the Nicaraguan will not be brought back, although the dispute over the legality of his detention and deportation remains unresolved.

Immigrant's Protection Against Deportation

López had been living in Minnesota, working in construction with employment authorization. In August 2024, an immigration judge granted him protection from deportation to Nicaragua due to the risk of torture in his home country.

While this protection did not remove his deportation order, it prevented authorities from sending him to Nicaragua. While in the U.S., he was subject to immigration supervision and had to meet certain conditions, including attending appointments with authorities.

On January 15, 2026, federal agents detained him again. After spending several months in detention centers in Texas and Louisiana, ICE deported him on August 28 to the Central African Republic, a country with which he had no familial or migratory ties.

Procedural Violations and Legal Challenges

In his October 30 order, available on CourtListener, Judge Bryan reviewed the circumstances of López’s detention and concluded that the government likely breached federal rules governing the revocation of supervised release.

He cited regulation 8 C.F.R. 241.13, which requires notifying the immigrant of the reasons for revoking their release and offering an initial informal interview to address the decision's grounds. It also mandates a subsequent custody review.

The court found insufficient evidence that ICE followed these procedures or that López González had received the necessary notification.

Implications for Deported Cubans

The case has sparked interest among Cubans deported to the Central African Republic, as Judge Bryan's initial order demonstrated that a federal court could compel the U.S. government to facilitate the return of a deported individual to a third country if potential rights violations and migration procedure breaches were present.

On October 21, 69 Cubans, including 64 men and five women, were transported to Bangui on a flight originating from Alexandria, Louisiana, making several African stops.

This group arrived almost two months after the Nicaraguan's deportation. Although different flights, the migrants face challenges from being sent to a foreign country, where they struggle to obtain documents, find work, and move freely.

The Eighth Circuit's suspension does not resolve the Cubans' cases, nor does it mean they have automatically lost any chance of returning to the U.S. Its significance lies in halting the execution of a court order that could serve as a precedent for other individual lawsuits against deportations to third countries.

The situation of each Cuban depends on their immigration history, the orders issued against them, and the procedures ICE followed before detaining or deporting them.
