text:
A lawyer for the father and daughter detained on a Sea-Tac jet bridge says no one assaulted officers and that both were already in the legal immigration process. Here is what those claims mean if they hold up.

The two people U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement took off an Alaska Airlines jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday, Nov. 21, are a father and his adult daughter, and both have immigration cases in progress, according to their attorney, Olia Catala, as reported by KING 5 on Sunday. Catala told the station that no assault occurred. She said the hot coffee that the Department of Homeland Security says was thrown at officers spilled on several people, including the daughter’s husband, a U.S. citizen, during a chaotic arrest by plain-clothes officers who, the family says, did not identify themselves.

That account directly contradicts DHS, which said in statements posted Saturday that travelers obstructed and assaulted officers and that Sofia Hernandez Mejia “will be charged with assaulting a federal officer.” As reported earlier, DHS describes her and Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza as Mexican nationals who overstayed visas. As of Sunday, no outlet had reported a filed criminal complaint, a court appearance, a habeas petition or the facility where either is held. Catala said Saturday evening that neither had been processed and the family had not been able to reach them. The attorney’s statements have so far been reported by KING 5 and outlets republishing its story; they are her client’s side of a disputed event, just as DHS’s statements are the government’s.

What the family’s lawyer says, and what DHS says

The relationship: Catala identified the two as father and daughter. Passenger Aidan Mendoza separately told KUOW he saw a girl screaming as agents took her father through a side door, consistent with that account.

How they entered: Catala said both came lawfully on tourist visas, the father bringing his daughter when she was 14. DHS agrees they entered on visas and says both stayed past their authorized period.

Pending cases: According to Catala, the father filed for asylum after arriving, and the daughter is pursuing permanent residence through her marriage to a U.S. citizen. These filings have not been independently confirmed, and their current stage is not public.

The coffee: DHS says the daughter hurled hot coffee at officers. Catala says it spilled in the struggle. KING 5 said it was seeking additional video of the moments before officers approached.

Criminal history: Catala said neither has any. DHS has not alleged a prior criminal record for either.

Can ICE detain someone with a pending asylum or marriage case?

Yes. A pending application is not lawful status. A person who overstays a visa is removable, and a filing with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services does not by itself stop ICE from arresting them or starting removal proceedings. A work permit, which the daughter is heard saying the family has in video of the arrest, shows permission to work but not protection from arrest, a point this site covered in recent Alabama detentions.

What a pending case does change is the strategy after arrest. Both cases described by Catala can generally continue inside removal proceedings rather than disappearing:

Asylum: An asylum application filed with USCIS that has not been granted is typically referred to, or renewed before, an immigration judge once removal proceedings begin. The judge then decides it, along with related protection claims.

Marriage-based green card: The spouse of a U.S. citizen is an “immediate relative.” Under USCIS policy, immediate relatives who were inspected and admitted, as visa entrants are, can usually adjust status even after an overstay. Once removal proceedings start, the immigration judge generally takes over jurisdiction to decide that adjustment application under 8 C.F.R. 1245.2.

Are they eligible for bond?

Probably eligible for a hearing, though release is never guaranteed. The Board of Immigration Appeals’ 2025 decision in Matter of Yajure Hurtado, which the American Immigration Council summarized as barring bond for many people who entered without inspection, turned on the lack of a lawful admission. People who were admitted on visas, as both are said to have been, are generally held under section 236(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows an immigration judge to set bond if the person shows they are not a danger or flight risk.

The assault allegation matters here. Even an uncharged allegation can weigh against release in a bond hearing, and a filed charge under 18 U.S.C. 111 could lead to criminal custody. That is why the factual dispute over the coffee carries consequences beyond any criminal case. If immigration custody becomes prolonged or a bond hearing is denied, a federal habeas petition in the Western District of Washington is the usual next step; Seattle-area judges have handled many such cases this fall, as this site reported in its coverage of the U.S. Attorney’s habeas reversal.

Where officials stand

Gov. Bob Ferguson said at a Saturday news conference that ICE should be abolished, according to KIRO 7 and the Lynnwood Times, and that he had asked Alaska Airlines and would ask other carriers at Sea-Tac to tell ICE it is not welcome at airports. He said his office is reviewing how agents reached the jet bridge and whether a state law on law enforcement face coverings was violated, a question complicated by a federal ruling last week that blocked Connecticut’s mask rule for federal officers. The Port of Seattle says it is discussing with DHS whether previously agreed protocols were breached. Alaska Airlines says it had no advance notice. DHS has defended the operation as a targeted arrest and has not addressed the attorney’s account.

Earlier coverage details DHS’s identification of the two and its assault claim and the Port’s limits on enforcement.

Quick answers

What is the latest on the Alaska Airlines jet bridge arrests? The family’s attorney says the two are father and daughter, denies any assault and says both have pending immigration cases. No criminal charge had been reported filed as of Sunday.

Why was the Alaska Airlines flight delayed? Flight 1306 to Los Angeles left about three hours late after the arrests at Gate N9, according to the Seattle Times, and KING 5 reported that four of six scheduled crew members chose not to work the flight.

Does being married to a U.S. citizen prevent an ICE arrest? No, but a person admitted on a visa can often still pursue a green card before an immigration judge.

Does a pending asylum case stop deportation? It does not stop arrest, but the claim generally must be heard by an immigration judge before removal.

Where are they being held? Not yet reported. People arrested in western Washington are usually taken to the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma; ICE’s online detainee locator typically updates after processing.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

Democratic Sen. Patty Murray is demanding answers from the Trump administration after masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested two passengers aboard an Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

The Washington senator condemned footage of the November 21 confrontation, which showed federal agents forcing a woman to the ground on a jet bridge as other travelers watched. The incident also delayed a flight bound for Los Angeles.

Murray made clear that she intends to hold the administration accountable, warning President Donald Trump that Democrats will have oversight power when the new Congress convenes in January.

Murray also said she was seeking answers from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) about the enforcement operation.

The confrontation took place around 8 a.m. at Gate N9 as passengers prepared to board Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 to Los Angeles.

ICE described the operation as a targeted arrest of Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national the agency alleged had overstayed his visa.

Video of the incident showed federal officers in unmarked jackets removing people from the boarding area. A woman could be heard shouting that agents were taking her daughter and that she had a work permit.

text:
A video of masked ICE agents arresting a father and his adult daughter inside an Alaska Airlines jet bridge at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning has since gone viral and sparked outrage from both the community and political leaders,

ICE confirmed that federal agents arrested Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and Sofia Hernandez Mejia during boarding for a flight from Seattle to Los Angeles on Nov. 21. The agency said both people arrested are originally from Mexico and have overstayed their visas, in violation of United State law.

PREVIOUS COVERAGE | ICE arrests 2 on Sea-Tac Airport jetway, disrupting flight boarding and sparking outrage

Olia Catala, a local immigration attorney, is representing both detainees and confirmed to KOMO News that they're currently being held in the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.

Ricardo and Sofia, who are father and daughter, came to the U.S. legally in 2015 with tourist visas, according to Catala. A person can typically stay in the U.S. for up to six months under a tourist visa.

Catala said Ricardo has a pending asylum application, and Sofia was originally listed as a derivative asylee on her father's application. Since then, Sofia has reportedly married a U.S. citizen and is in the process of obtaining a Green Card, Catala confirmed.

Catala alleges both of her clients have been allowed to stay in the U.S. legally because they have pending asylum, which is also how they have had work permits continuously renewed.

"Technically, ICE can arrest somebody in that circumstance and place them in removal proceedings, but generally speaking, if they have a pending application that puts them in this toll status, ICE hasn't gone after them," said Adam Boyd.

Boyd is also a local immigration and removal defense attorney, and he currently serves as chair of the Washington state chapter of the American Immigration Lawyers Association. Boyd is not involved in Sofia and Ricardo's case.

He said ICE arrests of non-citizens with pending immigration status and no criminal history, like Sofia and Ricardo, have allegedly become more common under the Trump administration. Boyd also confirmed that it's typical for an asylum application to remain pending for several years due to court backlog and the lack of a local office in Washington.

"An application filed in the Pacific Northwest, it's not unusual that it would be pending for 12 years before you get an interview on that application," he said as an example.

SEE ALSO | ICE buys Tacoma immigrant detention facility for $453M; GEO Group to provide services

ICE said in a statement shared Saturday that Sofia will also be charged with assaulting a federal officer because she "hurled hot coffee on the officers." Catala denied that the coffee was intentionally thrown.

She, and at least one traveler who witnessed and recorded the arrests, claimed the coffee was knocked out of someone's hands by agents after they "lunged" at Ricardo.

"[The officers] took the father to the ground and knocked the coffee out of the family member's hands, threw coffee, and that put coffee onto other passengers," said John Gaedeke, who was in the jet bridge when the arrests happened Saturday.

Regardless, Boyd explained an immigration judge is likely to take ICE's word for what happened between Sofia and the arresting officers, which he said will have implications for her potential release from custody.

"If it's written in a report that she assaulted the officers, it's going to be a serious, negative factor," Boyd continued, "and it might actually lead to her being denied bond."

Catala maintains that neither Sofia nor Ricardo has any sort of criminal history or prior arrests in the U.S. She said she will fight to have them both released from ICE custody on bond.

"This is happening way too often," she said over the phone. "Detention centers are filled with people who have no criminal records and are picked up this way."

KOMO News has reached out to ICE for confirmation of Sofia and Ricardo's lack of criminal history, as well as to Tacoma Immigration Court to inquire about scheduled court proceedings.

text:
The judge in the Princeton student’s habeas case pointed to two rulings involving men who crossed the border without inspection. Xie was admitted on a visa, which puts her on firmer legal ground.

The Eva Yi Xie bond case now turns on one question from the federal judge handling her habeas petition: is her case materially different from two earlier rulings that required bond hearings for people in ICE custody? Judge Anthony J. Trenga has given the government until 5 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 25, to answer. The Princeton neuroscience doctoral student was arrested at Reagan National Airport on Nov. 19 and is now held at the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Va. How the government answers will decide how fast she can get before an immigration judge on bond, and how hard the government can fight it.

Both rulings Judge Trenga cited involved men who entered the United States without inspection. Xie, by DHS’s own account, was admitted. That difference is likely to define the case.

The two rulings, and where their appeals stand

Hernandez Hernandez v. Crawford, No. 1:25-cv-01565, 2025 WL 2940702 (E.D. Va. Oct. 16, 2025). Sixto Hernandez Hernandez was held at the Farmville Detention Center under ICE’s July 2025 no-bond policy, which treats people who entered without inspection as subject to mandatory detention. Trenga ruled that his detention fell under 8 U.S.C. 1226(a), the provision that allows bond, and ordered a bond hearing within seven days. He also barred ICE from using the “automatic stay,” a regulation that lets the government keep someone detained after an immigration judge grants bond. The government appealed to the Fourth Circuit.

Lopez Garcia v. Guadian (4th Cir., Sept. 10, 2026). The Fourth Circuit decided the same question in two consolidated appeals from the same courthouse:

Oscar Lopez Garcia came from Guatemala as a child in 1996 without inspection. He has lived in Washington, D.C., for three decades and has two U.S.-citizen children.

Juan Jose Rivera came from El Salvador in 2005, also without inspection, and has no criminal record.

Both were arrested in October 2025 and later released on bond. In a 2–1 opinion by Judge Berner, joined by Senior Judge Keenan over Judge Rushing’s dissent, the court held that Section 1226, not Section 1225, governs people who have lived in the country for years, even if they were never admitted. The court also clarified that at the bond hearing, the detained person carries the burden of proof.

What the appeal means for Xie. The government’s appeal in Hernandez does not suspend Trenga’s ruling unless a court stays it, and no stay has been reported. More importantly, Lopez Garcia is now binding precedent for every federal court in Virginia, Maryland, West Virginia and the Carolinas. Whatever happens to the Hernandez appeal, a district judge in Alexandria must follow the circuit’s rule. The government’s realistic options are to ask the full Fourth Circuit to rehear the issue or to wait for the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court. On Oct. 1 the Court agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, a Second Circuit case. It asks whether 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(A) mandates detention of people “present in the United States without having been admitted.” No argument date has been set. The government’s brief is due Nov. 30 and the respondent’s on Jan. 13, so argument is likely in early 2027 and a decision by the end of June. If the Court sides with the government, Lopez Garcia would fall for people who entered without inspection.

The question presented is limited to people who were never admitted. Xie, by DHS’s account, does not fit that category, so the Supreme Court case should not decide hers directly.

Why her facts cut the other way

DHS told Newsweek that Xie was admitted on a temporary basis in March 2016 and was required to leave by Sept. 15, 2016. It did not say what visa she held. People who were admitted and overstayed have long been detained under Section 1226(a), with bond hearings available, even under the administration’s own reading of the law. The no-bond policy at issue in Hernandez, Lopez Garcia and the Supreme Court case was never aimed at them. So the dispute is not whether she gets a bond hearing, but what happens at one.

The government’s two paths by Nov. 25

No material difference. The government can file a notice conceding that her case raises no materially different issues. The Hernandez filings would then be folded in, and the court would rule without more briefing. Given the facts reported so far, the likely result is an order granting a bond hearing before an immigration judge. That is not release by itself.

Opposition. If the government argues her case is different, it must attach her immigration history, detention records and removal-case records. Those records could matter in several ways the public cannot yet see:

A prior removal order. If she was ever ordered removed, including in absentia, detention could shift to 8 U.S.C. 1231, where bond hearings are not available in the same way.

Parole, not admission. If her 2016 entry was a parole rather than a visa admission, the government could argue she was never “admitted.” That would bring her closer to the no-bond category. DHS’s statement says “admitted,” which points the other way.

Criminal history or prior arrests. DHS has not alleged any, and her lawyer says she has none. Either would weigh heavily at a bond hearing.

A prior bond denial or missed hearings. Earlier custody decisions or missed immigration court dates would undercut a flight-risk argument.

If the records match what DHS and her lawyer have said publicly, an opposition would have little to stand on. The timing is still tight: with the response due the day before Thanksgiving and any reply due Nov. 30, a release before the holiday would require the government to concede and the court to act at once.

Others admitted on visas who later sought asylum

Xie’s pattern has come up repeatedly this fall:

UC Berkeley student Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez (Colombia). DHS said she was admitted in September 2022 and authorized to stay until March 2023. She then applied for asylum and got a work permit. ICE arrested her at an SFO gate on Oct. 30. U.S. District Judge Dena Coggins ordered her released within days, finding that ICE had not provided a “constitutionally compliant pre-deprivation bond hearing,” according to KQED (coverage of the release order).

Phoenix couple Agustin Baccega and Gustavo Romanello (Argentina). ICE says the two acrobats were admitted at Los Angeles and Miami and overstayed visas that expired in 2021. Both have pending asylum cases and work permits. ICE arrested them at Sky Harbor on Nov. 7, and their lawyers said they would seek bond hearings (coverage of the Phoenix arrests).

Wisconsin state trooper. Detained at a Madison airport on Nov. 5, he holds a work permit as a derivative on his father’s asylum case. His lawyers said he was later released on an order of supervision (coverage of the trooper’s arrest).

In each case, the person’s lawful admission placed them under the bond-eligible statute. Where courts stepped in, the issue was how ICE detained them, not whether it could.

The bond hearing: flight risk and danger

At a bond hearing, the immigration judge asks whether she is a danger to the community and whether she is likely to flee, and she must prove neither. Her lawyers can be expected to point to:

nearly a decade in the U.S. since arriving as a minor;

family here;

a pending asylum case;

a valid work permit;

no criminal record;

doctoral research at Princeton.

The government’s answer is that she has been removable since 2016.

If bond is denied, or granted

If the immigration judge denies bond, she can appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals. The BIA is part of the Justice Department’s immigration court system, not a federal court, so it can review a bond decision. The statute, 8 U.S.C. 1226(e), bars only federal courts from second-guessing an immigration judge’s discretionary bond judgment. Legal and constitutional challenges, such as a claim that the hearing applied the wrong standard, can still go to federal district court through habeas, with appeal to the Fourth Circuit. She can also request a new bond hearing if her circumstances change materially.

If bond is granted, it has no fixed expiration and generally lasts while her removal case is pending. DHS can revoke it under Section 1226(b), but the BIA held in Matter of Sugay, 17 I&N Dec. 637 (BIA 1981), that ICE should not re-arrest someone on bond without a change in circumstances. Examples include a new arrest, a missed hearing or check-in, or a final removal order. Federal judges have pressed that point this year, including in the Seattle ruling on re-detention without notice. If she is ultimately ordered removed, detention authority shifts and the bond no longer protects her.

Her asylum case runs on a separate track

The bond hearing decides custody only. Under 8 C.F.R. 1003.19(d), it is “separate and apart” from the removal case, so the immigration judge will not decide her asylum claim there. She cannot be removed while the claim is pending. Detention may speed it up, since detained cases move on faster dockets, so her early-2028 hearing could move much sooner if she stays in custody.

How her claim is structured is still unknown. Her lawyer, Kerry Doyle, has said her family applied for asylum within a year of arriving. If Xie was a derivative on a parent’s application, the claim rests on the parent’s fear of persecution. A child generally keeps derivative status if under 21 when the parent filed. Whether she remains a derivative or has her own application, and whether ICE has taken any action involving her parents, has not been reported.

Why an airport

DHS has said people without lawful status should not fly domestically, and it told ABC News it reversed what it called a Biden-era policy that allowed it. Critics, including Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson after the jet-bridge arrests at Sea-Tac, argue these arrests are needlessly traumatic for detainees and bystanders. They also note that ICE generally already has the address of anyone with a pending case. DHS describes the arrests as targeted enforcement of existing law.

What to watch

Nov. 25, 5 p.m.: the government’s notice or opposition in Xie v. Warden, No. 1:26-cv-03839.

Nov. 30: Xie’s reply deadline if the government opposes; the government’s merits brief is due the same day in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha.

Bond hearing: if ordered, the immigration judge’s decision and any BIA appeal.

Immigration court: whether her asylum case moves to a detained docket.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

Sources

Xie v. Warden, Detention Center, No. 1:26-cv-03839 (E.D. Va.), docket and Nov. 20, 2026 order

Hernandez Hernandez v. Crawford, No. 1:25-cv-01565, 2025 WL 2940702 (E.D. Va. Oct. 16, 2025)

Lopez Garcia v. Guadian, Nos. 25-7044 and 25-7050 (4th Cir. Sept. 10, 2026)

text:
A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the US, where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

“They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people,” Catala said of the father and daughter. “She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it’s just heartbreaking.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa “in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the US illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a US citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia’s husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

“When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee,” Catala said.

“It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are,” Catala said. “There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on.”

“They just lunged forward. They didn’t identify themselves and then sort of hit this family from behind,” John Gaedeke, who was in line waiting to board the flight and filmed part of the confrontation on his cellphone, said of the officers.

Gaedeke said passengers on the jet bridge were screaming or crying “because it was just so emotional, and just to see the pain and anguish and then the speed and violence with which it happened.”

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.

text:
Bradley Jones has watched his wife’s pregnancy milestones through his phone screen.

During his shifts as a nurse in Tasmania, his phone buzzes with notifications. A video of his baby boy. Another scan missed.

“It feels awful not being present for this significant milestone or moment in our lives,” the 28-year-old says.

Tasimaporn, who lives in Thailand, is pregnant with their first child. Her February due date is rapidly approaching but the couple does not know when they will be able to live together.

When they applied for Tasimaporn’s partner visa last December after getting married, they were facing a likely wait time of two years. But an Australian government decision in July to prioritise the family visa applications of people already in the country placed offshore partner visas applications, like Tasimaporn’s, at the back of the queue.

The family visa stream, which allows the partners, children and parents of Australians to apply to live permanently in the country, has been swept into the national debate around reducing Australia’s net overseas migration.

One Nation this week proposed to scrap the permanent parent visa program alongside a 90% cut to Australia’s refugee intake if it held power.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Before signing the ministerial direction to prioritise certain applications under the Migration Act, the Department of Home Affairs warned its minister, Tony Burke, that deprioritising offshore family visa applications where children were involved “may be considered inconsistent” with Australia’s legal obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

In advice tabled in parliament this month in response to a request from the Senate for a production of documents, the department, which recommended Burke sign the direction, also warned that the ministerial direction could “increase exposure to legal challenges for unreasonable delay” from applicants outside Australia.

It said the change would require delegates to have “due regard to Australia’s international legal obligations” when assessing family visa applications.

‘Clearly inequitable’

The direction came into effect in the early months of Tasimaporn’s pregnancy. Jones says it felt like an “insult”.

“It’s not our fault that we met online and fell in love between two different countries,” he says.

“That’s just something that happened … and it’s the best thing that’s ever happened.”

He fears he could be separated from his son in the early years of his life.

“I won’t be there to change his nappies, to play with him, to get up in the night, or to share any of it with my wife,” he says.

“I think it’s important for mum and dad and the baby all to be together, growing up as a family.”

Peter van Vliet, the chief executive at the Migration Institute of Australia, says the departmental advice to Burke shows the government was warned about the human rights implications of separating families for long periods before the decision was made.

“A successful temporary skilled migrant with no connection to Australia can bring their partner to Australia within weeks of applying for a visa, but the life partners of actual Australian citizens are forced to wait years if their partner is offshore under Direction 117. This is clearly inequitable,” he says.

Van Vliet says the government should “get out of the way” and grant partner and child visas in queue order.

Dessie Hristova, the founder of Assent Migration Lawyers and co-chair of the migration law reform committee at the Law Institute of Victoria, says a visa applicant may be able to launch legal action on the basis of an unreasonable delay in the processing of an offshore visa.

“Ministerial directions cannot override, amend, restrict or operate inconsistently with the Migration Act 1958 or the Migration Regulations 1994,” she says.

Estimated wait time data from the Department of Home Affairs shows that an offshore partner visa lodged this week will, in 90% of cases, be processed within 35 months, compared with 30 months for onshore applicants.

Some 41,500 partner visas and 3,500 dependent child visas have been allocated under the family migration stream for 2026-27. A Senate hearing last month was told there were 81,000 onshore and 39,000 offshore partner visas currently in the system.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs said the reform sought to give the government greater control over who arrives, stays in and leaves Australia. They said the act allowed the minister to consider visa applications “in such order as he or she considers appropriate”.

“An onshore-focused migration program will support timely transitions to permanent residency for migrants already living, working and contributing to Australia, while reducing the program’s impact on net overseas migration,” they said.

“Although they have lower priority, offshore family visa applications will continue to be processed and granted.”

Jones is planning to visit Thailand in January, before Tasimaporn gives birth, He will stay for about four-and-a-half months before returning to work.

The pair are hopeful Tasimaporn can be granted another tourist visa so they can spend time together as a new family.

But Bradley says of the three visitor visas Tasimaporn has applied for since the couple met, two have been refused because the department determined she did not have strong enough ties or reasons to return home.

“Nothing is guaranteed,” he says.

text:
US immigration authorities faced criticism after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two passengers as they were boarding a flight in Seattle.

The incident happened on Saturday morning local time at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), when ICE said a man and a woman, both Mexican nationals, were arrested for allegedly overstaying their visas.

It said that, during its arrest of the man - named as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza - "other travellers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers", which it described as a "federal crime and a felony".

The Port said in a statement that it was "outraged" about the incident.

Alaska Airlines said the incident happened during the boarding of one of its flights to Los Angeles and that it was not given "appropriate notice of the enforcement action".

It also said it was "concerned" about the arrests and recognised "how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests".

Both the airline and the Port of Seattle, which owns and runs the airport, said they were looking into whether the proper protocols were followed.

The Port said: "Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port's participation or knowledge."

According to ICE, the woman they arrested - named as Sofia Hernandez Mejia - "hurled hot coffee on the officers" and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Olia Catala, a lawyer for both Mendoza and Mejia - who are father and daughter - told local NBC affiliate King 5 News that they have "absolutely no criminal history".

"They're not fugitives. They're going through a legal process," Catala added.

The family has reportedly said that the ICE officers were in plain clothes and approached Mendoza and Mejia without identification.

"You can imagine if somebody's running at you who is not dressed as an officer, you don't know who they are," said Catala.

"So, there was a lot of panic, a lot of chaos, officers grabbing her, coffee spilling."

Video of the arrests taken by eyewitnesses appears to show two agents wearing masks, plain jackets and khaki trousers.

One eyewitness, John Gaedeke, who was also boarding the plane, told the Reuters news agency he thought the agents were passengers and that they "didn't have any identification".

Gaedeke said the agents "pointed and then they said now, and then they just lunged forward, didn't identify themselves" before "tackling" a man.

"Coffee definitely went flying, but to me, it looked like the passenger was holding it in their hand, and when they were tackled, it went everywhere. I didn't see anyone throw coffee," he added.

The Port of Seattle said it had "continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS [the Department of Homeland Security] on whether any of these protocols were breached".

According to the port's website, federal agents have access to airport property and port officials cannot interfere with operations. It says that the port has not historically been given advanced information about immigration enforcement, even when this takes place on its property.

Alaska Airlines said it is "required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials".

"We do not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible," it added.

Washington's Democratic Governor Bob Ferguson told a press conference on Saturday that "ICE is completely out of control".

This year marks the 25th anniversary of Amnesty International’s annual Write for Rights letter-writing campaign.

The Napanee Amnesty group, supported by the Kingston group, is inviting the community to join in by calling on world leaders to respect and uphold human rights. They’re inviting the public to gather Dec. 5 at the Napanee branch of the Lennox and Addington Library from 10:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.

The campaign celebrates International Human Rights Day, which on Dec. 10 each year commemorates the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 by the United Nations. The principle of this campaign is simple. By making their voice heard, people can help free others from torture, harassment, or unjust imprisonment. From just 2,326 letters written in 2001, Write for Rights has grown to nearly four million actions—letters, social media messages and petition signatures—in 2025 and changed many lives. For some examples, see https://amnesty.ca/write-for-rights#success-stories.

Among the cases featured at the Napanee event this year will be Carlos Ricardo (Richard) Parias, an immigrant and citizen journalist shot by immigration agents during an arrest in Los Angeles a year ago. He is still in ICE custody even though a charge against him was dismissed, and he has not received adequate medical care.

Participants can also advocate for Marwa Arwafa, an Egyptian human rights activist who has been imprisoned for six years on “terrorism” charges as a result of her peaceful activism, which included speaking out against abuse of children.

The event will also call for the release of a Russian woman arrested for her work on indigenous rights, a critic of the Tanzanian government abducted from his home and held incommunicado for more than a year, and Pakistani lawyers who defended victims of state oppression.

Prewritten letters and petitions will be available, and Amnesty volunteers will be available to help those who want to write their own letters.

Neth Nahara, an Angolan mother, was sentenced to two years in prison for criticizing the country’s president on TikTok. After being featured as a Write for Rights case in December 2024, she was released in January of 2025.

text:
A U.S. federal appeals court suspended the order requiring Donald Trump's government to bring back a Nicaraguan immigrant from the Central African Republic, in a new legal twist that complicates the hopes of those expecting that the courts will open a path for the Cuban individuals deported to that same African country.

The decision was made last Thursday, November 19, by the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals, according to reports from CBS Minnesota and the network FOX 9.

The court accepted the Government's request to temporarily suspend the return of Kenis Adalberto López González, a Nicaraguan citizen who was deported to Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, last August.

The resolution pauses an order issued on October 30 by federal judge Jeffrey M. Bryan of the District Court of Minnesota, who had determined that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) likely violated its own regulations when it re-detained the immigrant and subsequently deported him from the country.

The judge had ordered the U.S. government to arrange and pay for López's return trip, allow him to re-enter the United States, and restore the conditions of immigration monitoring that he had before his arrest.

However, the Trump administration appealed the measure and succeeded in having its implementation suspended while the legal process continues.

That means that the Nicaraguan will not be returned for now, although the dispute over the legality of his detention and deportation is still ongoing.

A protected immigrant against deportation to Nicaragua

López resided in Minnesota, where he worked in construction and had employment authorization. In August 2024, an immigration judge granted him protection against his deportation to Nicaragua due to the risk of being subjected to torture in his home country.

That protection did not eliminate his deportation order, but it prevented the authorities from sending him back to Nicaragua.

While staying in the United States, he was subject to a migration supervision order and had to comply with certain conditions, including attending his appointments with the authorities.

On January 15, 2026, he was arrested again by federal agents. After spending several months in detention centers in Texas and Louisiana, ICE deported him on August 28 to the Central African Republic, a country with which he had no family or immigration ties.

In his court order dated October 30, available on CourtListener, Judge Bryan reviewed the circumstances of that detention and concluded that the Government likely violated the federal regulations governing the revocation of supervised release.

In particular, it cited regulation 8 C.F.R. 241.13, which requires that immigrants be notified of the reasons for the revocation of their release and offered an initial informal interview to respond to the reasons for that decision. It also includes a subsequent review of detention.

The court noted that it found insufficient evidence that ICE had followed those procedures or that López González had received the corresponding notification.

On November 9, Bryan rejected an initial request from the government to suspend his order. The administration then turned to the Eighth Circuit, which ultimately granted the suspension.

The government celebrates the decision while the deportee remains ill

During the litigation, the government's lawyers argued that forcing the United States to manage the return of a person from foreign territory represented a judicial interference in diplomatic relations with a sovereign state.

They also claimed that the authorities of the Central African Republic had provided diplomatic guarantees that the deportees received from the United States would not be persecuted or tortured.

After the decision of the appeals court was made known, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche publicly celebrated the suspension and presented it as a victory for the immigration policy of the Trump administration, as reported by CBS Minnesota.

The defense of the Nicaraguan, on the contrary, warned that the delay increases the risks to his health. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, reported that López González was diagnosed with malaria while he remains in the Central African Republic.

The African country is listed under a Level 4 travel advisory from the U.S. State Department, which recommends against traveling there due to risks of violence, crime, kidnappings, terrorism, and health issues.

What changes for Cubans deported to Bangui?

The case has sparked interest among Cubans expelled to the Central African Republic because the initial order from Judge Bryan demonstrated that a federal court could require the U.S. government to facilitate the return of a deported individual to a third country when there are possible violations of their rights and immigration procedures.

On October 21, 69 Cubans were transferred to Bangui, including 64 men and five women, on a flight that departed from Alexandria, Louisiana, and made several stops in Africa.

That group arrived nearly two months after the Nicaraguan's deportation. Although they are different flights, the migrants share challenges stemming from being sent to a country other than their own, where they face issues obtaining documents, working, and moving freely.

The suspension issued by the Eighth Circuit does not constitute a ruling on the cases of Cubans, nor does it mean they have automatically lost any chance of returning to the United States.

Its importance lies in the fact that, for now, it halts the execution of a court order that could serve as a reference for other individual lawsuits against deportations to third countries.

The situation of each Cuban depends on their immigration history, the orders issued against them, and the procedures followed by ICE before detaining or deporting them.

The Cuban-American attorney Wilfredo Allen had explained that the chances of returning to the United States vary significantly among the deportees, particularly depending on the existence of criminal records, pending immigration resources, or possible violations of due process.

Among the cases that have come to light is that of a Cuban who reported having been separated from his American wife and their three-year-old son following his deportation to Africa, despite having, according to his testimony, an approved family petition and a pending legal remedy.

The importance of immigration supervision orders

One of the most significant aspects of the López case is that the initial return order was not solely based on challenging the general deportation policy to third countries.

The judge specifically examined whether ICE had followed the rules to revoke the immigration supervision of the Nicaraguan before detaining him again.

That reasoning may be relevant for other immigrants who remain in the United States under supervision orders, including Cubans who hold Form I-220B and are required to check in periodically with ICE.

The regulations require certain guarantees before revoking that oversight, including notification of the reasons and an initial opportunity to respond. However, the application of these provisions depends on the specific legal situation of each individual.

Those under immigration supervision must keep their orders, employment authorizations, notices to appear, and any communication received from ICE.

If you face a new arrest or a possible deportation, an immigration lawyer can assess whether there are grounds to challenge the process through legal action.

The Supreme Court will decide on deportations to third countries

The legal battle also has a national dimension. The Supreme Court of the United States is scheduled to hear arguments in the case Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D. on December 9, related to the federal policy of deporting immigrants to countries other than their countries of origin.

Among the issues that the judges will examine is whether the Government must notify immigrants in advance about these transfers and provide them with a meaningful opportunity to report risks of persecution or torture in the destination country.

The Supreme Court suspended on September 29 a ruling that restricted the deportation policy to third countries, while it reviews the case. Therefore, this policy remains in effect during the judicial review.

text:
After the Republicans’ devastating losses in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump has said he is willing to work with the Democrats after they take control of Congress in January.

The next two years offer the Republican leader an opportunity to negotiate bipartisan agreements on some of the country’s most contentious issues.

While the president has hardened his stance in some ways—most notably by appointing hardliner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff—evidence suggests he may be seriously willing to work with the opposition to make historic progress.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Friday, November 20, President Trump warned he would use his veto power to block legislation he and his party disagreed with, arguing that doing so could be what it takes to force Democrats to negotiate with him.

While Democratic leaders promised to challenge the president’s policies and investigate his administration, Trump is also suggesting that the coming change in leadership in Congress could make it easier to pass legislation that voters support.

And for a president who has spent much of his life describing himself as the ultimate dealmaker, the next two years could let him build a different political legacy than the one he would leave behind if he resigned from office today.

Trump Threatens to Use Veto Power

Speaking at a press conference on Friday, President Trump outlined his plans for dealing with the incoming Democratic majorities.

He warned that controlling Congress would not allow Democrats to implement a radical new agenda.

“They’re going to send things my way, and I’m going to veto them,” he said. “And then they’re going to send more things that I’m going to veto.”

The president also argued, however, that the Democrats might ultimately realize that they have to negotiate if they intend to get anything passed.

Trump also identified immigration and “great healthcare” as possible areas where Democrats and Republicans could strike a deal.

“Great healthcare is possible,” Trump said.

“Can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country.”

Trump Has Always Described Himself as a Deal Maker

The president’s comments should not be read as a U-turn, but as consistent with an image that he has cultivated his whole life, particularly since his years as a New York real estate developer.

Trump built much of his reputation around his ability to negotiate tough business agreements.

He also published the book Trump: The Art of the Deal in 1987, followed by Trump: The Art of the Comeback in 1997 and Trump: How to Get Rich in 2004.

That reputation made him such a wildcard presidential candidate, and he has never abandoned his willingness to make deals.

During an interview with John Dickerson on CBS’ Face the Nation in 2016, Trump said that compromise was necessary to achieve results in politics. And almost a decade later, Trump made a similar point when he addressed Israel’s parliament.

“That’s all I do in my life — I make deals,” he told the Knesset on October 13, 2025.

Previous Immigration Offers

Trump has long promised to make deals with Democrats, including on the issues on which he is often accused of being too much of a hardliner.

In September 2017, Trump met with Democratic leaders Nancy Pelosi and Chuck Schumer to discuss protections for illegal aliens brought to the United States as children.

The discussions didn’t work out and produced competing accounts of what was actually said and what a possible agreement could look like.

No final agreement emerged — but Trump did try.

In January 2018, the White House offered another compromise.

Trump offered a pathway to citizenship for 1.8 million immigrants in exchange for border security measures and restrictions on legal immigration, which Democrats opposed.

Trump again offered to make an immigration deal during his 60 Minutes interview, broadcast on November 8.

He clearly seems to mean it.

Trump Can Return to Democratic Instincts

The next two years offer President Trump an opportunity to revisit the Democratic instincts that he was forced to abandon when he became the Republican candidate for president.

President Trump was a registered Democrat between 2001 and 2009, although he has changed party affiliation many times over the years.

His earlier political positions, however, show that he has long disagreed with most Republicans on major issues, including universal health care.

In October 1999, Trump told Larry King that he believed in universal healthcare, and he even advocated for it in his 2000 book, The America We Deserve.

With some Republicans already distancing themselves from Trump following the midterm defeats, Trump may now have less incentive to satisfy his party’s demands.

A deal on healthcare or immigration could prove popular with voters, but anger Republican hardliners.

Democrats, meanwhile, face a choice of their own: negotiate with a president they have spent years opposing, or risk entering the 2028 election with little legislative success to show for their significant congressional majorities.

SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- With Thanksgiving travel underway, California Senator Alex Padilla is proposing new restrictions on ICE operations at airports.

His legislation follows several high-profile immigration arrests at San Francisco International Airport, including one caught on camera earlier this year.

The proposal focuses on two major issues: when ICE can make arrests at airports and how federal agents access passenger information.

Both have been under scrutiny here in the Bay Area for months.

In March, federal agents were caught on video at SFO arresting a Guatemalan mother in front of her daughter. TSA had alerted ice about her travels.

RELATED: CA senators demand answers from DHS after ICE arrest tied to TSA data at San Francisco Airport

"We help ICE check against information and yes absolutely we do that," said Ha Nguyen McNeill with TSA in a previous interview with ABC7 Eyewitness News.

Now, Padilla wants to change those rules.

His new proposal would restrict TSA from sharing passenger information with ICE and also restrict immigration enforcement without a warrant.

"We have seen a pattern of these ICE arrests going on where ICE has known the information of somebody flying out. They have been able to gather all that data and know the time that somebody's flying out and where they're flying out of which gate," said Nikoles De Bremaeker, managing attorney of Centro Legal de la Raza.

It follows another high-profile arrest last month at SFO, when a UC Berkeley student was detained before a domestic flight. A federal judge later ordered her release.

RELATED: Judge orders UC Berkeley student released from ICE custody after SFO arrest

"If such legislation was in place requiring a judicial warrant, then this arrest would not have taken place," De Bremaeker.

In response to our request for comment on the legislation, the Department of Homeland Security said: "This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport."

DHS did not directly address the bill's proposed warrant or data-sharing restrictions.

Ahead of holiday travel, immigration attorneys say the arrests are already affecting how some people travel.

"We strongly recommend that anybody with an uncertain immigration status speaks with an attorney first before stepping into an airport," De Bremaeker said.

text:
A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday.

READ MORE: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

"They've done everything correctly, and these are educated people," Catala said of the father and daughter. "She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it's just heartbreaking."

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa "in violation of our nation's laws."

During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia's husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

WATCH: Lawmakers press Mullin on flight disruptions and ICE tactics

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

"When somebody's charging at you, you're going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said.

"It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they're not wearing a uniform, you don't know who they are," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what's going on."

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition.

"The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.

title: Migration Should Not Be a Death Sentence: From San Fernando to Ciudad Juárez
authors: Mexico Solidarity, Luis Eugenio Parés Sevilla
description:
From San Fernando to Ciudad Juárez: memory, routes, and pending responsibilities.
In August 2010, 72 migrants were murdered in San Fernando, Tamaulipas.
On March 27, 2023, another 40 died in a fire at a National Migration Institute (INM) facility in Ciudad Juárez.
After Ciudad Juárez, the National Migration Institute (INM) temporarily suspended operations at 33 detention centers and announced civil protection upgrades.
San Fernando produced laws, but it has not produced truth or full justice.
text:
This article by Luis Eugenio Parés Sevilla appears in the November 2026 issue of Let’s Talk About Migration (Hablemos de Migración), a magazine on migration issues published by the Frente Amplio de Mexicanos y Migrantes. Read and download the full November issue.

The lives Mexico was supposed to protect.

From San Fernando to Ciudad Juárez: memory, routes, and pending responsibilities.

Mexico is a territory of transit, but also of death. Two massacres of migrants, separated by thirteen years, reveal a disturbing pattern: the State responds with laws and promises, but the structure that produces the deaths remains intact.

In August 2010, 72 migrants were murdered in San Fernando, Tamaulipas. On March 27, 2023, another 40 died in a fire at a National Migration Institute (INM) facility in Ciudad Juárez. These are different cases: one a massacre attributed to Los Zetas, the other involving deaths in a fire while in state custody. Both raise the question of who was responsible for protecting them and what safeguards exist to prevent another tragedy.

Yes, there were institutional changes. In 2013, a Forensic Commission was created with the participation of authorities, independent specialists, and family organizations to identify victims of the San Fernando massacre and other massacres. Mechanisms were also established for reporting crimes and seeking information from abroad. However, the Foundation for Justice continued to report nine unidentified victims out of the 72 and unanswered questions about potential state responsibility. The convictions of members of the criminal group do not complete the investigation.

After Ciudad Juárez, the National Migration Institute (INM) temporarily suspended operations at 33 detention centers and announced civil protection upgrades. The National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) documented serious violations due to acts and omissions by its personnel. But inspecting buildings alone does not solve the problem of a detention system: effective evacuation, independent oversight, and clear accountability are also needed. On October 13, 2026, a judge dismissed the case against former commissioner Francisco Garduño, considering the conditions for suspending the proceedings to have been met; representatives of the victims announced they would appeal. That ruling does not clarify all the responsibilities for the fire.

The contrast is key. San Fernando produced laws, but it has not produced truth or full justice. Ciudad Juárez, on the other hand, did not even produce a real reform of the National Migration Institute (INM); the promised replacement of the institute remained just talk. The immigration detention centers, far from becoming spaces of protection, operated in fact as prisons under a policy of containment and militarization.

Fifteen years later, the equation repeats itself: some perpetrators are punished, but institutional responsibility is diluted. The families continue searching, the nameless bodies continue waiting, and the central question remains unanswered: who is responsible when the State is the custodian and death occurs under its watch?

Meanwhile, the caravans are changing. In October 2026, groups of families from Honduras, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Nicaragua were documented; some were seeking to settle and work in Mexico. Traveling together allows for sharing aid and gaining visibility, but it doesn’t guarantee safety. Documentation delays also fuel these movements. The response must link regularization and international protection, depending on the case, with safe transportation, prevention of extortion, and funding for shelters. The assistance provided by churches and organizations needs sustained public support.

Returning to Mexico demands a similar responsibility. “México te Abraza” (Mexico Embraces You) offers repatriated Mexican nationals’ documentation, housing, transportation, healthcare, and job placement. Its evaluation must go beyond simply providing services: how many people retain employment, find housing, and receive psychological support months later? Federal, state, and municipal governments need to coordinate follow-up. Foreign nationals deported to Mexico require differentiated protection and documentation services.

The disappearance traces a geography that crosses Darién, Mexico, the Rio Grande, Sonora, the Caribbean, the Mediterranean, and the Atlantic toward the Canary Islands. The trail can be lost in a jungle, a kidnapping, a shipwreck, or among disconnected institutional records. In Mexico, search commissions, prosecutors’ offices, forensic services, and consulates must coordinate; internationally, equivalent cooperation is needed. The IOM warns that restricting regular routes displaces migration toward more dangerous paths.

How many more tragedies does Mexico need to stop managing migrant suffering and take responsibility? No apology can replace justice, and no compensation guarantees that no one will die in detention again. We demand an investigation into the entire chain of responsibility, that those responsible be punished, and that a protection policy be funded that includes timely documentation, safe transit, dignified shelters, and immediate search and rescue operations.

Remembering involves identifying, investigating, repairing, and preventing. Success cannot be measured solely by how many people were contained or returned; it must include how many were able to reach their destination, remain in the country, or return alive and with their rights intact. No family should have to travel to another country to demonstrate that the life of the person they are searching for matters.

Dignity is not demonstrated with speeches, it is guaranteed with decisions, budget and accountability.

Protesters marched through Seattle-Tacoma International Airport demanding the removal of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after a viral cellphone video captured masked federal agents detaining a woman on a crowded jet bridge.

The enforcement action occurred around 8 a.m. as passengers were boarding an Alaska Airlines flight bound for Los Angeles.

The incident drew swift condemnation from state and local officials, while federal authorities defended their agents' actions and accused travelers of obstructing the operation.

Viral Video and Airport Security Questions

The backstory:

Cellphone footage recorded by bystanders shows masked federal agents pulling on a woman in an effort to remove her from the jet bridge. In the video, the woman can be heard saying agents were taking her father as nearby passengers rushed to ask for her name.

The Port of Seattle, which oversees the airport, stated it was not notified of the law enforcement operation in advance and described the scene on the jet bridge as "distressing." The lack of prior notice has prompted questions regarding airport security protocols and how federal agents accessed the boarding area of a commercial aircraft without the airport authority's knowledge.

State Leaders Condemn Enforcement Action

What they're saying:

Washington state leaders sharply criticized the arrests following the release of the footage.

Gov. Bob Ferguson condemned the incident, saying, "ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities. Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics. I’ll have more to say this afternoon."

U.S. Rep. Emily Randall echoed his criticism, calling the operation "state-sanctioned terror and violence." Randall vowed to hold the Trump administration accountable for its immigration enforcement policies.

Featured

ICE Defends Agents Amid Conflicting Witness Accounts

The other side:

In a statement posted to the social media platform X, ICE defended the operation, stating agents were conducting a targeted arrest of a man identified as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza.

Addressing the level of force seen in the footage, ICE accused travelers of escalating the encounter and committing a federal felony by obstructing an arrest. According to the agency, a female passenger threw hot coffee at officers. ICE stated agents arrested the woman, alleging she had overstayed a visa and would face charges for assaulting an officer.

However, witnesses recorded on the video disputed the agency's account in real time, stating the woman did not throw her coffee.

As of publication, ICE has not released body-worn camera footage or additional evidence to substantiate its claims regarding the crowd's actions. While Department of Homeland Security leadership has stated enforcement efforts prioritize violent criminals, no criminal records have been presented for either individual detained on the jet bridge.

text:
The governor of Washington state denounced federal immigration authorities on Saturday (Nov 21) for arresting two people on a jetway at a Seattle-area airport.

The incident involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers occurred around 8am PST at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as people boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles. ICE officers conducted an operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, who overstayed his visa, the agency said in a statement.

The officers also arrested a second individual, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, who threw hot coffee at them, ICE said in a post on social media. Mejia had also overstayed her visa, ICE said, adding that she would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Reuters was not able to identify lawyers for Mendoza or Mejia.

"ICE is completely and totally out of control and today we are confronted with yet more evidence of this," said Governor Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, at a news conference on Saturday.

Video of the incident circulated on social media and news outlets is "horrific" and "chilling", Ferguson said, adding that he told Alaska Airlines representatives that “they need to call on ICE to get out of our airports."

The governor said he would make the same request of every other airline that flies out of Sea-Tac airport.

Alaska Airlines said it is "concerned" by the federal action.

"Alaska Airlines was not provided advance notice of the enforcement action and we are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred," the company said in a statement.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council called the ICE arrest a "smash-and-grab" action that injected fear and chaos during a delicate time for air travel.

"Just days after our nation experienced widespread disruptions to air travel and flights being grounded, federal agents chose to carry out this operation at one of our busiest airports, during one the busiest travel weeks of the year," Sims said in a statement sent by the union, which includes local chapters representing flight attendants and ground crew at Sea-Tac airport.

Alaska Airlines said many passengers were put on other flights shortly after the incident and the originally scheduled flight departed at 11am.

text:
Elected Democratic officials expressed outrage Sunday over masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers aggressively arresting two passengers boarding a plane at the Seattle–Tacoma International Airport on Saturday.

Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., said Congress “needs to aggressively regulate” the government’s immigration tactics, calling the arrest of the two passengers in Seattle “just horrific.”

“We need immigration enforcement. We don’t need the reign of terror that Trump and Stephen Miller have brought down upon the American people,” Smith told MS NOW’s Antonia Hylton on “The Assignment” Sunday.

Videos of the incident widely circulated on social media show ICE officers forcibly holding down a passenger and dragging her out the door on an Alaska Airlines jet bridge while she screams loudly. Another passenger attempting to intervene appeared to be shoved by a masked officer. At least two people were detained.

Alaska Airlines said in a statement Saturday afternoon that it was not provided appropriate notice of the enforcement operation.

“We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306. We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests,” the airline said, adding that it is “working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred, including whether the proper protocols were followed.”

The Port of Seattle also said it was “outraged,” saying in a statement that “Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge. The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached.”

In a statement, ICE said that “during the arrest other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers—a federal crime and a felony” adding that one passenger, identified as a Mexican national who overstayed a visa, “hurled hot coffee on the officers.” ICE said that the individual will be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Smith and other leaders in the state vowed to seek justice and hold the agency and Trump administration to account.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called ICE “completely and totally out of control.”

“Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities,” the Democratic governor said in a statement Sunday. “Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics.”

Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., also said she was “outraged by disturbing video of ICE agents forcing a woman to the ground on a jet bridge at SeaTac. I’m demanding answers from DHS today & I’ll keep fighting to end this sick terror campaign.”

Smith expressed anger that “poorly trained” ICE agents at the Seattle–Tacoma airport were masked, wore no visible identification and disrupted the boarding process for everyone.

“This is no way for the federal government to be treating the people of our country,” he said.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash. called ICE’s behavior “totally unacceptable.”

“Violent arrests are the hallmark of fascist states, not a democracy. Soon, Democrats will take back control of Congress and we will continue the critical work to rein in these out of control agents and hold them accountable,” Jayapal said.

text:
A New Jersey congresswoman slammed a federal appeals court's decision not to dismiss the criminal charges against her Thursday as she considers whether to continue her appeal or return to court to face prosecution.

U.S. Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-10th Dist., is facing up to 17 years in prison if convicted.

She was arrested in May during a congressional oversight visit to the immigration detention facility at Delaney Hall in Newark. The visit turned into a confrontation with federal officers as they arrested Newark Mayor Ras Baraka.

Baraka was briefly detained before the charge against him was dropped. But McIver was later charged with assaulting and interfering with federal officers. She denied the allegations.

The 3rd Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals rejected McIver's appeal Thursday, leaving her with the option of appealing her case to the U.S. Supreme Court or proceeding to trial on the charges.

"Now, due to the disappointing decision by the Third Circuit, we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for," McIver said.

After McIver's arrest, President Donald Trump said she "was out of control" during the Delaney Hall incident.

McIver said Thursday she would continue to exhaust her legal options, warning that allowing the prosecution to proceed could set a chilling precedent for lawmakers carrying out congressional oversight.

She cited Democratic victories across the country in this month's midterm elections when calling for people to stand up to the Trump administration.

"This month, the American people clearly told us that they are against the president putting his own interests over the country's, that they are against ICE's reign of terror, and that they want action to stop this abuse," McIver said.

"I hope that everyone who feels that way will stand with me in my fight against these unjust charges because, while I am the first lawmaker they have tried to jail, I will surely not be the last," McIver added.

The U.S. Department of Justice expressed satisfaction with the decision.

"We are pleased with the court's decision, which proves the obvious: You cannot assault a federal officer, period," the department said in a statement. "That is a crime, and you will be held accountable, regardless of who you are."

The case also comes amid New Jersey's escalating fight to investigate conditions inside Delaney Hall. The state recently sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security in federal court, seeking to force the Trump administration to respond to requests for records in a civil rights investigation involving medical care, injuries and deaths at the facility.

The ACLU of New Jersey, National Women's Law Center and NAACP have also backed McIver's effort to have her charges dismissed, filing briefs in support of the congresswoman.

"Congresswoman McIver visited Delaney Hall to carry out congressional oversight of an immigration detention facility, an essential function of accountability that she has the legal authority to do," ACLU-NJ Executive Director Amol Sinha said in a previous statement.

The groups had previously condemned McIver's prosecution after an earlier effort to have the charges dismissed was rejected.
