title: Employment-Based Immigration After the Midterms: What to Watch in the Lame Duck Session
description:
There is no indication yet that congressional leaders or the White House have agreed on an employment-based immigration package.
Congress has previously paired additional access to employment-based immigration with measures addressing employer conduct, worker protection, and program integrity.
A negotiated omnibus, several “minibuses,” or an appropriations-and-extenders package could create room for immigration provisions.
For now, the circumstances support watching the lame duck session closely but not forecasting an immigration breakthrough.
What has not yet emerged is the political agreement required to move a defined employment-based immigration proposal through both chambers and obtain President Trump’s signature.
text:
By Angelo A. Paparelli

The November elections will shift control of Congress to the Democrats in January, while the current Republican-led Congress still has work to complete before it adjourns.

Funding of the federal government expires on December 11. This combination warrants attention from employers and mobility leaders because Congress has previously used lame-duck sessions and year-end appropriations legislation to enact significant immigration provisions.

There is no indication yet that congressional leaders or the White House have agreed on an employment-based immigration package. The more useful question at this stage is what circumstances could make one viable before the 119th Congress ends.

The historical precedent

Congress has enacted significant immigration legislation during previous lame-duck sessions. In 2000, year-end appropriations legislation incorporated the LIFE Act provisions (which provided significant adjustment-of-status and family-reunification relief, including a temporary extension of Immigration and Nationality Act § 245(i) that allowed certain otherwise ineligible individuals to adjust status to permanent residence in the United States despite specified immigration violations, and creation of the V and K-3/K-4 visa categories).

In 2002, Congress enacted the Homeland Security Act and fundamentally reorganized federal immigration administration.

The 2004 lame duck is particularly instructive for employers. The “Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2005” included the L-1 Visa and H-1B Visa Reform Acts. Congress created the exemption from the regular H-1B cap for up to 20,000 noncitizens with qualifying U.S. advanced degrees while also imposing additional fees, compliance requirements, and enforcement provisions.

That combination may be more relevant today than the numerical exemption standing alone. Congress has previously paired additional access to employment-based immigration with measures addressing employer conduct, worker protection, and program integrity.

More recent appropriations laws have continued this practice on a narrower scale through provisions involving supplemental H-2B visas (nonagricultural workers whom U.S. employers hire for seasonal or other temporary labor needs), E-Verify, Conrad State 30 (a program that helps underserved communities retain foreign-trained doctors who commit to work there for at least three years), special immigrant religious workers, and the EB-5 immigrant investor category.

The election changes the incentives on both sides

The expected transfer of congressional control creates an unusual negotiating environment, although it does not necessarily make an immigration agreement easier.

Republican leaders may have reason to complete selected legislative priorities while their party still controls both chambers. Retiring and defeated members may have greater latitude after the election to consider compromises that carried greater political risk before November 3.

There are countervailing considerations. Republicans may see little reason to make immigration concessions just before control changes. President Trump will remain in office after January and retain both veto authority and substantial executive power over immigration policy.

Democrats will gain congressional control and may prefer to negotiate from that stronger position. Senate procedure complicates that calculation because majority control does not eliminate the need for Republican votes on legislation requiring 60 votes for cloture.

The practical issue is therefore whether a bipartisan coalition available in December offers something that neither side can readily reproduce in the new Congress.

The December funding legislation matters

Current federal funding expires on December 11. Congress must address that deadline, but the form of the legislation will determine whether it offers a meaningful immigration vehicle.

A negotiated omnibus, several “minibuses,” or an appropriations-and-extenders package could create room for immigration provisions. A relatively clean continuing resolution would leave less room for negotiation.

Substantive immigration provisions also cannot simply be placed in an appropriations bill without regard to congressional procedure. House and Senate rules restrict legislative provisions in appropriations measures. Leadership can sometimes address those restrictions through special rules, waivers, or the structure of a broader negotiated package. Doing so requires a political decision, not merely agreement among immigration policymakers.

The December deadline therefore provides a potential vehicle. Whether immigration becomes part of it will depend on the larger funding negotiations.

What employment-based provisions might fit?

The established immigration extenders present the least novel possibility because Congress has repeatedly handled them in year-end legislation. Supplemental H-2B authority, E-Verify, Conrad State 30, and special immigrant religious workers fall into this category.

Other proposals would require a more substantial agreement, although Congress has already developed legislative language for several of them:

Recapture would make specified employment-based immigrant visa numbers that went unused in earlier years available again.

Anti-wastage provisions would seek to prevent congressionally authorized visa numbers from being lost in future fiscal years.

Adjustment-filing relief could allow certain backlogged applicants to file Form I-485 earlier and potentially receive employment authorization and advance parole without necessarily accelerating the ultimate availability of permanent residence.

Per-country reform would change how the existing employment-based numerical allocation is distributed among nationalities.

The House-passed Build Back Better bill in 2021 contained developed language addressing visa recapture and adjustment-related relief, although those provisions were not enacted. The EAGLE Act of 2022, a bill that reached the House floor, included detailed provisions addressing per-country limits, employment-based backlogs, and H-1B program integrity.

That history matters because negotiators would not necessarily need to develop these concepts from the beginning. It does not demonstrate that comparable provisions have sufficient support in the current Congress.

President Trump is an important part of the equation

The administration’s recent employment-immigration policies have emphasized protection of U.S. workers, employer layoffs, wages, outsourcing, and alleged program abuse. Those policies make broad employment-visa expansion difficult to envision without substantial safeguards.

President Trump’s own statements about highly skilled immigration have been more nuanced. He has spoken favorably about retaining talented foreign graduates of U.S. universities and about admitting workers with skills that he believes are not sufficiently available in the domestic workforce.

Those statements should not be treated as endorsements of visa recapture, adjustment filing, per-country reform, or any other specific proposal. They do suggest that targeted legislation focused on scarce skills and U.S.-educated talent could be considered differently from legislation perceived as facilitating the substitution of lower-cost foreign labor for U.S. workers.

The 2004 model may therefore be useful. A conceivable employment-based compromise could couple a limited immigration benefit with provisions addressing wages, recruitment, displacement, fees, compliance, or agency enforcement. Whether President Trump or congressional leaders would accept that bargain remains unknown.

What mobility leaders should watch

Developments in the coming weeks should provide considerably more insights than the historical analogies.

The first is the structure of the December funding legislation. The second is whether actual immigration text begins appearing in that process. Bipartisan sponsorship, participation by congressional leadership, and White House engagement would be more significant than the introduction of another standalone immigration bill. Any pairing of immigration relief with U.S.-worker protections or employer-compliance measures would also deserve close attention.

For now, the circumstances support watching the lame duck session closely but not forecasting an immigration breakthrough. Congress has the legislative vehicles, historical precedents, and previously drafted statutory language necessary to act. What has not yet emerged is the political agreement required to move a defined employment-based immigration proposal through both chambers and obtain President Trump’s signature.

title: ICE continues courthouse arrests, despite state's new PROTECT Act | WBUR News
description:
Some defense attorneys and immigrant advocates believe the arrests violate the new state law known as the PROTECT Act.
Five courthouse arrests took place the day the provision went into effect— twice the daily average for such arrests in 2025, Trial Court records show.
The PROTECT Act ban covers warrantless civil arrests — not ICE arrests for people facing federal criminal charges.
One could be overheard talking about the $50,000 signing bonuses for new ICE agents, while one said something about playing the rap song “Ice Ice Baby” in his car.
On a recent Monday at the Worcester district courthouse, ICE watchers appeared to outnumber ICE agents.
text:
Inside a Framingham district courtroom, a man in a flannel hoodie sat on a bench in the gallery, taking note of defendants as they appeared before a judge. He wasn’t wearing a badge or a uniform, but it would soon be clear that the man was with ICE.

He looked up after a bailiff escorted 24-year-old Rhyan Oliveira into the courtroom.

Oliveira faced three felony charges related to an alleged domestic violence incident the night before. He sat in the defendant's dock, listening to a Portuguese interpreter through headphones as a prosecutor read the allegations: that he tried to prevent his girlfriend from leaving the house, rammed her car with his BMW and threatened to kill her if she called police.

The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent typed into his phone as the prosecutor continued to say that the girlfriend had told police Oliveira sells cocaine, had access to a gun and kept cameras in the house to monitor both her and his stash. Oliveira’s public defender called these “baseless allegations,” that police found nothing when they searched the home, and said Oliveira had no criminal record.

As lawyers debated whether Oliveira should be released or remain in custody, no one mentioned the ICE agent sitting in the gallery — or the ones in the hallway and parking lot — who would all soon arrest him.

On Nov. 3, the state banned most warrantless civil immigration arrests at Massachusetts courthouses. But Oliveira was about to become one of more than the three-dozen ICE arrests since the ban took effect, according to data from the Massachusetts Trial Court.

Some defense attorneys and immigrant advocates believe the arrests violate the new state law known as the PROTECT Act. Five courthouse arrests took place the day the provision went into effect— twice the daily average for such arrests in 2025, Trial Court records show.

In the afternoon, Judge Sarah Kennedy ordered Oliveira released on conditions, including that he not contact his girlfriend. As he walked out of the courtroom and approached his mother and sister, the ICE agent in flannel followed closely behind.

Oliveira’s public defender, Christopher Quigley, broke the news to his mother and sister, who said they were there hoping to take him home from the court.

“I don’t think there’s really much we can do,” Quigley told them.

His sister started sobbing and vomited into a trash can. She sank to the floor and appeared to hyperventilate.

Two more plainclothes agents appeared in the lobby, now with gold ICE badges around their necks, and cuffed Oliveira. A fourth agent in green tactical gear and a mask waited at the entrance to the courthouse. They put Oliveira into an SUV and drove off.

The PROTECT Act ban covers warrantless civil arrests — not ICE arrests for people facing federal criminal charges. A search of federal court records turned up no criminal charges against Oliveira. The agency did not immediately respond to questions about Oliveira.

After the arrest, Oliveira’s mother told WBUR she and her daughter had no idea ICE had been in the courthouse until the moment they arrested her son.

Apparently, they were the only ones who didn’t know.

Interviews with immigrant advocates and public defenders indicate that ICE’s presence inside courthouses has become a regular part of working in the courts — with or without the PROTECT Act in place — and now they say ICE appears to be doubling down.

Marlborough

The PROTECT Act characterizes warrantless civil arrests at courthouses as “false imprisonment” under state law. It also authorizes the state attorney general to bring civil suits against federal officials for violations. The AG’s office said in a statement that it has received complaints about ICE conduct and encourages witnesses to come forward with information.

On a recent morning in Marlborough District Court, two men chatted outside the courtroom. One could be overheard talking about the $50,000 signing bonuses for new ICE agents, while one said something about playing the rap song “Ice Ice Baby” in his car.

Despite their lack of uniforms, defense attorney Trevor Clement said he could tell the men were federal agents, and he wanted everyone else to know too. He walked around the lobby, asking each person why they were in the courthouse — loudly enough for all to hear — calling out the two men as “ICE.”

“Be who you are. Say who you are. Know who you are. And absolutely, I'm gonna let other people know … you don't get to skulk around.”

defense attorney Trevor Clement

“Most people will give you an answer,” Clement told WBUR in an interview, “and then you had these, you know, bearded lumberjack-looking guys who would just give you a vague answer of, ‘It's a public courthouse,’ or, ‘I'm just here to watch.’ ”

People are rarely in court for those reasons, he added, so it isn’t hard to figure out who the ICE agents are.

“Be who you are. Say who you are. Know who you are,” Clement said. “And absolutely, I'm gonna let other people know … you don't get to skulk around.”

Clement said with agents in the courts, defendants face a serious dilemma. Either they remain in state custody, or they’re released into the hands of ICE — and the defendants don’t get to choose.

After identifying the agents in the lobby, Clement said he realized they were likely there for his client. When bail was set at $5,000, Clement told him he had two choices: “You can pay $5,000 to probably be picked up by ICE,’” he said, “Or you can sit in jail until this case is over … at which point, they'll then be standing at the doorway. Maybe.”

Clement’s client didn’t make bail, and he remains in state custody. But the agents didn’t leave the Marlborough courthouse empty handed. That morning they arrested a Brazilian woman facing a misdemeanor shoplifting charge.

Due process

The practice of ICE courthouse arrests “dismantles due process,” said Jen Klein, director of the immigration impact unit at the Committee for Public Counsel Services, the state agency that employs public defense attorneys across Massachusetts. In a statement, Klein said “staff attorneys have witnessed ICE agents violating the new law,” and the group is reporting incidents to the state attorney general’s office.

ICE officials said it’s “common sense” to detain suspects at courthouses, as that’s where they can find people facing criminal charges. The agency also said it’s safer to make an arrest after court security has screened people for weapons.

“Sanctuary politicians do not control federal law enforcement,” an ICE spokesperson said in a statement, citing the U.S. Constitution’s supremacy clause.

Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge who worked in Pennsylvania, agreed that Massachusetts’ PROTECT Act rests on shaky legal ground and could run afoul of the supremacy clause.

“States can't regulate the activity of the federal government, and courthouses are public places where anybody can go,” Arthur said.

In its final year, the Biden administration also increased ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses, Trial Court data shows. But in the first year of Trump’s second term, arrests more than doubled: court officials documented 2.5 per day.

"States can't regulate the activity of the federal government, and courthouses are public places where anybody can go."

Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge

Arthur is resident fellow in law and policy at the Center for Immigration Studies, a nonprofit that advocates for tighter restrictions on immigration. He believes that as states like Massachusetts refuse to cooperate with federal immigration policies, court arrests have become a bigger priority.

He said that claims about “due process” cut both ways — the enforcement of immigration law is also part of due process, and the state is making it difficult for ICE to arrest and deport people.

“If there is a due process right, for the people of Massachusetts and the people of the United States, that due process right is subverted when states like Massachusetts prevent [the Department of Homeland Security] from taking people into custody,” Arthur said.

Worcester

Volunteers for the LUCE Immigrant Justice Network of Massachusetts have been tracking ICE activity throughout the central and eastern parts of the state — in the streets and in courthouses — since the early days of President Trump’s second term.

On a recent Monday at the Worcester district courthouse, ICE watchers appeared to outnumber ICE agents. One LUCE observer sat in the courtroom; another was stationed at the sallyport behind the court, keeping eyes on an unmarked vehicle. Three more stood at the entrance, comparing notes on where agents were parked.

Social worker Jillian Phillips, one of the court watchers in Worcester, said ICE agents are thumbing their noses at the state’s restriction on courthouse arrests — and based on the accounts of LUCE observers, she thinks the state’s tally is an undercount. But Phillips pointed out that the law prohibits court staff from assisting or interfering with immigration arrests.

“Even if court officers do see it happening,” Phillips said, “you can't interfere with a federal arrest. So then, what actual options exist to hold people accountable?”

Phillips wants Attorney General Andrea Campbell to take steps to enforce the law, though she isn’t sure what the PROTECT Act can do to limit ICE arrests.

But for now, Phillips said, there’s one clear benefit of the law: court policy bans officers from handing over suspects behind closed doors. Before the PROTECT Act, the courts would allow agents into sallyports and courthouse lockups to take defendants into custody.

“We at least now have the opportunity to physically see the person and try to get help for them,” Phillips said, “whereas before, sometimes you didn't know if they took someone or not.”

text:
Federal courts are deciding how far ICE can go in re-detaining people already released, and the answer depends on why the person was free.

ICE re-arrest after release is being litigated in federal courts from Denver to Atlanta, and the cases involve three groups: habeas petitioners taken back into custody at the exit door, people released years ago while their cases proceed, and people with old removal orders reporting under supervision. Each group sits under a different legal rule, and that rule decides how much a release is worth.

Three kinds of release, three sets of rules

ICE re-arrest after release by a judge: what counts as freedom

In Denver, an ICE assistant field office director testified that she received a “direct order” to re-detain habeas petitioners “that had some type of criminality,” according to U.S. District Judge Charlotte N. Sweeney’s Nov. 18 order. Acting Field Office Director Nathan Rasper testified that the approach began in the district on Oct. 27 and rested on ICE’s statutory authority “to fix the situation of the forms, the technical.” The order counts eighteen such re-detentions. Sweeney found contempt but took no further action because Rasper swore the practice had stopped, as covered here earlier. A colleague, Judge S. Kato Crews, had already barred one re-detention unless the government first wins a bond hearing by clear and convincing evidence.

Minnesota’s bench is split. MPR News reports that Judges Jeffrey Bryan and John Tunheim found instant re-arrests at the Whipple Federal Building violated their orders, while Chief Judge Eric Tostrud and Judge Jerry Blackwell did not, and that Tunheim now writes that the government “SHALL NOT re-detain” a petitioner without adequate notice and a pre-detention bond hearing. Security video of two Whipple arrests shows how fast they happen.

The government does not claim court orders can be ignored. A DHS spokesperson told MPR on Oct. 27 that ICE “may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision,” and called any suggestion otherwise “sabotage.” Bryan himself wrote that a habeas order does not bar every future arrest. The practical effect is that protection depends on each order’s wording, which varies by judge within one courthouse.

The changed-circumstances rule for people on bond

For people released while their cases proceed, the statute is broad: the government “at any time may revoke a bond or parole,” rearrest the person “under the original warrant” and detain them, under 8 U.S.C. 1226(b). In Matter of Sugay, the Board of Immigration Appeals read an implicit limit into that power, requiring a change of circumstances. According to Judge P. Casey Pitts’s Dec. 19, 2025, order in Garro Pinchi v. Noem, DHS had followed that practice, dropped it in May 2025, and in July 2025 adopted the view that 8 U.S.C. 1225 mandates detention for everyone who entered without admission. Pitts stayed the policy for ICE’s San Francisco office; the government appealed on Jan. 29, 2026. Four plaintiffs in the Atlanta field office filed a class action seeking the same relief on Nov. 12.

The open question is whether this fight survives the Supreme Court’s review of ICE’s mandatory detention reading. A government win would likely make the changed-circumstances rule largely irrelevant for people who entered without inspection, because their detention would be mandatory.

Supervision orders and an old removal order

People with final orders stand on the weakest ground. Regulations let ICE revoke supervision when it is “appropriate to enforce a removal order,” but require notice of the reasons and “an initial informal interview promptly” after the return to custody. Noune Phompor, ordered removed in 2009 and released because Laos would not take him, was arrested Sept. 1. His attorney told the Peninsula Daily News that a magistrate judge found “effectively no pre-detention process” constitutionally deficient on Nov. 19. That account comes from one outlet; the order was not available for review. If it reads as described, the ruling asks for process before custody, beyond what the regulation requires.

What the data does and does not show

No public dataset counts re-detentions. The available numbers are tallies from court records and reporting: eighteen in Colorado in Sweeney’s order, at least eight in Minnesota confirmed by MPR, and at least 20 nationwide in the year before Nov. 2 counted by The Guardian. The surrounding scale is measurable. ProPublica’s analysis of court data counts 97,050 immigration habeas cases filed since January 2025, as of Nov. 17, 2026, and notes some duplicates. ICE’s average daily detention population rose from 39,314 on Jan. 20, 2025, to 67,180 on July 30, 2026, according to the Government Accountability Office. Those figures measure detention and litigation volume, not whether re-arrests are becoming more common.

What to watch

Late February or early March 2027: expected oral argument in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, according to the ACLU, which represents the detained man.

Atlanta: a ruling on the Sosa Martinez request to halt the policy during the case.

Ninth Circuit: the government’s appeal of the Garro Pinchi stay, and any appeal in the Phompor case.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

title: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson Calls for Abolishing ICE Following Sea-Tac Airport Arrests
description:
"It is time to abolish Donald Trump's ICE," Ferguson declared.
His remarks represent a direct call to dismantle a major federal law enforcement agency, rather than simply change its leadership or operating procedures.
Federal officials said she was also arrested and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
The airline emphasized that it must comply with applicable laws and regulations but does not direct or coordinate federal immigration enforcement.
The controversy has also raised questions about a Washington law Ferguson signed earlier this year.
text:
Speaking during an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and elected officials in Des Moines, Ferguson sharply criticized the Trump administration's immigration enforcement tactics after masked federal agents detained two people on a crowded jet bridge as passengers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles.

"It is time to abolish Donald Trump's ICE," Ferguson declared.

Ferguson argued that the agency's problems extend beyond individual enforcement operations and reflect deeper institutional failures.

"The culture of ICE is bankrupt," Ferguson said. "It lacks morals. It lacks any decency."

The Democratic governor said the United States still needs immigration enforcement and border security but called for ICE to be replaced with a system that is effective, ethical and humane.

His remarks represent a direct call to dismantle a major federal law enforcement agency, rather than simply change its leadership or operating procedures.

Ferguson also urged commercial airlines operating at Sea-Tac to publicly pressure the federal government to remove ICE from airports.

During the news conference, Ferguson said he had spoken with representatives of Alaska Airlines and intended to make similar requests of other carriers serving Seattle.

The governor's comments followed an incident Saturday morning involving Alaska Airlines Flight 1306, which was preparing to depart Seattle for Los Angeles.

According to an official statement from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, agents conducted a targeted operation at approximately 8:05 a.m. to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national whom the agency said had overstayed his visa.

Federal officials said the situation escalated when other passengers interfered with the arrest.

ICE alleged that a second individual, identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, threw hot coffee at federal officers during the confrontation. Federal officials said she was also arrested and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Those allegations are based on ICE's account of the incident, and the announcement of an intended criminal charge does not establish guilt.

Videos circulating online showed masked agents restraining individuals on the jet bridge as nearby passengers watched and questioned what was happening.

Ferguson characterized the video as horrific and chilling and questioned the federal government's handling of the operation.

The Port of Seattle issued a statement Saturday expressing outrage over the incident, saying the enforcement action occurred without its participation or advance knowledge.

Port officials said they were communicating with the Department of Homeland Security to determine whether previously established airport enforcement protocols had been violated.

Alaska Airlines also issued a statement confirming it had not received appropriate notice of the operation.

The airline emphasized that it must comply with applicable laws and regulations but does not direct or coordinate federal immigration enforcement.

The controversy has also raised questions about a Washington law Ferguson signed earlier this year.

On March 19, the governor signed Senate Bill 5855, which restricts law enforcement officers from concealing their identities with facial coverings while interacting with the public.

The law explicitly includes federal immigration enforcement officers, although it provides exceptions for certain undercover operations, protective equipment and other specified circumstances.

Ferguson said he believes the masked agents involved in Saturday's operation violated the state law and indicated that officials were examining how agents obtained access to the airport's secure boarding area.

Whether the operation violated the statute has not been established through a court ruling. Applying state restrictions to federal officers also raises questions about federal authority.

Despite Ferguson's demands, neither Washington's governor nor the Port of Seattle has the legal authority to independently abolish ICE or prohibit federal officers from carrying out otherwise lawful immigration enforcement.

ICE was established in 2003 as part of the Department of Homeland Security. Eliminating the agency and permanently restructuring its responsibilities would require action at the federal level.

The Port of Seattle acknowledges on its official website that it cannot interfere with lawful federal enforcement operations at the airport.

Ferguson's call adds his voice to a broader national debate over whether ICE should be reformed, replaced or eliminated altogether.

Supporters of abolishing ICE argue that the agency's enforcement practices and institutional structure require fundamental change, while opponents maintain that federal authorities need the resources and personnel to enforce immigration laws and carry out deportations.

For now, Ferguson's proposal remains a political demand rather than an enacted policy.

No specific federal restructuring plan accompanied his Saturday announcement, and the governor has not identified legislation that would replace ICE with a different immigration enforcement agency.

NEWARK, N.J. (VINnews) — A federal appeals court has rejected Rep. LaMonica McIver’s effort to dismiss criminal charges stemming from a confrontation with federal officers during a congressional oversight visit to an immigration detention facility, prompting the New Jersey Democrat to warn that she may be the first of many lawmakers targeted by the Trump administration.

Join our WhatsApp group

Subscribe to our Daily Roundup Email

The 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to rehear the case en banc after an earlier panel ruling left the charges in place. McIver, who represents New Jersey’s 10th Congressional District, faces up to 17 years in prison if convicted on counts of assaulting and interfering with federal officers.​

The charges arose from a May 2025 visit to Delaney Hall in Newark, where McIver and other lawmakers went to inspect conditions at the privately operated immigration detention center. The visit escalated into a physical confrontation as agents moved to arrest Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Baraka was briefly detained, but charges against him were later dropped. McIver has denied the allegations and argued that the prosecution interferes with Congress’s oversight authority.​

In a statement after the appeals court decision, McIver said the ruling brings the country “one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.” She pledged to continue exploring legal options and urged supporters to stand with her, citing recent midterm election results as evidence of public opposition to the administration’s immigration policies. “While I am the first lawmaker they have tried to jail, I will surely not be the last,” she said.​

The Justice Department welcomed the decision. “You cannot assault a federal officer, period,” the department said in a statement. “That is a crime, and you will be held accountable, regardless of who you are.”​

The case has drawn support from groups including the ACLU of New Jersey, the National Women’s Law Center, and the NAACP, which have argued that McIver was carrying out a core congressional function. Separately, New Jersey has sued the Department of Homeland Security seeking records related to conditions at Delaney Hall amid broader scrutiny of the facility.​

McIver, who recently won reelection, has maintained that the charges represent political retaliation for her oversight work. She and her legal team are weighing whether to petition the U.S. Supreme Court or proceed to trial.​

text:
An Alaska Airlines pilot reportedly walked away from his aircraft during boarding on Saturday morning after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two passengers on a Seattle jet bridge. Two flight attendants were also said to be so overwhelmed by the incident that they asked to be replaced.

The arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) as passengers boarded Alaska flight AS1306 to Los Angeles, which ended up being delayed by more than three hours. Video footage of the incident, which has sparked widespread outrage, shows masked officers struggling with travelers near the aircraft door.

Alaska Airlines Pilot Walks Off, Flight Attendants Ask To Be Replaced

The incident occurred on Saturday morning as Alaska passengers were boarding a Boeing 737-800 bound for Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). Speaking to local radio station KUOW, passenger Aidan Mendoza said masked ICE agents struggled with a man and a woman on the jet bridge at Gate N9, leaving around 50 passengers pressed against the jet bridge wall.

Amid the chaos, Mendoza said an Alaska pilot walked back up the jet bridge looking uncomfortable and unsure of what to do, adding that "he didn't come back." KUOW also reports that two Alaska flight attendants were so overwhelmed that they asked to be "subbed out." Mendoza decided not to board the flight, saying a gate agent removed him from the passenger list before customer service refunded his ticket.

In a statement to Simple Flying, an Alaska spokesperson did not confirm whether any crew members had to be replaced, but said it was "not provided advance notice of the enforcement action" and is "working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred." The spokesperson added,

"We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306. We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests."

ICE Says Other Travelers Impeded Its Operation

In a statement, ICE said it had launched an operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza (who is unrelated to passenger Aidan Mendoza), a Mexican national who it said had overstayed his visa. The agency claimed other travelers "began to obstruct and assault" officers during the arrest, while a second passenger, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, "hurled hot coffee on the officers." ICE said Hernandez Mejia, also from Mexico, had overstayed her visa and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

The Port of Seattle, which operates the airport, said it was "outraged" by the incident, emphasizing that immigration enforcement at SEA takes place without its involvement or knowledge. According to the Port, local federal immigration authorities had previously agreed to protocols at the airport, and it is now investigating whether any of those agreements were breached.

Saturday's arrests drew strong criticism from Washington officials, including Governor Bob Ferguson, who said ICE was "completely and totally out of control." Ferguson added that he was looking into how the agents accessed the jet bridge and whether they violated a state law prohibiting law enforcement officers, including federal immigration agents, from wearing face coverings.

Immigration Arrests At US Airports

ICE has stepped up arrests at US airports since the summer to apprehend travelers overstaying visas. Other notable cases include a woman from Ecuador escorted off a jet bridge in Denver in July, and a Southwest Airlines flight attendant taken into custody while on the job at Nashville International Airport (BNA).

Airlines have little control over immigration enforcement at the gate. Airlines for America (A4A), which represents the largest US carriers, said in August that it was holding discussions with ICE and TSA to ensure proper procedures were in place when law enforcement activity takes place at airports.

The woman who was arrested, identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was also found to have overstayed her visa, the department said, adding that she would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

The agency did not say where the two were taken.

Officials demand answers

The footage prompted sharp condemnation from Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, who called ICE “completely and totally out of control” and described the video as “horrific” and “chilling” at a news conference on Saturday.

Ferguson also questioned whether the agents violated a Washington state law he signed in March that restricts law enforcement officers from wearing facial coverings.

“Masked agents who do not identify themselves drag screaming individuals off a jetway as they’re about to do something very ordinary in our country: board a flight. There is no justification for this brutality,” Ferguson said during the news conference.

He added that state officials were investigating the circumstances of the arrests, including how the agents accessed the jet bridge.

Ferguson also urged Alaska Airlines and other carriers to demand that federal immigration agents leave airports.

Alaska Airlines said it did not receive advance notice of the enforcement operation and was working with Ferguson and the Port of Seattle to determine whether established protocols had been followed.

The Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, said in a statement that it has raised its concerns with the relevant federal authorities about whether regulations were breached.

At Saturday’s news conference, Port of Seattle Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed characterised the arrests as particularly distressing because of when they took place.

“We are entering the holidays. That is one of the most heartbreaking things about this moment today. There are so many people in that airport that are travelling to go and connect with their families,” Mohamed said. “And that family is separated.”

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson also condemned the operation, describing the agents’ tactics as “unacceptable and un-American”.

Protesters gathered at the airport on Saturday evening, in the hours after the confrontation, to condemn the arrests and call for accountability from federal authorities.

Disapproval of Trump’s immigration crackdown

The arrests come as President Donald Trump continues to pursue what he has promised will be the largest deportation effort in US history.

But voters have expressed concern about the tactics used during his immigration crackdown. Some experts believe the topic became a political liability for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.

A Fox News poll from September found that 53 percent of registered voters believed the administration’s immigration enforcement had gone too far. The figure rose to 60 percent among independent voters and two-thirds of Hispanic respondents.

In a November 8 interview with the CBS News television programme 60 Minutes, Trump acknowledged that his administration’s deportation policies may have been too aggressive, saying, “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”

In the midterms, the Democratic Party won majorities in both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, flipping both chambers from Republican control.

In the wake of that victory, several high-profile members of the left-wing party have pledged to seek reforms to immigration enforcement operations in the US.

Senators Alex Padilla and Jacky Rosen, for instance, have introduced legislation that would prevent ICE from carrying out arrests at or near airports without a judicial warrant first.

Patty Murray, another Democratic senator, also said she was demanding answers from DHS and warned in a post on X that the administration would face consequences when the incoming Congress is sworn in early next year.

“Trump answers to a Democratic Congress on January 3rd – there WILL be accountability,” she wrote.

"Just days after our nation experienced widespread disruptions to air travel and flights being grounded, federal agents chose to carry out this operation at one of our busiest airports, during one the busiest travel weeks of the year," Sims said in a statement sent by the union, which includes local chapters representing flight attendants and ground crew at Sea-Tac airport.

text:
The president pushed back on the incoming House speaker's criticism of his chief of staff while expressing optimism about working with Democrats in the next Congress.

President Donald Trump is standing by his newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller after House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the controversial adviser a "stone-cold racist" and accused him of architecting the administration's aggressive immigration crackdown.

During a Saturday, Nov. 21, appearance on Fox News' "Saturday in America," Trump defended Miller's role in shaping his administration's border policies, pushing back on Jeffries' criticism while suggesting he remained open to working with Democrats when they take control of Congress next year.

"The one thing with Stephen, he was very strong on the border," Trump told Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany. "So he called him a racist. But we had to be strong."

Trump went on to repeat claims about the number of people who entered the United States during the Biden administration, alleging that 25 million people, including "killers, murderers," drug dealers and rapists, had been allowed into the country. He used those claims to defend his administration's approach to border enforcement, which Miller helped develop.

The president's comments came after Jeffries sharply criticized Miller in an interview with The New York Times published Saturday. Asked whether he could envision sitting down with the White House chief of staff, Jeffries rejected the possibility.

"No. I made clear that Stephen Miller's a stone-cold racist. Why would I deal with him at this point in time?" Jeffries told the newspaper.

The Brooklyn Democrat went on to describe Miller as "the architect of Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine," arguing that the administration's immigration policies have been marked by "cruelty," "chaos" and "death."

Miller, who replaced Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff on Nov. 9, has been one of the central figures behind Trump's immigration agenda. His elevation to the administration's top staff position signaled the president's continued commitment to the hardline enforcement strategy that has drawn criticism from immigrant advocates and Democratic lawmakers.

The White House has pushed back against Jeffries' characterization of Miller. Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told the New York Post that Miller has a record of working across party lines on issues including public safety reform, drug pricing transparency and nuclear energy.

But Trump's defense of Miller was accompanied by a notably more conciliatory message toward Jeffries, who is positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.

"I think Hakeem will see that, and I look forward to working with Hakeem," Trump said, referring to Miller's character. "I give him a lot of congratulations."

Trump acknowledged the historic significance of Jeffries potentially becoming the first Black person to hold the speakership, calling his selection by House Democrats "pretty spectacular" and saying it was "a big deal."

Jeffries was nominated by House Democrats to lead their caucus as speaker following the party's victories in the November midterm elections. Democrats are preparing to assume control of the House and Senate, setting up a new political dynamic for the remainder of Trump's term.

Although Jeffries has made clear that he does not intend to work directly with Miller, his comments do not necessarily rule out negotiations with the broader Trump administration. In his interview with The New York Times, Jeffries pointed to other administration officials, including Vice President JD Vance, as potential channels for communication.

Trump, meanwhile, suggested he was interested in finding common ground with Democrats on legislation, including health care and immigration. He also reiterated his support for temporarily capping credit card interest rates at 10%, an issue he has previously raised despite criticism from some conservatives.

"I don't want to veto every time," Trump told McEnany, referring to the prospect of Democratic legislation reaching his desk. "I'm sure that they'll send something up and we can negotiate."

The president also praised Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, signaling that he sees opportunities to work with Democratic leadership in both chambers.

Still, the exchange highlights a potential tension heading into the next Congress: Democrats will have to navigate negotiations with an administration whose immigration agenda they have strongly opposed, while Trump will have to contend with a Democratic-controlled legislature.

For Jeffries, drawing a distinction between engaging with the president and working with Miller appears central to that challenge. For Trump, defending one of his most influential advisers while expressing an interest in bipartisan cooperation reflects the competing priorities that could shape the next two years in Washington.

title: Alex Pereira-Alves Deportation to Africa Feared After Latest ICE Move - WEHOville
description:
According to other Brazilian detainees, they may be transferred to Louisiana before being flown to Brazil.
Equatorial Guinea has a documented history of violence, persecution and discrimination against LGBTQ people.
Even more disturbing, the administration has already sent Brazilian and Cuban nationals to Equatorial Guinea.

text:
Sunday Nov 22 11:30 a.m.

Alex’s best friend, Jeff Markwardt, spoke with Alex Sunday morning. According to other Brazilian detainees, they may be transferred to Louisiana before being flown to Brazil. But ICE still hasn’t told Alex where he’s being sent or when. “It could be tonight. It could be next week,” Markwardt said. “The uncertainty continues, and Alex remains in the dark about what happens next.”

The confusion, chaos and cruelty continue, with Alex still waiting for answers.

Saturday Nov 21 9:30 p.m. Alex Pereira-Alves thought he was finally getting closer to home. Instead, ICE has moved the longtime gay West Hollywood resident from El Paso, Texas, to Florence, Arizona, raising a terrifying possibility: that he could be deported to Equatorial Guinea instead of Brazil, where his mother and sister are waiting for him.

And for Alex, the stakes could be life-threatening. Equatorial Guinea has a documented history of violence, persecution and discrimination against LGBTQ people. Although consensual same-sex relations are not generally illegal there, human rights reports have documented harassment, abuse and mistreatment of gay people, with little protection from authorities. A Reuters investigation published last month documented how the Trump administration has deported LGBTQ immigrants to African countries where their safety is at risk.

Now Alex is scared to death he could be next. ICE has not told him where he is going.

He’s so frightened that he’s begun making arrangements for someone to care for his beloved dog, Bella, if he dies.

In a phone call with WEHOonline Saturday night, Alex’s best friend, Jeff Markwardt, and neighbor Marna Deitch said Alex had called with the disturbing news. Rather than being placed on a flight to Brazil, as had been expected, Alex had spent the last several hours on a bus traveling from Texas to Arizona alongside 17 Cuban detainees and three Africans. He was the only Brazilian on the bus.

Alex was so terrified he broke down crying during the bus ride as fears grew that ICE could be sending him to Equatorial Guinea instead of Brazil, despite a judge’s order directing his return home.

What’s especially troubling is the fact Arizona has become a hub for the Trump administration’s deportation flights to Africa.

An Arizona Mirror investigation described how ICE has used Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport for flights to African nations, including flights carrying immigrants who have no connection to the countries where they are being sent.

Even more disturbing, the administration has already sent Brazilian and Cuban nationals to Equatorial Guinea. In August, a Brazilian man and four Cubans were among six detainees flown to the Central African nation after refusing to disembark from a deportation flight in Liberia, according to an Associated Press report.

For Alex, that precedent is terrifying.

An earlier removal order named Equatorial Guinea as his destination. A subsequent immigration court order on Nov. 5 directed his removal to Brazil.

But Alex says ICE has not told him where he is going.

Alex’s attorney, Jane Oak, has previously contacted ICE to clarify that the latest removal order specifies Brazil. Markwardt said he contacted her again Saturday night, seeking confirmation that ICE intends to honor that order.

The latest transfer is especially cruel considering that just a day earlier, Alex was finally feeling some relief. He described conditions at the El Paso detention facility as “night and day” better than Adelanto, where he spent more than three months. Now he’s in Florence, where he says conditions are even worse than Adelanto. There are no beds, and he’s sleeping on a mat on the floor near one or two other Brazilian detainees. And still, nobody will tell him where he’s going next.

Deitch, who has been helping advocate for Alex, said he is carrying a copy of the judge’s removal order with him, but worries it may offer little protection once he leaves American soil. And as she pointed out during the conversation, she’s not even sure how much protection it offers him here in the United States.

Alex should be on his way home to Brazil. Instead, he’s frightened for his life, not knowing whether ICE will send him home to his family or to a country where he could face persecution simply for being gay. It’s a cruel position to put anyone in. We’ll continue following his case and keep you posted as we learn more.

title: Are immigration agents targeting people of color in Northern California? The ACLU is investigating
description:
A Sacramento-area man says he was driving to a landscaping job with a longtime friend when federal immigration agents followed their truck into a grocery store parking lot.
Julio, whose real name is being withheld because he fears retaliation, said several agents approached the vehicle and identified themselves as immigration officers.
The organization has also been documenting vehicles left behind after reported encounters with immigration agents.
The Department of Homeland Security rejected allegations that immigration agents are targeting people based on race or ethnicity.
Investigators would need to establish common patterns to prove federal immigration officers are racial profiling individuals in the region.
text:
A Sacramento-area man says he was driving to a landscaping job with a longtime friend when federal immigration agents followed their truck into a grocery store parking lot.

Julio, whose real name is being withheld because he fears retaliation, said several agents approached the vehicle and identified themselves as immigration officers.

Julio said the agents eventually handcuffed him and held him in a vehicle for about 15 minutes before releasing him. His friend was taken into custody.

“You don’t feel as safe anymore,” Julio said in Spanish. “Sometimes you don’t feel safe going out because you think they could arrest you at any moment, even though you haven’t done anything.”

Julio has lived in the United States for over 25 years and works as a landscaper. He said the encounter has changed how he goes about his daily life, even as he continues working and caring for his family.

Giselle Garcia with NorCal Resist, a mutual aid-organization and immigrant-rights group, said agents never told Julio why they had approached the truck. The paperwork he later received instructing him to report to ICE for a check-in also did not give a reason for the encounter.

Garcia explained that Julio has no criminal history and had no legal immigration status at the time. He had entered the country without inspection and recently applied for a U visa, a form of immigration relief available to certain victims of crimes who cooperate with law enforcement.

That’s significant because under a May federal court ruling, ICE generally cannot arrest, detain or deport individuals with a pending U visa application.

“It doesn’t seem like they actually had that reasonable suspicion to pull him over,” Garcia said.

Garcia added that Julio’s friend later signed paperwork agreeing to leave the country, which she says is common among people the organization hears from.

“The majority of these individuals have unfortunately signed voluntary departure after being detained,” she said. “And there’s a lot of different factors. One, they come from very hard working class families that don’t have the funds to hire an attorney… others have expressed they felt forced to sign that document because of ICE officers saying ‘You have to, you have to, you have to.’”

Garcia said accounts like Julio’s are part of a broader pattern of federal immigration enforcement they are trying to document.

NorCal Resist’s rapid-response network has flagged nearly 80 cases for possible racial profiling since Oct. 25, according to Garcia. The nonprofit has sent those cases to the ACLU of Northern California for review.

The groups have not announced a lawsuit over the recent enforcement activity, but the ACLU says it’s gathering accounts and looking for evidence of broader patterns.

Looking for patterns in traffic stops

Emilia Garcia, an investigator with the ACLU of Northern California, said the organization is interviewing people who have been stopped to understand what happened and whether agents gave a reason for the encounter.

She said the goal is to learn whether officers appeared to know anything about someone before stopping them, or whether the person was approached seemingly at random.

“ICE is pulling people over either because they see that they’re a person of color or they see a vehicle that looks like it might be driven by a person of color,” the ACLU investigator said. “We’ve been seeing huge numbers of work trucks with either construction or landscaping materials, maybe pulling trailers or with racks on the back, being pulled over.”

NorCal Resist is helping identify potential cases and connect people with the ACLU. Programs Director Giselle Garcia said the organization has been flagging and referring cases it believes warrant further scrutiny.

The referrals include cases the group believes may involve racial profiling or other potentially unlawful enforcement practices.

“Our role is providing the real human stories that prove these abuses are happening,” Garcia said, describing how NorCal Resist’s Migra Watch observers find abandoned vehicles and make door-to-door visits to alert families that someone has been taken.

Garcia added that NorCal Resist has completed intakes for more than 140 detainments since Oct. 6. The organization has flagged about 80 of these cases so far as potentially involving racial profiling.

These cases have not all been independently verified as instances of profiling by the ACLU.

Garcia also said many of the reported encounters have happened during the morning commute between 5:30 a.m. and 9 a.m. and that most in the reports have been men of color.

“With the exception of two or three women out of these 73, they’ve all been men. Brown men,” she said in an earlier interview.

Garcia said another pattern is that many of the people being detained have had little or no prior contact with the immigration system have no criminal record.

“They don’t even have A-numbers assigned when we talk to their families,” she said, referring to Alien Registration Numbers, unique identifiers used in immigration records.

The organization has also been documenting vehicles left behind after reported encounters with immigration agents. In one case near Marysville, Garcia said an employer contacted the group after four workers failed to show up.

“Our observers through Migra Watch found that vehicle on the side of the highway,” Garcia recounted. “We saw coffee cups and lunches throughout the car so we knew it was at least four people.”

Garcia said the employer didn’t know their full names so they weren’t able to track them all down to get them help.

“How many of these kinds of detainments are going unaccounted for and people being eaten up by the system?” she added.

The Department of Homeland Security rejected allegations that immigration agents are targeting people based on race or ethnicity.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE” a department spokesperson said in a statement. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S. — NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity.”

The spokesperson said ICE officers use reasonable suspicion to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests, consistent with the Fourth Amendment. However, they did not elaborate on what constitutes “reasonable suspicion” when asked.

DHS also declined to discuss specific enforcement operations citing security and officer safety concerns.

What counts as racial profiling?

UC Davis law professor and immigration law expert Kevin Johnson said immigration officers generally need reasonable suspicion that someone is in the country unlawfully before making an investigative stop.

“And the Supreme Court has said that the officers are required to consider the totality of the circumstances, which includes attire, location of the stop, Mexican appearance and a variety of other factors,” he said. “But the court left it pretty open to the officers to consider what they want to consider in an immigration stop.”

Johnson is referring to a1975 Supreme Court ruling that found apparent Mexican ancestry alone cannot justify an immigration stop, but that it could be considered alongside other factors.

The legal debate has resurfaced in Southern California where the ACLU and other groups sued over immigration raids and alleged that federal agents were stopping people based on their perceived Latino identity and other characteristics.

Last month, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction barring immigration agents from conducting detentive stops based on racial stereotyping in seven Southern California counties.

But the ruling was not a final decision and the Trump administration has appealed. The injunction applies to Southern California, not the Sacramento region.

Johnson said a separate lawsuit in Northern California could potentially lead to similar restrictions if investigators document evidence that agents are relying on racial appearance, language or work attire to make stops.

Investigators would need to establish common patterns to prove federal immigration officers are racial profiling individuals in the region.

“You’d look at who is being apprehended and whether they were almost exclusively Latino,” he said. “You’d want to look at data of who’s being stopped, indicators like Spanish surname… You’d want to look at as much data as you can about the kinds of stops, where the stops are and what the officers when confronted say are the basis for the stop.”

“It’s hard to get that kind of information in advance of a lawsuit, but you certainly can collect data and talk to people who’ve been apprehended by ICE either on the streets or in workplaces or in arrests, including immigration check-ins.”

Johnson added that while he believes ICE officers are engaging in similar practices in the greater Sacramento area as in Southern California, the outcome of any potential case would depend on the facts gathered.

Still gathering evidence

Emilia Garcia said the ACLU is still in the fact-gathering stage and has not announced a lawsuit over the recent enforcement activity in Northern California.

Investigators are speaking with individuals who have been stopped and their families to learn whether the encounters point to a broader pattern.

“Myself and my co-workers interview them to understand ‘What did ICE say when they stopped you?” she said. “‘Did they have any reason to stop you? Did they know who you were before they stopped you or did they just sort of randomly stop you on the street, or in your work truck as you were going to a job?’”

The ACLU investigator said NorCal Resist’s rapid-response network is helping them connect with individuals who have been arrested or detained — and their families — so the ACLU can follow up with them.

For Julio, the encounter has left him feeling less secure in his daily life.

“You go to the store without thinking twice,” he said in Spanish. “You think, ‘I haven’t done anything wrong. I’m just going to pick something up.’ And then, after getting your groceries, suddenly they’re right there behind you. It’s unjust, honestly.”

And the experience has also made him think about his family and the possibility of being separated from his children.

“Leaving your children, not knowing whether you’ll make it back to them or not,” he said in Spanish. “All of this is very difficult.”

. . .

About the data: The data analyzed for this story was collected by NorCal Resist, an immigrant-rights organization that documents immigration enforcement activity reported by affected individuals and their families. It is not a comprehensive record of ICE arrests or operations in Northern California. Many enforcement actions may go unnoticed or unreported, meaning the dataset represents only a portion of the activity taking place in the region.

ICE is the only agency with comprehensive records of its own enforcement operations. CapRadio requested this information from the agency and DHS but did not receive the requested data. As a result, the analysis reflects the incidents documented and verified by NorCal Resist and should not be interpreted as a representative sample of all immigration arrests or enforcement activity.

Garcia also said many of the reported encounters have happened during the morning commute between 5:30 a.m. and 9 a.m. and that most in the reports have been men of color.

“With the exception of two or three women out of these 73, they’ve all been men. Brown men,” she said in an earlier interview.

Garcia said another pattern is that many of the people being detained have had little or no prior contact with the immigration system have no criminal record.

“They don’t even have A-numbers assigned when we talk to their families,” she said, referring to Alien Registration Numbers, unique identifiers used in immigration records.

The organization has also been documenting vehicles left behind after reported encounters with immigration agents. In one case near Marysville, Garcia said an employer contacted the group after four workers failed to show up.

“Our observers through Migra Watch found that vehicle on the side of the highway,” Garcia recounted. “We saw coffee cups and lunches throughout the car so we knew it was at least four people.”

Garcia said the employer didn’t know their full names so they weren’t able to track them all down to get them help.

“How many of these kinds of detainments are going unaccounted for and people being eaten up by the system?” she added.

The Department of Homeland Security rejected allegations that immigration agents are targeting people based on race or ethnicity.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE” a department spokesperson said in a statement. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S. — NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity.”

The spokesperson said ICE officers use reasonable suspicion to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests, consistent with the Fourth Amendment. However, they did not elaborate on what constitutes “reasonable suspicion” when asked.

DHS also declined to discuss specific enforcement operations citing security and officer safety concerns.

What counts as racial profiling?

UC Davis law professor and immigration law expert Kevin Johnson said immigration officers generally need reasonable suspicion that someone is in the country unlawfully before making an investigative stop.

“And the Supreme Court has said that the officers are required to consider the totality of the circumstances, which includes attire, location of the stop, Mexican appearance and a variety of other factors,” he said. “But the court left it pretty open to the officers to consider what they want to consider in an immigration stop.”

Johnson is referring to a1975 Supreme Court ruling that found apparent Mexican ancestry alone cannot justify an immigration stop, but that it could be considered alongside other factors.

The legal debate has resurfaced in Southern California where the ACLU and other groups sued over immigration raids and alleged that federal agents were stopping people based on their perceived Latino identity and other characteristics.

Last month, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction barring immigration agents from conducting detentive stops based on racial stereotyping in seven Southern California counties.

But the ruling was not a final decision and the Trump administration has appealed. The injunction applies to Southern California, not the Sacramento region.

Johnson said a separate lawsuit in Northern California could potentially lead to similar restrictions if investigators document evidence that agents are relying on racial appearance, language or work attire to make stops.

Investigators would need to establish common patterns to prove federal immigration officers are racial profiling individuals in the region.

“You’d look at who is being apprehended and whether they were almost exclusively Latino,” he said. “You’d want to look at data of who’s being stopped, indicators like Spanish surname… You’d want to look at as much data as you can about the kinds of stops, where the stops are and what the officers when confronted say are the basis for the stop.”

“It’s hard to get that kind of information in advance of a lawsuit, but you certainly can collect data and talk to people who’ve been apprehended by ICE either on the streets or in workplaces or in arrests, including immigration check-ins.”

Johnson added that while he believes ICE officers are engaging in similar practices in the greater Sacramento area as in Southern California, the outcome of any potential case would depend on the facts gathered.

Still gathering evidence

Emilia Garcia said the ACLU is still in the fact-gathering stage and has not announced a lawsuit over the recent enforcement activity in Northern California.

Investigators are speaking with individuals who have been stopped and their families to learn whether the encounters point to a broader pattern.

“Myself and my co-workers interview them to understand ‘What did ICE say when they stopped you?” she said. “‘Did they have any reason to stop you? Did they know who you were before they stopped you or did they just sort of randomly stop you on the street, or in your work truck as you were going to a job?’”

The ACLU investigator said NorCal Resist’s rapid-response network is helping them connect with individuals who have been arrested or detained — and their families — so the ACLU can follow up with them.

For Julio, the encounter has left him feeling less secure in his daily life.

“You go to the store without thinking twice,” he said in Spanish. “You think, ‘I haven’t done anything wrong. I’m just going to pick something up.’ And then, after getting your groceries, suddenly they’re right there behind you. It’s unjust, honestly.”

And the experience has also made him think about his family and the possibility of being separated from his children.

“Leaving your children, not knowing whether you’ll make it back to them or not,” he said in Spanish. “All of this is very difficult.”

. . .

About the data: The data analyzed for this story was collected by NorCal Resist, an immigrant-rights organization that documents immigration enforcement activity reported by affected individuals and their families. It is not a comprehensive record of ICE arrests or operations in Northern California. Many enforcement actions may go unnoticed or unreported, meaning the dataset represents only a portion of the activity taking place in the region.

ICE is the only agency with comprehensive records of its own enforcement operations. CapRadio requested this information from the agency and DHS but did not receive the requested data. As a result, the analysis reflects the incidents documented and verified by NorCal Resist and should not be interpreted as a representative sample of all immigration arrests or enforcement activity.

title: Trump defends Stephen Miller after Hakeem Jeffries calls him a 'stone-cold racist' - TheGrio
description:
President Donald Trump is standing by his newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller after House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the controversial adviser a “stone-cold racist” and accused him of architecting the administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown.
The president’s comments came after Jeffries sharply criticized Miller in an interview with The New York Times published Saturday.
Asked whether he could envision sitting down with the White House chief of staff, Jeffries rejected the possibility.
The White House has pushed back against Jeffries’ characterization of Miller.
For Jeffries, drawing a distinction between engaging with the president and working with Miller appears central to that challenge.
text:
President Donald Trump is standing by his newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller after House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the controversial adviser a “stone-cold racist” and accused him of architecting the administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

During a Saturday, Nov. 21, appearance on Fox News’ “Saturday in America,” Trump defended Miller’s role in shaping his administration’s border policies, pushing back on Jeffries’ criticism while suggesting he remained open to working with Democrats when they take control of Congress next year.

“The one thing with Stephen, he was very strong on the border,” Trump told Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany. “So he called him a racist. But we had to be strong.”

Trump went on to repeat claims about the number of people who entered the United States during the Biden administration, alleging that 25 million people, including “killers, murderers,” drug dealers and rapists, had been allowed into the country. He used those claims to defend his administration’s approach to border enforcement, which Miller helped develop.

The president’s comments came after Jeffries sharply criticized Miller in an interview with The New York Times published Saturday. Asked whether he could envision sitting down with the White House chief of staff, Jeffries rejected the possibility.

“No. I made clear that Stephen Miller’s a stone-cold racist. Why would I deal with him at this point in time?” Jeffries told the newspaper.

The Brooklyn Democrat went on to describe Miller as “the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine,” arguing that the administration’s immigration policies have been marked by “cruelty,” “chaos” and “death.”

Miller, who replaced Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff on Nov. 9, has been one of the central figures behind Trump’s immigration agenda. His elevation to the administration’s top staff position signaled the president’s continued commitment to the hardline enforcement strategy that has drawn criticism from immigrant advocates and Democratic lawmakers.

The White House has pushed back against Jeffries’ characterization of Miller. Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told the New York Post that Miller has a record of working across party lines on issues including public safety reform, drug pricing transparency and nuclear energy.

But Trump’s defense of Miller was accompanied by a notably more conciliatory message toward Jeffries, who is positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.

“I think Hakeem will see that, and I look forward to working with Hakeem,” Trump said, referring to Miller’s character. “I give him a lot of congratulations.”

Trump acknowledged the historic significance of Jeffries potentially becoming the first Black person to hold the speakership, calling his selection by House Democrats “pretty spectacular” and saying it was “a big deal.”

Jeffries was nominated by House Democrats to lead their caucus as speaker following the party’s victories in the November midterm elections. Democrats are preparing to assume control of the House and Senate, setting up a new political dynamic for the remainder of Trump’s term.

Although Jeffries has made clear that he does not intend to work directly with Miller, his comments do not necessarily rule out negotiations with the broader Trump administration. In his interview with The New York Times, Jeffries pointed to other administration officials, including Vice President JD Vance, as potential channels for communication.

Trump, meanwhile, suggested he was interested in finding common ground with Democrats on legislation, including health care and immigration. He also reiterated his support for temporarily capping credit card interest rates at 10%, an issue he has previously raised despite criticism from some conservatives.

“I don’t want to veto every time,” Trump told McEnany, referring to the prospect of Democratic legislation reaching his desk. “I’m sure that they’ll send something up and we can negotiate.”

The president also praised Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, signaling that he sees opportunities to work with Democratic leadership in both chambers.

Still, the exchange highlights a potential tension heading into the next Congress: Democrats will have to navigate negotiations with an administration whose immigration agenda they have strongly opposed, while Trump will have to contend with a Democratic-controlled legislature.

For Jeffries, drawing a distinction between engaging with the president and working with Miller appears central to that challenge. For Trump, defending one of his most influential advisers while expressing an interest in bipartisan cooperation reflects the competing priorities that could shape the next two years in Washington.
