text:
Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

WATCH: Lawmakers press Mullin on flight disruptions and ICE tactics

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws."

During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

WATCH: ICE touts record number of deportations in agency's history

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition.

"The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. "We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform."

Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem.

"Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos," she said.

title: Trump's immigration crackdown drives international students away from US universities
description:
That hesitation appears to be increasingly common among international students, and the number who enroll at American schools has plummeted in the last two years.
During the 2023 to 2024 school year, more than 1.1 million international students came to the United States, a record high, according to the International Education Institute.
International students typically pay a higher tuition than domestic students.
There are also, of course, less tangible ways foreign students affect US colleges, including in social life.
DHS denies its actions have significantly driven away foreign students and adversely affected schools.
text:
Until 2025, students from Brazil, Nigeria, Thailand, Turkey, Turkmenistan and Zambia eagerly accepted a full scholarship to attend Indiana University in Bloomington, a town in the midwestern United States where fans are passionate about the Hoosiers – the school’s basketball and football teams.

The town also hosts the Little 500, a famous bicycle race that can attract more than 25,000 people. And most importantly for prospective students, the school has well-regarded academic programs.

“There was a general sense that this was the beginning of a great new phase in people’s lives,” said Christoph Irmscher, who for 13 years directed the Wells Scholars Program, which covers the full costs of attendance, including living expenses.

But things changed in January 2025, when Donald Trump started his second term and launched a shocking immigration crackdown.

That year, Irmscher offered the award to a Black man from South Africa and a woman from Central America. Both declined.

“People are cautious now, and it’s more like weighing the benefits versus the disadvantages” and whether to take a risk, said Irmscher, who grew up in Germany and came to the United States in 1993 on a scholarship through the Fulbright Program, a federal initiative.

That hesitation appears to be increasingly common among international students, and the number who enroll at American schools has plummeted in the last two years.

Their absence on campuses takes money away from colleges, causes a brain drain and robs American students of the chance to meet their counterparts from around the world. It also ripples out into the wider economy – especially in the many small college towns dotted across the US.

In fall 2026, there was a 15% decrease in foreign students studying for the first time at a US college or university as compared to last year, according to the Institute of International Education. That follows an 18% dip in fall 2025.

“To think that the system could go on functioning politically, socially, economically without those students is to misunderstand what US higher education has always been, for as long as it’s been the best in the world,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors.

To study in the United States, a foreign student must get accepted by a college or university and get the federal government to approve a visa, like an F-1 for academic programs or an M-1 for vocational or non-academic programs.

During the 2023 to 2024 school year, more than 1.1 million international students came to the United States, a record high, according to the International Education Institute.

But interest in coming to the United States has waned, college leaders say, since Trump retook office in January 2025 and deployed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents across the country to conduct raids and arrest and deport alleged undocumented immigrants.

Images of masked officers roaming US cities spread across the globe and unsettled people in America and abroad.

Indiana University, Bloomington saw its international student enrollment decrease 15%, from 4,428 in fall 2025 to 3,768 this year, according to university data.

In addition to the federal actions, the Republican-led state also passed legislation this year requiring schools to conduct background checks on students from China, Iran, North Korea and Russia before allowing them to attend. Irmscher, who stepped down from the Wells position last summer, described the requirement as “totally unnecessary” because the federal government already conducts such checks on visa applicants.

“In the culture of social media and TikTok, these clips of ICE agents brutalizing people on the street have an enormous ripple effect,” Irmscher, an English professor, said. “If you look different, if you feel that you are different, I’m sure that is something that affects your decision.”

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment dropped 46%, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall.

That was largely due to potential students having trouble obtaining visas, according to provost Nigamanth Sridhar.

In May 2025, the Trump administration ordered US embassies to stop scheduling visa interviews for foreign students as it prepared to implement social media screening for applicants.

“We have people who want to go to Harvard and other schools; they can’t get in because we have foreign students there,” Trump said at the time.

In January 2026, the state department announced it had revoked 8,000 student visas. In October, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also proposed a rule that would require schools to pay a $70,000 fee for each international student who participates in a training program that allows students to take jobs related to their major during or after their time in school.

That enrollment drop cost Cleveland State between $2m and $4m, Sridhar estimated. International students typically pay a higher tuition than domestic students.

There are also, of course, less tangible ways foreign students affect US colleges, including in social life.

Sridhar, a former computer science professor who came to the United States from India in 1999 to attend graduate school at Ohio State University, said that international students bring “a diverse group of viewpoints to campus in various kinds of conversations, whether they are in the classroom or outside the classroom”, which creates a “richness and intellectual diversity”.

After a 2025 earthquake in Myanmar killed thousands and left millions needing humanitarian assistance, a student from the country studying at Indiana University organized a fundraiser with Burmese food where she spoke about the country.

“It was not just a culturally enriching event. It was also an exercise in putting yourself into the shoes of somebody else in ways that are normally not accessible to students in landlocked America,” Irmscher said.

When students come here to study, they also sometimes immigrate, like Irmscher and Sridhar, and positively impact American society. The Trump administration tried to obstruct that path by introducing a rule in July 2026 that prohibited student visa recipients from staying in the country for more than four years without federal government approval. It often takes longer than that to complete a degree.

Dubal, who is also a law professor at the University of California, Irvine, is the daughter of Indian immigrants who came to the United States in the 1960s to study and pursue careers. Her father, a biochemist, had a blood testing laboratory in Houston; her mom, a physician, had pain clinics in Lexington, Kentucky.

“She spent the entirety of her career helping people who were often poor from underserved communities, from rural communities, who had occupational injuries as a result of mining, as a result of factory work, and both of them spent their lives contributing immensely to their communities,” Dubal said.

DHS denies its actions have significantly driven away foreign students and adversely affected schools.

“This ‘reporting’ is completely misleading and not backed up by any real evidence,” a spokesperson stated in an email to the Guardian. “The performative outrage is incredible. Where was the outrage when foreign nationals were abusing the system, violating the terms of their student visas, and making a mockery of our immigration laws? If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege.”

Asked for evidence of “rampant fraud”, the agency did not respond.

In October, the Trump administration announced it would investigate nine universities to determine if they committed fraud through a student visa program.

“Something weird is going on at these universities,” vice-president JD Vance said. “They are using these visas way too much. They are using them to undercut the wages of American grad students.”

The administration has not been entirely successful in trying to implement new restrictions on international students hoping to study in the country. This week, a federal judge blocked the rule that limited students’ stays in the United States to four years.

“Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity—providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States—that Congress sought to permit and encourage,” the judge stated.

Dubal is optimistic – particularly in the wake of the Democrats’ wins in the midterm elections – that higher education can overcome the Trump administration’s treatment of foreign students. Rather than focus on keeping them out, lawmakers should instead concentrate on reducing the cost of higher education, she said.

“If the Trump administration cares about whether or not native-born Americans are getting access to higher education, the answer to that is not to push out immigrants,” Dubal said. “It is to make it more accessible. And how do you make it more accessible? You lower the prices.”

title: Eva Yi Xie: DHS Gives Arrest Reason as Judge Sets Nov. 25 Deadline
description:
As reported earlier, her lawyers say she is an asylum applicant with a case pending in immigration court until early 2028.
DHS described a targeted enforcement operation at Reagan National on Nov. 19 to arrest Xie.
What Judge Trenga ordered The order, entered Nov. 20 in Xie v. Warden, Detention Center, No.
Sources CourtListener: Xie v. Warden, Detention Center, No.
25-7044 (Sept. 10, 2026) SCOTUSblog: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court (Nov. 17, 2026)
text:
DHS now says the Princeton doctoral student overstayed a 2016 admission, while a federal judge in Virginia has barred her transfer and tied the case to the Fourth Circuit’s bond-hearing ruling.

The Department of Homeland Security has given its first account of why it arrested Eva Yi Xie, the Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student detained at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Nov. 19. In a statement to Newsweek late Friday, DHS said Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, with a required departure date of Sept. 15, 2016, and that a pending application does not give her legal status. The department said she will remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings.

Hours earlier, U.S. District Judge Anthony J. Trenga of the Eastern District of Virginia barred ICE from moving Xie out of the district and ordered the government to answer her habeas petition by 5 p.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 25. The order’s structure matters more than its deadline: it asks the government to say whether her case is materially different from earlier rulings that required bond hearings for people in ICE custody. As reported earlier, her lawyers say she is an asylum applicant with a case pending in immigration court until early 2028.

What DHS says about her status

According to the DHS statement as reported by Newsweek:

A planned arrest. DHS described a targeted enforcement operation at Reagan National on Nov. 19 to arrest Xie.

An overstay. DHS said she was admitted temporarily in March 2016 and was required to leave by Sept. 15, 2016.

No student status. DHS said she never held valid authorization to study in the United States and that a pending application does not confer legal status.

Air travel. The statement tied the arrest to the administration’s position that people without lawful status should not fly within the country, and noted that DHS offers detainees a free flight and $3,000 to leave voluntarily.

Her lawyer, Kerry Doyle, has given a different emphasis. She told The Daily Princetonian that Xie came to the United States lawfully as a minor, that her family applied for asylum within a year of arrival, and that ICE had not told Xie why she was arrested. Doyle has also said, according to The Washington Post as summarized by other outlets, that Xie holds a valid work permit and has no criminal record. The two accounts overlap more than they conflict: both describe a lawful 2016 entry followed by an expired stay and a pending asylum claim. The dispute is over whether that history justified a warrantless arrest and detention without a bond hearing.

What Judge Trenga ordered

The order, entered Nov. 20 in Xie v. Warden, Detention Center, No. 1:26-cv-03839, does three things, according to the court docket:

No transfer. The government and anyone acting with it are enjoined from removing Xie from the Eastern District of Virginia until the court says otherwise.

A choice by Nov. 25. By 5 p.m. that day, the government must file either a notice that her case raises no materially different factual or legal issues from Hernandez v. Crawford, an October 2025 ruling of the same court, and the Fourth Circuit’s Lopez Garcia v. Guadian, or an opposition explaining the differences.

Two tracks. If the government files the notice, the filings from Hernandez will be incorporated and the court will rule without further briefing. If it opposes, it must attach records of Xie’s immigration history, detention and removal proceedings, and her reply is due by 5 p.m. on Nov. 30.

Named respondents include Robert Guadian, director of ICE’s Washington Field Office, and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. A Justice Department lawyer entered an appearance for the government the same day.

What the Hernandez and Lopez Garcia rulings require

In Hernandez v. Crawford, Judge Trenga ordered on Oct. 16, 2025, that the petitioner receive a bond hearing before an immigration judge under 8 U.S.C. 1226(a) within seven days. He also barred the government from using the regulatory automatic stay that can keep a person detained after an immigration judge grants bond. The government appealed.

On Sept. 10, 2026, a divided Fourth Circuit panel ruled on the same question in Lopez Garcia v. Guadian. Judge Berner, joined by Senior Judge Keenan, held that long-time residents arrested inside the country must receive a bond hearing and be eligible for release. Judge Rushing dissented. The court rejected the government’s July 2025 position that people who entered without inspection are subject to no-bond detention under 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(A).

Xie’s facts differ in a way that may help her. The no-bond policy targets people who were never admitted, and DHS’s own statement says she was admitted in 2016. Noncitizens who were admitted and then overstayed have generally been held under Section 1226(a), which allows bond. If the government accepts that framework, the likely result is a bond hearing before an immigration judge, not automatic release. At that hearing, Fourth Circuit precedent puts the burden on the detained person to show she is neither a danger nor a flight risk. The government could still argue in an opposition that her case differs. Her separate argument that the warrantless arrest itself was unlawful remains before the court.

The national backdrop

Nine federal circuits, including the Fourth, have rejected the government’s no-bond reading, while the Fifth and Eighth Circuits have adopted it. On Oct. 1 the Supreme Court agreed to hear the government’s appeal in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, a Second Circuit case, with a decision expected by the end of the term. Airport arrests of people with pending asylum cases have become a recurring pattern, as earlier coverage of a Phoenix case showed, and overstay-based detentions have raised similar questions.

Quick answers

Why did ICE arrest Eva Yi Xie? DHS says she overstayed a temporary admission that ended in September 2016 and never held student status. Her lawyer says she has a pending asylum case, a work permit and no criminal record.

Can ICE move her to another state? Not for now. Judge Trenga’s order bars her removal from the Eastern District of Virginia pending further order.

When will the judge decide? The government’s response is due Nov. 25. If it does not contest the Hernandez framework, the court can rule without more briefing. If it opposes, briefing closes Nov. 30.

Will she be released? Not necessarily. The rulings the judge cited led to bond hearings, where release depends on an immigration judge’s assessment of flight risk and danger.

Does her pending asylum case protect her? It generally prevents removal while the case is pending, but it does not bar detention.

New Jersey: A doctoral researcher at Princeton University has been detained by US immigration authorities after attending a major neuroscience conference in Washington, DC, raising concerns across the university community and prompting an emergency legal challenge.

Eva Yi Xie, a 24-year-old third-year neuroscience PhD student, was taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on November 19, 2026, at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Virginia. She was reportedly preparing to board a domestic flight after attending the Society for Neuroscience’s annual conference.

Xie had traveled to Washington to present her research on neural circuits and decision-making. Her detention quickly prompted concern among her academic colleagues, who sought assistance from university officials and elected representatives.

Princeton University arranged legal representation for the student and confirmed that it was maintaining contact with her family, attorneys and research colleagues. The university has also expressed hope that she will be able to return to her studies.

The case has attracted national attention because of questions surrounding her immigration history, pending asylum proceedings and the circumstances of her arrest.

Xie moved to the United States from China with her family in 2016. She attended the Bronx High School of Science in New York before enrolling at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

She graduated from MIT in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics, along with a concentration in economics. She subsequently joined Princeton’s neuroscience doctoral program and began conducting research in Professor Carlos Brody’s laboratory.

Her research focuses on how neural circuits process information and influence decision-making. She was attending the Washington conference to present academic work when immigration officers detained her.

According to her attorney, Kerry Doyle, Xie’s family applied for asylum within a year of arriving in the United States. Her application was referred to immigration court, where her next hearing is scheduled for January 2028.

Doyle told The Daily Princetonian that Xie also holds a valid employment authorization document and has no criminal history. Her legal team has challenged the circumstances of her detention, arguing that immigration authorities took her into custody without a warrant.

The Department of Homeland Security offered a different account of her immigration history. It said Xie entered the United States temporarily on March 16, 2016, with a required departure date of September 15, 2016, and alleged that she overstayed her authorized period.

DHS also argued that a pending immigration application does not automatically provide lawful immigration status. The agency’s position has become a central issue in the dispute between federal authorities and Xie’s legal representatives.

Following her detention, Xie was initially held at an ICE facility in Chantilly, Virginia. Her lawyers subsequently filed an emergency habeas corpus petition in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, asking a federal judge to review the legality of her custody.

On November 20, a federal judge ordered immigration authorities not to transfer Xie outside the Eastern District of Virginia while the legal proceedings continue. The government was directed to respond to the petition by 5 p.m. on November 25.

The court order does not constitute a release decision or a final ruling on the legality of her detention. Her attorneys are continuing to pursue legal options, including the possibility of a bond hearing.

Princeton University Graduate School Dean Rodney Priestley described the detention as distressing for members of the academic community. He said the institution had arranged legal support and would continue assisting Xie’s family and colleagues.

Professor Carlos Brody, her academic adviser, also expressed concern about the situation and highlighted her contributions to neuroscience research. Fellow graduate students have called for her release and urged lawmakers to seek answers from federal immigration authorities.

New Jersey Senator Andy Kim’s office confirmed that it was in contact with Xie and working on the case. Senator Cory Booker also said his office had contacted ICE and requested an explanation for the detention.

The Society for Neuroscience, which organized the conference Xie attended, said it was monitoring the situation and remained in contact with Princeton University. The organization also offered support to the researcher, her family and colleagues.

The case has raised wider questions about immigration enforcement involving international researchers and students traveling within the United States. Universities and academic organizations are increasingly concerned about how immigration-related complications could affect international participation in research conferences and educational programs.

Princeton University continues to support Xie through its legal and administrative channels as her case moves through federal court proceedings.

text:
The date 1 September, or 9/01 Day, is a festive day for Memphians. The date mirrors the city’s 901 area code, and gives residents a reason to come together to celebrate the city and the people who love it. When 9/01 Day falls on a weekday, as it did this year, the celebration starts the weekend prior, extending the festivities. Groups across the city hosted celebrations featuring food vendors, DJs, musicians and members of the Memphis Grizzlies, the local NBA team, while dozens of local businesses offered $9.01-themed specials.

But for the families of 121 people, this past 1 September will be remembered for a different reason – just days prior, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained their friends and relatives, conducting one of the largest single-day raids in the country this year, and the largest known one in Memphis.

On Beale Street during the 9/01 Day celebration, a 9 year old child, Valentina*, stood solemnly, holding a sign that read: “ICE took my mom!” (*The Guardian is using a pseudonym to protect the child and her family’s identity.)

On 30 August, Valentina’s mother and sister had both been at work at El Corralón, a bar on the edge of Memphis’ Berclair neighborhood, which is primarily Hispanic. Valentina went to sleep anticipating celebrating her birthday with family and friends the next morning. Instead, she awoke to the news that her family members were among the 121 people who were detained by ICE.

According to reports, more than one dozen agents entered the building that night, and quickly spread across the bar. They turned off the music and ordered those inside to gather on the dancefloor. Some people screamed; others attempted to hide. Some prayed.

El Corralón had been under investigation by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI), which had a warrant signed on Wednesday of the week leading up to the raid, to search the premises for illegal gambling machines and potential drug activity. Saturday, when the nightclub was full of patrons, TBI executed the warrant. One by one, agents asked people if they were in the country legally. People were zip-tied, taken outside and led onto buses that waited to take them to detention centers.

A statement released by the Department of Homeland Security shortly after the raid highlighted five of those arrested, whose crimes, the department alleges, range from cocaine possession to assault, prostitution and child endangerment. Maria Oceja, a co-founder of Vecindarios 901, a volunteer group that monitors the actions of the Memphis Safe taskforce, said the raid predominantly targeted innocent people. “This is just another example of that rising level of authoritarianism and white supremacist tactics that we’re seeing,” Oceja said.

El Corralón, which has been closed since the raid, had a “juke joint environment”, she said. Spanish language music blared and working class people could have a drink on a Saturday night. Many of the workers and patrons were parents. The morning after the raid, Hunter Demster, a co-founder of Vecindarios 901, said Valentina’s family tried to figure out next steps. “Her mom was a breadwinner and worked three different jobs trying to keep food on the table and the utilities paid,” Demster said. He’s friends with Valentina’s older sister, Camila, who is now responsible for her younger siblings. “Now her entire family is devastated. When I went over there the next day, I asked her, ‘What do you need?’ The sorrow and almost the vacancy in her eyes was jawdropping. The pain was palpable.

“These are our friends and our neighbors and for every one of those 121 people, there’s another family going through that exact same thing. They’re figuring out how they’re going to navigate life without a loved one. It is a gutwrenching, horrible, traumatic experience for a family member.”

For days after the raid, no one knew where the girls’ mother was. Eventually, volunteers learned she was being held in a detention center in Louisiana, Gisela Guerrero, lead organizer for Memphis Interfaith Coalition for Action and Hope (Micah), said. “A lot of immigrant children right now, regardless of their age, are very clear about the possibility of their parent being taken away any day. It’s scary. It’s overwhelming,” she told the Guardian.

An ICE spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian that the agency does “not pick and choose which laws to enforce or where to enforce them”. The spokesperson said that the detainments make “the Memphis community safer”. According to the agency, 69 of the 121 have been removed from the country. “The rest will remain in ICE custody pending their immigration proceedings, and they will receive due process,” the statement read.

On the night of the raid, portions of the street were blocked off by federal agents according to Dexter Britt, a volunteer and co-chair for the immigration and inclusivity team with the Micah who made it to El Corralón, shortly after 1am. He saw the Memphis police department (MPD), sheriffs, state troopers and other personnel, he said. Buses and vans idled, waiting to be filled with people who were detained.

Britt said that there were also community members observing and documenting what was happening. He saw family members, including children, who were there to catch a glimpse of their relatives, perhaps for the last time. “You start seeing people getting ushered out of the building,” Britt told the Guardian. “I remember hearing the chains shackling as they were loading people into the vans, into the buses. It was very harrowing to hear.”

The Memphis mayor, Paul Young, issued a statement saying that MPD was not involved in the planning or execution of the raid. Instead, he said, they assisted with crowd and traffic control after people began gathering in the area. According to witnesses, multiple agencies – TBI, Tennessee Highway Patrol, and ICE – seemingly worked in conjunction with each other.

On 15 September 2025, Donald Trump signed a presidential memorandum creating the multi-agency Memphis Safe taskforce. The initiative, which includes the national guard, highway patrol officers, and agents from more than federal agencies, began operating in the city on 29 September. Though the memorandum establishing the taskforce alleged that Memphis was “suffering from tremendous levels of violent crime that have overwhelmed its local government’s ability to respond effectively”, crime in the city was at a 25 year low prior to the taskforce’s arrival.

In the year since it began operating, members of the taskforce have killed four people, all Black men, including 20-year-old Tyrin Johnson who was fatally shot in the back. A woman was killed after being ejected from a vehicle when it crashed while being pursued by members of the Memphis Safe taskforce. Five young people were killed in a crash involving the MPD and a man died during a traffic stop by members of the taskforce. An analysis by the Institute for Public Service Reporting Memphis identified 75 vehicle pursuits over the taskforce’s first five weeks of operation.

According to the Tennessee Lookout, immigration arrests and detentions multiplied nearly four-fold in Tennessee during Trump’s first year back in office. Weeks after the Memphis Safe taskforce was created, more than 400 people were arrested. The taskforce has made nearly 23,000 arrests, 64% of which were for non-violent crimes. A growing number of businesses are calling for an end to the taskforce’s operations in the city, while others are mobilizing to document its actions. “It’s not just impacting immigrant communities who are Latino or Hispanic, but it’s also impacting Black Memphians because the city is majority Black,” Britt said. “There’s a lot of harm being done to the Memphis community because of the presence of these agents who are really just here to intimidate.”

The El Corralón raid happened the same weekend that people detained at a detention center in Macon, Tennessee, protested “deplorable conditions” and abusive tactics inside” the facility. Some of those detained at El Corralón were initially sent to the center in Macon.

In mid-October, the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, and federal and state leaders visited Memphis to discuss the taskforce. Unlike similar operations in Minneapolis or Chicago, which had intense surges that lasted a few months, there is no end date to the Memphis Safe taskforce’s occupation of the city. Though Blanche celebrated the taskforce’s record and presence, he said that it would be in the city “as long as it takes. We haven’t won yet. It’s not over”.

On 20 October, the Memphis City Council passed a resolution calling for the removal of the taskforce. The non-binding resolution said that the El Corralón raid raised “concerns about due process and the impact of federal immigration enforcement on local communities, including the disruption and separation of Memphis families”.

“Memphis is literally an occupied city with law enforcement agencies all doing immigration work, causing real harm to the city of Memphis,” Demster said of the taskforce. He said that people are afraid to leave their homes. “This is un-American. They’re violating people’s rights by not giving them due process. They’re criminalizing people when they have done nothing wrong. This is the beginning of fascism. This is the beginning of a dictatorship.”

Filling the gap

On 31 August, photos of Valentina holding her sign and mentioning her birthday were posted across social media. Demster and other volunteers purchased a birthday cake and presents and dropped them off for the child. “In the midst of such horror, at least it put a smile on that baby’s face,” he said. “She literally hugged the cake. ‘Devastating’ doesn’t measure up to what people are experiencing at this point … . It’s just another example of how they’re not out for the worst of the worst. They are out for people with brown skin.”

Vecindarios 901, Micah, Indivisible Memphis, Latino Memphis, TIIRC, World Relief and organizations collaborated to see how they could support the families. In the week following the raid, many of the organizations met with families of detainees to help connect them with legal aid and other resources.

“We had a seven-year-old who was saying, ‘I don’t think I’m going to see my mom anymore,’” Guerrero said. “We had a 14-year-old who was trying to figure out what he needed to do to be responsible for his younger siblings. We had a senior in college who’s trying to figure out how he is going to pay tuition. Because his parents, hardworking people, are now detained.”

Guerrero said that about 100 people from various families stopped by the meeting. They were grandparents, aunts, neighbors, coworkers and children themselves who are now responsible for younger children who were left behind.

“There are children who lost both of their parents in that raid,” Amber Hampton, of Indivisible Memphis, a chapter of the nationwide civil rights organization, said. “You’re talking about children who are now displaced, who have to possibly move, change schools because their parents are no longer there and they have to go with a different caregiver.”

At a city council meeting shortly after the raids, family members told city council people about the impact of the taskforce. More than 40 children, some of whom testified, were left without parents. Children also testified when the city council decided to vote to call for the taskforce’s removal.

“There’s a lot of confusion, especially with the younger kids,” Demster said. “Families are scattering to try to keep their heads above water, to pay these utility bills, to find food, to fill that void of the parent being targeted and detained and deported. One of the hardest things about this work is talking to these children and seeing the pain and seeing the devastation of these families. For every one person that were taken in that raid, there’s usually two to four family members here in Memphis that were devastated.”

text:
A Georgetown University research and advocacy institute signed a Nov. 5 letter to senior congressional leadership, asking them to expand oversight over redirected peacemaking funds.

In the letter, the Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace and Security (GIWPS), which researches women’s role in peacebuilding, called on members of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives appropriations committees to protect conflict prevention grants that the Trump administration reappropriated. GIWPS was one of 28 groups to sign the demands after President Donald Trump instead directed the funds to energy security projects.

Kim Hart, the GIWPS policy and programs director, said the funds are crucial to establishing the United States’ international leadership.

“Not only do we think this is a problem morally and ethically, but it’s also a problem in terms of America’s foreign policy interests,” Hart told The Hoya. “And cutting these funds undercuts critical programming that advances America’s interests overseas.”

The letter drew particular attention to three reprogrammed initiatives — $2.85 million to prevent atrocities, $8 million for the peacebuilding organization Young African Leaders Initiative and $18.75 million for the Middle East Partnership for Peace Act, an organization that promotes dialogue between Israelis and Palestinians. Reprogramming, while not typically illegal, redirects funds from Congress’ dedicated purpose.

Hart said the Trump administration has overhauled the federal funding landscape.

“This is part of a larger trend that we’ve seen under the Trump administration of systematically eliminating key offices, capacities and funding that advances peace and security around the world, so this is not an isolated incident,” Hart told The Hoya. “It’s part of a much bigger trend where we’ve seen key portfolios eliminated or used for other purposes, and I find that to be deeply problematic as a taxpayer and as an expert on peace and security.”

In 2025, the Trump administration shut down the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) — one of the leading U.S. international aid agencies. In fiscal year 2025, federal agencies dispersed $38 billion less than the year before.

Nisha Singh (GRD ’21) — senior global policy and advocacy manager for Women for Women International, a nonprofit organization that also signed the letter — said the Trump administration’s grant redirection will weaken support for peacebuilding programs.

“It is coupled with this broader strategy around weakening the infrastructure, creating uncertainty around the future of a lot of these programs,” Singh told The Hoya.

“If people think they can’t rely on it, then there’s going to be fewer and fewer advocates for it in the future,” Singh added.

Hart said she hopes Congress will intervene in future reprogramming issues.

“I’m hopeful that the new Congress will take more robust action to prevent that from happening and to ensure that some of these really critical funds stay online in the future and that there’s guardrails to protect against this type of action,” Hart said.

The funds will be redirected to issues that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed would “support exigent energy security needs for partners facing coercive supply cutoffs, market disruptions and inflated costs.”

Singh said it is important to equally question the value of the funds’ new destination.

“We’re really talking about moving money from an account that is investing in community-driven peace in Israel and Palestine to fossil fuel companies, or moving money from middle- to low-income countries to a fund led by corporations in the U.S,” Singh said.

“We call it America first. Are we really talking American corporations first?” Singh added.

Amelia Lightfoot (CAS ’27), who studies government and justice and peace studies, said university-affiliated institutions should continue supporting causes aligned with Georgetown’s values.

“I do think that standing by the Jesuit values that matter so much to the school are at the core of what makes it a good institution,” Lightfoot told The Hoya. “It would be a shame if, for example, the Women’s Institute didn’t sign onto this.”

Hart said she is grateful to be a part of a university and professional community that is willing to stand behind this letter.

“I think we should all feel really, really proud that Georgetown has continued to stand up for what it knows to be right, which includes supporting women; it includes supporting inclusion and diversity,” Hart said. “It’s not easy to stand up to political pressure, and I think it’s really nice to work and I assume to go to school somewhere that is willing to take a stand for what it knows to be right.”

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

After paying $495.6 million for a prison whose owner had discussed selling it to Minnesota for $75 million, the Trump administration now asks taxpayers to trust it with another $50 billion.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is requesting an additional $50.1 billion following a nationwide aviation ground stop. The package includes $10.1 billion for air-traffic modernization, with the remainder for airport infrastructure, terminals, control centers and towers. America needs reliable air travel. But a staggering price tag is not proof of competence.

Urgency is not a plan.

Congress must determine which purchases address immediate failures, which serve longer-term needs and which projects are ready. An emergency cannot become a blank check.

The administration’s immigration spending provides ample reason for caution. The Government Accountability Office found that ICE invested billions in six detention-expansion initiatives without necessary analysis or planning. ICE purchased 11 warehouses for approximately $1.07 billion, then decided to sell seven. The agency reported more than $20 million in unrecoverable costs associated with those properties.

Then came Minnesota. DHS paid CoreCivic $495.6 million for its vacant Prairie Correctional Facility. The company had previously discussed selling it to Minnesota for $75 million. CoreCivic and DHS dispute the figures’ comparability; DHS cites independent appraisals and federal requirements. Those explanations deserve examination, not automatic acceptance. Senator Maggie Hassan has opened an investigation.

A price more than six times the earlier figure demands documents, not reassurances.

The aircraft purchases raise similar questions. The New York Times reported that DHS agreed to pay $108 million for a converted Boeing 737 featuring bedrooms, marble showers and a bar. The seller’s chairman had contributed to a political action committee supporting then-Secretary Kristi Noem. DHS also agreed to pay $106 million for two Gulfstream jets the seller reportedly acquired for approximately $83 million.

Bloomberg reported Oct. 20 that seven Boeing 737s acquired for deportations had barely flown. Its Oct. 29 follow-up reported the fleet’s first removal flights after months of limited use. The price spreads, political connections and underuse demand scrutiny. They do not, by themselves, establish corruption.

Meanwhile, Trump has weakened spending oversight. He fired 17 inspectors general in the opening days of his second term. According to Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, 29 of 72 federal inspector general positions were vacant at the end of 2025. Not all vacancies resulted from firings, and acting leaders can continue oversight. Nevertheless, prolonged leadership gaps raise accountability concerns.

Now Trump has nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director of the Office of Management and Budget, to lead GAO for a 15-year term. Former Interior Inspector General Mark Greenblatt warned that Ueland could evaluate decisions he helped make.

The Senate must examine that potential conflict before confirmation. GAO must serve Congress and taxpayers, not shield the administration whose spending it examines.

None of this means aviation modernization should be rejected. Biden’s bipartisan infrastructure law provided $25 billion for aviation over five years, including $5 billion for air traffic facilities. Congress subsequently provided $12.5 billion through the July 2025 reconciliation law.

In a Nov. 14 statement, Representatives Rick Larsen and André Carson said $4.3 billion of that $12.5 billion had been obligated and approximately $1 billion spent.

Unspent money alone proves nothing. Complex projects take time. DOT reports operational upgrades, including telecommunications replacements and new tower technology, and says Congress restricts transfers among funding categories. Those claims deserve independent verification, alongside an accounting of what remains unfinished.

Congress must determine what previous appropriations purchased, which improvements are operational and why additional funding is needed.

Equipment alone cannot operate an aviation system. In March 2025, the National Weather Service temporarily suspended routine weather balloon observations in Omaha and Rapid City, explicitly citing inadequate staffing. That does not explain the aviation ground stop. It illustrates a broader point: technology cannot substitute for operational capacity.

Managing a national aviation network requires technical expertise, competent management and disciplined execution. Congress must evaluate the actual plan, not simply accept promises.

Gross federal debt exceeds $40 trillion. Necessary investment makes credible estimates, measurable milestones and independent oversight more essential, not less.

With Democrats set to control both chambers when the new Congress convenes in January, they must insist on transparent contracts and measurable results. Taxpayers should not finance promises while independent scrutiny is weakened.

An administration asking taxpayers to trust it with another $50 billion must first account for the billions it has already spent.

text:
"Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision, and that's very disappointing," Bowen said, hours after the latest draft drew a fresh wave of criticism. "Ultimately, looking back, many parties who are people of good faith had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues, and despite many, many attempts, on reflection those red lines were not able to be met."

The European Union, Panama, and small island nations were among those that rejected the proposal. Explaining the EU's position, the Irish climate and environment minister, Darragh O'Brien, said that "it is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels."

While Big Oil-backed US President Donald Trump has ditched the Paris Agreement and declined to send a delegation to COP31, even though his country is the largest historical climate polluter, other major petroleum producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia lobbied against mentioning fossil fuels. Panama's climate minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told Politico that "the world is hostage to petroleum producers. That is the truth... And they will not stop."

In the lead-up to the conference, scientists warned that temporarily surpassing the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C threshold for temperature rise this century, relative to preindustrial levels, is now inevitable, and the world is barreling toward "an irrecoverable overshoot" of that target absent a rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions.

Jasper Inventor, head of the Greenpeace International delegation at COP31, said that "it's bitterly disappointing to leave without a clear outcome or a credible pathway to end fossil fuels. We stopped a bad deal that favors fossil fuels, but leaving without a deal is still a failure for communities on the climate frontlines. As always, it is the world's most vulnerable communities who bear the consequences of this failure. We've run out of time to avoid overshoot, but we can still keep 1.5°C alive."

Climate campaigners from around the world joined Inventor in expressing frustration that "COP31 has failed to deliver any meaningful outcomes on climate action," as Oxfam International climate change policy lead Nafkote Dabi put it after two weeks of talks. "Shame on rich polluting countries for once again turning their backs on communities fighting for survival in a climate crisis they did little to cause. Shame on the presidencies for prioritizing profits and ego over progress."

"And shame on all the countries that stubbornly blocked and distracted from discussions meant to deliver crucial funding to people watching their homes swallowed by floods, their crops wither in droughts, and their lives upended by deadly heat," said Dabi. "Instead of implementation, COP31 has delivered yet another victory for rich polluting countries and fossil fuel interests. The co-presidencies—who both remain heavily invested in fossil fuels and are profiting from climate destruction—attempted to broker a decision without a single mention of fossil fuels in favor of false solutions."

Nikki Reisch, a director at the Center for International Environmental Law, explained that "the proposed cover decision did not advance the provision of climate finance, said nothing about the root cause of the crisis, and made no mention of states' legal obligations to prevent and repair climate harm, as clarified by the International Court of Justice. On loss and damage, it fared no better as it offered little more than expressions of deep concern about mounting impacts. And a text that welcomed a scale-up of future fantasy fixes like carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies and proven-to-fail industry favorites like carbon capture and storage (CCS), without so much as a whisper about fossil fuels, would have been a massive giveaway to polluters."

Calling out the hosts, Global Climate and Health Alliance executive director Jeni Miller stressed that "the rightly rejected 'Antalya Pact' comes as climate change compounds this year's super El Niño, causing severe droughts in Fiji and Bolivia, extreme flooding in the western US, and wildfires in Southeast Asia, and putting millions of additional people at risk of hunger or famine."

Amiera Sawas, head of research and policy at the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, highlighted that "while Global North countries rejected the outcome on the basis that there was no language on transitioning away from fossil fuels, these same countries have not themselves presented serious or credible phaseout plans, nor do they intend to support others in their transitions. Many wealthy countries continue expanding fossil fuel extraction despite their international legal obligations, while developing countries carrying unpayable debt can't plan an exit at all."

"The EU and some of its most powerful member states have blocked progress or, worse, reneged on past commitments," Sawas continued. "Demanding the words 'fossil fuels' in the cover text while blocking mandated agenda items and pointing fingers at developing countries is acting in bad faith. We need real commitments to a fair and financed phaseout of fossil fuels that delivers on the Paris Agreement, not collapses it. That means a just transition, where those most responsible pay their fair share and workers, communities, and Indigenous peoples have a meaningful say in what it looks like."

Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa, declared that "this has been the worst ever COP, and its collapse needs to be a wake-up call for the world. Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook."

Romain Ioualalen, global policy lead at Oil Change International, similarly asserted that "this will go down as one of the worst COPs in history. COP hosts Australia and Türkiye have failed to steward the negotiations. This sad stalemate only benefits fossil fuel interests while people and communities will continue paying the highest price for the crisis they didn't create."

"Don't fall for the EU's attempt to portray themselves as heroes. They are the ones who are largely to blame for this result... But let's be clear: The outcome on the table was dangerous," he continued, welcoming the proposal's defeat. "Countries failed to rise to the moment, but we refuse to lower the bar. The countries and communities fighting for climate justice are not backing down, and the road to COP32 in Ethiopia must be about action."

Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, also emphasized how bad the final deal was: "After decades of broken pledges and hollow commitments, an agreement built on yet more empty promises would have been unforgivable and no substitute for the transformative action we urgently need. So the dramatic rejection of the presidency's final text by some, though underscoring the lack of consensus that's been reached, restores some level of faith in its recognition that a deal of this caliber is no deal at all."

"What matters now is not when governments reconvene, it's how they do so," he argued. "The world doesn't need more meetings with woolly commitments. We need global governments, including the UK, to come back to the negotiating table ready to deliver. That means cutting emissions fairly at home, transitioning our economies in a way that leaves no one behind, and providing the public climate finance so desperately needed to protect people, livelihoods, and our planet from unimaginable harm."

Savio Carvalho, head of campaigns and networks at 350.org, also looked ahead: "You'd think that in the middle of the worst fossil fuel crisis in history, after a year of devastating wildfires, floods, and collapsing glaciers, world leaders would finally rise to the moment. But they didn't. We averted a truly bad outcome because many countries stood up to the fossil fuel industry and rejected dangerous distractions. But we still left COP31 without a clear plan to exit coal, oil, and gas. There's no real money on the table to help countries survive the climate breakdown that is already at our doorstep."

"The world needs governments with the courage to stand with people and the planet, even when the fossil fuel industry pushes back," Carvalho added. "This isn't the end. We'll keep pushing until governments end the age of fossil fuels. Every meeting and every decision in the year ahead counts. The time for delay is over."

ICE's parent agency, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said late Saturday that "officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa."

"During the arrest, other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers—a federal crime and a felony," DHS claimed. "The individual who threw the hot coffee was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay. She was subsequently arrested as well. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."

Earlier Saturday, the Port of Seattle, which operates Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, said in a statement that "we are outraged about this morning's incident involving ICE and two passengers as travelers boarded AS 1306 to Los Angeles. Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the port's participation or knowledge."

"The port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to, protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached," the port said.

"However, the port remains committed to the safety of all of our travelers and staff and airline team," the airport operator added. "This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

The Alaska Airlines flight, "originally scheduled for 8:10 am, departed late at 11:03 am" local time, according to The Seattle Times.

Alaska Airlines said that "we are aware of an incident involving law enforcement that occurred in the jet bridge area during the boarding process for Alaska Flight 1306 from Seattle to Los Angeles. We understand that situations like this can be distressing. We were not previously aware of the law enforcement activity, and we are actively reviewing the details and engaging the appropriate contacts and authorities. The safety and well-being of our guests and employees remain our top priority."

Michele Storms, executive director at the ACLU of Washington, said in a statement that the organization "strongly condemns" the arrest operation.

"The Trump administration's practice of conducting immigration enforcement with masked and unidentifiable agents has resulted in civil rights violations at an unprecedented scale," Storms continued. "Their cruelty turns everyday locations like schools, bus stops, grocery stores, and airports into sites of fear and chaos, and complicates holding agents accountable for abuses. ICE violence is intentional and will not stop unless Congress or the courts hold this rogue agency to account."

Some elected Democrats from the state have also spoken out. US Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), a frequent critic of ICE's operations under President Donald Trump, said on social media that "I am [incredibly] disturbed by the reports of this detention at Sea-Tac. My office is working to gather more information on the situation."

"This is yet another incredibly terrifying moment for immigrant communities. Whether you’re an immigrant or citizen, be sure you know your rights," added Jayapal—who is an immigrant from India—sharing a link to an informational page on her congressional website.

Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson declared that "ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities. Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics."

As for Eva Yi Xie, the 24-year-old Princeton student, NBC News reported Saturday that she is being held at the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia, according ICE's website.

While DHS claimed in a statement that "Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States" and her "pending application does not confer legal status in the United States," Xie's attorney, Kerry Doyle, asserted that "her arrest and detention is without legal basis, as ICE and DHS are fully aware."

This article has been updated with comment from the ACLU of Washington and the US Department of Homeland Security.

The White House claimed that "Trump is ensuring that Americans' confidential information and national and homeland security work is protected, and that the executive branch is able to serve the American people efficiently and economically."

However, his move was widely seen as part of a broader effort by the president to limit Democrats' planned probes into not only the federal government and its contractors but also Trump and businesses that may have benefited from his return to power.

Acknowledging the anticipated Democrat-led investigations, the White House fact sheet says that "certain congressional leaders have threatened to intrude on these executive prerogatives by seeking confidential executive branch information from executive agencies and harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."

Lisa Gilbert, co-president of of the watchdog group Public Citizen, stressed in a Saturday statement that "contractors are paid with Americans' tax money and must be the best for the job, full stop."

"However, throughout the Trump administration we've seen widespread abuse of the contracting process, with lucrative contracts doled out to political allies, inexperienced startups, and flatly unqualified bidders, for everything from major ICE operations to Trump's vanity projects," she noted, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel joined 19 other state attorneys general in a November 18, 2026 letter urging congressional leaders to hold hearings on Trump administration immigration enforcement. The coalition includes attorneys general from Illinois, Minnesota and Wisconsin.

Why it matters

The letter asks Congress to examine alleged constitutional violations by ICE and CBP agents, detention practices and alleged waste within the Department of Homeland Security. The request comes as the administration has pushed back broadly against Democratic plans to investigate it after the election.

The administration reported 491,000 immigration arrests and 483,000 deportations in fiscal year 2026, while DHS paid $2.2 billion for four CoreCivic prisons. Whether the alleged rights violations and purchase practices hold up under scrutiny remains unresolved.

The players

Department of Homeland Security

The federal department overseeing ICE and CBP, whose enforcement practices and prison purchases are the subject of the letter.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement

The federal agency responsible for interior immigration enforcement, arrests and deportations that the attorneys general asked Congress to examine.

CoreCivic

A private prison operator that sold four facilities to DHS for $2.2 billion, including a Minnesota prison.

The details

The letter states that ICE and CBP agents have violated constitutional rights through unlawful stops and arrests, racial profiling and excessive force. It cites the use of tear gas and force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Portland and Newark, and three January 2026 shootings by federal agents in Minneapolis, two of which were fatal. The attorneys general did not prescribe specific legislative changes and said Congress should first establish the extent of any abuses through hearings.

Timeline

January 2026: Three shootings involving federal agents occurred in Minneapolis.

2025: CoreCivic offered a Minnesota prison to the state for $75 million.

November 8, 2026: U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appeared on CNN's State of the Union questioning Democratic oversight.

November 18, 2026: The attorneys general sent the letter to congressional leaders.

November 21, 2026: The White House and DHS had not publicly responded to the letter.

The attorneys general's request is a counter-move to the administration's pushback against Democratic investigation plans, and it asks Congress to hear from affected residents, immigrant advocates and state officials before any legislative response. The coalition frames the enforcement actions as having antagonized and terrorized communities nationwide.

The letter could lead to congressional hearings that examine how immigration enforcement and detention are conducted, affecting residents who interact with federal agents or detention facilities. Any resulting oversight could shape the policies that determine how arrests, deportations and prison contracts are handled nationwide.

The takeaway

State-level scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement is moving toward congressional hearings, which would put the administration's arrest, deportation and detention figures under formal review. The outcome will depend on whether Congress acts on the coalition's request.

text:
A 29-year-old Indian-origin man in Texas has been taken into custody by U.S. immigration authorities after being convicted of transferring private photographs from a female customer’s mobile phone to his own device. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) announced on Sunday that Raghul Anandakrishnan was transferred into its custody from a county jail in Texas. He will remain detained by the agency until his immigration court proceedings are completed. According to ICE, the criminal case stemmed from a complaint filed by a woman who alleged that a wireless store employee accessed her phone and transferred her private images without permission, leading to his conviction for attempted invasive visual recording.

​Incident at Austin Wireless Store

​The incident occurred in June 2026 while Anandakrishnan was working at a Total Wireless store in Austin, Texas, according to local police records and filings in a Travis County court. A female customer visited the store with her mobile phone, and investigators alleged that Anandakrishnan gained access to the device and sent two of her private photographs to his own phone using AirDrop. The police investigation also revealed that he accessed the customer’s Snapchat account during the interaction. Following the woman’s complaint, law enforcement officers investigated the unauthorized access to her device and the transfer of her personal images, resulting in his arrest.

​Arrest, Bail, and Criminal Conviction

​Travis County jail records show that Anandakrishnan was arrested and booked on June 7 on initial charges related to invasive visual recording and a computer security breach. Total bail across both charges was set at $10,000, and the court imposed restrictions barring him from contacting the complainant. He was subsequently convicted of attempted invasive visual recording, though full details regarding the court’s final verdict and sentencing terms were not disclosed in the available records. After completing his time in county jail following the criminal conviction, he was handed over to federal immigration officials.

​Immigration Custody and Pending Proceedings

​In a statement posted on the social media platform X, ICE confirmed that Anandakrishnan was taken from county custody and will remain detained pending the outcome of his immigration case. Federal authorities have not yet disclosed his specific immigration status, his current detention facility, or the scheduled date for his next hearing. Under U.S. immigration law, foreign nationals convicted of criminal offenses may face separate administrative proceedings to determine their eligibility to remain in the country. For Anandakrishnan, the upcoming immigration court process will examine his legal status and residency eligibility, though officials have not indicated when hearings will begin or how long a final decision might take.

text:
When Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 after campaigning on mass deportation, his administration got to work expanding immigration detention and reshaping the nation’s immigration courts to make it more difficult for jailed migrants to seek release. Almost two years later, data show just how successful those policies have been.

The number of people jailed in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention nationwide is up roughly 80 percent since President Joe Biden left office. The Trump administration has foreclosed most avenues through which jailed migrants have historically sought release. For the shrinking share of the jailed population that does access an immigration bond hearing, the average bond denial rate has jumped. It rose to about 60 percent in the first year of Trump 2.0, up from about 53 percent in the last year of Biden’s tenure. The denial rate has continued to rise this year.

Even when a bond is granted, freedom remains out of reach for many caught in the Trump administration’s deportation machine because median bond amounts have also increased. Those amounts have even doubled from 2024 to the first months of 2026 in some of the federal circuit court jurisdictions with the most immigration bond cases, according to data compiled and analyzed by Bklg.org.

“This is a linchpin in the administration’s deportation strategy,” Michael Tan, deputy director of the Immigrants’ Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), told Truthout. “The primary reason they’re subjecting people to detention with no avenue for release is to coerce them into giving up their immigration cases, their claims to legal status, to remaining in the country, and to acquiesce to a deportation because they can’t stand being locked up for so long.”

Even for those who do not agree to so-called self-deportation, outcomes tend to be worse for those who fight their immigration cases while detained. Those who are released are more likely to have their immigration cases resolved with permission to remain in the U.S. than with deportation orders. Once freed, a person tends to have more resources and more time to participate in their case, gather evidence, and access other needed support. “It’s a lot harder to fight your immigration case when you’re in a jail cell,” Tan told Truthout. Especially, he added, “when ICE moves people all over the place, and so it’s not the case that you’ll be detained often in your community or near your family [and] your lawyer. Instead, ICE is routinely shipping people to far-flung locations.”

Fisayo Okare, digital communications manager at Envision Freedom Fund, told Truthout that migrant community members with whom her organization works regularly face these pressures. “Families are thinking of whether it’s worth it or not to even remain in the country or just choosing to voluntarily deport,” she said. The nonprofit Envision Freedom Fund is the largest immigration bond fund in the nation; it helps cover bonds for individuals jailed in New York or New Jersey and those who will return home to the area on release. Since the fund launched in 2018, it has provided over $15 million in bond support to help secure the release of over 1,600 people from immigration jails.

An October report from Envision Freedom Fund shows how the increase in the number of migrants jailed and struggling to access release is affecting communities in New York and New Jersey. The volume of requests for support that the bond fund receives has risen so much that it projects it will cover nine times as many bonds in 2026 as in 2024, if it can raise the funds needed to meet demand through the end of the calendar year.

The average bond amounts submitted to the fund for support have also risen from $6,200 in 2024 to $14,200 in 2026. Half of the requests the fund has received this year have involved bonds exceeding $10,000, and it has seen bonds set as high as $85,000 since Trump returned to the White House. The fund has also tracked tens of thousands of individuals who have been booked in to detention facilities in New York and New Jersey and then transferred to more than 100 other detention facilities across 25 states.

“The fact is that we’re forced to bond so many more people out now because the sheer volume of the system — everything is increasing,” Ben McCoubrey, Envision Freedom Fund’s data and advocacy manager, told Truthout.

It has never been easy for those in ICE jails to access bond, a process that entails securing a bond hearing in immigration court, finding a lawyer to present the case, then convincing the immigration judge to grant a bond, and ultimately finding someone outside with U.S. citizenship or a green card and the funds needed to post the bond. But the obstacles to accessing bond are now greater than ever before thanks to what Tan characterized to Truthout as the Trump administration’s “takeover of the immigration courts.”

Since Trump returned to office, he has signed executive orders to expand detention and restrict release. Based on those directives, ICE’s lawyers have made legal arguments and issued guidance meant to subject as many immigrants as possible to mandatory detention and limit their access to bond. Those directives have become standard practice following administration-friendly decisions from the Board of Immigration Appeals, which governs the immigration courts and judges from within the Department of Justice.

The Trump administration has also purged dozens of immigration judges and recruited replacements that it now calls “deportation judges,” rather than immigration judges. Many of these new judges come from the ranks of former military lawyers, ICE lawyers, and prosecutors with little or no experience or training in immigration law.

“They’ve fired immigration judges that they think, in their view, are too friendly to immigrants and replaced them with so-called deportation judges [and] for the judges who remain, who didn’t get fired, we know that the administration is exerting pressure on them to deny relief, and to really crack down, and serve as foot soldiers in a mass deportation campaign,” Tan told Truthout. “They’ve taken an immigration court system that is supposed to be neutral and fair and made it into an arm of the immigration enforcement system.”

The ACLU has litigated the Trump administration’s mandatory detention scheme in every circuit court where it could be heard, a total of 11 of the nation’s 13. Only two circuits have concurred with the administration’s interpretation of the law. Nine have rejected it, opening the door for more individuals to access bond hearings in the 40 states covered by those circuits. The Supreme Court will hear the issue in a case arising from the Second Circuit, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, next year; Tan told Truthout a decision is expected by the end of June. The outcome will affect access to bond hearings for those in ICE jails nationwide.

While the legal fight continues, the humanitarian crisis created by the Trump administration’s policy changes is deepening. Envision Freedom Fund’s recent report helps put a human face on the issue. “We paint a picture of what’s happening in the context of detention and deportation, how things are growing, and go beyond what we see when it’s just [the number of] people getting released on bonds,” McCoubrey told Truthout about the report’s aims.

The report includes stories of immigrants who have suffered medical neglect and other traumas in ICE jails and are navigating the lasting effects after being bonded out with Envision Freedom Fund’s support.

One man for whom the fund helped cover a $50,000 bond to secure his release in July 2026 shared that he “felt unmeasurably happy when [he] got released from the jail.” He had been jailed for over two months, and after release, said, “I believed that now everything will be okay. Because when I was in there, I was stressing a lot. I didn’t know what would happen because nowadays it’s really tough.” Just two weeks after the man’s release, his asylum case was granted — ending a more than four-year wait that began in 2022.

More recently, Okare told Truthout that Envision Freedom Fund secured release for a man in his mid-thirties who had been transferred from Delaney Hall in New Jersey to an ICE jail in Georgia. The fund then coordinated with partners to arrange transportation to bring him home in time to be with his wife and witness the birth of his child. “His wife was actually in the hospital when we got the bond request, and he got out right in time,” she said.

Okare told Truthout that stories like these are common in the work of Envision Freedom Fund and other immigration bond funds operating nationwide. For each of the tens of thousands of people jailed in the country’s ICE detention facilities, there are families missing a parent or a sibling and communities missing a neighbor.

As the Trump administration continues pulling these communities apart, Okare told Truthout that organizations like hers will keep fighting to make them whole again: “[We’re] not just paying their bond but ensuring that they get out and make it back to their community.”
