text:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. (VINnews) — A prominent Jewish legal association has called on U.S. authorities to review the immigration status of a British cleric serving as rector of a church in Michigan after he publicly advocated for driving Jews out of the United States.

Join our WhatsApp group

Subscribe to our Daily Roundup Email

The American Association of Jewish Lawyers and Jurists sent a letter to Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun, the State Department’s special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism. The group, led by its president Robert Garson, asked officials at the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security to determine whether legal grounds exist to revoke the visa of Calvin Robinson, rector at St. Paul’s Church in Grand Rapids.

Robinson, who moved to the United States in 2024 and became rector the following year, has made repeated statements targeting Jews. On a Nov. 13 podcast appearance with white nationalist Joe Enders, Robinson said people discuss mass deportation of Muslims but not Jews, adding, “I think driving out the Jews is the answer.” He has also claimed Jews disproportionately control industries such as Hollywood, music and pornography, engaged in Holocaust denial, and written that “it is the Jews. It has always been the Jews. Not all of them, but always them.”

In the letter, reviewed by Jewish News Syndicate, Garson described Robinson’s comments as reflecting “disturbing hostility toward Jews” and a “breathtaking ignorance of American history.” He called the cleric’s vision “not merely antisemitic” but “fundamentally un-American,” noting the absurdity of a British cleric lecturing American Jews about belonging in a country where their contributions to its founding, defense and institutions are well established. Garson highlighted the long history of Jewish presence in America and principles of religious freedom emphasized by George Washington.

St. Paul’s Church, founded in the 19th century within the Episcopal Church, left that body in 1980, later joined and then departed the Anglican Catholic Church in 2025, and is now affiliated with the Christian Episcopal Church. Robinson joined as priest-in-charge in 2024.

The Anglican Catholic Church revoked Robinson’s license to serve as a priest on Jan. 30, 2025, citing alleged antisemitic statements or sympathy with antisemitic groups. Church officials said Robinson had previously disavowed antisemitism in writing after a warning but continued provocative conduct and lacked the temperament required of a parish priest. He has remained at the Michigan church after the congregation voted to leave the Anglican Catholic Church.

Garson, who has represented President Trump in litigation and was appointed by him to the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Council, specifically urged a review of Robinson’s status based on advocacy for the collective exclusion of American citizens. U.S. officials have not publicly commented on the request.

The case highlights ongoing concerns within the Jewish community about rising antisemitic rhetoric from public figures and the potential for such speech to influence immigration decisions when it involves calls for the removal of Jewish Americans.

title: ICE Detention Contractors Must Report Congress Requests to White House
description:
ICE detention contractors, along with every other company holding a federal contract, must now notify the White House and their contracting agency of any congressional request about their government work, under Executive Order 14438, which President Trump signed on Nov. 20.
Yet few contractors sit closer to the coming oversight fight than the private companies that run detention facilities, staff clinics and move detainees for ICE.
The order lists no exception, but it must be carried out “consistent with applicable law,” and a statute outranks an executive order.
What to watch OMB guidance and DHS notices to ICE contractors under Section 3.
4712, contractor employee whistleblower protections McGrain v. Daugherty, 273 U.S. 135 (1927) Image: Official White House portrait of President Donald J. Trump (public domain)
text:
An order signed Nov. 20 requires every federal contractor, including the companies that run ICE detention centers, detainee medical care and removal flights, to alert the White House to congressional requests and follow its instructions on what to hold back.

ICE detention contractors, along with every other company holding a federal contract, must now notify the White House and their contracting agency of any congressional request about their government work, under Executive Order 14438, which President Trump signed on Nov. 20. The order also requires them to obey White House and agency instructions on withholding communications the administration says are covered by executive privilege, a rule that arrives weeks before Democrats take control of the House and its investigative committees in January.

The text never mentions immigration. Yet few contractors sit closer to the coming oversight fight than the private companies that run detention facilities, staff clinics and move detainees for ICE. In August, 87 House Democrats led by Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey wrote to DHS and ICE about deaths in custody, naming GEO Group, CoreCivic, LaSalle Corrections, Akima Global Services, Management & Training Corporation and Amentum. Their letter said more than 50 people had died in ICE custody since Jan. 20, 2025, and asked which private contractors provide medical care and how many violations had led to penalties or terminations. With a House majority, those requests can come with subpoenas attached.

ICE was holding 65,765 people as of July 11, 2026, according to the most recent figure on the quick-facts page compiled by TRAC at Syracuse University. Spending on the system has already drawn auditors’ attention, including a GAO finding on warehouses ICE bought far above their value.

What Executive Order 14438 requires of contractors

Notice: Section 2(a) says contractors must “immediately” notify the White House and contracting agencies of any pending or future congressional request “respecting the contractors’ communications or work with the executive branch.”

Withholding: They must follow instructions on withholding communications that the White House or the agency has “determined are protected by executive privilege.” The order does not define what qualifies.

Subcontractors: Covered as well, with prime contractors responsible for their compliance.

Enforcement: Agencies “shall consider” contract termination or cancellation and suspension or debarment, “consistent with applicable law.”

Next steps: Agencies must “promptly inform” contractors, and the Office of Management and Budget is to issue compliance guidance. No deadline is set for either.

The White House argument and the Democratic reply

Section 1 of the order states that Congress cannot seek information from agencies, employees or contractors “without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions,” and describes the goal as “preventing and prohibiting uncoordinated disclosures.” The accompanying fact sheet accuses unnamed congressional leaders of “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government,” without citing a specific request.

The Associated Press reported that the order is part of a broader push to resist oversight once Democrats take over in January. Earlier this month, White House Counsel William Scharf wrote to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the incoming House Oversight chair, that some planned investigations may “cross the line into blatant criminality,” according to the letter published by PBS NewsHour. Garcia answered that “it appears Donald Trump has something to hide.”

Where the order’s reach likely ends

Privilege has limits. Executive privilege protects certain executive branch communications. A detention operator’s own staffing logs, medical protocols and incident reports are a different category, and much of what detention oversight seeks is likely to fall outside any credible privilege claim. Disputes would probably center on contractors’ exchanges with ICE about contract performance, which the administration could call deliberative.

Subpoenas still bind. An executive order cannot cancel a congressional subpoena. Federal law makes it a crime for any person summoned by a committee to refuse to testify or produce papers, and the Supreme Court recognized Congress’ power to compel information for a legislative purpose in McGrain v. Daugherty (1927). The practical effect is that the order is more likely to slow and channel voluntary cooperation than to block compelled testimony. The open question is what happens to a company caught between a subpoena and a White House instruction, since the government’s broad right to end contracts for its convenience is the real leverage here.

Whistleblowers keep their statute. Under 41 U.S.C. 4712, contractors may not retaliate against employees who disclose evidence of gross mismanagement, abuse of authority or violations of law to a member of Congress or a committee. The order lists no exception, but it must be carried out “consistent with applicable law,” and a statute outranks an executive order. A detention nurse who reports medical lapses to a committee keeps that protection. The order also states that it creates no right enforceable in court.

Access to detention information is already contested, from New Jersey’s lawsuit over an ignored subpoena tied to Delaney Hall to Washington state’s push to inspect the Tacoma facility ICE is buying.

What to watch

OMB guidance and DHS notices to ICE contractors under Section 3.

The Dec. 11 funding deadline, the next point at which Congress sets terms for DHS money.

The first committee requests to detention companies after the new Congress convenes in January, and any detention-deaths reporting bill that would put disclosure duties into law.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

text:
Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws."

During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the US illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition.

"The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. "We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform."

Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem.

"Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos," she said.

text:
President Donald Trump will likely veto many of the bills that Democrats pass once they take control of Congress next year, he said Friday, though he suggested negotiations on healthcare and immigration were possible.

“They’re going to send things my way and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send more things and I’m going to veto them,” he said. “But I think after a month or so, they’re going to send things, and I’m going to say, ‘I’m going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’”

Trump then referred to House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, both of New York, as “smart” and indicated he would be willing to work with them on some issues.

“There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare. I am open to great healthcare,” he said. “Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.”

Trump said several Democrats have called him in recent weeks, including Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who he said wanted to discuss border security.

“I received a phone call two days ago from the new governor-elect of Texas. She was really nice. It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border,” he said. “And I think we’ll be able to work something out because that’s a very important thing.”

Must-pass items

Trump and Democratic leaders in Congress will need to negotiate much more than healthcare and immigration once divided government begins in January.

They will need to work out bipartisan agreement on the dozen annual government spending bills that fund scores of departments and agencies as well as the thousands of programs they administer. Failing to accomplish the work, or approving a stopgap spending bill instead, would lead to yet another shutdown.

Congress and the White House will also likely need to negotiate another debt-ceiling increase early next year. Without agreement, the country would default for the first time in modern history, very likely plunging the economy into a tailspin.

Not addressing the debt ceiling before the remainder of the $5 trillion in new borrowing authority approved by Republicans in last year’s “big, beautiful” law expires would limit the federal government to only spend what it brings in.

That would lead to ramifications more significant than a government shutdown, including the possibility that Social Security checks would not go out on time and that medical providers wouldn’t be reimbursed for Medicare or Medicaid patients treatment.

text:
Parents and children separated at the U.S.-Mexico border between March 7, 2017, and January 20, 2021, who belong to the Ms. L. class are covered by a $48.75 million settlement with government contractor MVM, Inc. that a federal judge preliminarily approved in November 2026. The court set a June 17, 2027, claim deadline, with each valid claim receiving at least $3,000; notice to class members is due by December 15, 2026.

What Happened?

On November 17, 2026, U.S. District Judge Dana M. Sabraw of the Southern District of California preliminarily approved a $48,750,000 class action settlement between MVM, Inc. and families separated at the U.S.-Mexico border. The case is Padre v. MVM, Inc., No. 3:24-cv-01265-DMS-AHG. MVM did not oppose the motion for preliminary approval.

MVM is a private government contractor that provides security, staffing and transportation services to federal agencies. The lawsuit, filed July 23, 2024, alleged that MVM participated in the separation of children from their parents under the federal family separation policy that began in 2017, including by transporting separated children, and asserted claims under the Alien Tort Statute, federal civil rights statutes and California law. MVM denies all allegations of wrongdoing, liability and damages, and the settlement is not an admission of fault. Judge Sabraw found the agreement likely to be approved as fair, adequate and reasonable at a final hearing set for July 23, 2027.

Status Preliminarily Approved Order of November 17, 2026 · final hearing July 23, 2027

Settlement Fund $48.75 million About 8,900 class members · minimum $3,000 per valid claim

Who Is in the Settlement Class?

The court certified a settlement class of all persons who qualify as class members of the settlement class certified in Ms. L. v. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, No. 3:18-cv-00428-DMS-AHG, and who were separated from their parent or child between March 7, 2017, and January 20, 2021. Judge Sabraw also presides over the Ms. L. case, which ended in a 2023 settlement with the federal government providing reunification-related relief and other benefits. The MVM case seeks relief for essentially the same class.

The court estimated the settlement class at about 8,900 people. The order notes that most class members came to the United States from Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Mexico, and that some now live outside the United States.

How Payments Will Work

Under the settlement allocation plan the court approved, every class member who submits a valid claim form will receive a baseline award of no less than $3,000. Class members may also apply for an additional criteria-based award or an extraordinary injury award, which are calculated under a points system tied to the circumstances of each separation. The value of those additional awards will be adjusted uniformly depending on the number of valid claims and the points assigned.

The claim form can be submitted online or printed and mailed. According to the order, it asks for basic identifying information that the settlement administrator will verify, uses drop-down menus and check boxes to describe the circumstances of the separation, and allows an optional narrative statement for those seeking an extraordinary injury award. Attorneys’ fees, costs and any service awards come from the fund, subject to the court’s approval, and class counsel must file that request by January 21, 2027.

Key Dates

December 15, 2026: deadline to send direct notice to class members

January 21, 2027: class counsel’s motion for attorneys’ fees, costs and service awards

February 22, 2027: deadline to request exclusion or object

May 27, 2027: motion for final approval

June 17, 2027: deadline to file a claim

July 23, 2027, 1:30 p.m.: final approval hearing

The court approved a notice program that includes direct mail, email and phone contact where available, a press release, an internet search campaign and targeted digital notice. JND Legal Administration is the settlement administrator, Huntington Bank is the escrow agent, and Hausfeld LLP is class counsel. An official settlement website address had not been published in the court order when this page was written.

How the Case Reached Settlement

MVM moved to dismiss the complaint in November 2024. On March 3, 2025, the court granted that motion in part and allowed the plaintiffs to amend claims found to be time-barred. On June 26, 2026, the claims for enforced disappearance, torture, and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment were dismissed with prejudice. The parties began mediation in October 2024 and held a two-day settlement conference before U.S. Magistrate Judge Goddard in March 2026, then continued negotiating until they reached the $48.75 million agreement.

In weighing the deal, the court noted that MVM disputed the claims, argued that the federal government should have been joined, and maintained that it acted under its contractual obligations and was therefore immune from liability. The court also noted that settling before depositions and trial spares class members from testifying about their experiences.

Questions

Who is covered by the MVM settlement?

The settlement class is everyone who qualifies as a member of the class certified in Ms. L. v. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and who was separated from a parent or child between March 7, 2017, and January 20, 2021. The court estimated the class at about 8,900 people.

How much will each class member receive?

Each class member who submits a valid claim form will receive a baseline award of no less than $3,000. Class members can also seek additional criteria-based or extraordinary injury awards under a points system, and those amounts depend on how many valid claims are filed.

What is the claim deadline?

The court’s schedule sets June 17, 2027, as the deadline for class members to file a claim. The deadline to request exclusion or object is February 22, 2027, and the final approval hearing is July 23, 2027.

Did MVM admit wrongdoing?

No. MVM denies all allegations of wrongdoing and liability, and the settlement is not an admission of fault. The court has not decided who is right.

Who is running the settlement?

The court appointed JND Legal Administration as settlement administrator and Hausfeld LLP as class counsel. Notice is scheduled to go out to class members by December 15, 2026.

title: Vance thinks doubling-down on anti-immigrant rhetoric will work. He's wrong. - MS NOW
authors: James Downie, Amanda Marcotte, Steve Benen
description:
Say what you will about JD Vance — and I have — but no one ever accused the vice president of lacking self-confidence.
Kevin Stitt after the Oklahoma Republican called for Trump to work with the newly elected Democratic congressional majority on immigration reform.
After boosting rumors that Haitian migrants kidnapped pets and spread disease, Vance labeled it “amnesty” to allow them to keep Temporary Protected Status.
Vance is not required to stand by Trump’s immigration agenda.
Publicly criticizing Republicans who express a desire to moderate on immigration is a choice — one Vance clearly wants to be seen making.
text:
Say what you will about JD Vance — and I have — but no one ever accused the vice president of lacking self-confidence. When it comes to the issue of immigration post-midterms, he’s typically bold in his assessment that Donald Trump’s White House is on the right track.

On Thursday, Vance lashed out at Gov. Kevin Stitt after the Oklahoma Republican called for Trump to work with the newly elected Democratic congressional majority on immigration reform. Pointing at the “huge swing in the midterms,” Stitt argued that there was a way to keep a “strong border” while making sure the U.S. had enough immigrants to meet labor market needs.

That idea, Vance replied on X, “is morally and electorally disastrous,” and “to a lot of people, this sounds like an effort to give amnesty.” This echoed his warning in the immediate aftermath of the midterms that it was “gaslighting” to argue that Trump’s mass deportation efforts played a role in turning voters against Republicans.

Simply put, the vice president is wrong. Trump’s deportation agenda is broadly unpopular on its own. It has also exacerbated the economic woes that topped the list of concerns for voters. While the Trump administration seems determined to continue this inhumane policy, doing so likely will hurt the GOP nominee in 2028 — something that should worry Vance if he plans to run.

The vice president frequently invokes “amnesty” as a scare word to malign more moderate views on immigration. After boosting rumors that Haitian migrants kidnapped pets and spread disease, Vance labeled it “amnesty” to allow them to keep Temporary Protected Status. Around the same time, he demonized a Democratic bill that would allow undocumented immigrants to start a five-year process to become lawful permanent residents. He flings the word “amnesty” at legal immigrants, while also falsely accusing them of causing crime and inflation.

Saying “amnesty” all the time, however, cannot erase the exit polls that showed most Americans oppose Trump’s aggressive deportation tactics and believe immigration helps the country. Even the president, in a post-election interview with Ross Douthat of CBS News, admitted that it’s unpopular to deport “good people” who are “paying taxes,” as his administration has focused on doing.

For Trump, who can’t run for president again, there’s no personal downside to doubling down on his cruel immigration agenda. He already showed his contempt for midterm voters by promoting Stephen Miller, widely reported to be the driving force behind the mass deportations, as White House chief of staff. The lame-duck president and his right-hand man likely feel free to unleash Immigrations and Custom Enforcement on even more daycare workers, teenage clerks and parents dropping kids off at school.

More articles

Vance, however, is considering a presidential run. If he wants to win, he should reconsider his confidence that voters would reward a hard-line stance against their immigrant neighbors. Two more years of Trump’s deportations won’t just further offend people morally, either. The resulting economic damage will cause a lot of headaches for the next Republican nominee.

As NPR reported Thursday, immigration drives economic growth and increases the number of jobs available for everyone. Deliberately shrinking the population by millions of people, which is the stated goal of the Trump deportation campaign, is like building a giant vacuum to suck billions of dollars out of the economy. That deficit can’t be made up by American citizens having more babies, no matter how much Vance would like to pretend otherwise. Babies, while cute, don’t work jobs and pay taxes like immigrant adults do.

Vance is not required to stand by Trump’s immigration agenda. Even if he doesn’t want to be caught publicly disagreeing with Trump, as he came close to doing with the Iran war, silence is always an option. Publicly criticizing Republicans who express a desire to moderate on immigration is a choice — one Vance clearly wants to be seen making.

Since the vice president is smart enough to read a poll, this seems like an odd path to travel. But he is facing considerable pressure from right-wing media. As Media Matters documented, popular MAGA pundits like Tucker Carlson and Megyn Kelly have been pushing the Trump administration to inflict even more pain on immigrants, by making it even harder to work and earn money. On Steve Bannon’s “War Room” podcast, Heritage Foundation fellow Mike Howell called on Miller to “unleash the dragon” and “deport millions.” Anyone who spends a lot of time on X, which Vance appears to do, will see a steady drumbeat of racist vitriol against immigrants.

Wallow in these waters long enough, and you might get a distorted view of where Americans stand on this issue. But MAGA podcasts and right-wing social media chatter do not reflect the average opinion, which is far more forgiving toward undocumented immigrants and positive toward immigration in general. Right-wing pundits are loud, but the voters had their say on Election Day, and they do not like the Trump-Miller approach to immigration. If Vance takes the same approach, he’ll likely find out that it’s a political loser for him, as well.

text:
Masked US immigration officers have detained two people on an airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers boarded a flight to Los Angeles, prompting criticism from Washington state Governor Bob Ferguson and concerns from Alaska Airlines.

The arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport around 8 a.m. local time (1600 UTC) on Saturday. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who had overstayed his visa.

Agents also arrested Sofia Hernandez Mejia, who they alleged threw hot coffee at the ICE officers during the confrontation. ICE said she had also overstayed her visa and would face a charge of assaulting a federal officer.

Videos of the incident circulated on social media, showing officers struggling with a person on the ground as passengers look on. One woman could be heard shouting that her daughter was being taken away and that she had a work permit.

Washington governor slams 'out of control' ICE

Governor Ferguson, a Democrat, described the footage as "horrific" and "chilling", accusing ICE of being "completely and totally out of control."

He urged Alaska Airlines to ask federal immigration authorities to leave the state's airports and said he would make the same appeal to other airlines operating at Seattle-Tacoma.

Alaska Airlines said it had received no advance notice of the enforcement operation and was working to understand the circumstances.

The airline also expressed concern over the incident, which it said had been distressing for passengers and employees.

The operation drew criticism from April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, who said it had caused fear and disruption during one of the busiest travel periods of the year.

The flight was delayed, with Alaska Airlines saying many passengers were transferred to other flights. The original service eventually departed at 11 a.m. local time.

His wife told 13WHAM, “Every letter, every visit, every phone call, every act of kindness mattered. We learned that a community is not defined only by where people live, but by how they show up for one another when it matters most.”

Machado was arrested in mid-October during what the Department of Homeland Security described as a targeted enforcement operation. title: US deportees in South Sudan went hungry as guards pocketed money from relatives, families say
description:
For those expelled to South Sudan, and their families, the ordeal has come at an additional cost.
Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods.
In addition to the Phans, The Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers.
South Sudan sought sanctions relief and other concessions, though details of the arrangement remain unclear.
But the Trump administration has signaled it has no intention of getting involved, and U.N. agencies say they are unable to help.
text:
JUBA, South Sudan — Migrants deported by the Trump administration to countries other than their own have endured hunger, thirst and other deprivations while being detained indefinitely in places with poor human rights records and little oversight.

For those expelled to South Sudan, and their families, the ordeal has come at an additional cost.

Guards have solicited and received thousands of dollars from detainees' families, who were told the money would be used to improve conditions for their loved ones. Instead, the guards pocketed most of the money, families said, while detainees went for days without food or clean water, and months held incommunicado.

"They used our desperate situation," said Ngoc Phan, a U.S. citizen whose husband Tuan Phan had been detained in South Sudan for nearly a year before he was repatriated to Vietnam in June. "If that's not exploitation, I don't know what is."

It is the inevitable outcome, she said, of a U.S. immigration policy that places deportees in the custody of countries struggling with poverty and corruption, then looks the other way.

Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods. The economy is in tatters, and government workers rarely receive wages.

In all, Ngoc Phan said she forked over roughly $4,000 intended for food, water and a cellphone. She sent several hundred dollars on multiple occasions and each time, her husband said, guards would give him a few bananas and apples, and some peanuts.

Tuan Phan, 44, said he lost 20 pounds while under confinement at a gated three-story building in Juba, the capital, and that tensions grew between detainees and guards as living conditions worsened. One detainee who wanted a window open for fresh air was struck in the face by a guard, and another who complained about a lack of soap was locked in his room for days and only let out to eat, he said.

"I feared for my life every day I was there," he said.

In addition to the Phans, The Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers. Most spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation against the detainees.

AP also reviewed money-transfer receipts and messages between guards and four detainees' relatives.

When asked about AP's findings, a spokesperson from South Sudan's Foreign Ministry said detainees are given adequate food, water and medical care, and are allowed regular contact with relatives and lawyers while it works to resolve their individual cases. The spokesperson said the government pays for all the associated costs.

MIGRANTS DEPORTED TO A COUNTRY BESET BY SEVERE POVERTY AND CORRUPTION

Under a series of murky agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to more than 30 countries that are not their own, advocates say, all part of the broad U.S. crackdown on immigration. Many were asylum seekers with U.S. court orders protecting them from being returned to their home countries because they could face persecution or torture.

The countries taking deportees have struck deals to receive millions of dollars in payments from the U.S., or have sought goodwill in negotiations over trade, migration or aid, documents show. South Sudan sought sanctions relief and other concessions, though details of the arrangement remain unclear.

In July 2025, after a legal battle that ended with a Supreme Court ruling, Phan and seven other migrants with criminal convictions — including for murder and sexual assault — were deported to South Sudan. In a press release heralding their expulsion, the Trump administration referred to the men — originally from Mexico, Cuba, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and South Sudan — as "barbaric criminal illegal aliens."

All eight had completed their sentences in the U.S. before being taken into immigration custody. One more deportee has been detained in South Sudan.

The Trump administration defends its policy as a means of quickly deporting migrants who have final removal orders, but whose home countries refuse to accept them.

Alma David, a lawyer representing one of the detainees still in Juba, said her client has been arbitrarily held for over a year despite not being charged with a crime.

"These are people who had lives and friends and families and who were scooped up and flown to a faraway country and locked up," she said.

WORRIED FAMILIES SENT MONEY AS DETAINEES' FOOD AND WATER RAN OUT

The first time Ngoc Phan sent money to a guard was in November 2025, after hearing from a lawyer that several detainees in Juba had complained about food shortages. She sent $300. After that, requests for money started coming in more frequently.

Whenever food ran out, guards would instruct Tuan Phan to call his wife and tell her to send money. Occasionally, a guard would contact her directly, requesting cash without indicating what it was for, messages show.

Three other detainees had similar experiences, their relatives and a lawyer said. Payments made on their behalf to four individuals identified as guards ranged from $100 to $1,000 at a time, money-transfer receipts show. A $1,000 payment was made after a guard demanded money for suits, shirts and shoes that he said a detainee needed to travel back to his home country, according to text messages and a money-transfer receipt.

Food and other supplies were depleted quickly, Tuan Phan said, as up to a dozen guards lived and ate alongside the detainees. Sometimes the men ate only bread or rice, or went days without eating.

When they had no drinking water, some detainees collected rainwater, he said. "They give you a jug of water and say it needs to last a week. But then when it runs out it can be another 10 days before you get more."

Fuel shortages led to weekslong blackouts, and when the plumbing stopped working, the smell of feces filled the building, he said.

In September, one detainee called his niece in the U.S. to tell her to stop sending money after an earlier payment never reached him.

SOUTH SUDAN SAYS THE US HAS 'RELINQUISHED' RESPONSIBILITY

Relatives and lawyers for detainees still stuck in South Sudan say they have little faith the detention will end or conditions will improve without pressure from the U.S. government or international organizations.

But the Trump administration has signaled it has no intention of getting involved, and U.N. agencies say they are unable to help.

The staff at the U.S. Embassy in Juba has been instructed by the Trump administration not to visit the detainees or follow up on their treatment, according to a U.S. congressional aide who discussed the subject with embassy staff during a visit in August 2025. The aide spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

The U.S. embassy referred questions to the State Department, where a spokesperson did not address whether the embassy had received such instructions.

A spokesperson for the U.N.'s International Organization for Migration said the agency is unable to step in without a request from South Sudan.

In a statement, South Sudan's Foreign Ministry said the U.S. "fully relinquished responsibility and no longer has any legal jurisdiction over, or ties to, these individuals."

text:
Federal immigration agents conducted an arrest inside a crowded Alaska Airlines jetway at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning, sparking a chaotic struggle, and spurring multiple viral videos of the scene.

The arrests quickly drew sharp rebuke from Governor Bob Ferguson, who said he was "outraged" by the incident and that ICE is “completely and totally out of control.” Gov. Ferguson said it was an example of "ICE’s deeply un-American tactics."

The Department of Homeland Security issued a statement in response to Gov. Ferguson's post, saying in part that they were arresting people for overstaying their visas, adding that ICE officers were obstructed and assaulted during the incident.

The confrontation unfolded around 8 a.m. at Gate N9 as travelers boarded Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 to Los Angeles. In a written statement, the Port of Seattle said the incident involved U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and two passengers.

“We were just walking in the tunnel like a normal check-in,” said passenger Aidan Mendoza, 20. “Then there was yelling. And I thought instantly like, ‘Oh, somebody's fighting.’ ... And like everyone around me, we all got dead silent 'cause we were like, Well, what's going on?”

In a statement to KUOW, Alaska Airlines confirmed the incident, adding “We understand that situations like this can be distressing. The law enforcement activity was not previously known to us, and we are actively reviewing the details and engaging with the appropriate contacts and authorities. The safety and well-being of our guests and employees remain our top priority.”

Airport arrests have become a growing part of ICE strategy to remove immigrants from the U.S. ICE made nearly 50,000 arrests in July, according to NPR, as part of this expanded enforcement. There have been at least two other arrests at Sea-Tac Airport (SEA) since August, according to KING 5.

The Port of Seattle called the incident "outrageous."

“Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge,” the Port said in a statement to KUOW.

“The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with the Department of Homeland Security on whether any of these protocols were breached.”

KUOW has not confirmed these were ICE agents. Mendoza, the passenger, said he did not see weapons, masks, or visible ICE badges or insignias. ICE did not respond to a KUOW request for comment.

The witness video shows masked men tussling with a woman and a man, both on the ground, at the space between the jetway and the airplane, as coffee cups flew. Their names were not released.

For more than 10 minutes, Mendoza said, a girl sat on the floor screaming as agents pulled her father through a side door, as bystanders yelled at officers to let him go.

"She was sitting on the floor screaming hysterically, and the whole family was begging for the dad," Mendoza said.

Mendoza described 50 or so silent, terrified passengers who hugged the jetway wall as the family screamed.

Mendoza said he watched as a pilot walked off the flight.

“He started walking up the jetway, and you could tell by his face he was very uncomfortable, and he didn't know what to do.”

Mendoza said the pilot kept walking and “He didn’t come back.” Two flight attendants were reportedly so overwhelmed that they asked to be subbed out.

Mendoza decided not to board the flight after this incident. A visibly rattled gate agent removed him from the list, and customer service refunded his ticket.

"How can we go to Los Angeles and have fun with our family when we just watched a family get torn apart?" Mendoza said.

Federal law grants ICE access to public and post-security terminals, according to Port of Seattle guidance. Port policy bars its police from aiding civil immigration arrests.

text:
WASHINGTON – An arrest by US federal immigration agents at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport sparked outrage among officials and politicians on Nov 21, and intensified scrutiny of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and investigate the agency’s tactics.

Masked federal agents confronted passengers on a jet bridge as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles, forcing a woman to the ground in a chaotic encounter captured on video.

The confrontation delayed the flight.

The Port of Seattle said it was “outraged” by the incident, which involved ICE and two passengers.

ICE said its officers were attempting to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who they said had overstayed his visa, when other passengers interfered with the operation.

The agency said a second passenger, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, allegedly threw hot coffee at officers and was also arrested.

She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer, according to ICE.

Alaska Airlines said in an e-mailed statement that it had no advance notice of the enforcement action and was working to determine whether proper protocols were followed.

The airline said it was concerned by the incident, which it described as distressing for passengers and employees, and emphasised that it does not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement.

“I’m outraged by disturbing video of ICE agents forcing a woman to the ground on a jet bridge at SeaTac,” Senator Patty Murray, a Washington Democrat, said in a post on X.

“Trump answers to a Democratic Congress on January 3rd – there WILL be accountability.”

Democrats are preparing to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, promising investigations into President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Lawmakers have identified ICE’s enforcement practices, treatment of detainees and use of federal authority among the targets of planned congressional oversight, which could include hearings, subpoenas and demands for agency records.

In October, undercover federal immigration agents arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport in another encounter captured on video.

Washington governor Bob Ferguson, also a Democrat, called Nov 21’s incident “just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics”, saying the agency was “completely and totally out of control”.

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that immigration enforcement actions at the airport occur without its participation or knowledge.

Washington state officials condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday after plainclothes officers in masks detained two people who were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.
The Port of Seattle said the incident happened as travelers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight from Seattle to Los Angeles.
The agency added that during the arrest other travelers allegedly "began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers."
In the statement, DHS said she is also a Mexican national "and visa overstay."
"Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port's participation or knowledge," the statement said.
text:
Washington state officials condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday after plainclothes officers in masks detained two people who were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

Part of the incident was caught on video by onlookers. The video appears to show at least one person being detained by the officers on the bridge into the airplane. The officers are seen holding people down on the ground and pushing away bystanders. A woman is heard saying that she and the other person have work permits.

The Port of Seattle said the incident happened as travelers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight from Seattle to Los Angeles.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that ICE conducted "a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza" who the agency alleged "overstayed his visa."

The agency added that during the arrest other travelers allegedly "began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers."

"One passenger hurled hot coffee on the officers," the DHS spokesperson alleged. "Other passengers began obstructing federal officers."

That woman who allegedly threw the coffee was detained and identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia. In the statement, DHS said she is also a Mexican national "and visa overstay."

"She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer," DHS said in a statement.

DHS did not say where the two people were taken after they were detained.

Washington Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson said in a news conference later in the day that officials were still working to understand what happened but said the video of the incident was "horrific and chilling."

"Masked agents who do not identify themselves dragged screaming individuals off a jetway as they are trying to do something ordinary in our country, boarding an airplane," he said.

The Port of Seattle echoed the governor's sentiment, saying in a statement it was "outraged" over the incident. "Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port's participation or knowledge," the statement said.

"The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached," the Port of Seattle said.

"This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred," the agency added.

Rep. Adam Smith, a Democrat, said in an X statement that the incident was "absolutely unacceptable."

"ICE's conduct across our country is putting people in harm's way, undermining public trust, and stoking fear in our communities," Smith said in his statement.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson also slammed ICE over the incident in a X statement, calling the tactics used in the video "unacceptable and un-American."

"I am outraged by videos of masked ICE agents causing chaos and dragging a woman off the jetway at Sea-Tac airport," she said.

Alaska Airlines said in a statement it did "not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible."

"In this instance, Alaska Airlines was not provided advance notice of the enforcement action, and we are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred, including whether the proper protocols were followed," the airline added.

Alaska Airlines said it would be working with the governor and Port of Seattle "to ensure the collaborative standards and practices that have kept our air system safe and secure for decades are respected moving forward."

ABC News' Alyssa Pone contributed to this report.

title: ICE Home Raid Lawsuit Tossed on Standing, Warrant Question Left Open
description:
According to KRGV’s reporting on the complaint, filed in February, ICE officers arrived around 7 a.m. on Jan. 9, and a video obtained by the station shows them jumping a fence into the yard.
The warrant question the court left open An administrative immigration warrant, such as a Form I-200 or I-205, is signed by an immigration officer, not a judge.
Whether an officer-signed administrative warrant satisfies those rules is the open question in a growing number of cases.

text:
A federal judge in McAllen, Texas, has dismissed a Donna family’s ICE home raid lawsuit without ever deciding the question at its heart: whether immigration officers holding only an administrative warrant could lawfully enter the family’s yard and home. U.S. District Judge Randy Crane ruled on Nov. 9 that the family lacked standing to seek the forward-looking relief it requested and dismissed the case without prejudice, KRGV reported on Nov. 21.

The outcome matters beyond one Rio Grande Valley household. As ICE makes arrests at homes nationwide, families who want a court to declare a raid unlawful keep hitting the same wall: someone harmed once usually cannot get an injunction without showing a likelihood of being harmed again. That rule can end a case before a judge examines what officers did.

What the family alleged. According to KRGV’s reporting on the complaint, filed in February, ICE officers arrived around 7 a.m. on Jan. 9, and a video obtained by the station shows them jumping a fence into the yard. The suit says officers pointed guns at Humberto Garcia and pinned him down, produced no warrant when his sister asked for one, and made the youngest child, whose condition makes her bones break easily, kneel at gunpoint before entering to take the father. The parents were in the process of obtaining lawful permanent residence, and the mother was later deported to Mexico, KRGV reported. These are the family’s allegations. The court made no findings on them, and KRGV’s reports included no response from ICE or DHS.

The complaint raised Fourth and Fifth Amendment claims and sought a declaration that the officers acted unconstitutionally. It also pointed to an ICE memo that, the family says, told officers they could enter homes on administrative warrants. In a Sept. 3 motion to dismiss, the government argued that the family could not sue on behalf of the noncitizen parents, that its claimed injury was too speculative to support standing and that the complaint failed to state a claim.

The warrant question the court left open

An administrative immigration warrant, such as a Form I-200 or I-205, is signed by an immigration officer, not a judge. That distinction is the whole fight. In Payton v. New York (1980), the Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment bars police from entering a home without consent to make a routine arrest unless they have a warrant, and courts have long read that to mean a warrant issued by a neutral magistrate. DHS’s own regulation, 8 C.F.R. 287.8(f)(2), says immigration officers may not enter a residence, including its curtilage, to question occupants about their status without a warrant or consent. A fenced yard is classic curtilage.

Whether an officer-signed administrative warrant satisfies those rules is the open question in a growing number of cases. Judge Crane did not reach it. According to KRGV, he wrote that he did not need to decide whether officers had permission to enter, because standing controlled.

Why standing ended the ICE home raid lawsuit

The governing precedent is City of Los Angeles v. Lyons (1983), in which a man choked by police could not obtain an injunction against the city’s chokehold policy because he could not show he would be stopped and choked again. Past exposure to illegal conduct, the Court said, does not by itself create a live case for prospective relief. KRGV reported that Crane applied the same reasoning: the family had not shown a real and immediate threat of future injury, and the threat had not been shown to be “certainly impending,” the standard the Supreme Court articulated in Clapper v. Amnesty International USA (2013). KRGV did not say which precedents the order cited.

The practical effect is that a one-time raid is hard to challenge with declaratory or injunctive claims, however serious the conduct alleged. The damages routes are narrow too. Egbert v. Boule (2022) sharply limited Bivens suits against individual federal officers, and the Federal Tort Claims Act requires an administrative claim to the agency within two years before suing the United States. KRGV did not report whether the family has pursued either. A dismissal without prejudice leaves room to refile.

Class actions attacking an ongoing practice are better placed to show the continuing threat Lyons demands, and challenges brought while a person is still detained avoid the problem another way, which is how courts reached the merits in the Maine ruling on a warrantless arrest of a Special Immigrant Juvenile teenager. Evidence about how ICE trains officers and documents arrests, from a draft watchdog report on training cuts to the FBI database breach affecting ICE warrant records, is likely to matter most in those broader suits.

What to watch

Appeal window: when the United States is a party, a notice of appeal to the Fifth Circuit is generally due within 60 days of the judgment.

Amended claims: whether the family refiles with damages or tort claims that do not depend on showing a future threat.

The warrant question elsewhere: rulings in pending cases that do reach whether an administrative warrant permits entry to a home or its curtilage.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

title: Guantánamo Bay 2.0? The rise of legal violence inside US detention centers
description:
Many held in Guantánamo Bay have claimed that members of the United States military physically and mentally assaulted them during their detention.
Detainees’ testimonies of violent punishments by ICE agents are all too reminiscent of the experiences of Guantánamo Bay prisoners.
Guantánamo Bay was established in 2002 to detain individuals believed to be linked with the perpetrators of the September 11 attacks.
Ending legal violence Like many who were imprisoned in Guantánamo Bay, most of the migrants in detention today have not been convicted of any crime.
If these steps are not taken, the use of legal violence and the policies of impunity that underpin them will only grow.
text:
The United States government has a long history of dehumanizing foreigners both inside and outside its borders. The treatment of prisoners in Guantánamo Bay and of migrants currently detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) provide just two recent examples of the extensive use of criminalizing language to justify targeting these groups. The George W. Bush administration routinely labeled those incarcerated in Guantánamo Bay as “terrorists” and associated them with the September 11 attacks, often without direct evidence. Today, the Donald J. Trump administration labels migrants as “animals,” “criminals,” and “rapists.” This type of dehumanizing language suggests that detainees do not deserve legal rights, and it leads to the broad erosion of the civil protections that shield people—whether or not they are US citizens—from arrest without charge and trial or harsh and unusual punishment.

The state’s curtailment of due process and other civil rights in these cases has led to a rise in legal violence: harm inflicted by a government body while enforcing state policy. Many held in Guantánamo Bay have claimed that members of the United States military physically and mentally assaulted them during their detention. Similar abuse is still taking place today against migrants in ICE detention centers. Detainees’ testimonies of violent punishments by ICE agents are all too reminiscent of the experiences of Guantánamo Bay prisoners.

The US government and military have not taken the lessons of the War on Terror to heart, and the United States is still using violence against people it detains. There has been very little pressure from legislators or the courts to dissuade the government from using legal violence—a direct failure of the very systems that allowed this kind of violence to become legal in the first place.

Mass incarceration and violence toward migrants

Since Trump took office as president of the United States for the second time, his administration has pushed ICE to detain anyone deemed to be residing in the country illegally. This has led to the mass incarceration of Latinos and other migrants all over the nation. According to The Guardian, a total of 68,400 individuals were held in detention as of December 2025. The majority of detainees have no previous criminal record. A recent Human Rights Watch report documented dozens of executive orders rolling back migrants’ right to due process, guaranteed by the Fifth Amendment, and limiting their ability to seek legal redress while detained.

These new executive orders have systematically allowed the state to punish those detained prior to legal due process or the filing of charges. The result is legal violence inflicted against migrants detained in defiance of their constitutional rights. For example, officers are now legally allowed to interrogate suspected illegal migrants using violence and make arrests without warrants.

The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) has done very little to limit the powers granted to ICE. In fact, some recent SCOTUS rulings have expanded ICE’s powers. In September 2025, SCOTUS eliminated restrictions on ICE’s use of racial profiling when making arrests. In the case of Noem v. Vasquez-Perdomo SCOTUS ruled that ICE could conduct raids in public places opening the door to using race, ethnicity, and language to determine their targets. This is unambiguously racial profiling and encourages violence toward especially Latinos regardless of their immigration status.

Several reports documenting migrant accounts of violence committed by detention officers and ICE have been released since Trump’s executive orders and SCOTUS’s legal decisions on immigration enforcement. One of many migrants who spoke with the ACLU reported that detention officers had beaten him, breaking his tooth and damaging his ear to the point that he began to lose hearing. This violence was carried out in one of the largest detention centers in the country, located at the Fort Bliss military base in Texas.

One man in a Florida detention center, speaking to Human Rights Watch, recalled officers turning up the air conditioning to intentionally freezing levels in the cells. Several people in the same location are also being denied life-saving medications needed to treat chronic illnesses.

Are detention centers the new Guantánamo Bay?

Guantánamo Bay was established in 2002 to detain individuals believed to be linked with the perpetrators of the September 11 attacks. The Center for Constitutional Rights has outlined the violent experiences of prisoners detained at Guantánamo Bay, which included practices like those used today in ICE detention centers.

The Bush administration authorized the use of violent practices in Guantánamo Bay by declaring that those imprisoned there were “unlawful enemy combatants” and thus ineligible for the protections of the Geneva Conventions. By eliminating application of the Geneva Conventions, the Bush administration removed a major barrier imposed by international law to prevent the torture of prisoners. More recently, the Trump administration has similarly rejected the Geneva Conventions by cutting funding for the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and condemning their operations.

The Center for Constitutional Rights has shared the experience of Abu Zubaydah, who was subjected to waterboarding, sleep deprivation, stress positions, and confinement inside a coffin-sized box. Ahmed al-Darbi similarly reported that officers played painfully loud music for several hours and chilled his cell to extremely cold temperatures until he confessed to the crime he was accused of. The government framed these practices as interrogation, but it’s clear that they constitute torture.

Many of the prisoners in Guantánamo Bay were never formally charged with any crime. Instead, they were imprisoned indefinitely and subjected to intense and violent interrogation tactics in hopes of eliciting confessions. These abusive practices were justified by a Military Order that allowed prisoners suspected of terrorism to be held outside US jurisdiction. This was an intentional move to limit the court’s reach and provide for increased use of force against those held in Guantánamo Bay and impunity for the officers who carried it out.

Ending legal violence

Like many who were imprisoned in Guantánamo Bay, most of the migrants in detention today have not been convicted of any crime. Legal violence does not change; only its target does.

To prevent the continuation of legal violence, we must challenge the system. The executive and military orders that allowed violence and mistreatment of prisoners in Guantánamo Bay laid the foundation for the laws currently supporting ICE’s violent and indiscriminate campaign of immigration enforcement. The United States Constitution already prohibits abuse inside penitentiaries and detention centers. Cruel and unusual punishments are strictly prohibited.

The courts must consistently apply the protections provided by the United States Constitution, and they must disempower ICE. This includes protecting due process rights for migrants, firing officers who act with racial bias, eliminating officers’ rights to interrogate detainees using violence, and investigating each facility where abuse has been reported. If these steps are not taken, the use of legal violence and the policies of impunity that underpin them will only grow.

title: Mikie Sherrill, governor of New Jersey: 'Democrats have to move fast and show wins right away'
description:

However, the New Jersey governor warns that the biggest “challenge” facing her party when it takes control of Congress in January will be the need to act decisively and quickly.

They’ve seen how quickly Trump could move, and he moves really quickly at breaking things.
text:
Mikie Sherrill has a firm conviction about the state of the Democratic Party. “We are in our strongest position in decades because we are all united,” she says without hesitation, following the resounding Democratic victory in the November 3 midterm elections.

However, the New Jersey governor warns that the biggest “challenge” facing her party when it takes control of Congress in January will be the need to act decisively and quickly. “You have to move fast and show wins right away because people are cynical, they’re struggling, and they want to see effective government. And as soon as you start to deliver that, they can start to breathe again because they think, ‘Okay, help is coming.’”

Two weeks have passed since the Democrats swept the midterm elections when Sherrill, 54, welcomes EL PAÍS for an interview at the New Jersey State House, the third-oldest state capitol in the United States. Sherrill arrived in its opulent coral-colored hallways last January as the second woman to serve as governor of the country’s most densely populated state (with 9.5 million residents) and the first Democratic woman to hold the office.

Sherrill considers herself a product of the Trump era. She is part of what she describes as “a new generation” of Democratic leaders shaping the party’s direction at a time when the rulebook of politics has been torn up. And the party’s North Star, she says, must be the working class.

Focusing on the cost of living has proven to be a winning strategy for Democrats, as the midterm elections made clear. Voters repeatedly cited Trump’s handling of the economy as their main concern when casting their ballots. It was a message Trump himself successfully exploited in 2024, even though he subsequently failed to deliver on his promises and, in fact, made matters worse with the war in Iran and his tariffs.

Now Democrats are reaping the rewards of those broken promises. Their campaigns drew inspiration and lessons from the victories last year of figures such as Sherrill in New Jersey, Zohran Mamdani in New York City, and Abigail Spanberger in Virginia. All won on platforms centered on affordability, which went on to become the party’s “model,” according to the governor.

“A lot of people would say affordability is a boring campaign, and that you need to run on fascism or democratic institutions or standing up to Trump... And those are all incredibly important things, but it’s not boring to people when they can’t afford their rent and you’re running on trying to fix that for them. It’s not boring when they cannot afford their utility costs and a corrupt president is making billions,” Sherrill argues.

But her own experience as governor over the past nearly 12 months has led her to reiterate a message she delivers not so much as advice but rather as a warning: “Moving quickly to deliver for people is key if you want to hold the public trust.” Democrats must stop the “bleeding” caused by Trump and address the affordability crisis and put an end to corruption within his administration, she says.

A veteran with an acute sense of urgency

Sherrill has said that her sense of urgency stems from her time in the military. Inspired by her grandfather, a World War II veteran, the governor knew from an early age that she wanted to be a pilot. She enrolled at the United States Naval Academy and graduated from flight school in the first class of women qualified to take part in combat operations. She subsequently served as a pilot in Europe and the Middle East. After nine years in the military, she went on to study law and became a federal prosecutor before running for Congress.

Her political career began during Trump’s first presidency, when she was elected in 2018 to represent New Jersey’s 11th Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives in Washington. That year, Democrats wrested control of Congress from Trump’s Republican Party, just as they did this November. Sherrill herself played a role in this year’s victory: she helped flip two congressional seats in New Jersey from Republican to Democratic hands and also campaigned for the now Democratic governors-elect of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, and Ohio, Amy Acton.

Now, as she considers the task facing Democrats as they regain power during the final two years of Trump’s presidency, she says she often draws on what she learned in the military about effective leadership, believing that the political class in this country has been “really, really poor” in that regard.

“Leadership is enunciating a vision. And you can take a disparate group of people and get them committed to that vision because it’s compelling and they trust you that you can get it done. That’s the military. And we recruit from all over the nation. We have people from every different background, and we all come together because we believe in the country. And so that’s what leadership in the Democratic Party is going to look like” after the midterms, she says.

When discussing the future of her party, the governor shows little interest in engaging in the debate over its different factions and divisions. “To me, there’s not one face that says, this is who the Democratic Party looks like. How could one person embody all that it means to be an American?” she asks.

“I hear all this stuff about how we have different ideas, and so it’s going to be ungovernable. I just don’t understand how you think you can govern America with just one person. It’s why we chose not to have a king,” she adds, fully aware that Trump considers himself one.

Sherrill, who belongs to the moderate and pragmatic wing of her party, brushes aside the question of whether the Democratic establishment will be able to coexist with the democratic socialists, who won a record number of seats and positions across the country in these elections. She considers that debate “artificial” and too far removed from people’s everyday concerns. “I can’t tell you the last time someone came to me and said, ‘Mikie, I’m worried about the moderates,’ or ‘I’m worried about the DSA candidates.’ Everybody comes up to me and says, ‘Mikie, I’m worried about affordability. I’m worried about Donald Trump,’” she insists.

Her own record shows that she shares some ideas with both the moderate wing of the party and its more progressive faction. One example is her position on immigration. Sherrill has been highly critical of the White House’s crackdown on immigrants. And although she has not gone so far as to call for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), as more progressive figures such as Mamdani have done, she has taken several steps to limit the immigration agency’s activities in New Jersey.

New Jersey was, for example, among the first states to ban immigration agents from covering their faces during their brutal enforcement operations. In response, the Trump administration sued the governor. The legal battle is ongoing. Sherrill has also called for the closure of the first detention center opened during Trump’s second presidency, Delaney Hall, located in Newark. The former prison, which was converted into a detention facility, has come under heavy criticism over its inhumane conditions. Last summer, hundreds of detainees launched a hunger strike that lasted a month. At least three people have died after being held at Delaney Hall.

“I don’t believe in private detention facilities. Delaney Hall should be shut down,” Sherrill says firmly.

A roadmap for 2028

The governor believes that the work she is doing in New Jersey should serve as a roadmap not only for Democrats in Congress over the next two years, but also for the party as it looks ahead to the 2028 presidential election. The Democratic nominee will face Trump’s successor since the president will be unable to run again. In that election, Sherrill says she would like to see a candidate much like herself.

Would she herself consider running in 2028? “I’m very happy being governor of New Jersey,” she replies with a laugh. “What I really want to see in 2028 is leadership that looks a lot like what we’ve done in New Jersey, meaning taking action right away.”

On paper, Sherrill has many of the qualities that make her an attractive candidate for the job: she is a military veteran, a former prosecutor, and a former member of Congress. However, her name does not appear on lists of potential presidential contenders, although she has said she has received calls from people asking whether she would be willing to run.

For now, she prefers to highlight her accomplishments as governor, including signing legislation to curb algorithmic rent pricing; signing a package of laws restricting state and local authorities’ cooperation with the federal government’s anti-immigration crackdown; and taking the Trump administration to court and winning a lawsuit to secure federal funding for the construction of a new rail tunnel connecting New Jersey and New York.

“You have to be fighting for the people you serve. That looks like getting in court really quickly. Not waiting, not trying to cut a deal; just when Trump’s acting illegally, take him to court. Don’t try to negotiate with him. Why are you negotiating for money, for example, for the Gateway Tunnel, when he is legally obligated to turn it over? There’s no negotiation there. There’s court, and he loses, and you keep moving. Having that kind of leadership is really important,” she says.

For the governor, this is the new formula for doing politics. “People are not okay with government inefficiency right now. They’ve seen how quickly Trump could move, and he moves really quickly at breaking things. So if you are going to be great at serving people, you need to move really quickly in rebuilding new things.”

text:
President Trump said at a White House news conference on Friday, Nov. 20, that he could reach an immigration deal with Democrats once they take control of the House in January, while warning that he would veto bills that do not meet his terms. The remarks, reported by USA Today, are his clearest signal yet that the White House sees immigration as a subject for bargaining in the next Congress, and they came one day after Vice President JD Vance publicly rejected a Republican governor’s call for exactly that kind of bargain.

Nothing in the law changed, and no framework or bill text came with the comments. But for employers of long-settled workers, Dreamers, TPS holders and the staff drafting January’s agenda, the question is shifting from whether the president will talk to what he would sign.

Two messages in one news conference

According to USA Today, Trump called House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become Speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer “smart,” and said he could negotiate compromises with them. “If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too,” he said. In the same answer he set out his leverage: Democrats are “going to send things my way and I’m going to veto them,” he said, unless they agree to conditions he did not spell out.

On immigration, Trump described a Nov. 18 call with Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who plans to undo Texas’s H-1B freeze. “She wants to have a strong border,” Trump said, adding that he thought they could work something out. He also voiced sympathy for immigrants who arrived years ago and hold jobs. “They work well and they work hard,” USA Today quoted him as saying.

That second line is the one that matters for legalization. It tracks Trump’s Nov. 8 remark on 60 Minutes that his approach may have been too tough, and his Nov. 11 C-SPAN comments that tax-paying farm and hotel workers were not the enforcement focus, which came with no written policy change. It also sits uneasily beside Vance’s Nov. 19 statement that legal status for people who broke immigration law would be “morally and electorally disastrous,” as covered here when he rebuffed Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt. Trump did not say whether helping long-term workers means green cards, work permits or simply continued enforcement priorities.

Democrats are attaching conditions of their own. Jeffries has said Democrats cannot work with Stephen Miller, the White House official most closely tied to the administration’s enforcement agenda, USA Today reported. Trump praised Miller at the same news conference.

The bills Democrats would bring to the table

Talks would start from existing proposals. The one Jeffries has prioritized is the American Dream and Promise Act, H.R. 1589, from Rep. Sylvia Garcia, D-Texas. As USA Today described it, the bill would offer permanent residence to certain people brought to the U.S. as children and to people who held protected status because of conditions in their home countries, if they have been in the country since 2021, pass a background check and meet an education, military or work requirement. Garcia’s Discharge Petition No. 25, filed July 20 to force a vote in this Congress, has not added a signature since Sept. 2, according to the House Clerk’s record, and it dies with the Congress on Jan. 3. Jeffries has promised to move the bill early in the next Congress either way.

Two other measures offer different templates. The bipartisan Dignity Act, which pairs border spending with a work-authorized status, has been gaining House cosponsors, nearly all Democrats. The Protect Our Neighbors Act, introduced Nov. 19, would let final removal orders lapse after 10 years and open a conditional green card route.

Why the arithmetic still favors the status quo

A Democratic House will not need discharge petitions, because the majority controls the Rules Committee and the floor. The Senate is different. Most bills need 60 votes to end debate, and overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers. Versions of the Dream and Promise Act passed the House in 2019 and 2021 and never received a Senate vote. The last broad bill to clear the Senate, S. 744 in 2013, passed 68 to 32 and died in the House.

Trump’s veto framing makes the White House, not the Senate, the likely first gate. A viable package would probably trade border and enforcement measures, the subject of his Hinojosa call, for relief aimed at narrower groups such as Dreamers or long-employed workers, the shape of the Dreamer talks that collapsed in early 2018. The open question is whether the president’s coalition, now split in public, would follow him.

For now, DACA renewals, TPS designations and Form I-9 obligations are unchanged, and no one gains status from the president’s words.

Dates to watch

Dec. 11: the current stopgap funding law expires, putting DHS funding and E-Verify in play before any reform talks begin.

Jan. 3, 2027: the 119th Congress ends; H.R. 1589, its discharge petition and other pending bills must be reintroduced.

Any White House framework: a written proposal would be the first sign the remarks are becoming policy.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.
